title: Parkside purveyors of artisanal jenever
desc: Popular in the Netherlands, jenever is a juniper-based spirit comparable to gin. This video from Amsterdam Calling showcases Distillery ’t Nieuwe Diep, which creates and serves a dizzying variety of booze from a renovated pumping station in Flevopark.

title: The shop embracing analog photography
desc: Safelight Berlin is a camera shop that finds, fixes, and resells old analog cameras. In this video from Shopify, the store’s founders Chris and Alessandro advocate for the “happy accidents” and community camaraderie that traditional film cameras provide.

title: A haven for tram enthusiasts
desc: Opened in 1975 by “a group of tram fanatics,” the Electric Tram Line Museum houses 20 restored antique trains. In this video, Gessell from Amsterdam Calling visits on a Sunday when the museum takes the midcentury streetcars out for a spin on a 7km route.

title: Nu jeans e ’na maglietta
creator: Nino D’Angelo
desc: The title means ‘Jeans and a T-shirt.’ The blond neomelodico Nino D’Angelo, raised in the airport suburb of San Pietro a Patierno, sang for a working-class Naples that saw itself in his cheap clothes and blow-dried hair.

title: Munasterio ’e Santa Chiara
creator: Roberto Murolo
desc: The title names the Santa Chiara cloister with its majolica-tiled garden. A wartime exile’s ache for home: ‘I don’t want to know if Naples is still beautiful — let me keep it the way it was.’

title: A fugitive painter finds sanctuary and his masterpiece
desc: Caravaggio fled to Naples in 1606 after killing a man in Rome, and painted The Seven Works of Mercy for this charity within months, still hanging where he left it. He’d flee again after Naples, only to die in mysterious circumstances four years later.

title: Cristian Mungiu — Director
desc: The director of Palme d’Or winner 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days grew up under Ceaușescu and came of age as a filmmaker just as communism fell, part of a wave of Romanian directors who turned the transition’s absurdities into award-winning cinema.

title: A reforming prime minister is shot
desc: Serbia’s reforming prime minister, who had sent Milošević to face war crimes charges in The Hague, was shot by a sniper outside a government building in 2003. Cabinet minister Gordana Matković recalls that day.

title: The real doctor behind Sherlock Holmes
desc: Bell diagnosed patients’ occupations and recent travels before they said a word, using observation alone — a party trick he taught his students at this medical school. One of them, Arthur Conan Doyle, turned his old professor into Sherlock Holmes.

title: A design festival built by one family, not city hall
desc: Now drawing 150,000 visitors, Helsinki Design Week grew out of this neighborhood without significant public funding, powered instead by one family’s multigenerational stewardship, in a city declared the world’s happiest for eight years running.

title: An immigrant engineer designs a nation’s economic model
desc: Farouk al-Kasim, an Iraqi engineer who moved to Norway for his wife’s medical care, convinced officials here to limit yearly drilling licenses and save oil wealth rather than spend it, laying the groundwork for the world’s largest sovereign fund.

title: A king’s medical advice invents a national snack
desc: One theory holds that tapas began when a doctor advised Alfonso X to eat something while drinking, prompting a decree that bars serve snacks alongside alcohol. Centuries and countless small plates later, the tradition remains an essential evening ritual.

title: A piracy-fighting idea outgrows music entirely
desc: Ek and co-founder Martin Lorentzon launched Spotify from Stockholm in 2008, betting a legal option could beat piracy where lawsuits couldn’t. Recording in this studio, Ek traces the company’s pivot from music streaming into podcasts and audiobooks.

title: What Emperor Hadrian Lost: A Walk Through Ancient Rome
creator: Antinous the Tour Ghost
desc: A first-person ‘ghost’ tour narrated by Hadrian’s lost lover, tracing the emperor’s mark on Rome. From his riverside mausoleum, it winds through squares and alleys to the great domed temple and an old colonnade, ending at a monumental square.

title: The Veins of Ancient Rome: A Walk through the Park of the Aqueducts
place: San Policarpo church, Parco degli Acquedotti
creator: Lara Moscovchuk
desc: A scenic engineering walk through a green park of ancient aqueducts on the city’s edge. From a modernist church, it follows dirt trails beneath towering arches, past cisterns and an old Roman road, ending at an ancient villa’s water reservoir.

title: A dying poet spends his last winter beside the Spanish Steps
desc: John Keats died in a room at the foot of these steps in 1821, at just twenty-five, tuberculosis worsening through the Roman winter. This traces the Romantic poet’s short, brilliant life, a century before Roman Holiday made the same stairs a screen icon.

title: A financier’s ties to the Vatican Bank end in a hanging
place: Tower of Nicholas V (Vatican Bank), Vatican City
desc: Roberto Calvi ran Vatican-linked Banco Ambrosiano near this medieval tower, home to the Vatican Bank, before fleeing Italy in 1982 amid a collapsing financial empire. He turned up hanged under a London bridge days later, a death still disputed today.

title: A paranoid emperor builds reflective walls to spot assassins
desc: Domitian lined his throne room with polished marble so reflective he could watch for anyone approaching from behind, terrified of an assassination he couldn’t avoid. He demanded to be addressed as lord and god while ruling from this hilltop palace.

title: A biblical prophet glares down at Julius II’s unfinished tomb
desc: Michelangelo carved this seated Moses for Pope Julius II’s planned tomb, a monument meant to include over forty statues before money and politics scaled it down to almost nothing. Legend holds Michelangelo struck its knee, commanding it to speak.

title: A god’s grasp turns fleeing skin into laurel leaves
desc: Bernini carved this marble mid-transformation, capturing the nymph Daphne’s fingers sprouting into laurel leaves as she flees Apollo’s grasp. He was just 24 when he finished it, already redefining what stone could seem to do.

title: A column moves mountains, literally and figuratively
desc: Hadrian raised this 115-foot column after Trajan’s sudden death in 117 AD, its spiral relief wrapping upward through 190 meters of carved scenes from the Dacian Wars. Each marble drum weighs roughly 32 tons, quarried and shipped from Tuscany.

title: A colonnade opens its arms to welcome every visitor
desc: Bernini designed this oval colonnade of 284 columns in the 1650s to embrace arriving pilgrims like open arms, a deliberate contrast to the closed, walled atrium of the original basilica it replaced. He worked under six different popes shaping St. Peter’s.

title: A myth about a fiddle obscures a real catastrophe
desc: Ancient sources say the Great Fire of 64 AD broke out near this stadium, burning for six days, though the myth of Nero fiddling while it raged is almost certainly false. He blamed Christians for the disaster, one of history’s first recorded persecutions.

title: A friar burns for insisting the universe has no edge
desc: Bruno was burned alive on this square in 1600 for refusing to recant his belief in an infinite universe with countless worlds. Unlike Galileo, who abjured decades later, Bruno’s statue now faces the Vatican, a deliberate symbol of free thought.

title: Two rival architects glare at each other across a square
desc: This square still traces the exact oval shape of Domitian’s ancient athletic stadium, now centered on Bernini’s Fountain of the Four Rivers facing Borromini’s church, built by two rival Baroque architects who reportedly couldn’t stand each other.

title: Breaking a sacred vow means being sealed alive underground
desc: Six priestesses tended Vesta’s sacred flame in this temple, believed to safeguard Rome itself for as long as it burned. Breaking the vow of chastity carried the ultimate penalty: being sealed alive underground with only a few days of food and water.

title: A tennis-court brawl ends a rival and a career in Rome
desc: Caravaggio killed a man near this street’s namesake tennis court in a 1606 brawl, forcing him to flee Rome under a death sentence. He painted some of his greatest work in exile, chasing a pardon he’d win only after dying mysteriously four years later.

title: A quarter million Romans lose their minds over chariots
desc: This track could hold roughly 250,000 spectators, more than four times the Colosseum’s capacity, all gathering to watch chariot races. Champion charioteer Gaius Appuleius Diocles won 1,462 of his 4,257 races here, retiring wealthier than most emperors.

title: An altar’s shadow tells time across a giant sundial
desc: The Senate commissioned this altar in 13 BC to honor Augustus’s return from campaigns abroad, positioning it so a giant obelisk’s shadow crossed its center each year on his birthday. Buried under later buildings for centuries, it was reassembled by 1938.

title: A vision before battle changes an empire’s religion
desc: The Senate raised this arch after Constantine defeated his rival at the Milvian Bridge in 312 AD, a battle he later claimed he’d won after seeing a sign in the sky. It marks a turning point toward Christianity becoming the empire’s dominant faith.

title: Ancient temples wear a church like a disguise
desc: Columns from two Republican-era temples, vowed during the wars against Hannibal’s Carthage, are still visible fused into this church’s walls. Rome’s eventual victory over its greatest rival freed the city to expand its river port and grow into an empire.

title: A Trojan priest’s death agony gets rediscovered centuries later
desc: This marble group depicting a doomed Trojan priest and his sons was unearthed in 1506 and installed here within weeks, reshaping Renaissance art overnight. Michelangelo reportedly rushed to see it the same day it was dug up.

title: A philosopher on horseback survives by being mistaken
desc: This bronze survived the Middle Ages’ habit of melting pagan statues because medieval Romans mistook the rider for Constantine, the first Christian emperor. He’s one of the last Five Good Emperors, who wrote private philosophy while leading campaigns.

title: A monument celebrates the destruction of a temple
desc: Reliefs inside this arch show Roman soldiers carrying off the Temple of Jerusalem’s menorah after the city’s sack in 70 AD, built to honor Titus after his death and deification. The image remains a resonant, painful symbol in Jewish diaspora memory.

title: A tyrant builds Rome’s most lavish bathhouse
desc: This complex could hold 1,600 bathers at once, with libraries, gardens, and gyms alongside the pools, commissioned by an emperor remembered for murdering his own brother to secure the throne. Its towering brick walls still stand nearly full height today.

title: An emperor builds a pleasure palace on the city’s ashes
desc: Nero built this vast palace complex, complete with an artificial lake and a rotating dining room, on land cleared by the fire that devastated Rome in 64 AD. Its extravagance helped turn the public against him; he was dead within four years.

title: More than a club becomes a rallying cry
desc: FC Barcelona grew from a football club into a symbol of Catalan identity itself, especially under Franco when the team became one of few places to express it openly. This episode traces the club’s greatest players and what matchday feels like here.

title: A historian and travel writer skip the obvious sights
desc: Past the crowds on La Rambla, this episode digs into the medieval quarter’s overlooked corners, tracing the pivotal moments and Catalan cultural pride that the postcard version of Barcelona tends to skip, alongside a hunt for the city’s best bites.

title: A red-light district becomes a food destination
desc: Chef Alfredo Marcus walks Monocle through El Raval, once Barcelona’s red-light district and now, after fifteen years of change, one of its most interesting places to eat.

title: Closing streets to cars, block by block
desc: Barcelona closed nine-block clusters to through traffic, capping speeds at 10kph and handing the freed street space to trees, benches, and playgrounds — a low-tech fix for a city with some of Europe’s worst urban air and noise.

title: Handed to Franco, a president is executed
desc: Catalonia’s civil-war president Lluís Companys was handed to Franco by the Gestapo and shot by firing squad in the moat of this hilltop fortress in October 1940 — the only serving European head of government executed by fascists.

title: Catalonia’s last stand becomes a national holiday
desc: Catalonia’s militia held this ground through a 13-month siege, until Bourbon troops broke through on September 11, 1714. The defenders are buried here; Catalans still mark that date, the Diada, as their national day.

title: Building a cathedral its architect wouldn’t finish
desc: Gaudí was hit by a tram and died before he could finish this church, mistaken for a beggar and refused care. A century later, architects are still piecing together how he wanted it built from fragments of his smashed plaster models.

title: Orwell’s wife runs the office while he fights
desc: At the former POUM headquarters near here, Eileen O’Shaughnessy ran the office while her husband George Orwell fought at the front, fending off Stalinist informants and a brutal police crackdown during the war’s most paranoid weeks.

title: A monk’s math book invents modern bookkeeping
desc: Florentine bankers here recorded transactions in two columns generations before Luca Pacioli, a friend of Leonardo da Vinci, published the 1494 textbook that codified their system into Summa, the book that gave the world double-entry bookkeeping.

title: A Florentine gives his name to two continents
desc: The Vespucci family chapel is here, and tradition holds a young Amerigo appears in Ghirlandaio’s fresco on the wall. He later sailed for Spain and Portugal, realized the Americas were a new continent rather than Asia, and lent them his first name.

title: An orphaned Medici becomes France’s most feared queen
desc: Catherine was born in this palace in 1519 and orphaned within weeks. Sent to France at fourteen to marry the future king, she ruled as regent through decades of religious war, earning a reputation as the serpent queen that historians still debate.

title: A cousin lures Florence’s duke to his own murder
desc: On the promise of a secret liaison, Lorenzino de’ Medici lured his cousin Alessandro, Florence’s first duke, to an apartment near here and stabbed him to death in 1537. His own killer’s identity stayed a mystery for centuries.

title: A teenage apprentice outshines his own master
desc: Leonardo trained for a decade in Andrea del Verrocchio’s workshop, whose Doubting Thomas sculpture still fills a niche on this building’s exterior. Legend holds Verrocchio saw his student’s work on a shared painting and never picked up a brush again.

title: The one bridge a retreating army wouldn’t blow up
desc: Retreating German forces dynamited every bridge across the Arno on the night of August 3, 1944, sparing only this one. Accounts differ on why, from Hitler’s fondness for the city to a local man who talked the demolition crew out of it.

title: A barefoot boy becomes shoemaker to Hollywood
desc: Ferragamo made his first pair of shoes at age nine, emigrated to design for Hollywood’s silent stars, then brought his workshop home to this 13th-century palace in 1938. The museum inside now holds ten thousand of his shoe prototypes.

title: A friar burns Florence’s art in a public square
desc: In February 1497, followers of the monk Savonarola piled up wigs, mirrors, dice, and paintings — some believe Botticelli’s own — and burned it all here. Excommunicated weeks later, Savonarola was himself burned on this same square within a year.

title: Rivals debate where to put a giant
desc: In 1504, a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci had to decide where to install Michelangelo’s just-finished David, originally meant for the cathedral roof. They chose this square instead, right outside the seat of Florence’s government.

title: Assassins strike during Sunday Mass
desc: During Sunday Mass here in 1478, assassins hired by the rival Pazzi family stabbed Lorenzo de’ Medici’s brother Giuliano to death at the altar. Lorenzo, wounded, escaped into the sacristy, and Florence’s streets erupted in reprisal killings within hours.

title: Crediting Persian engineering for Florence’s dome
desc: For six centuries, guides have credited Brunelleschi’s double-shell brick dome to sheer genius. This episode traces the herringbone brickwork instead to Persian domes, carried to Florence by merchants trading silk along the same routes.

title: A banker converts fortune into hidden power
desc: Cosimo de’ Medici built this palace as the headquarters of a banking fortune he then spent decades converting into political control of Florence without ever holding formal office — a template for concealed power his family would refine for generations.

title: Orange-blossom incense fills streets for a week each spring
desc: Brotherhoods carry gilded floats of Christ’s Passion through the city each Holy Week, some processions lasting through the night into dawn. Even as religious belief declines across Spain, the spectacle still draws crowds moved by the music and pageantry.

title: A queen builds an empire, then an inquisition to police it
desc: Isabella and Ferdinand ran their court from this palace, funding Columbus’s voyages, conquering Granada, and launching the Spanish Inquisition, all in 1492. To some she remains Europe’s first great queen; to others, one of history’s most ruthless.

title: A veterans’ camp produces two Roman emperors
desc: Roman general Scipio founded this settlement in 206 BC to house war veterans after defeating Carthage nearby. It later produced Trajan, born here in 53 AD and remembered as Rome’s best ruler, and his successor Hadrian, both emperors born outside Italy.

title: A mosque’s minaret survives as a cathedral’s belltower
desc: Christian conquerors built the world’s largest Gothic cathedral around this surviving Almohad minaret rather than tearing it down. Nearby Santa Cruz, once home to Seville’s Jewish community, emptied out when the Inquisition forced them out.

title: A libertine’s grief rebuilds him into a saint-like patron
desc: Don Miguel de Mañara spent his youth in spectacular debauchery before grief and a religious vision drove him to found this charity hospital in 1674, filling its church with Murillo paintings meant to confront visitors with their own mortality.

title: A ritual that’s either high art or organized cruelty
desc: This 18th-century ring, among the oldest active in Spain, refined the corrida de toros into the elaborate ritual it is today. The episode traces its evolution and weighs both sides of a debate Hemingway helped export worldwide: tradition, or cruelty.

title: Sailors and potters build a neighborhood apart from Seville
desc: Trianeros have long insisted they’re from Triana rather than Seville, a riverside barrio of sailors, bullfighters, and flamenco artists across the water from the grand palaces. This former factory traces the neighborhood’s tile and pottery tradition.

title: Grief and defiance turn into a dance form
desc: Flamenco grew out of Andalusian Roma culture, fusing guitar, song, rhythm, and dance into something travel writers have struggled to describe. This museum’s founder, dancer Cristina Hoyos, built it to preserve an informally passed-down art form.

title: A prequel outshines the sequel it was written after
place: Plaza de Alfaro (Rosina’s balcony), Santa Cruz
desc: Rossini’s comedy, set in these winding streets, tells how Count Almaviva wins Rosina with barber Figaro’s help, decades before Mozart’s Marriage of Figaro. Rossini’s 1816 premiere was a near-disaster, sabotaged by fans loyal to a rival version.

title: A river tower once chained ships out of the harbor
desc: Moorish engineers built this riverside tower as part of Seville’s defenses, once paired with a matching tower across the water so a chain could block enemy ships from entering. Centuries later, Pedro the Cruel used it to imprison his own wife.

title: Seeds, diseases, and gold reshape two hemispheres
place: General Archive of the Indies (Archivo de Indias)
desc: This building holds the paperwork behind Spain’s entire American enterprise, run through Seville’s Casa de Contratacion trade monopoly. The episode looks past Columbus to the exchange of crops, animals, and disease that reordered two continents.

title: A skinny girl from a bombed town becomes a screen goddess
desc: Loren grew up steps from here in wartime poverty, sheltering from Allied bombing raids and once cut by flying shrapnel as a child. She tells the BBC how hardship in this town shaped one of cinema’s most celebrated actresses.

title: A wine-fueled chat descends into the city’s spookiest depths
desc: Beneath this square, Greek quarrymen and Roman aqueduct-builders carved tunnels that later sheltered families during WWII bombing raids. A local guide leads a wine-soaked chat through superstitions still alive above ground today.

title: A queen survives four husbands and a mob’s fury
desc: Joanna I ruled Naples from this castle for over three decades in the 14th century, outliving four husbands and surviving accusations she had the first one strangled. A hostile chronicle branded her a she-wolf; historians now see a ruler boxed in by men.

title: An Argentine outsider becomes a city’s patron saint
desc: Maradona’s seven seasons at this stadium delivered Naples its only two league titles, turning a team and city long dismissed by wealthier northern Italy into champions. Locals still light candles to him and keep vials of his hair as relics.

title: AI finally reads scrolls burned solid by Vesuvius
desc: Vesuvius carbonized an entire philosophy library at this villa in 79 AD, leaving scrolls too fragile to unroll for over two centuries. Former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman’s Vesuvius Challenge now uses CT scanning and AI to digitally unwrap and read them.

title: A queen’s visit births a legend, real or not
desc: This 1780 pizzeria claims to have invented the Margherita for Queen Margherita’s 1889 visit, topping it red, white, and green for the Italian flag. Food historian Annie Gray traces the messier, more interesting truth behind pizza’s global rise.

title: A city frozen mid-day by a volcano’s fury
desc: Vesuvius released 100,000 times the thermal energy of the Hiroshima bomb in a single afternoon in 79 AD, burying this town and its residents under ash so completely that their final moments remain frozen in plaster casts nearly 2,000 years later.

title: A 19th-century tannery becomes an experimental stage
desc: Papakonstantinou converted the largest tannery in the 19th-century Balkans into a multi-stage venue in 2011, right as Greece’s economic crisis hit hardest. She explains why reworking the ancient Classics felt like the only honest response.

title: A photographer chases sixty years of changing light
desc: McCabe first photographed Athens as a student in 1954, and his black-and-white images of a traffic-light-free golden era helped reshape the world’s image of postwar Greece. He explains why the best light for the Acropolis isn’t when tourists assume.

title: A novelist sends her heroine to a prison island
desc: British author Victoria Hislop’s novel follows a young woman imprisoned on this island for joining the communists in the Greek Civil War. Hislop, an adopted Athenian since 1977, discusses how the city’s history reshaped her writing.

title: Negotiating Greece’s bailout from the inside
desc: Greece’s own finance minister, Euclid Tsakalotos, describes negotiating the 2015 bailout from the inside, as protesters filled this square outside parliament, seventy years after gunfire here opened the civil war.

title: Students defy a junta from behind Polytechnic gates
desc: Journalist Alan Johnston reports on the 1973 student occupation of this campus in defiance of the junta, crushed when a tank crashed the gates, the moment that first cracked the dictatorship’s authority for good.

title: Ancient tragedy’s long afterlife on other stages
desc: Playwrights competed here each spring with trilogies performed for the whole city as a religious festival. This episode traces tragedy’s form from this stone hillside theater to twentieth-century Cuban stages, still asking the same questions.

title: An empty gallery built for stolen marble
desc: The museum’s top floor, glass-walled and aligned with the Parthenon above it, was built with an empty gallery waiting for the sculptures Lord Elgin removed in the early 1800s and Greece has sought back ever since.

title: Mark Mazower: A revolution’s chaotic road to a nation
desc: Athens itself changed hands in the 1820s war for independence, rebels holding the Acropolis through two Ottoman sieges. Mazower discusses the revolution’s chaos, foreign intervention, and its unlikely success.

title: Writing war’s first unsentimental history
desc: Pericles delivered his funeral oration for Athens’ war dead in this cemetery. Thucydides, who lived through the war himself, turned it into history’s first attempt at objective, unsentimental war reporting.

title: Choosing hemlock over exile
desc: The rock-cut cells on this hill are traditionally, though not certainly, identified as where Socrates spent his final days. Plato’s Crito and Phaedo describe him refusing to escape, then drinking hemlock calmly.

title: Flute music at the fall of an empire
desc: Seventy-six years after its triumph at Salamis, Athens surrendered here in 404 BC, and the victorious Spartans tore down the Long Walls to Piraeus to flute music, ending the city’s imperial age.

title: Trapping Persia’s fleet in a narrow strait
desc: Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into the narrow strait just offshore here, where Athenian triremes trapped and destroyed it in 480 BC, the naval victory that saved Athens and later built its empire.

title: Routing an empire on the plain of Marathon
desc: In 490 BC, heavily outnumbered Athenian hoplites routed a Persian invasion force on this plain. The burial mound over their dead still stands here, on the field where democracy’s first great test was won.

title: Vradiazei
creator: Stelios Kazantzidis
desc: The title means “Night Falls.” The great mournful voice of postwar Greece was born here in Nea Ionia, a district thrown up for Asia Minor refugees; his ache is the ache of that uprooted, hard-up quarter.

title: A code-breaker is prosecuted for who he loved
desc: Turing built the world’s first stored-program computer at this university after his codebreaking work helped win the war, then was convicted of gross indecency in 1952 for a relationship with a Manchester man and sentenced to chemical castration.

title: A widow builds a cathedral of books
desc: Enriqueta Rylands secretly negotiated a 210,000-pound purchase of a private collector’s 40,000 books, then spent a decade building this neo-Gothic book cathedral as a memorial to her late husband, a Manchester textile magnate.

title: New Order gambles a fortune on a cavernous nightclub
place: Site of the Haçienda club, Whitworth Street West
desc: Joy Division’s surviving members regrouped as New Order after singer Ian Curtis’s 1980 death, then poured royalties into a vast nightclub here in 1982. On opening night almost nobody danced; within a few years the Haçienda defined a city’s sound.

title: A refueling stop ends a football team’s golden age
desc: Flying home from a European match in February 1958, Manchester United’s plane crashed on a third takeoff after refueling in Munich, killing 23 people including eight players. Manager Matt Busby, critically injured, rebuilt the club within a decade.

title: Forty people watch punk rock get invented
desc: An estimated 40 people paid 50p to see the Sex Pistols play here in June 1976. Future members of Joy Division, The Fall, Buzzcocks, and The Smiths were reportedly in the room, and much of Manchester’s music scene traces back to that one night.

title: A gunpowder factory gives a neighbourhood its name
desc: An 18th-century gunpowder works run by the Balfour family gave this district its unlikely name, long before it became a hub of workshops and, later, a greyhound stadium. Ruth Gray chats with the owner of one of the area’s oddest surviving properties.

title: A Victorian garden cemetery goes back to nature
desc: Opened in the 1840s as a fashionable Victorian garden cemetery, this graveyard beside the Water of Leith has since been swallowed by wildflowers and ancient elms. Ruth Gray walks its overgrown paths to trace who’s buried here and how nature reclaimed it.

title: A coronation stone comes home after 700 years
desc: Seven hundred years after Edward I seized Scotland’s coronation stone and built it into England’s own throne, a 400-mile police-escorted convoy brought it back on St Andrew’s Day 1996, where it now sits beside the Honours of Scotland.

title: Leith’s forgotten role as a whisky engine room
place: The Vaults (Scotch Malt Whisky Society), Leith
desc: Recorded inside this 18th-century bonded warehouse, once one of nearly a hundred that made Leith a global whisky engine room of blending and shipping, the Scotch Malt Whisky Society’s storyteller traces the port’s trade back to 1898.

title: Three thousand years on an extinct volcano
desc: From a Bronze Age settlement to a Wars of Independence battleground to Mary Queen of Scots’ refuge, this fortress on an extinct volcano has been besieged more than almost any castle in Britain. Dan Snow walks the grounds with a senior guide.

title: Rubbing a skeptic’s toe for luck
desc: Visitors rub the toe of this bronze statue for luck, an irony Hume would have appreciated since he spent his life arguing no one can prove cause leads to effect. Runciman traces Hume’s ideas on debt and credit to today’s fights over money.

title: A ploughman poet conquers Edinburgh society
desc: A farmer’s son from Ayrshire arrived here in 1786 already a literary sensation, and Edinburgh’s high society lionized him as a heaven-taught ploughman. This museum, dedicated to Burns alongside Scott and Stevenson, explores his uneasy fit in the city.

title: Writing Harry Potter with a view of the castle
place: Elephant House café, George IV Bridge
desc: Rowling wrote parts of the second and third Harry Potter books at a table in this cafe, drawn by the view of the castle. She told the UK’s Poet Laureate she’d love to still write there, but fame made it “just not humanly possible” anymore.

title: A dog’s fourteen-year vigil at his owner’s grave
desc: A Skye Terrier reportedly kept vigil at his owner’s grave in the kirkyard behind this statue for fourteen years after his death in 1858, refusing to leave even when the city tried to have him put down for lacking a dog license.

title: A councillor’s double life inspires Jekyll and Hyde
place: Heart of Midlothian mosaic (site of the Old Tolbooth)
desc: Respected cabinetmaker and city councillor William Brodie was hanged here in 1788 for a string of burglaries he’d committed by night, using his locksmith trade to copy keys to his own clients’ homes. His double life later inspired Jekyll and Hyde.

title: Grave-robbers turn to murder to supply anatomists
desc: Edinburgh’s medical schools paid well for fresh cadavers and asked few questions — a gap Burke and Hare filled by murdering sixteen people in 1828. This museum, run by the institution whose demand created the market, still displays Burke’s skeleton.

title: A husband’s murder seals a queen’s downfall
place: Site of Kirk o’ Field, Old College
desc: Mary’s second husband, Lord Darnley, was recovering from illness in a house that once stood on this spot when it was blown up in February 1567; his strangled body was found in the garden, and Mary’s swift remarriage to a suspect sealed her downfall.

title: Prenzlauer Berg’s Hidden Jewish Heritage: A Berlin Walking Tour
creator: Efrat Y.
desc: A history walk uncovering Prenzlauer Berg’s pre-war Jewish community and its persecution. Starting outside a U-Bahn station, it passes a historic cemetery and a grand surviving synagogue, ending at a lively neighborhood square.

title: A clockmaker’s revenge curses his own masterpiece
desc: Legend holds that city councilors blinded the clock’s maker to stop him building a rival elsewhere, so he sabotaged the mechanism and it sat silent for a century. Historians now credit Mikuláš of Kadaň as the builder; the blinding story looks invented.

title: One brewery outlasts five centuries of Prague’s history
desc: Brewing continuously since 1499, this dark-lager house survived the Thirty Years’ War, two world wars, and forty years of communist nationalization before returning to private hands. The show ranks it against eleven other historic Prague pubs.

title: A confessor is drowned for keeping the queen’s secrets
desc: Legend holds that King Wenceslas IV had his wife’s confessor, Jan of Nepomuk, thrown from this bridge into the Vltava in 1393 for refusing to reveal what she confessed. He became the patron saint of bridges and, curiously, of keeping secrets.

title: In the footsteps of Franz Kafka: A Prague Walking Tour
creator: Jana Vesela
desc: A literary-biography walk through the writer’s home turf, with readings from his work where it was set. From the square named for him by his birthplace, it passes his childhood homes and the old main square, ending near a café he loved downtown.

title: An emperor builds a Rome of his own on the Vltava
desc: Charles IV laid the first stone of this entirely new district in 1347, doubling Prague’s size and filling it with churches meant to rival the holiest sites in Christendom, determined to build a capital worthy of a Holy Roman Emperor.

title: A bureaucrat writes nightmares about bureaucracy at night
place: Former Workers’ Accident Insurance office, Na Poříčí 7
desc: Kafka spent fourteen years at this building investigating factory injury claims, protecting his 8-to-2 schedule so he could write in the afternoons. His insurance-office bureaucracy fed directly into The Trial’s nightmarish, unaccountable legal system.

title: Tanks roll into the square as reform crumbles overnight
desc: Soviet-led tanks filled this square on August 21, 1968, crushing Alexander Dubček’s brief experiment in socialism with a human face. Journalist Jan Čulík recalls the crackdown’s slow grind through the 1970s, including his own arrest by the secret police.

title: A clay giant sleeps in a synagogue attic
desc: Legend holds that Rabbi Judah Loew built a clay protector for Prague’s Jewish community and hid it in this synagogue’s attic when its work was done. The tale grew out of Emperor Rudolf II’s real court, where alchemists chased the philosopher’s stone.

title: Two prime ministers split a country in six days
desc: Czech and Slovak leaders Václav Klaus and Vladimír Mečiar divided an entire country’s assets behind closed doors rather than put it to a public vote, negotiating from offices like this one. Not a single life was lost, giving the split its nickname.

title: Radio staff seize their own building to spark an uprising
desc: On May 5, 1945, Czech Radio staff seized this building and broadcast an appeal for armed resistance, sparking the Prague Uprising days before war’s end. American forces freed western Bohemia, but Soviet troops took Prague, shaping the next four decades.

title: A duke’s own brother arranges his murder at church
desc: Wenceslas I ruled Bohemia as a genuinely pious duke before his brother Boleslav had him killed on the way to Mass in 935. His remains rest in this cathedral, and the murdered ruler became both a saint and the Good King Wenceslas of the Christmas carol.

title: Three men thrown from a window ignite a European war
desc: Protestant noblemen threw two Catholic governors and their secretary from a 70-foot castle window in May 1618, and all three survived, landing in a moat or saved by angels depending who you ask. The stunt sparked the Thirty Years’ War, killing millions.

title: Budapest’s Jewish Quarter: A Walk Through its Past and Present
creator: Tas Tóbiás
desc: A neighborhood walk through Budapest’s Jewish Quarter, from synagogues to present-day cafes and markets. Starting at a square near a neoclassical church, it passes a triangle of three synagogues and a Holocaust memorial park, ending at a former palace.

title: A dragon’s cave becomes a kingdom’s founding myth
place: Dragon’s Den cave (Smocza Jama), Wawel Hill
desc: Legend holds that Prince Krak killed a cave-dwelling dragon here with poisoned livestock before founding the city that bears his name. A modern statue at the cave’s mouth breathes real fire every few minutes, still drawing crowds to the story.

title: A merchant’s orphaned son upends the universe
desc: Copernicus studied here in the 1490s before traveling to Italy and eventually proposing that the Earth orbits the Sun, not the reverse. The theory sat mostly unread for decades before reshaping astronomy, published the same year he died.

title: A pierogi crawl through Europe’s largest medieval square
desc: Best visited under a blanket of winter snow, according to Monocle’s guide, this square anchors a food scene built around comforting classics. Flynn Symonds shows off his favorite spots for pierogi in a city better known for its wartime history.

title: A servant volunteers to be shot to prove a point
desc: In 1901, inventor Jan Szczepanik publicly tested an improved silk bulletproof vest here, firing a revolver at his own servant to prove it worked. The design built on Polish priest Kazimierz Zeglen’s original, later saving a Spanish king’s life.

title: A Nazi party member’s factory becomes his redemption
desc: Novelist Thomas Keneally stumbled onto this story in 1980 while buying a briefcase from a Kraków survivor in Beverly Hills. He tells Witness History why a Nazi party member who saved over a thousand Jewish workers at this factory made such a subject.

title: War refugees invent Dada, a movement to reject meaning itself
desc: Artists fleeing WWI gathered nightly at this nightclub in 1916, staging deliberately absurd performances out of disgust with the war and bourgeois values. A rare archive recording captures founder Richard Huelsenbeck describing Dada’s birth firsthand.

title: A 167-year-old bank collapses over a single weekend
desc: Secret negotiations unfolded around this square in March 2023 as regulators arranged a takeover before markets reopened, ending Credit Suisse’s 167-year run. Journalist Duncan Mavin traces a bank whose scandals stretched back almost to its founding.

title: A public debate decides which religion wins a city
desc: Zwingli defended his 67 Theses in a public disputation here in 1523, winning the council’s backing for Reformed Christianity. Splitting the Swiss Confederacy along religious lines, the conflict escalated until Zwingli died at the Battle of Kappel in 1531.

title: A snowman’s exploding head predicts the summer weather
desc: Zurich’s guilds parade to this square each April and burn the Böögg, a giant snowman effigy stuffed with firecrackers. Locals swear the faster its head detonates, the better the coming summer will be, a tradition tied to a 1525 workday law.

title: A young psychiatrist takes psychotic delusions seriously
desc: Jung worked at this asylum from 1900, developing word-association experiments that helped confirm Freud’s theories before he even met him. Their intense, six-year collaboration ended in a bitter split over what the unconscious actually was.

title: Eating sausage during Lent sparks a religious revolution
desc: Zwingli preached from this pulpit in 1522 defending a printer’s workers who’d publicly eaten sausage during the Lenten fast, a deliberate provocation that snowballed into the Swiss Reformation. He died six years later defending the city he’d converted.

title: Heavenly Club
creator: Les Sauterelles
desc: The first Swiss song to top the national chart, in 1968. Toni Vescoli’s beat group were the kings of the Niederdorf, the old-town lanes whose cellar clubs were Zurich’s answer to Merseybeat.

title: Flâneurs of Belleville
creator: Jennifer Solheim
desc: A guide to the Parisian art of aimless wandering, along the seam between two working-class neighborhoods. From a metro exit, it drifts past a scholar’s favorite backstreets, doll shops, and pastry salons, ending in a hillside park.

title: Two nobles beheaded, a revolt ignited
desc: William of Orange fled this city in 1567 rather than face the Duke of Alba, whose Council of Troubles beheaded two nobles who’d stayed behind — Egmont and Hoorn — on this square, igniting the Dutch Revolt that Orange led from exile.

title: A Brussels sign painter creates Belgium’s biggest export
desc: Housed in a Victor Horta building, this museum traces the career of Brussels-born Georges Remi, or Hergé, whose boy reporter Tintin first appeared in a local newspaper supplement in 1929 and became Belgium’s best-known export.

title: A chance encounter turns a sign painter into a surrealist
desc: This museum holds the world’s largest Magritte collection. The episode traces how a reproduction of a De Chirico painting, seen by chance, pushed the Brussels-born sign painter toward the eerie, everyday-object surrealism that made him famous.

title: Is the traditional beer cafe dying?
place: La Fleur en Papier Doré café
desc: Recorded live inside this cramped, art-covered pub that once hosted Magritte and the Belgian Surrealists, a panel debates whether Brussels’ traditional beer café is a dying institution or one that just keeps reinventing itself.

title: A 15-year-old emperor comes of age
desc: Forty years before his abdication in the same hall, a 15-year-old Charles was declared of age here in 1515, his regent’s authority publicly revoked and her official seals smashed with hammers in front of the assembled nobility.

title: An emperor gives up the largest empire in Europe
desc: On October 25, 1555, Charles V leaned on the shoulder of a young William of Orange and, in the great hall of this palace, gave up rule over his seventeen provinces to his son Philip, ending Europe’s largest empire in a single ceremony.

title: A shipping clerk exposes Congo’s atrocities
desc: Built to showcase Leopold’s colony, this museum once displayed 267 Congolese people in a human zoo at the 1897 exhibition here. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook trace how a shipping clerk’s suspicions exposed the regime’s atrocities.

title: A nurse’s execution reveals she really was a spy
place: Tir National memorial (Edith Cavell execution site)
desc: A British nurse who ran a WWI escape network for Allied soldiers was shot by German firing squad on this spot in 1915. Historian Helen Fry argues the evidence shows Cavell really was passing intelligence, not just sheltering fugitives.

title: Red paint marks a colonial king’s statue
place: Leopold II equestrian statue, Place du Trône
desc: Protesters have doused this statue in red paint for two decades, symbolizing the blood of the roughly 10 million Congolese who died under Leopold’s personal rule of the Congo Free State, run from Brussels for his own profit.

title: A fish market tells the story of who came here
desc: Fishermen have sold their daily catch straight off the boat at this quay for generations, in a city where bouillabaisse itself tells an immigrant story: a Provençal fishermen’s stew reshaped by Italian, Corsican, and North African hands.

title: Greek settlers bring wine and olives to Gaul
desc: Greek colonists planted the region’s first vineyards and olive groves around this harbor, turning Massalia into a gateway for wine, tin, and trade routes reaching north to the Atlantic and inland along the Rhône.

title: A bribed quarantine unleashes plague on the port
desc: A ship’s captain bribed his way past quarantine to unload silk cargo here in May 1720, unknowingly releasing plague-carrying fleas into the city. It killed roughly half of Marseille’s residents, the last major bubonic plague in Western Europe.

title: A Greek bride’s choice founds France’s oldest city
desc: Legend holds a local princess picked a Greek sailor from Phocaea as her husband at her own wedding feast, granting him land at this harbor around 600 BC. The colony that grew here, Massalia, later hosted Hannibal’s army passing toward Italy.

title: Volunteers sing a war song into being
desc: Volunteer soldiers from Marseille marched up this street and onward to Paris in 1792, singing a new song they’d picked up from a young officer’s patriotic gathering. Parisians who’d never heard it before started calling it La Marseillaise.

title: A king builds a fortress with its guns turned inward
desc: After Marseille’s consuls defied royal authority in 1659, Louis XIV marched 7,000 troops into the city, then built this fortress with its cannons pointed at the town rather than the sea. He also opened the port to expanded Mediterranean trade.

title: Saturday Night
creator: Herman Brood
desc: Herman Brood was the Netherlands’ one true rock ‘n’ roll star, gloriously reckless, and this 1978 song was his breakthrough. After he died in 2001, thousands lined the streets as his coffin was carried to Paradiso, the venue that had been his home.

title: Coffee, fashion, and circumcision festivals fill the sultan’s court
desc: From this palace, the Ottomans ran an empire stretching from Hungary to Morocco for six centuries. This episode skips the wars for law codes, coffeehouse culture, sartorial rules, and the public circumcision festivals thrown for young princes.

title: Cannons finally break a thousand-year-old wall
desc: These walls turned back every siege for a thousand years until Sultan Mehmed II’s cannons breached them here after 53 days in 1453. Constantine XI, the last Byzantine emperor, reportedly died fighting nearby as the city, and Roman rule, finally fell.

title: A 13th-century poet still fills tattoo parlors and coffee mugs
desc: Istanbul’s first Mevlevi lodge, built in the 1490s, trained dervishes in the spinning meditation Rumi’s followers developed after his death. Melvyn Bragg and guests unpack his verse and how he became a best-selling poet in the modern West.

title: A chubby cat’s slouch earns her a bronze statue
desc: Tombili became an internet meme for the way she slumped against a step here, one paw draped over her belly. When she died in 2016, a petition for a memorial drew thousands of signatures; the statue was stolen within a month and returned after outcry.

title: A Monocle correspondent reads the pulse of a divided city
desc: Monocle’s Istanbul correspondent walks this ferry-crossed waterfront to take the city’s temperature, from municipal politics under Erdogan to the small design fixes and everyday rhythms that make a metropolis straddling two continents function.

title: Every clock in this palace stopped at 9:05
desc: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk died in this palace’s bedroom on November 10, 1938, and its clocks have been kept frozen at that exact minute since. NPR’s Throughline unpacks how the man who dissolved an empire built a national identity Turkey still argues over.

title: A defector’s fatal call reaches the wrong Englishman
desc: In 1945, a Soviet official in Istanbul secretly offered British intelligence the names of Moscow’s agents inside MI6, unaware the officer receiving his message at this building, Kim Philby, was one of them. Philby tipped off Moscow; the defector vanished.

title: A kidnapped teenager becomes the sultan’s only wife
desc: Captured as a teenager and sold into Suleiman’s harem, Hurrem broke tradition by becoming his legal wife rather than a concubine, a rise so unprecedented that court gossips called her a witch. This bathhouse, built in her honor, still operates today.

title: Istanbul exiles thousands of dogs to a barren island
desc: In 1910, Ottoman authorities rounded up Istanbul’s stray dogs and abandoned them on this uninhabited island, where witnesses reported hearing them howl for days before starving. The episode traces the city’s fraught relationship with its street animals.

title: An underground lake hides a carved Medusa head
desc: Byzantine engineers built this 6th-century reservoir to supply the Great Palace with water, supported by 336 columns scavenged from older ruins, including two bases carved with the face of Medusa, still submerged and upside-down at the cistern’s edge.

title: Two Serbian scientists who made it in America
desc: This museum holds Tesla’s ashes and papers, though he never lived in Belgrade. The episode traces how two Serbian-born scientists, Tesla and telecommunications pioneer Mihajlo Pupin, made their names an ocean away in America.

title: Building socialism’s showcase from farmland
desc: Twin concrete towers linked by a sky bridge mark the western gateway to the city Tito built from farmland after 1948, planned as a showcase of socialist modernism free of any one architect’s signature.

title: Belgrade Walking Tour: Where Every Empire Left Its Mark
creator: Aleksandar Bastic
desc: A local historian’s sweep through two millennia of conquest: from the seat of parliament, walk a boulevard built over a Roman legion’s road, past a hotel that hosted Einstein and later Gestapo HQ, ending at a hilltop fortress above two rivers.

title: Refusing to choose sides in the Cold War
desc: In this hall in September 1961, Tito hosted Nehru, Nasser, and Nkrumah to found a bloc of nations refusing to pick a side between Washington and Moscow — a movement that still counts most of the world’s countries as members.

title: Defying Stalin and surviving
desc: Yugoslavia’s parliament sits empty of this drama, but it’s the clearest symbol of the state that, in 1948, became the first communist government to defy Moscow and survive — a split that reshaped the Cold War.

title: Did Europe’s first civilization begin outside Belgrade?
desc: Excavations at this Danube-side village uncovered a Neolithic culture with its own script, predating Sumerian cuneiform, and evidence of copper smelting older than anywhere else on record, though the biggest claims remain hotly disputed.

title: Suleiman succeeds where Mehmed II failed
desc: Sixty-five years after Hunyadi’s victory, Suleiman the Magnificent returned and succeeded where Mehmed II had failed, opening the road that put Belgrade under Ottoman rule for most of the next three centuries.

title: Surviving a missile strike on live TV
desc: A NATO missile hit this state broadcaster’s headquarters at 2am, killing 16 staff on shift. Technician Dragan Sukovic survived and tells Witness History what it was like inside the building when the missile struck.

title: A third siege in five centuries
desc: In October 1915, Austro-Hungarian and German forces crossed the Sava and Danube under this fortress’s guns, and Belgrade fell after fierce street fighting — the third time in five centuries the citadel had been stormed from outside.

title: Tito’s death unravels a country
desc: Tito lies buried in the winter garden he once worked in. His death here in 1980 removed the one figure holding six republics together, and within a decade the country he built had torn itself apart in war.

title: Trading secrets in Belgrade’s cafes
desc: After Tito’s death in 1980, a CIA officer met his Yugoslav intelligence source in Belgrade’s cafes and hotels, trading a gym bag of secret documents while Moscow circled a weakened, non-aligned Yugoslavia.

title: Monks illuminate a manuscript that still needs protecting
place: Book of Kells, Old Library, Trinity College
desc: Monks working around 800 AD illuminated this Gospel manuscript with such intricate detail that Trinity’s Old Library, its home since the 1600s, still turns a fresh page daily to keep any one spread from fading under constant view.

title: An aristocrat rejects his title to lead a rebellion
place: The Lord Edward pub, Christchurch Place
desc: Recorded above a pub named for him, this episode traces Lord Edward Fitzgerald, born into aristocracy but determined to be, in his sister’s words, a Paddy and no more. He helped lead the 1798 rebellion and died of wounds sustained resisting arrest.

title: A sickly childhood breeds Dracula’s imagination
desc: Stoker spent his first seven years bedridden in this Georgian house while his mother filled his head with horror stories. A Dublin walking-tour guide leads a visit to the home, now painted blood-red, that shaped the imagination behind Dracula.

title: Ireland’s only Nobel physicist splits the atom
desc: Recorded decades after his 1932 breakthrough at Cambridge, Ireland’s only Nobel physics laureate describes in his own voice the experiment that first split an atom’s nucleus, before returning to teach at Trinity for forty more years.

title: Trad’s journey from marginal to mainstream
desc: Tom Mulligan, who has run session nights at this pub for over 35 years, traces trad’s unlikely journey from a marginalized rural genre to a defining sound of modern Ireland, and its newest threat: Dublin property prices closing venues one by one.

title: Gunfire interrupts a football match
desc: On November 21, 1920, British forces opened fire into this stadium during a Gaelic football match, killing 14 including Tipperary player Michael Hogan — hours after Michael Collins’s squad had assassinated British officers across the city.

title: A single day in Dublin, chapter by chapter
desc: Leopold Bloom really did buy lemon soap at this pharmacy on June 16, 1904, the single day Joyce’s novel covers street by street. The shop still sells the same soap, and volunteers still read the book aloud here every week.

title: A literary salon shapes a future wit
desc: Wilde was born in this Georgian townhouse in 1854 to parents already prominent in Dublin’s cultural scene: his father a surgeon, his mother a poet who hosted literary salons where the young Oscar mingled with the leading writers of the day.

title: A mathematician carves an equation into a bridge
desc: Recorded on the annual walk retracing Hamilton’s route, this audio guide tells how a mathematician, mid-walk with his wife, stopped to carve the founding equation of quaternion algebra into this bridge’s stone in 1843.

title: A 9,000-year lease begins a brewing dynasty
desc: Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease on this site in 1759. Historian Turtle Bunbury digs the brewery’s own archive for stories the tour skips, from carthorses and canals to the welfare schemes that made a Guinness job one for life.

title: A charity premiere becomes participatory art
place: Site of the Great Music Hall, Fishamble Street
desc: On this street’s Music Hall in 1742, Handel’s Messiah premiered to a packed charity audience, half the choir borrowed from Christ Church Cathedral down the road. Freakonomics visits the spot to ask why the piece still draws people back to sing it.

title: A basement discovery reveals a city built for war
desc: The hosts found a Cold War-era bomb shelter in their own Stockholm basement and traced why the city built so many. Stockholm’s metro tunnels, blasted deep into bedrock partly for this reason, could double as shelter for tens of thousands if needed.

title: A king’s promised amnesty turns into a mass execution
desc: King Christian II invited Swedish nobles to a celebratory feast in 1520, promised amnesty, then had 82 of them executed in this square over two days. The massacre backfired, fueling the rebellion that ended Danish rule and put Gustav Vasa on the throne.

title: A king’s floating fortress sinks in twenty minutes
desc: Thousands lined the waterfront to watch this warship’s 1628 maiden voyage, only to see it capsize barely a mile out, top-heavy with cannons and carvings meant to broadcast Swedish power. Salvaged nearly intact in 1961, it’s now this museum’s sole exhibit.

title: A sitting Speaker reflects on his historic office
desc: In a rare interview, the hosts sit down with Andreas Norlén, Speaker of Sweden’s Parliament, who reflects on the centuries of history behind his office, which era he’d have most wanted to hold it in, and how he views the current king’s reign.

title: A worker’s shoes reveal a disaster the Kremlin hid
desc: A radiation detector went off on a worker’s shoes here on April 28, 1986, two days after an explosion the USSR hadn’t admitted to. Sweden’s questions forced Moscow to publicly confirm Chernobyl, the world’s first outside acknowledgment of the disaster.

title: Banned from the city, he moves his explosives to a park
desc: After nitroglycerin experiments killed his younger brother and several workers, Stockholm banned Nobel’s testing within city limits. He moved production to a barge and later this inlet, going on to hold 355 patents while building an explosives empire.

title: A neutral nation quietly houses another country’s escaped navy
desc: Three Polish submarine crews escaped occupied Poland in September 1939 and were interned here rather than fight on, in the small town of Mariefred outside Stockholm. The hosts trace camp life and how the crews got along with their Swedish neighbors.

title: A log floating ashore names Sweden’s future capital
desc: Legend credits Birger Jarl with founding this city in 1252, where a floating log supposedly washed ashore, giving Stockholm its name, log islet. Historians debate whether Birger or his son issued the founding letter, and runestones suggest older origins.

title: A businessman becomes an accidental Holocaust hero
desc: Inspired by a film about a fictional Nazi-resisting archaeologist, Wallenberg volunteered for a Budapest post and issued passports saving tens of thousands of Hungarian Jews. Arrested by Soviets after the city’s liberation, he vanished into the Gulag.

title: A king dances into an assassin’s waiting pistol
place: Royal Swedish Opera (site of Gustav III’s opera house)
desc: Warned in advance and still defiant, Gustav III attended a masked ball at the opera house he’d built and was shot in the back at close range in 1792. He lingered two weeks before dying, giving conspirators an awkward interval to plan their own defense.

title: A stabbing in a shopping aisle shocks a nation
desc: Sweden’s popular foreign minister, considered a likely future prime minister, was stabbed while shopping here in September 2003, days before a euro referendum. Her death shattered a sense of safety unbroken since a prime minister’s murder decades earlier.

title: A childhood haunted by death shapes an artist’s vision
desc: Munch lost his mother and older sister to tuberculosis before he turned fifteen, and spent his career processing that grief through paintings so raw that some visitors have reported feeling physically unwell in front of them.

title: A secret detour wins the race to the South Pole
desc: Amundsen told the world he was sailing this ship to the Arctic, then secretly diverted to Antarctica, racing Robert Falcon Scott to the South Pole. Amundsen’s team reached it first, on December 14, 1911; Scott’s team died on the return journey.

title: Thieves steal ‘The Scream’ in under a minute
desc: Two thieves climbed a ladder into this gallery on the opening morning of the 1994 Winter Olympics, cut the painting free, and left a note reading Thanks for the poor security. It turned up undamaged three months later, ransom unpaid.

title: A confused will creates the world’s most contested prize
desc: Alfred Nobel’s brief, three-times-rewritten will never explained why he chose peace as a prize category, or why a Norwegian committee should award it rather than his native Sweden. The ceremony was held in this very hall from 1947 to 1989.

title: A historian traces Oslo from Viking outpost to modern capital
desc: This medieval fortress has guarded Oslo’s harbor since the 1290s, surviving sieges, fires, and a total relocation of the city itself. Historian Eleanor Rosamund Barraclough walks its walls to trace the capital’s evolution into modern Norway.

title: A Doll’s House shocks Europe into rethinking marriage
desc: Ibsen spent his last eleven years in this apartment, having already scandalized Europe with A Doll’s House, whose heroine Nora shocked audiences simply by walking out on her husband and children to find her own life.

title: A record shop basement becomes a genre’s ground zero
place: Former Helvete record shop, Schweigaards gate
desc: Guitarist Øystein Aarseth opened this record shop in 1991, and its basement became the meeting place for the inner circle of Norwegian black metal. Within three years, arson attacks on historic churches and a murder had shattered the scene.

title: A raft of balsa wood crosses the Pacific to prove a theory
desc: In 1947, Heyerdahl sailed this balsa-wood raft from Peru to Polynesia to test his theory that South Americans could have settled the Pacific islands. The museum’s curator explains what drove a man with no sailing experience to attempt it anyway.

title: A brother’s masterpiece hides in permanent darkness
desc: Emanuel Vigeland spent decades painting this former studio, now his mausoleum, with frescoes spanning life’s arc from conception to death. Overshadowed by his more famous brother Gustav, he insisted visitors experience it in near-total darkness.

title: A wartime flood story becomes a beloved family
desc: Jansson wrote the first Moomin book from an apartment near this spot in 1945, inventing round white trolls as comfort during wartime. Her niece Sophia describes growing up amid the creativity that made Moomin one of Finland’s biggest exports.

title: Oodi Central Library Tour: Helsinki’s Community Hub of the Future
creator: Arto Mieskolainen
desc: An in-building walk through Helsinki’s central library, named the world’s best library in 2019. From the ground floor, it passes a maker space with free 3D printers and a rosewood sculpture from Renaissance geometry, ending on the top-floor reading level.

title: A rubber-boot company conquers the world’s pockets
desc: At its 2007 peak, this company’s revenue topped 50 billion euros and its ringtone was recognizable worldwide, drawing engineers from across the globe to a Finnish firm that started out making rubber boots and paper before smartphones ended its reign.

title: A tone poem disguised itself to dodge Russian censors
desc: Sibelius premiered Finlandia here in 1900 under fake names like Happy Feelings at the Awakening of Finnish Spring to slip past Russian censorship, before it became the unofficial anthem of a nation that wouldn’t exist for another 17 years.

title: A parliament votes itself out of the Russian Empire
desc: On December 6, 1917, Finland’s parliament met near this building and voted 100 to 88 to declare independence from a collapsing Russian Empire, a fragile break that plunged the new country into civil war within weeks.

title: Cold War spies hide behind ordinary Helsinki lives
desc: This seaside park sits inside Helsinki’s old embassy district, ground zero for a Cold War where Soviet agents trained locally and Finnish officials were quietly assigned their own pet Russians, a shadow relationship the show argues never really ended.

title: A concert hall becomes a Cold War summit stage
desc: Alvar Aalto’s white marble hall on the bay has hosted concerts and conferences since 1971, including the 1975 summit that produced the Helsinki Accords, a Cold War human rights agreement negotiated on Finland’s deliberately neutral ground.

title: A museum devoted entirely to the male member
desc: Founded in 1997 by Sigurdur Hjartarson, this museum now displays over 300 specimens from more than 100 species, from whales to hamsters, plus a cafe serving beer beside the gift shop’s novelty merchandise. It added its first human specimen in 2011.

title: Cold War tensions get decided on a chessboard
desc: Volatile American Bobby Fischer took on Soviet champion Boris Spassky here in 1972’s Match of the Century, a Cold War proxy battle over a chessboard. An Icelandic policeman who became one of Fischer’s few close companions shares what he was really like.

title: Björk takes apart her own heartbreak anthem
desc: Björk has reworked her catalogue with Icelandic musicians at this glass concert hall. Here she pulls apart ‘Stonemilker,’ the opening track of her 2015 breakup album Vulnicura, layer by layer, from its aching string arrangement to its rawest lyrics.

title: Six innocent people confess to murders that can’t be proven
desc: Six young Icelanders confessed to two 1974 murders after solitary confinement and sleep deprivation at a prison on this street, despite no bodies, witnesses, or evidence ever surfacing. Iceland’s Supreme Court acquitted five of them 44 years later.

title: A backwater country becomes a genetics goldmine
desc: Neurologist Kari Stefansson founded this company in 1996 to mine Iceland’s unusually documented genealogy and homogeneous population for medical research. Two-thirds of Icelandic adults participate, yielding discoveries linked to Alzheimer’s and cancer.

title: A blacklisted socialist wins Iceland’s only Nobel Prize
desc: Laxness lived in this house for over 50 years after winning the 1955 Nobel Prize in Literature, having already been jailed abroad for his writing and later blacklisted in America for opposing a permanent US military base at Keflavik.

title: The most photographed statue wasn’t even the real hero
desc: This bronze Leif Erikson, a gift from the US in 1930, stands before Iceland’s most photographed backdrop. Yet the sagas credit a different sailor, Bjarni Herjolfsson, with spotting North America first, after getting lost en route to Greenland.

title: An airline promises impossibly cheap flights, then vanishes overnight
desc: WOW Air’s founder promised ultra-cheap transatlantic flights through this airport, growing the startup into Iceland’s second-largest airline within five years. It collapsed into bankruptcy overnight in March 2019, stranding thousands with no warning.

title: A tiny navy wins a war without firing a shot
desc: Icelandic coast guard vessels spent decades cutting British trawlers’ fishing nets rather than firing on them, extending their waters from 4 to 200 miles despite facing the Royal Navy. Furious protesters smashed every window at this embassy in 1973.

title: A chieftain’s tossed pillars choose Iceland’s capital
desc: Legend holds Ingolfur Arnarson threw his high-seat pillars overboard and vowed to settle wherever they washed ashore, landing here in 874. This museum sits atop the excavated remains of a Viking-age longhouse, believed to be Reykjavik’s oldest structure.

title: A tiny country’s banks grow ten times bigger than its economy
desc: Icelandic banks headquartered along this street borrowed so aggressively abroad their combined assets hit ten times the country’s GDP by 2007. When global credit froze in 2008, all three collapsed within a week, a failure unique among Western nations.

title: Two professors argue over medieval Iceland’s body counts
desc: This exhibition holds the medieval manuscripts recording Iceland’s family sagas: tales of feuds, outlaws, and blood debts written between the 9th and 13th centuries. Two professors work through them chapter by chapter, awarding prizes for Best Bloodshed.

title: Nadia Comăneci: The Gymnast Who Made Olympic History with a Perfect 10
desc: Ceaușescu turned the fourteen-year-old’s 1976 perfect 10 into state propaganda the moment she landed back in Romania. By 1989, weeks before the regime fell, she trudged through winter mud to defect across the Hungarian border.

title: The Execution of Romanian Dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu
desc: Ceaușescu addressed a crowd from the balcony over this square on December 21, 1989, expecting cheers. Jeers turned to gunfire, then revolution; four days later he and his wife were executed, ending Europe’s last hardline communist regime.

title: Dracula (Vlad the Impaler)
desc: A charter Vlad III signed here on September 20, 1459 is the first written record of Bucharest’s existence. He ruled Wallachia from this riverside court, and his brutal tactics against Ottoman invaders later fed Bram Stoker’s Dracula.

title: Muistatko Monrepos’n
creator: Annikki Tähti
desc: The title means ‘Do You Remember Monrepos?’ — a park in Vyborg, the city Finland lost to the USSR. Helsinki-born Annikki Tähti’s lament for a vanished Karelia was Finland’s first gold record. She sings it again in Kaurismäki’s ‘The Man Without a Past.’

title: Get On
creator: Hurriganes
desc: Hurriganes played stripped-down rock’n’roll with a thick Finnish accent and became a national institution. Drummer-singer Remu Aaltonen, Helsinki-born, founded them in this northern suburb in 1971.

title: Finlandia, Op. 26
creator: Jean Sibelius
desc: Written as covert protest music under Russian censorship, its hymn section became Finland’s unofficial second anthem. Sibelius trained at the Helsinki Music Institute and conducted the premiere here in 1899; Hiltunen’s steel-pipe monument stands in Töölö.

title: Ciel d’hiver
creator: Kaija Saariaho
desc: The title means ‘Winter Sky.’ Saariaho was born in Helsinki and studied at the Sibelius Academy before Paris and IRCAM made her one of the great composers of her generation. She endowed the organ at Musiikkitalo, home to the orchestra that recorded this.

title: Grand Canal Revelations: Venice’s Right Bank Vaporetto Audio Tour
creator: Erla Zwingle
desc: A waterbus ride along the Grand Canal’s right bank, starting at the modern glass bridge by the bus station, past merchants’ palaces, the Rialto market and a palazzo said to be cursed, ending at the old customs house point.

title: Castello’s Hidden Corners: A Walk around a Vibrant Venice Neighborhood
creator: Erla Zwingle
desc: A neighbourhood walk through working-class, seafaring Castello, starting at the naval history museum, past the shipyard gates, a Slavic confraternity hall and a huge Gothic friars’ church, ending at an old boatyard facing a hospital church.

title: Politics and Power in Serenissima: From the Doge’s Palace to Venice’s Arsenale
creator: A History of Italy Podcast
desc: A political-history walk starting outside the Doge’s Palace, the seat of the old Republic’s government, past its prisons, a Greek refugee church and a looted Athenian lion, ending at the walled state shipyard that built its fleets.

title: In and Around St. Mark’s Square: A Walk with Context
creator: Context Travel
desc: An art historian’s tour of a thousand years of Venetian power, starting in St Mark’s Square and taking in the clock tower, the gold-domed basilica, the old mint and the Bridge of Sighs before ending in a small waterside royal garden.

title: Bucharest’s Highlights and Beyond: Monarchy, Communism and Modern Times
creator: Florin Preda
desc: A history walk through Bucharest’s monarchy, communist, and modern eras. Starting outside a neoclassical concert hall, it passes the balcony where a dictator gave his last speech and a royal palace, ending among medieval ruins tied to Dracula’s prince.

title: Bucharest Beyond the Boulevards: From Revolution to Royal Secrets
creator: Cristian
desc: A history walk down Bucharest’s grandest boulevard, from Ottoman trade hub to revolutionary battleground. Starting outside a historic bank, it passes a university square that sparked a revolution and a mansion-turned-casino, ending at a government square.

title: Reykjavik Revealed: A Tour of its Main Sights and Hidden Gems
creator: Matt / Voyageurs d’Islande
desc: A city-overview walk pairing Reykjavík’s headline sights with local secrets. From the great basalt-inspired church, it takes in a waterfront concert hall, the harbour, a steel viking-ship sculpture, and the old pond, ending downtown.

title: Suomenlinna Walking Tour: A Guide to Helsinki’s Island Fortress
creator: Helsinki Tour
desc: A history walk through a UNESCO-listed island sea fortress, reached by ferry from the mainland. From the ferry terminal, it passes a WWII-era submarine open for viewing and one of Europe’s oldest operational dry docks, ending near the fortress museum.

title: Capital of Contrasts: A Helsinki Walking Tour
creator: Arto Mieskolainen
desc: A loop through Helsinki’s history, from Swedish and Russian rule to independence, led by a local guide. From the central cathedral square, it passes a vast underground bomb shelter and a mermaid statue central to the city’s biggest street party.

title: Helsinki Walking Tour: Historical Highlights of the Finnish Capital
creator: Helsinki Tour
desc: An introductory walk through Helsinki’s central squares and harbor. From the cathedral square, it passes a salt warehouse turned presidential palace and Western Europe’s largest Orthodox cathedral, ending on the main shopping street.

title: Kallio Walking Tour: Workers, Rebels and Pioneering Women
creator: Ed Morrow
desc: A walk through Helsinki’s historic working-class district, tracing labor and women’s-rights history. From a market square, it passes where a future revolutionary hid and a pioneering library, ending at a kindergarten by Finland’s first female architect.

title: Downtown Oslo: Exploring the City’s Highlights and History
creator: Stormposten Lars Engerengen
desc: A history walk along Karl Johan Avenue from the waterfront to the fjord. From City Hall Square, it passes the Nobel Peace Center and the National Museum with Munch’s The Scream, and the Palace gardens, ending at Bjørvika bay, the old Viking settlement.

title: Akerselva Walking Tour: Oslo’s Industrial and Working-Class Story
creator: Stormposten Lars Engerengen
desc: A history walk along the Akerselva river’s industrial corridor. From Vaterland Park, it passes through Grønland and Grünerløkka, former immigrant districts now sought-after, ending at Hønse-Lovisa’s House, named for a figure who sheltered single mothers.

title: Gamla Stan Walking Tour: A Guide to Stockholm’s Old City
creator: Walter Gustav Molander
desc: A circular walk through the Old Town’s four islands with a local guide. From the Old Town metro, it loops past a royal burial church, the pink cathedral, the great square, the royal palace, and the city’s narrowest alley before returning.

title: Stockholm walking tour: the landmarks and legends of Gamla Stan and beyond
creator: Mikael Shainkman
desc: A historian’s stroll from the medieval Old Town to the modern centre. From an Old Town square, it passes a Viking runestone, the royal palace, and the Nobel museum, unpacking Swedish empire, royal bloodshed, and the term ‘Stockholm syndrome’.

title: Sweden’s Past and Present: Stories from Stockholm’s Old Town
creator: Plati Perspektyva
desc: A story-driven walk from Parliament through the Old Town to the modern centre. From opposite Parliament, it threads the medieval quarter, the ‘Northern Venice’ bridges, and a Nobel-laureate hotel, ending in the square that named ‘Stockholm syndrome’.

title: Royal Djurgården Tour: A Cycle Around Stockholm’s Royal National City Park
creator: Explore Stockholm City
desc: A cycle loop around Djurgården, the royal park island east of the centre. From its blue gate, it follows waterside trails past a royal summer palace, gardens, a lighthouse, and the maritime museum, through an embassy district back to the bridge.

title: Stockholm’s Musical Legacy: An Audio Guide to the ABBA Story
creator: Irina Kåvik
desc: A music walk tracing ABBA’s rise from Eurovision to global fame. From the central park where fans marked the band’s 50th anniversary, it passes the opera house and crosses to the island studio, ending by the harbour near the national museum.

title: Central Stockholm: A Guide to the Modern City
creator: Plati Perspektyva
desc: A modern-Stockholm walk through design, Swedish values, and royal drama. From the busy shopping street, it crosses the main squares and the city’s ‘Broadway’ into upscale Östermalm, ending at the royal palace and the gateway to the Old Town.

title: Stockholm by Bus: A Local’s Tour of the Capital’s Highlights
creator: Mia & Mikael Brejcha
desc: A hop-on/hop-off public-bus tour across the islands, by a local couple. From a central market square, it loops through Östermalm and Södermalm’s viewpoints, past a former prison island and City Hall, back to the centre. Bus fare not included.

title: Drottningholm Palace Park: A Stockholm Walking Tour
creator: Mia & Mikael Brejcha
desc: A walk through the royal family’s palace gardens, a UNESCO site west of the city. From the palace quay, it winds through baroque avenues and English gardens past a Chinese pavilion and an antique court theatre, ending by the palace tennis courts.

title: The Best of Oslo’s City Centre: From the Royal Palace to Aker Brygge
creator: Victoria Vanegas
desc: A city-center walk from the Royal Palace through the University of Oslo and Parliament to the harbor. It passes the National Theatre, Nobel Peace Center, and City Hall, ending at Aker Brygge.

title: The Philosopher’s Last Walk
creator: Rasmus Nielsen Bitsch
desc: A biographical walk tracing the life of Denmark’s most famous philosopher, Søren Kierkegaard. Starting outside his birthplace, it passes a towering astronomical tower and a grand cathedral, ending at his grave in a leafy cemetery.

title: Copenhagen’s Royal History: The King’s Square to the Queen’s House
creator: James Cowan
desc: A royal history walk tracing Copenhagen’s rise from muddy medieval outpost to European capital. Starting at a grand royal square, it passes a colorful former sailors’ harbor once home to a famous fairy-tale author, ending at a four-palace royal complex.

title: Discovering Copenhagen: Its Modern Marvels and Historical Landmarks
creator: Pernille Schlander
desc: A sightseeing walk from Copenhagen’s grand royal square to its famous harborside mermaid statue. Starting at the square, it passes a colorful canal harbor, a marble-domed royal church, and a star-shaped fortress, ending at the Little Mermaid.

title: Copenhagen MonsTour
creator: HidDenmark
desc: A folklore walk uncovering the dragons, trolls, and merfolk hidden in Copenhagen’s landmarks. From the central station, it passes a dragon fountain at town hall and a castle island tied to a witch-trial prison, ending at an underwater mermaid sculpture.

title: In the Footsteps of Hans Christian Andersen: A Copenhagen Walking Tour
place: Royal Danish Theatre (Old Stage), Kongens Nytorv
creator: Pernille Schlander
desc: A literary biography walk tracing Hans Christian Andersen’s Copenhagen. From the Royal Danish Theatre, it passes the colorful harbor where he lived and wrote his fairy tales and a marble-domed royal church, ending near a historic canal-side square.

title: The Day the Soldiers Came: Copenhagen’s Seizure in 1940
creator: James Cowan
desc: A WWII walk tracing the hours-long Nazi invasion of Copenhagen in April 1940. At a wartime memorial near the harbor, it passes a fortress captured within minutes and a palace square where Danish guards made a stand, ending at the wartime king’s statue.

title: Copenhagen’s Cozy Corners: A Hygge Tour of the Danish Way of Life
creator: Pernille Schlander
desc: A mindful walk exploring the Danish concept of hygge through Copenhagen’s cozy corners. Starting at a grand royal square, it passes a colorful canal harbor and a royal garden, ending at a beloved amusement park.

title: Copenhagen’s Urban Echoes: A Walking Tour Through Vibrant Vesterbro
creator: Pernille Schlander
