title: Piazza Fontana: The Italian Conspiracy
place: Piazza Fontana, site of the agricultural bank
creator: Marco Tullio Giordana
desc: Original title Romanzo di una strage. Marco Tullio Giordana on the 12 December 1969 bombing of an agricultural bank on Piazza Fontana, a square behind the Duomo, which killed 17. The courts later blamed a neo-fascist cell. No one was punished.

title: House of Gucci
creator: Ridley Scott
desc: Ridley Scott’s drama from Sara Gay Forden’s book, with Lady Gaga as Patrizia Reggiani and Adam Driver as Maurizio Gucci, whom she had killed in 1995. He was shot on the steps of his office at Via Palestro 20, a street along the public gardens.

title: I Am Love
creator: Luca Guadagnino
desc: Original title Io sono l’amore. Luca Guadagnino’s drama about a rich Milan textile family, with Tilda Swinton as the Russian-born wife who falls for a young chef. The family home is Villa Necchi Campiglio, a 1930s villa now run as a house museum.

title: Il Posto
creator: Ermanno Olmi
desc: Original title means “the job.” Ermanno Olmi’s quiet drama about a shy teenager from the town of Meda who commutes into Milan, sits the entrance tests for a big company and finds a dead-end desk. Trains from Meda end at Cadorna station.

title: Who Will Write Our History
creator: Roberta Grossman
desc: Documentary with re-enactments about historian Emanuel Ringelblum’s secret group, which buried an archive of ghetto life in milk cans. Two of its three caches were dug up after the war. Parts are on show at the Jewish Historical Institute.

title: The Zookeeper’s Wife
creator: Niki Caro
desc: Jessica Chastain plays Antonina Żabińska, who with her husband Jan sheltered Jews in Warsaw Zoo during the occupation. Shot in Prague, not Warsaw. The real zoo is in Praga, the district on the Vistula’s east bank, and the Żabińskis’ villa is open.

title: The Pianist
creator: Roman Polański
desc: Roman Polański’s film of Władysław Szpilman’s memoir, with Adrien Brody as the pianist. In 1942 his family was sent from the Umschlagplatz, the ghetto’s railway loading yard, to Treblinka. A white marble memorial stands there on Stawki Street.

title: Warsaw Uprising
creator: Jan Komasa
desc: Real colour and black-and-white footage shot by Home Army cameramen in 1944, edited into a story of two young reporters, with voices added by lip-readers. Made by Jan Komasa with the Warsaw Rising Museum, which shows the original reels.

title: Kanał
creator: Andrzej Wajda
desc: Andrzej Wajda’s film about a Home Army company escaping through the sewers (kanały) as the 1944 Uprising collapses. Bleak and short. On Dworkowa Street a memorial marks the manhole where Germans shot more than 100 insurgents as they climbed out.

title: Leave No Traces
place: Jezuicka Street police station, Old Town
creator: Jan P. Matuszyński
desc: In 1983 militia officers beat student Grzegorz Przemyk to death in a police station on Jezuicka Street, in the Old Town. The state then spent years covering it up. This film follows the friend who saw it. Long, at nearly three hours.

title: A Film Unfinished
creator: Yael Hersonski
desc: Israeli director Yael Hersonski examines ‘Das Ghetto’, unfinished Nazi propaganda film shot in the Warsaw ghetto in 1942, setting staged scenes against survivors’ accounts. On Chłodna Street, light poles mark the footbridge joining the ghetto’s two parts.

title: Popiełuszko: Freedom Is Within Us
creator: Rafał Wieczyński
desc: Biopic of Jerzy Popiełuszko, the priest whose ‘Masses for the Homeland’ drew thousands of Solidarity supporters until secret police officers murdered him in 1984. He is buried at St Stanisław Kostka Church in Żoliborz, where he served.

title: Stones for the Rampart
creator: Robert Gliński
desc: Drawn from Aleksander Kamiński’s 1943 book about real scouts in the Home Army underground. Its climax is Operation Arsenal, the March 1943 raid by the Arsenal on Długa Street that freed Jan Bytnar from a Gestapo truck. He died of his torture days later.

title: Odd Man Out
place: Crown Liquor Saloon, Great Victoria Street
creator: Carol Reed
desc: Director Carol Reed’s film about a wounded gunman (James Mason) hunted through the city on his last night. Partly shot in Belfast. Its pub scenes copy the Crown Liquor Saloon, the Victorian gin palace on Great Victoria Street, still pouring today.

title: Belfast
creator: Kenneth Branagh
desc: Actor-director Kenneth Branagh’s account of his own childhood in 1969, when riots broke out and his family weighed leaving. Shot in black and white. Branagh grew up on Mountcollyer Street in north Belfast; the family left for England when he was nine.

creator: Yann Demange
desc: Director Yann Demange’s thriller about a young British soldier stranded in West Belfast after a riot in 1971, early in the Troubles. Fiction, filmed in England. The peace wall on Cupar Way still separates the Catholic Falls from the Protestant Shankill.

title: Good Vibrations
creator: Lisa Barros D’Sa and Glenn Leyburn
desc: Comedy-drama about Terri Hooley, who opened a record shop and label in the 1970s and put out the Undertones’ “Teenage Kicks”. Punk crossed sectarian lines. The Harp Bar on Hill Street, now in the Cathedral Quarter nightlife area, was the scene’s home.

title: Hunger
creator: Steve McQueen
desc: Artist Steve McQueen’s first feature, about IRA prisoner Bobby Sands, who starved himself to death in the Maze prison in 1981 aged 27. Hard to watch, with long silent stretches. His mural is on the side of the Sinn Féin office on the Falls Road.

title: Kneecap
place: Cultúrlann McAdam Ó Fiaich, Falls Road
creator: Rich Peppiatt
desc: Writer-director Rich Peppiatt’s loosely true comedy about Kneecap, a West Belfast hip-hop trio who rap in Irish and play themselves. Crude and political. The Cultúrlann, an Irish-language arts centre on the Falls Road, is a hub of the revival they rap for.

title: Titanic Town
creator: Roger Michell
desc: Julie Walters plays a mother in 1972 Andersonstown, a Catholic estate in west Belfast, who starts a peace campaign and ends up despised by the IRA and the British Army alike. From Mary Costello’s novel based on her own mother. Funny as often as grim.

title: Framing John DeLorean
creator: Don Argott and Sheena M. Joyce
desc: Documentary with dramatised scenes, Alec Baldwin as carmaker John DeLorean, whose gull-winged DMC-12 was built with British government money at a factory in Dunmurry on Belfast’s edge. It closed in 1982, the year of his arrest on drug charges.

title: Distant Voices, Still Lives
creator: Terence Davies
desc: Director Terence Davies’s memory film of his own family in working-class Liverpool in the 1940s and 50s: a violent father, a patient mother, songs sung in pubs. It is slow. Davies grew up in Kensington, an inner-city district east of the centre.

title: Nowhere Boy
creator: Sam Taylor-Johnson
desc: Teenage John Lennon caught between his strict Aunt Mimi and his lively mother Julia, until Julia was killed by a car in 1958. Mimi’s house, Mendips on Menlove Avenue, now belongs to the National Trust and can be visited on tours.

title: Good Ol’ Freda
creator: Ryan White
desc: Freda Kelly was 17 when she became the Beatles’ secretary and ran their fan club for over a decade. Then she stayed in Liverpool, worked as a typist and said almost nothing for fifty years. She first saw them at the Cavern Club.

title: Of Time and the City
creator: Terence Davies
desc: Terence Davies’s documentary about the Liverpool he grew up in and left, cut from archive film under his own spoken commentary, fond and bitter by turns. The Museum of Liverpool keeps a carriage from the Overhead Railway, the elevated dock line seen in it.

title: Letter to Brezhnev
creator: Chris Bernard
desc: Two young women from Kirkby, a 1950s overspill town just outside Liverpool, meet Soviet sailors on a night out, and one writes to Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev to get back to hers. Written by Frank Clarke and made on a tiny budget.

title: Dockers
creator: Bill Anderson
desc: Television film about the Liverpool dock strike of 1995–98, when some 500 dockers were sacked after refusing to cross a picket line. Writers Jimmy McGovern and Irvine Welsh made it with the sacked men, whose pickets stood at the Royal Seaforth Dock gates.

title: Small Faces
creator: Gillies MacKinnon
desc: Director Gillies MacKinnon’s drama about three teenage brothers caught up in the street gangs of 1968 Glasgow. One wants to be an artist. A key scene plays out in Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, the red sandstone museum in the West End.

title: Ratcatcher
creator: Lynne Ramsay
desc: Lynne Ramsay’s first feature: a boy in a tenement during the 1973 binmen’s strike, when rubbish piled up across the city. Slow and quiet. The canal at its centre is the Forth and Clyde, which runs through Maryhill in the north of the city.

title: Comfort and Joy
creator: Bill Forsyth
desc: Director Bill Forsyth’s comedy about a radio DJ caught between rival ice-cream van firms. It came out just as Glasgow’s real ice-cream wars turned deadly: six of the Doyle family died in an arson attack on their Ruchazie flat in April 1984.

title: My Name Is Joe
creator: Ken Loach
desc: Ken Loach’s drama about a recovering alcoholic coaching a boys’ football team and falling for a health visitor. Peter Mullan won Best Actor at Cannes. It was shot in Ruchill, a north Glasgow district, with local non-actors. The dialect is thick.

title: Red Road
place: Site of the Red Road flats
creator: Andrea Arnold
desc: Andrea Arnold’s first feature. A CCTV operator watching the city on screens spots a man from her past. Much of it unfolds in the Red Road flats, once among Europe’s tallest housing blocks. They were demolished between 2012 and 2015.

title: Under the Skin
creator: Jonathan Glazer
desc: Jonathan Glazer’s science-fiction film with Scarlett Johansson as an alien driving a van, picking up men. Many street scenes were shot with hidden cameras on real shoppers on Argyle Street, the city’s main shopping street. Strange and slow.

title: The Angels’ Share
creator: Ken Loach
desc: Director Ken Loach and writer Paul Laverty’s comedy about Robbie, a young Glaswegian sentenced in the city’s sheriff court to community service, who finds a nose for whisky. The Sheriff Court stands on the south bank of the Clyde in the Gorbals.

title: A Youth in Germany
creator: Ernst Toller
desc: A young playwright’s memoir of the trenches and of leading Munich’s short-lived Soviet Republic in 1919, which cost him five years in jail. A plaque in the pavement on Kardinal-Faulhaber-Straße marks where premier Kurt Eisner was shot.

title: Bayern: Creating a Global Superclub
creator: Uli Hesse
desc: A German football writer’s history of FC Bayern, founded in Schwabing in 1900. It covers Kurt Landauer, the Jewish president the Nazis drove out, and Beckenbauer’s great sides. The club now plays at the Allianz Arena stadium in the north.

title: A Memoir of the Warsaw Uprising
creator: Miron Białoszewski
desc: Poet Miron Białoszewski’s record of the Uprising from the cellars, where civilians queued for water and moved from ruin to ruin. No battles, just daily life under bombs. The Old Town around its market square was flattened that summer and rebuilt by 1953.

title: The Mersey Sound
creator: Adrian Henri, Roger McGough and Brian Patten
desc: Penguin’s 1967 collection of three Liverpool poets: painter Adrian Henri, Roger McGough and Brian Patten. Funny, sad, plain-spoken poems about love, pubs and the city. Their patch was Hope Street, which runs between the city’s two cathedrals.

title: The Cruise
creator: Marek Piwowski
desc: Marek Piwowski’s cult comedy, originally Rejs. Stowaways on a Vistula pleasure boat elect a committee and hold absurd meetings, a sly picture of communist life. Mostly amateur actors. Poles quote it constantly. The boat sails from Warsaw’s riverbank.

title: Hillsborough
creator: Daniel Gordon
desc: Daniel Gordon’s documentary on the 1989 Hillsborough stadium crush in Sheffield and the families’ long fight to overturn the police version of events. The memorial to the dead stands beside Anfield, Liverpool FC’s stadium.

title: Chronicle of Poor Lovers (Cronache di poveri amanti)
creator: Carlo Lizzani
desc: Lizzani’s adaptation of Vasco Pratolini’s novel follows the families of one working-class lane in 1925 as Fascist squads take hold. It shows the old Santa Croce quarter as people lived in it. Via del Corno, the short street behind the Palazzo Vecchio.

title: Life Is Bearable at Times (Chwilami życie bywa znośne)
creator: Katarzyna Kolenda-Zaleska
desc: A rare portrait of Wisława Szymborska, the Nobel-winning poet who avoided cameras, with Woody Allen and Umberto Eco among the guests. She lived in Kraków for 70 years, long at the writers’ house on Krupnicza Street.

title: Olympia 52
creator: Chris Marker
desc: Chris Marker’s first feature, a French documentary about the 1952 Summer Olympics, the first Games with a Soviet team. It catches a small, war-worn capital hosting the world. The Olympic Stadium, with its white tower, where the Games took place.

title: Zombie and the Ghost Train (Zombie ja Kummitusjuna)
creator: Mika Kaurismäki
desc: Mika Kaurismäki’s bleak-funny descent: a drunken bass player drifts through Helsinki’s bars, army and gutters toward the ghost train of the title. Kallio, the working-class quarter of dive bars and bedsits his decline plays out in.

title: Molecole
creator: Andrea Segre
desc: Andrea Segre was stuck in Venice when Covid emptied it in 2020. He filmed the silent city and wrote to his late father, a scientist. Rowers train on the deserted Giudecca Canal, the wide channel between Giudecca island and the Zattere.

title: Saviour Square
creator: Krzysztof Krauze, Joanna Kos-Krauze
desc: A young family loses its savings when the developer of its new flat goes bust, and moves in with a domineering mother-in-law. Bleak and hard-going. Fiction, named for the round square of arcaded 1950s blocks around the Church of the Holiest Saviour.

title: George Best: All by Himself
creator: Daniel Gordon
desc: Daniel Gordon’s documentary on footballer George Best, from the Cregagh estate in east Belfast to Manchester United stardom and a long fall into alcoholism. He won 37 caps for Northern Ireland, whose home ground is Windsor Park stadium.

title: Violent Playground
creator: Basil Dearden
desc: Director Basil Dearden’s drama about a Liverpool policeman, played by Stanley Baker, moved to youth work and up against a teenage arsonist played by David McCallum. It was shot around Gerard Gardens, inner-city council tenements since demolished.

title: Leonardo and the Last Supper
creator: Ross King
desc: Art historian Ross King on how Leonardo da Vinci painted the Last Supper in the 1490s for Duke Ludovico Sforza, while war closed in on Milan. It is short and clear. The mural is still on the dining-hall wall of the Santa Maria delle Grazie convent.

title: Accidental Death of an Anarchist
creator: Dario Fo
desc: A farce by Nobel-winning playwright Dario Fo. In December 1969 anarchist Giuseppe Pinelli fell to his death from a window of Milan’s police headquarters, held after the Piazza Fontana bank bombing that killed 17. Fo mocks the official story.

title: The Sack of Rome
creator: Alexander Stille
desc: Journalist Alexander Stille on Silvio Berlusconi, the Milan builder who made a TV fortune, owned AC Milan and became prime minister. It covers the 1990s Clean Hands bribery inquiry, run from the Palace of Justice, the city’s vast 1930s courthouse.

title: The House of Gucci
creator: Sara Gay Forden
desc: Fashion journalist Sara Gay Forden on how a Florentine leather firm became a global brand and a family war. In 1995 Maurizio Gucci was shot dead on the steps of his office at Via Palestro 20. His ex-wife, Patrizia Reggiani, was convicted of ordering it.

title: The Doll
creator: Bolesław Prus
desc: Prus’s 1890 novel follows Wokulski, a self-made merchant hopelessly in love with an aristocrat. It is Warsaw’s great novel, and it’s long. A plaque on Krakowskie Przedmieście, the royal road, marks the house where readers placed his shop.

title: Obsessive Genius: The Inner World of Marie Curie
creator: Barbara Goldsmith
desc: A short, clear life of the physicist Marie Curie, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. She was born Maria Skłodowska in 1867 in a house on Freta Street in the New Town, now a small museum, and studied in secret classes under Russian rule.

title: In My Father’s Court
creator: Isaac Bashevis Singer
desc: Nobel novelist Isaac Bashevis Singer remembers his boyhood at No. 10 Krochmalna Street, where his rabbi father settled the neighbours’ quarrels. The poor Jewish street of thieves, tailors and widows was destroyed in the war. The street name survives.

title: The King of Children: The Life and Death of Janusz Korczak
creator: Betty Jean Lifton
desc: Janusz Korczak was a doctor and children’s author who ran a Jewish orphanage. In 1942 he refused rescue and went with his 200 children to the deportation trains. His orphanage on Jaktorowska Street still stands, and is still a children’s home.

title: Shielding the Flame
creator: Hanna Krall
desc: Journalist Hanna Krall interviews Marek Edelman, the last surviving commander of the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, who became a heart surgeon. He talks flatly, with no heroics. The fighters’ last bunker at Miła 18 is now a grassy mound with a stone.

title: Rising ’44: The Battle for Warsaw
creator: Norman Davies
desc: British historian Norman Davies on the Warsaw Uprising, the Home Army’s 63-day revolt against German occupation in 1944, while the Soviets waited across the river. It’s long and openly partisan. The Warsaw Rising Museum fills an old tram power station.

title: Iron Curtain: The Crushing of Eastern Europe 1944–1956
creator: Anne Applebaum
desc: Historian Anne Applebaum on how Soviet-backed communists took over Poland, Hungary and East Germany after the war. Warsaw’s Constitution Square, built around 1952 with giant stone workers on its facades, is that era set in stone.

title: A Minor Apocalypse
creator: Tadeusz Konwicki
desc: Novelist Tadeusz Konwicki’s dark comedy: a writer is asked to burn himself alive outside the Communist Party’s offices and spends a day wandering Warsaw’s shortages and queues. It ends at the Palace of Culture and Science, Stalin’s 1955 gift to the city.

title: Thomas Andrews: Shipbuilder
creator: Shan Bullock
desc: A short life of Thomas Andrews, the Harland & Wolff designer who went down with the Titanic in 1912, written by novelist Shan Bullock that same year. Andrews worked in the shipyard’s drawing offices. The building is now a hotel.

title: These Days
creator: Lucy Caldwell
desc: Novelist Lucy Caldwell follows two sisters through the German air raids of spring 1941, the Belfast Blitz. Around 900 people died in one April night, many in the packed streets of North Belfast around York Street.

title: Immortal: The Approved Biography of George Best
creator: Duncan Hamilton
desc: Sportswriter Duncan Hamilton on footballer George Best, who left the Cregagh housing estate at 15 for Manchester United and became football’s first pop-star celebrity. Drink ended his career early. The city airport now carries his name.

title: The Lonely Passion of Judith Hearne
creator: Brian Moore
desc: Brian Moore’s first novel: a lonely, devout piano teacher in a shabby boarding house in the streets near Queen’s University, where respectability was everything. Moore left Belfast and never moved back. A fiction pick; the city is its subject.

title: The Star Factory
creator: Ciaran Carson
desc: Poet Ciaran Carson’s memoir of growing up Irish-speaking off the Falls Road in the 1950s. It wanders from street names to old factories and his postman father’s stories. The title comes from a shirt factory near the family home on Raglan Street.

title: Milkman
creator: Anna Burns
desc: Anna Burns’s Booker winner: a teenager stalked by a paramilitary in the 1970s, during the Troubles, the 30-year conflict over Northern Ireland’s future. Nothing is named, but it draws on Ardoyne, the north Belfast district where Burns grew up.

title: Northern Protestants: An Unsettled People
creator: Susan McKay
desc: Journalist Susan McKay, herself from a Protestant family, interviews unionists and loyalists about faith, fear and belonging. It is the counterweight to books about the republican side. The Shankill Road is the heart of loyalist West Belfast.

title: Eureka Street
creator: Robert McLiam Wilson
desc: Novelist Robert McLiam Wilson’s comedy about two friends, one Catholic and one Protestant, in Belfast around the 1994 ceasefires. It is funny until a bomb goes off a few streets from City Hall, the domed civic building at the centre.

title: Redburn: His First Voyage
creator: Herman Melville
desc: Herman Melville’s half-autobiographical novel of a boy sailor’s first voyage, drawn from his own 1839 trip to Liverpool. The Liverpool chapters show docks, beggars and emigrant ships. His ship ties up at Prince’s Dock, north of the Pier Head.

title: The Slave Ship: A Human History
creator: Marcus Rediker
desc: Historian Marcus Rediker on the ships that carried enslaved Africans across the Atlantic, built from sailors’ and captives’ own accounts. Liverpool sent more slaving voyages than any other British port. The Town Hall’s frieze includes carved African heads.

title: Dead Wake
creator: Erik Larson
desc: Erik Larson on the Cunard liner Lusitania, torpedoed off Ireland in May 1915 with nearly 1,200 dead. She was bound from New York for Liverpool, her home port. Cunard ran its fleet from the Cunard Building on the Pier Head waterfront.

title: Twopence to Cross the Mersey
creator: Helen Forrester
desc: Helen Forrester’s memoir of a family gone bankrupt and dropped into the slums of 1930s Liverpool. She was kept home from school to mind her six siblings. The title is the ferry fare back to the Wirral. The boats land at Woodside terminal in Birkenhead.

title: An Awfully Big Adventure
creator: Beryl Bainbridge
desc: Novelist Beryl Bainbridge worked as a teenage stagehand at the Liverpool Playhouse and drew on it for this dark comic novel. A stagestruck girl joins a repertory company in the bomb-damaged city of 1950. The theatre still stands on Williamson Square.

title: Tune In: The Beatles: All These Years, Volume 1
creator: Mark Lewisohn
desc: Beatles historian Mark Lewisohn on the band up to the end of 1962, nearly all of it in Liverpool. It’s long. John Lennon met Paul McCartney at a church fête at St Peter’s in Woolton, a village suburb, on 6 July 1957.

title: Red or Dead
creator: David Peace
desc: Novelist David Peace retells Bill Shankly’s fifteen years managing Liverpool FC from 1959, in a deliberately repetitive, chant-like style. It’s long, over 700 pages. Shankly’s bronze statue stands outside Anfield, the club’s stadium, by the Kop stand.

title: Liverpool: Wondrous Place
creator: Paul Du Noyer
desc: Music writer Paul Du Noyer, a Liverpudlian, tells the city’s music story from sea shanties and the Beatles to punk and the Cream nightclub. The Cavern Club on Mathew Street is a rebuild. The original cellar was filled in in 1973.

title: Hillsborough: The Truth
creator: Phil Scraton
desc: Criminologist Phil Scraton on the 1989 crush at Sheffield’s Hillsborough stadium, where 97 Liverpool fans died, and the police cover-up that followed. His work fed the 2012 inquiry. Crowds held a vigil at St George’s Hall, the civic hall, when it reported.

title: Charles Rennie Mackintosh
place: Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh Building
creator: Alan Crawford
desc: Architectural historian Alan Crawford’s compact illustrated life of Glasgow’s great architect and designer. His masterpiece was the Glasgow School of Art building on Renfrew Street. It burned in 2014 and again in 2018. Restoration is still under way.

title: When the Clyde Ran Red: A Social History of Red Clydeside
creator: Maggie Craig
desc: Historian Maggie Craig on Red Clydeside, the strikes and protests of 1910–1922. In 1915 Govan housewife Mary Barbour led a rent strike that forced a national rent freeze. Her statue has stood at Govan Cross, the old town square, since 2018.

title: Growing Up in the Gorbals
creator: Ralph Glasser
desc: Ralph Glasser’s memoir of a poor Jewish childhood in the Gorbals tenements, south of the river, in the 1920s and ’30s. He worked in a barber’s and a garment factory, won a place at Oxford, and cycled there. The tenements were cleared in the 1960s.

title: Lanark
creator: Alasdair Gray
desc: Novelist and painter Alasdair Gray’s novel, half realist, half fantasy. Its hero, art student Duncan Thaw, grows up in Riddrie, the east-end council estate where Gray grew up. It argues that Glasgow needs artists to imagine it. It’s long.

title: Windswept & Interesting
place: Site of Alexander Stephen & Sons shipyard, Linthouse
creator: Billy Connolly
desc: Comedian Billy Connolly’s memoir of a hard Glasgow boyhood and how he found his voice. Before folk music and stand-up he was a welder at Alexander Stephen & Sons, a shipyard at Linthouse on the Clyde. The yard closed in 1968. It is very funny.

title: New Selected Poems
creator: Edwin Morgan
desc: Poems by Edwin Morgan, Glasgow’s first poet laureate and later Scotland’s national poet. He wrote about the city for sixty years: tenements, demolitions, a Glasgow Green park poem about men meeting in the dark. He came out publicly at seventy.

title: Jock Stein: The Definitive Biography
creator: Archie Macpherson
desc: Broadcaster Archie Macpherson’s life of the former miner who managed Celtic Football Club. In 1967 his team, all born near Glasgow, became the first British side to win the European Cup. Their ground is Celtic Park, the stadium in Parkhead.

title: Laidlaw
creator: William McIlvanney
desc: Novelist William McIlvanney’s first Glasgow detective story, often called the start of Scottish crime writing known as Tartan Noir. A girl is found murdered in Kelvingrove Park, the Victorian park in the West End. The city’s pubs and streets do the rest.

title: Shuggie Bain
creator: Douglas Stuart
desc: Douglas Stuart’s Booker Prize-winning novel about a boy and his alcoholic mother in 1980s Glasgow, as the shipyards and pits closed. It begins in the Sighthill tower blocks north of the centre. The towers were demolished in 2016. Stuart grew up there.

title: Mitridate, re di Ponto, K. 87: Overture
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
desc: Mozart was 14 when his first opera seria, “Mithridates, King of Pontus,” opened on 26 December 1770 at the Teatro Regio Ducale, the court theatre in the Palazzo Reale palace beside the Duomo. That theatre burned in 1776; La Scala replaced it.

title: L’elisir d’amore: Una furtiva lagrima
creator: Gaetano Donizetti
desc: Donizetti’s comic opera “The Elixir of Love” premiered in 1832 at the Teatro della Canobbiana, now the Teatro Lirico on Via Larga. This tenor aria, “A furtive tear,” is its best-known number. The theatre was renamed for singer Giorgio Gaber in 2021.

title: Nabucco: Va, pensiero
place: Casa Verdi rest home, Piazza Buonarroti
creator: Giuseppe Verdi
desc: The Hebrew slaves’ chorus, “Go, thought, on golden wings,” made Verdi’s name at La Scala in 1842. When his body was moved in 1901 to the rest home for musicians he founded, Casa Verdi on Piazza Buonarroti, crowds sang it. He lies in its crypt.

title: Messa da Requiem: Dies irae
creator: Giuseppe Verdi
desc: Verdi wrote his Requiem to honour novelist Alessandro Manzoni, author of “The Betrothed,” and conducted the first performance on 22 May 1874 in San Marco church in Brera, a year after Manzoni’s death. “Dies irae” means “day of wrath.”

title: Madama Butterfly: Un bel dì vedremo
creator: Giacomo Puccini
desc: Puccini’s “Madama Butterfly” was booed at its La Scala premiere on 17 February 1904. He withdrew it, revised it, and it triumphed in Brescia months later. In Cio-Cio-San’s aria, “One fine day we’ll see,” she hopes that her American husband returns.

title: Polonaise in A-flat major, Op. 53 “Heroic”
creator: Fryderyk Chopin
desc: Chopin grew up in Warsaw and left at 20, never to return. His heart did: his sister smuggled it home, and it rests in a pillar of Holy Cross Church. This stirring polonaise, a Polish court dance, became a wartime emblem of national pride.

title: Halka: Mazur
creator: Stanisław Moniuszko
desc: Halka, by composer Stanisław Moniuszko, is the founding Polish national opera: a highland girl seduced and abandoned by a nobleman. Its full version premiered in Warsaw’s Grand Theatre in 1858; his statue stands outside. The mazur is a quick Polish dance.

title: Kattorna
creator: Krzysztof Komeda Quintet
desc: Pianist Krzysztof Komeda, who scored Roman Polanski’s early films, recorded his album Astigmatic at the National Philharmonic hall in December 1965. Often called the high point of Polish jazz, it opens with this theme from a Danish film.

title: In München steht ein Hofbräuhaus
creator: Maxl Graf
desc: The title means “In Munich there’s a Hofbräuhaus.” Berlin composer Wiga Gabriel wrote this waltz in 1935, reportedly borrowing from Munich’s city hymn. When it reached the Hofbräuhaus beer hall, he conducted it there and was rewarded with a giant mug.

title: Soldi
creator: Mahmood
desc: Singer Mahmood, Sardinian mother and Egyptian father, grew up in Gratosoglio, the high-rise estate on Milan’s southern edge. “Money” is about a father who left, with an Arabic line; it won Sanremo in 2019 and came second at Eurovision.

title: Szampan
creator: sanah
desc: “Champagne,” a breezy hit by Warsaw-born singer Sanah (Zuzanna Grabowska), a classically trained violinist. On 22 September 2023 she became the first Polish woman to sell out the National Stadium, the bowl-shaped arena on the Vistula’s east bank.

title: I’ll Tell Me Ma
creator: Van Morrison & The Chieftains
desc: A children’s skipping song whose chorus crowns “the belle of Belfast city”; Van Morrison recorded it with Irish folk group the Chieftains on Irish Heartbeat. Belfast City Hall, the domed civic heart of the city, stands for her.

title: Solang der alte Peter
creator: Franzl Lang
desc: The title means “As long as old Peter stands.” Munich’s unofficial anthem, adapted around 1880 by local folk singer Michl Huber from a Viennese tune, promises the city’s easy warmth will last as long as the tower of St Peter’s Church.

title: O mia bela Madunina
creator: Giovanni D’Anzi
desc: Songwriter Giovanni D’Anzi’s dialect anthem, “Oh my beautiful little Madonna,” salutes the gilded Virgin on the highest spire of the Duomo cathedral, a Milanese symbol since 1774. Fans still sing it at the San Siro stadium.

title: Ma mi
creator: Ornella Vanoni
desc: Theatre director Giorgio Strehler wrote these dialect words, “But me,” for singer Ornella Vanoni (1934–2025): a resistance prisoner held in San Vittore prison who refuses to name names. It belongs to her “canzoni della mala,” songs of the Milan underworld.

title: Porta Romana
creator: Giorgio Gaber
desc: Milanese singer and theatre-maker Giorgio Gaber (1939–2003) sings of the working-class streets and bars around Porta Romana, the 1596 stone gate on the old Spanish walls where the road to Rome left the city.

title: Il ragazzo della via Gluck
creator: Adriano Celentano
desc: Adriano Celentano grew up at No. 14 on Via Gluck, behind the Central Station. “The boy from Via Gluck” mourns the fields there lost to postwar concrete, an early Italian protest song about urban sprawl, sung at the 1966 Sanremo festival.

title: Vengo anch’io. No, tu no
place: Derby Club site, Viale Monte Rosa
creator: Enzo Jannacci
desc: Doctor, songwriter and comic Enzo Jannacci (1935–2013) had his biggest hit with this absurdist refrain, “I’m coming too. No, not you.” He was a pillar of the Derby Club on Viale Monte Rosa, the cabaret where Milan’s satirical comedy scene grew up.

title: Luci a San Siro
creator: Roberto Vecchioni
desc: Songwriter Roberto Vecchioni remembers courting by car in the dark near the San Siro stadium: “Lights at San Siro,” with the floodlights of Inter and AC Milan’s shared ground as the backdrop. It became one of the best-loved Milan songs.

title: Badabum Cha Cha
creator: Marracash
desc: Rapper Marracash, born Fabio Bartolo Rizzo to Sicilian parents, grew up in the Barona housing estates on Milan’s southwest edge. This lead single from his 2008 debut album helped take Milan street rap into the Italian charts.

title: Ta ostatnia niedziela
creator: Mieczysław Fogg
desc: “This Last Sunday,” Jerzy Petersburski’s tango of a final farewell, was a 1935 hit for Warsaw crooner Mieczysław Fogg. Petersburski led a band at the Adria, the interwar city’s smartest dance hall; Fogg later sang for fighters in the 1944 uprising.

title: Sen o Warszawie
creator: Czesław Niemen
desc: “A Dream of Warsaw”: singer Czesław Niemen’s soaring song of longing to return to the city. Fans of Legia, Warsaw’s main football club, adopted it as their anthem and sing it en masse at the club’s stadium on Łazienkowska street.

title: Warszawa
creator: David Bowie
desc: In 1976 David Bowie’s train stopped at Warszawa Gdańska station and he walked the grey streets nearby, buying records of Polish folk music. The wordless chant he sang with Brian Eno on the album Low borrows from one of those folk songs.

title: Mniej niż zero
place: Polish Radio Three building, Myśliwiecka street
creator: Lady Pank
desc: “Less Than Zero” made Warsaw band Lady Pank, led by guitarist Jan Borysewicz, stars under martial law. It topped the weekly chart of Polish Radio Three, the station that gave a generation its rock, broadcast from this building on Myśliwiecka street.

title: Ballade No. 1 in G minor, Op. 23 (The Pianist)
creator: Janusz Olejniczak
desc: Pianist Janusz Olejniczak played the Chopin heard in Roman Polanski’s The Pianist. Władysław Szpilman, a Jewish pianist who escaped the Warsaw Ghetto, survived hiding in a ruined house at Niepodległości avenue 223, where a German officer found him.

title: Ukryty w mieście krzyk
creator: Pezet / Noon
desc: “A Cry Hidden in the City,” from rapper Pezet and producer Noon’s album Muzyka klasyczna, is a moody night drive through Warsaw. Pezet came up in Ursynów, the vast 1970s concrete housing district on the southern edge of the city that bred its rap scene.

title: Godzina W
creator: Lao Che
desc: “W-Hour” was 5 pm on 1 August 1944, when the Home Army began the Warsaw Uprising, a 63-day revolt against German occupation. Rock band Lao Che made a whole album about it, launched at the Warsaw Rising Museum, which hosts their anniversary concerts.

title: Softly, Softly
creator: Ruby Murray
desc: Ruby Murray, raised off the Donegall Road in south Belfast, took this ballad to No. 1 in Britain in 1955 and once had five singles in the Top 20 in the same week. Belfast unveiled a blue plaque to her in 2019.

title: Gloria
creator: Them
desc: Them, the band fronted by a teenage Van Morrison, built this three-chord stomp in their residency at the Maritime Hotel’s R&B club. Countless garage bands copied it; the old seamen’s hotel on College Square North is long gone.

title: Cyprus Avenue
creator: Van Morrison
desc: Van Morrison, born a mile away on Hyndford Street, turned this leafy, well-off east Belfast avenue into the centrepiece of his 1968 album Astral Weeks. In 2015 he played a 70th-birthday concert on the street itself.

title: Belfast Boy
creator: Don Fardon
desc: English singer Don Fardon’s tribute to footballer George Best, the Manchester United winger who grew up on the Cregagh council estate in east Belfast. Best’s boyhood home on Burren Way is still visited by fans.

title: Stairway to Heaven
creator: Led Zeppelin
desc: Led Zeppelin, the London rock band, played this song live for the first time at the Ulster Hall on 5 March 1971, months before it came out on record. The Victorian concert hall on Bedford Street still hosts gigs.

title: Big Time
place: Good Vibrations record shop, Great Victoria Street
creator: Rudi
desc: Belfast punks Rudi made this the first single on Good Vibrations, the label run by record-shop owner Terri Hooley from Great Victoria Street. His shop gave young fans a scene across the sectarian divide during the Troubles.

title: Alternative Ulster
creator: Stiff Little Fingers
desc: Stiff Little Fingers, from Belfast, shouted about life under the Troubles, the decades of conflict over Northern Ireland’s future, with soldiers on every corner. Punks crowded the Harp Bar on Hill Street to hear bands like them.

title: Annie’s Song
creator: James Galway
desc: Flautist James Galway, who grew up in working-class north Belfast and learned in local flute bands, took this instrumental of John Denver’s love song to No. 3 in Britain. The pin is the York Road, spine of his old district.

title: Glue
creator: Bicep
desc: Belfast DJ duo Bicep wrote this wistful track out of nostalgia for 1990s rave. Shine, the long-running club night at Queen’s University Students’ Union, anchored the Belfast dance scene they grew up in.

title: You’ll Never Walk Alone
creator: Gerry and the Pacemakers
desc: Gerry Marsden’s band took this show tune from Rodgers and Hammerstein’s musical “Carousel” to No. 1 in 1963. Fans on the Kop, the home end at Liverpool FC’s Anfield stadium, adopted it as their anthem, and it is still sung before every home match.

title: Anyone Who Had a Heart
creator: Cilla Black
desc: Cilla Black worked the cloakroom at the Cavern Club, the Mathew Street cellar where the Beatles played, before Brian Epstein signed her. Her version of this Burt Bacharach song went to No. 1 in 1964; a statue of her now stands outside the club.

title: Ferry Cross the Mersey
creator: Gerry and the Pacemakers
desc: Gerry Marsden wrote this for the 1964 film of the same name, about the boats linking Liverpool and Birkenhead. The Mersey Ferries still leave from the Pier Head terminal, and the song plays on board as they cross the river.

title: Penny Lane
creator: The Beatles
desc: Paul McCartney’s picture of the street and bus terminus near where he and John Lennon grew up: the barber, the bank, the fireman and the “shelter in the middle of the roundabout,” which still stands at Smithdown Place by Penny Lane.

title: Strawberry Fields Forever
creator: The Beatles
desc: John Lennon grew up near Strawberry Field, a Salvation Army children’s home in Woolton, and played in its garden as a boy. The red gates are a pilgrimage spot, and the site now has a visitor centre about the home and the song.

title: Maggie Mae
creator: The Beatles
desc: A 40-second scrap of an old Liverpool sailors’ song on the Beatles’ “Let It Be,” about a woman who robbed a sailor “down Lime Street.” The street runs past Lime Street station, the city’s main railway terminus, and St George’s Hall.

title: Children of the Ghetto
creator: The Real Thing
desc: Brothers Chris and Eddie Amoo of the Real Thing, Britain’s first Black chart-topping band, wrote this about their own district, Liverpool 8, or Toxteth. Granby Street was the heart of its Black community, one of the oldest in Britain.

title: Electricity
creator: Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark
desc: Andy McCluskey and Paul Humphreys, teenagers from Meols on the Wirral peninsula across the Mersey from Liverpool, formed OMD in 1978. This debut single, about wasted energy, came out on Manchester’s Factory Records in 1979.

title: Relax
place: Site of Eric’s club, Mathew Street
creator: Frankie Goes to Hollywood
desc: Singer Holly Johnson came out of the punk scene at Eric’s, the late-1970s club opposite the Cavern on Mathew Street. His band Frankie Goes to Hollywood’s debut was banned by BBC Radio 1 in 1984 and became one of Britain’s best-selling singles.

title: The Killing Moon
creator: Echo & the Bunnymen
desc: Ian McCulloch’s band Echo & the Bunnymen grew out of Liverpool’s post-punk scene; In May 1984 they led fans on “A Crystal Day” around the city, ending with a concert in St George’s Hall, the columned concert hall on Lime Street.

title: All Together Now
creator: The Farm
desc: Peter Hooton’s band the Farm set the 1914 Christmas truce, when British and German soldiers stopped fighting, to Pachelbel’s Canon. A statue of the truce football match stands in St Luke’s, a church gutted in the 1941 Blitz and left roofless.

title: Dreaming of You
creator: The Coral
desc: The Coral formed in Hoylake, a seaside town at the tip of the Wirral peninsula, as teenagers in the 1990s. This short, Merseybeat-tinged single from their 2002 debut album is the song most people know them by.

title: Let’s Dance to Joy Division
creator: The Wombats
desc: The Wombats met as students at LIPA, the performing arts school co-founded by Paul McCartney in his old school building on Mount Street. Matthew Murphy’s song is about dancing badly to the Manchester post-punk band Joy Division.

title: I Belong to Glasgow
creator: Will Fyffe
desc: Dundee-born music-hall comedian Will Fyffe said he wrote this tipsy anthem after a cheerful drunk talked to him at Glasgow Central Station. Its chorus, “Glasgow belongs to me,” is still sung in the city’s pubs a century on.

title: Rock Island Line
creator: Lonnie Donegan
desc: Lonnie Donegan, the “King of Skiffle,” was born in the East End district of Bridgeton in 1931. His sped-up take on Lead Belly’s railroad song set off a craze for washboards and tea-chest basses that put guitars in the hands of the young Beatles.

title: Shout
creator: Lulu and the Luvvers
desc: Lulu, born Marie Lawrie, was 15 and living in the tenements of Dennistoun in the East End when she belted out this Isley Brothers cover. It went Top 10 in Britain, and she has been closing shows with it ever since.

title: The Jeely Piece Song
creator: Adam McNaughtan
desc: A child in a new tower block can’t get a jeely piece (a jam sandwich) thrown down from the 20th floor. Folk singer Adam McNaughtan’s comic protest about the 1960s high-rises is pinned here at the site of the Red Road flats, demolished in 2015.

title: Delilah
creator: The Sensational Alex Harvey Band
desc: Rock showman Alex Harvey grew up in the Gorbals, the tenement district on the south bank of the Clyde. His band turned Tom Jones’s murder ballad into a stomping piece of theatre, and their live recording reached the UK Top 10.

title: Blue Boy
creator: Orange Juice
desc: Edwyn Collins’s band made this jangling single for Postcard Records, run by Alan Horne from a tenement flat on West Princes Street. Postcard’s “Sound of Young Scotland” gave British indie music a template for the decade.

title: Waterfront
creator: Simple Minds
desc: Jim Kerr’s band sing about the Clyde riverside on this bass-driven anthem, and filmed its video at the Barrowland Ballroom, the old East End dance hall that became the city’s favourite rock venue.

title: Tinseltown in the Rain
creator: The Blue Nile
desc: Paul Buchanan and Robert Bell met as students at the University of Glasgow before forming The Blue Nile. This string-swept single from “A Walk Across the Rooftops” turns a wet night in the city into something cinematic.

title: Dignity
creator: Deacon Blue
desc: Ricky Ross’s band sing about a council road sweeper saving up to buy a little boat he’ll call Dignity. It is pinned at the City Chambers on George Square, the grand Victorian headquarters of the council he works for.

title: The Concept
creator: Teenage Fanclub
desc: Teenage Fanclub came out of Bellshill, a town on Glasgow’s eastern edge whose 1980s guitar scene became known as “the Bellshill Sound.” This six-minute opener of “Bandwagonesque” fades out on a long, harmony-laden coda.

title: The State I Am In
creator: Belle and Sebastian
desc: Stuart Murdoch’s band recorded their first album, “Tigermilk,” as a project for the Electric Honey label run by music students at Stow College. This wry, confessional opener began a cult that grew well beyond Glasgow.

title: Why Does It Always Rain on Me?
creator: Travis
desc: Singer Fran Healy was an art student at the Glasgow School of Art, Charles Rennie Mackintosh’s building on Renfrew Street, when Travis took shape. This rueful hit about bad luck and grey skies made them one of Britain’s biggest bands.

title: Take Me Out
creator: Franz Ferdinand
desc: Before Franz Ferdinand, Alex Kapranos booked bands at the 13th Note, a vegetarian café and basement venue on King Street. The band’s tempo-shifting breakthrough single was nominated for a Grammy and took Glasgow art-rock worldwide.

title: Geraldine
creator: Glasvegas
desc: Glasvegas come from Dalmarnock, an East End district by the Clyde. Singer James Allan wrote this wall-of-sound ballad in the voice of a social worker, and sings it in his own unvarnished Glasgow accent.

title: The Mother We Share
creator: CHVRCHES
desc: Glasgow synth-pop trio CHVRCHES, led by singer Lauren Mayberry, a law graduate of the University of Strathclyde, broke out with this bright, glassy debut single. It set up a career of stadium tours and festival headlines.

title: Bombs, rumours and the government’s morale reports
place: St Luke’s bombed-out church, Leece Street
desc: A talk from The National Archives on how the wartime government measured the morale of Liverpudlians during the Blitz, some of the heaviest bombing in Britain. St Luke’s Church, burned out in May 1941, stands roofless on Leece Street as a memorial.

title: Stroll Through Time: A Walking Tour of Glasgow’s West End
desc: A history of the university district and its scientists, alumni and music venues, starting at a station on the small orange underground, passing the Gothic university cloisters and a grand red sandstone museum, ending in a pub inside a converted church.

title: Ghouls and Gruesome Tales: A Glasgow Ghost tour with Where Now
desc: Ghost stories and grim history told by a local comedian, starting on the main civic square and taking in grave-robbing, a hilltop Victorian cemetery and a reputedly haunted hotel, finishing at one of the city’s oldest pubs near the river.

title: Glasgow: The Merchant City
desc: A history of Glasgow’s trade wealth, from tobacco and cotton to heavy engineering and the city’s ties to slavery and abolition, starting in the main civic square and passing a cone-hatted equestrian statue, ending on a Georgian square uphill.

title: Glasgow through the ages: A sightseeing walk from the Cathedral to Glasgow Green
desc: A history walk through the oldest part of Glasgow, starting at the medieval cathedral and the legend of its patron saint, then down the old pilgrims’ high street past a herb garden and history murals, finishing in the city’s oldest public park.

title: Religion, Ireland and ninety minutes of football
desc: The Department of Information on the Old Firm, the rivalry between Glasgow’s Celtic and Rangers, rooted in Irish Catholic immigration and Protestant loyalism. Celtic play at Celtic Park in the East End, known locally as Parkhead.

title: The only house left from medieval Glasgow
desc: STV News on Provan’s Lordship, built in 1471 opposite the cathedral as part of a hospital, the oldest house in Glasgow and one of just four medieval buildings left in the city. It is now a free museum with a physic garden behind it.

title: The rent strike that beat Glasgow’s landlords
desc: Scottish History Out Of Order on Mary Barbour, the Govan housewife who in 1915 led tenants against wartime rent rises; the strike forced Parliament to freeze rents. Her statue, leading a crowd of women, stands at Govan Cross.

title: Why the Duke wears a traffic cone
place: Duke of Wellington statue, Royal Exchange Square
desc: The local history channel Astonishing Glasgow on Carlo Marochetti’s 1844 equestrian statue of the Duke of Wellington outside the Gallery of Modern Art, which has worn a traffic cone on its head, put there by late-night climbers, since the 1980s.

title: A century of the Barras
desc: Glasgow Building Preservation Trust marks a hundred years of the Barras, the East End weekend market that Maggie McIver started by renting out barrows, the handcarts that gave it its name, before building the covered market and the Barrowland dance hall.

title: A hill of Victorian merchants’ monuments
desc: The volunteer Friends of Glasgow Necropolis show the garden cemetery opened in 1833 on the hill behind the cathedral, where the city’s merchants and industrialists competed in stone under a column topped by reformer John Knox.

title: Miss Cranston’s tea rooms, restored
place: Mackintosh at the Willow, Sauchiehall Street
desc: A Doors Open Days film on the Willow Tea Rooms on Sauchiehall Street, designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh for tea-room owner Kate Cranston and opened in 1903. A trust rescued the building and reopened it in 2018 as Mackintosh at the Willow.

title: A tenement flat left as it was in 1965
desc: Rick Steves visits the Tenement House in Garnethill, where shorthand typist Agnes Toward lived from 1911 to 1965. The National Trust for Scotland keeps her flat as she left it, with gaslight, a coal range and beds built into wall recesses.

title: Trams, locomotives and a tall ship on the riverbank
desc: The Daily Record’s short tour of the Riverside Museum, Glasgow’s transport museum, a zigzag shed by architect Zaha Hadid at the mouth of the River Kelvin. The museum keeps old trams, Clyde-built locomotives and the tall ship Glenlee.

title: A shipowner’s 9,000 objects in a glass-walled park museum
desc: STV News goes behind the scenes at the Burrell Collection in Pollok Country Park, the art, armour, tapestries and ceramics shipping magnate William Burrell gave the city in 1944, rehoused after a six-year refurbishment that ended in 2022.

title: Repairing a medieval cathedral the medieval way
desc: Historic Environment Scotland on conserving Glasgow Cathedral, the 13th-century church on the site of St Mungo’s grave and the only medieval cathedral on the Scottish mainland to come through the 1560 Reformation almost intact.

title: Virginia leaf and the merchants who grew rich on it
desc: A clip from the BBC series Union on how the 1707 union with England opened colonial trade to Glasgow, whose tobacco lords grew rich on leaf grown by enslaved people in Virginia. The 1775 Tobacco Merchant’s House survives on Miller Street.

title: A museum of ordinary Glaswegian life
desc: In Glasgow Museums’ Glasgow Histories series, Peter Mortimer tells the story of the People’s Palace, the 1898 red sandstone museum of the city’s social history on Glasgow Green, the oldest park in the city, with a glasshouse Winter Gardens behind.

title: Building the QE2 in the last great Clyde yard
desc: BBC footage from 1967 of the workers at John Brown & Company in Clydebank, just downriver from Glasgow, building the liner Queen Elizabeth 2. The yard’s giant 1907 Titan crane still stands on the riverbank.

title: The world’s third-oldest underground, still one small circle
desc: Transport filmmaker Geoff Marshall rides the Glasgow Subway, opened in 1896 after London’s and Budapest’s: one 15-station loop under both banks of the Clyde, with trains small enough to earn the nickname the Clockwork Orange.

title: Gable-end murals across the city centre
desc: Rick Steves on the giant murals painted on Glasgow’s city-centre gable walls, a trail whose best-known stop is the artist Smug’s modern St Mungo, the city’s patron saint, cradling a robin on High Street.

title: The pedestrian spine of the Victorian city centre
desc: Rick Steves walks Buchanan Street, Glasgow’s pedestrianised main shopping street, which runs downhill from the Royal Concert Hall to Argyle Street between Victorian sandstone frontages, glass-roofed arcades and street musicians.

title: A sandstone palace of art built for an exhibition
desc: Travel writer Rick Steves visits Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, the red sandstone building opened for Glasgow’s 1901 International Exhibition, where free admission puts Salvador Dalí’s Christ of St John of the Cross near a hanging Spitfire.

title: The restaurant that claims chicken tikka masala
desc: The Judge Reviews talks to Asif of the Shish Mahal, the West End curry house whose founder Ali Ahmed Aslam said he invented chicken tikka masala there around 1971 by adding a tomato sauce to dry tandoori chicken for a customer.

title: Suffragette bodyguards against the Glasgow police
desc: In March 1914 police stormed the stage at St Andrew’s Halls to arrest suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst, and her jiu-jitsu-trained bodyguard fought back. Only the halls’ facade survived a 1962 fire; the Mitchell Library now fills it.

title: Hundreds of children hunt a vampire in a graveyard
desc: One night in 1954 hundreds of Gorbals children armed with knives and stakes stormed the Southern Necropolis, a Victorian cemetery, hunting an iron-toothed vampire. The Hebejeebies podcast asks how the rumour started and who got blamed.

title: From the Gorbals to guarding Abraham Lincoln
desc: Actor Alex Norton narrates the story of Allan Pinkerton, born in 1819 in the Gorbals, the old tenement district south of the river, who emigrated to the US, foiled a plot against Abraham Lincoln and founded the Pinkerton detective agency.

title: The speech the New York Times compared to Gettysburg
desc: Former Scottish justice secretary Kenny MacAskill on “A rat race is for rats”, the 1972 address by shipyard union leader Jimmy Reid on becoming rector of the University of Glasgow. The New York Times printed it in full.

title: A ship launched with its builders aboard
desc: In July 1883 the steamer Daphne capsized moments after launch at Alexander Stephen’s Linthouse yard on the Clyde, drowning 124 of the shipyard workers still aboard. Scottish History Out of Order visits their graves in Craigton Cemetery.

title: The novelist who painted the city’s ceilings
desc: Sorcha Dallas, custodian of the Alasdair Gray Archive, on the Glasgow writer and artist behind the novel Lanark. His murals are all over the city; the largest is the starry ceiling of Òran Mór, a former church turned arts venue on Byres Road.

title: A modernist world’s fair in a south side park
desc: This Day in Scottish History recalls the 1938 Empire Exhibition in Bellahouston Park, south of the Clyde, which drew nearly 13 million visitors to its modernist pavilions and 300-foot Tait Tower. The Palace of Art is one of the few buildings left.

title: Photographing the slums before the demolition crews
desc: Glasgow’s Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons on photographer Thomas Annan, hired in 1868 to record the closes, narrow alleys off the Saltmarket and High Street, before the city cleared them: some of the first photographs of slum housing.

title: How Glasgow taught the world to pass
desc: Richard McBrearty of the Scottish Football Museum at Hampden Park, Scotland’s national stadium, on early Glasgow football: Queen’s Park, the amateur club that pioneered the passing game, and the Irish community clubs that followed.

title: A dance hall built by a market queen
desc: Writer Alison Irvine on the Barrowland Ballroom on the Gallowgate, opened on Christmas Eve 1934 by market trader Maggie McIver as an East End dance hall. Its neon sign and sprung floor later made it one of Britain’s best-loved rock venues.

title: The wife Mackintosh said was three-quarters of his work
place: The Mackintosh House, Hunterian Art Gallery
desc: The National Trust for Scotland’s podcast on artist Margaret Macdonald Mackintosh, wife and collaborator of Charles Rennie Mackintosh. The Hunterian Art Gallery at the University of Glasgow has rebuilt the interiors of the couple’s home.

title: The art school that burned twice
place: Glasgow School of Art, Mackintosh Building
desc: Cultural historian Robyne Calvert on architect Charles Rennie Mackintosh and his Glasgow School of Art on Renfrew Street, finished in 1909 and gutted by fires in 2014 and 2018.

title: Tanks in the city after a riot in the main square
desc: Versus History talks to writer Donny O’Rourke about 31 January 1919, when police charged strikers campaigning for a 40-hour week in George Square, Glasgow’s civic square. The government sent troops, and tanks waited in the cattle market.

title: Shipyard workers refuse to let their yards close
desc: In 1971 the government let Upper Clyde Shipbuilders fail. Led by shop stewards Jimmy Reid and Jimmy Airlie, workers kept building ships instead of striking. One of the yards was Fairfield in Govan, whose 1890s offices still face Govan Road.

title: Art therapy for the most violent men in Scotland’s prisons
desc: In 1973 the Special Unit at Barlinnie Prison, Glasgow’s Victorian jail in Riddrie, began giving violent long-term prisoners art materials and a say in their own regime. Its best-known inmate, gangster Jimmy Boyle, left as a sculptor.

title: Sixty-six fans die on a stairway after a New Year derby
desc: On 2 January 1971, as fans left the Old Firm derby between Glasgow’s two big clubs, Rangers and Celtic, a crush on Stairway 13 at Ibrox Stadium killed 66 people. The disaster led to Britain’s first stadium safety law in 1975.

title: Saint, cathedral, trading port, workshop of the Empire
desc: A one-episode history of Glasgow, which grew up around the medieval cathedral of St Mungo, the city’s patron saint, and became a transatlantic trading port and then one of the world’s great shipbuilding and engineering cities.

title: Tobacco fortunes and the streets they built
desc: Historian and broadcaster Neil Oliver on Glasgow’s 18th-century tobacco lords, whose wealth came from plantations worked by enslaved people, and on the Merchant City, the quarter of streets and mansions they built east of George Square.

title: Rab C. Nesbitt
creator: Ian Pattison
desc: Writer Ian Pattison’s BBC Scotland sitcom about Rab C. Nesbitt, an unemployed street philosopher in a string vest, played by Gregor Fisher, and his family in Govan, the old shipbuilding district on the south bank of the Clyde.

title: Still Game
creator: Ford Kiernan and Greg Hemphill
desc: Ford Kiernan and Greg Hemphill’s sitcom about two pensioners, Jack and Victor, in a tower block in a fictional Glasgow scheme. It ran on and off until 2019. Live stage versions sold out the Hydro, the big arena by the Clyde, for weeks.

title: Taggart
creator: Glenn Chandler
desc: Writer Glenn Chandler’s Glasgow murder series ran for 27 years, set around Maryhill police station. “There’s been a murder” became a catchphrase. The Glasgow Necropolis, the Victorian hilltop cemetery behind the cathedral, was a favourite location.

title: Tea and Taste: The Glasgow Tea Rooms 1875–1975
place: Willow Tea Rooms building, Sauchiehall Street
creator: Perilla Kinchin
desc: Design historian Perilla Kinchin on how Glasgow, a city of temperance campaigners, built a tea-room culture. Businesswoman Kate Cranston hired Mackintosh to design the Willow Tea Rooms on Sauchiehall Street in 1903. You can still have tea there.

title: It Wisnae Us: The Truth About Glasgow and Slavery
place: Gallery of Modern Art, Royal Exchange Square
creator: Stephen Mullen
desc: Historian Stephen Mullen’s short guide to how Atlantic slavery paid for the city centre. Tobacco lord William Cunninghame built a mansion in 1778 off Queen Street. It is now the Gallery of Modern Art. The title is Scots for “it wasn’t us.”

title: The Beatles, Docks and Rock ’n’ Roll: Liverpool’s Musical Heritage
desc: From the Albert Dock along the waterfront to the Cavern Club on Mathew Street, mixing Beatles history with the story of the port that shaped the city.

title: Hidden Histories: Liverpool’s Links to the Transatlantic Slave Trade
desc: A walk through the buildings and street names of central Liverpool that still carry the city’s ties to the transatlantic slave trade, which made its 18th-century fortune.

title: The cathedral that would have outdomed St Peter’s
desc: Architect Edwin Lutyens designed a Catholic cathedral for Liverpool with a dome larger than St Peter’s in Rome. Work began in 1933 and halted with the war; only the brick and granite crypt was built, and the 1967 cathedral now sits on top of it.

title: Victorian painters who rejected the art academy
desc: National Museums Liverpool introduces the Pre-Raphaelites, the Victorian painters around Dante Gabriel Rossetti, John Everett Millais and William Holman Hunt. The Walker Art Gallery on William Brown Street has one of the major collections of their work.

title: A temple for concerts and courts opposite Lime Street
desc: Historian Steve Binns on St George’s Hall, the neoclassical concert hall and law courts of 1854 opposite Lime Street station. Its young architect, Harvey Lonsdale Elmes, died before it was finished; its floor of some 30,000 Minton tiles is usually covered.

title: An electric railway on stilts along the docks
desc: Rail historian Ruairidh MacVeigh on the Liverpool Overhead Railway, an electric elevated line opened in 1893 above the Dock Road, past docks such as Stanley Dock. Known as the dockers’ umbrella, it closed in 1956 and was pulled down soon after.

title: Everton fans tell their own club’s story
desc: Everton supporters tell the history of their club, founded by a Methodist chapel side in 1878. From 1892 Everton played at Goodison Park in Walton, one of the oldest purpose-built football grounds, before moving to Bramley-Moore Dock in 2025.

title: A swaying wall of singing on the Anfield terrace
desc: A 1974 BBC film on the Kop, the vast standing terrace behind one goal at Anfield, Liverpool FC’s stadium, named after Spion Kop, a Boer War hill. Its crowd swayed and sang as one. The terrace became all-seated in 1994.

title: Toxteth’s 1981 riots, told from inside the neighbourhood
desc: The 1981 Toxteth riots as seen from L8, the postcode of Liverpool’s long-established Black community. Granby Street, the district’s old shopping street, was at the heart of the area worst affected by the unrest and the neglect that followed.

title: Granada’s current-affairs cameras return to Toxteth
desc: Granada TV’s World in Action returns to Toxteth, the inner-city district where July 1981 saw days of rioting between young people and police after an arrest. Upper Parliament Street, where the Rialto ballroom burned, was at its centre.

title: The Chinese seamen shipped out of Liverpool after the war
place: Chinese seamen memorial plaque, Pier Head
desc: In 1945–46 the British government quietly deported hundreds of Chinese merchant seamen from Liverpool, many leaving wives and children who never learned why. A plaque on the Pier Head waterfront has remembered them since 2006.

title: Europe’s oldest Chinese community, filmed in 1981
desc: Archive footage of Liverpool’s Chinatown, home to Europe’s oldest Chinese community, which grew from seamen of the Blue Funnel shipping line in the late 1800s. Its centre is Nelson Street, now marked by a large ornamental arch built in 2000.

title: Concrete, clock towers and two copper birds
desc: Walter Aubrey Thomas’s Royal Liver Building, finished in 1911 for an insurance society, was among the first big reinforced-concrete buildings. Its two Liver Birds, the city’s mythical emblem, watch over the Pier Head waterfront and the river.

title: Twenty-two-year-old architect, seventy-four years of building
desc: Architect Giles Gilbert Scott won the competition for Liverpool’s Anglican cathedral in 1903, aged 22. Building ran from 1904 to 1978, long after his death, producing Britain’s largest cathedral on a sandstone ridge above the city.

title: A museum on the dock where slaving ships were fitted out
place: International Slavery Museum, Royal Albert Dock
desc: An introduction to the International Slavery Museum, opened in 2007 inside the Merseyside Maritime Museum on the Royal Albert Dock. It covers the transatlantic slave trade, Liverpool’s central part in it, and racism and resistance since.

title: Liverpool’s slave-trade past, read in its streets and stones
desc: Liverpool ships carried well over a million enslaved Africans across the Atlantic. Behind the Town Hall, the merchants’ square of Exchange Flags holds the 1813 Nelson monument, whose four chained captives are often read as an echo of that trade.

title: Thirty years of digging, and no reason given
place: Williamson Tunnels Heritage Centre, Smithdown Lane
desc: Tobacco merchant Joseph Williamson paid men for about 30 years to dig tunnels under his Edge Hill estate and never said why. Jimmy Akin and Dom Bettinelli weigh seven theories. Part of the maze is open at the Williamson Tunnels Heritage Centre.

title: A radical city and its fight with Westminster
desc: Historian David Swift, author of Scouse Republic, on Liverpool’s radical politics and its 1980s decline, when the Labour council, run from the Municipal Buildings on Dale Street, defied Margaret Thatcher’s government over its budget.

title: A church fête, a skiffle band and a boy with a guitar
desc: On 6 July 1957 John Lennon’s skiffle group the Quarrymen played the summer fête at St Peter’s Church in Woolton, a south Liverpool suburb. That afternoon a friend introduced him to 15-year-old Paul McCartney. The Retrospectors tell the story.

title: A seventieth birthday on the Mersey ferry
desc: Liverpool-born politician and novelist Edwina Currie, who turned 70 the same year as BBC Radio 3, marks its birthday with an essay on the ferry across the River Mersey, which sails from the Pier Head terminal.

title: How a port city came to talk Scouse
desc: Linguist Tony Crowley, who grew up in central Liverpool, on Scouse, the city’s accent and dialect, named after lobscouse, a sailors’ stew. Scotland Road, the old Irish working-class district north of the centre, is where much of that mix of voices settled.

title: The women who worked the sugar refinery on Love Lane
place: Tate & Lyle refinery site, Love Lane
desc: Authors Duncan Barrett and Nuala Calvi on The Sugar Girls of Love Lane, their book of stories from women who worked at Tate & Lyle’s sugar refinery on Love Lane, in the dockside Vauxhall district, in the 1960s. The refinery closed in 1981.

title: Britain’s biggest cathedral, raised over an old quarry
desc: Uncharted Liverpool on the Anglican Liverpool Cathedral: why it was built on St James’s Mount, above a former quarry turned cemetery, who designed it, and the odd details inside. Begun in 1904 and finished in 1978, it is Britain’s largest cathedral.

title: A concrete tent under a stained-glass crown
place: Metropolitan Cathedral of Christ the King
desc: Writer David Trigg and Laura Moffatt of Art + Christianity tour the art of the Metropolitan Cathedral of Christ the King, England’s largest Catholic cathedral, a circular 1967 church under John Piper’s glass lantern, with former organist Terry Duffy.

title: The first intercity railway nearly dies in Parliament
desc: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway of 1830 was the first intercity line worked only by steam, yet engineer George Stephenson nearly sank it in Parliament. Its Liverpool end climbed to Edge Hill, where the 1836 station still takes passengers.

title: Wartime sailors deported, families left behind
desc: Thousands of Chinese seamen kept supplies reaching Liverpool in the Second World War. After 1945 the British authorities forced many out, leaving wives and children behind. Many sailed for the Blue Funnel Line, based at India Buildings on Water Street.

title: A Cunard liner torpedoed on its way home to Liverpool
desc: On 7 May 1915 a German U-boat sank the Cunard liner Lusitania off Ireland as it sailed from New York to Liverpool; about 1,200 died. Witness History draws on archive survivor accounts. Cunard’s old headquarters, the Cunard Building, stands at Pier Head.

title: Ninety-seven fans, a cover-up and a city’s long fight for the truth
desc: Lindsay Graham recounts the 1989 FA Cup semi-final crush at Sheffield’s Hillsborough stadium that killed 97 Liverpool fans, and the police smears that followed. Inquests in 2016 found they were unlawfully killed. Their memorial stands at Anfield stadium.

title: Four Liverpool teenagers and the cellar club where it started
desc: Historians Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook on the Beatles, who played the Cavern Club, a cellar club on Mathew Street, close to 300 times in 1961–63. The original cellar was filled in in 1973; today’s club is a rebuilt version a few yards away.

title: How a city remembers the trade that built its wealth
place: International Slavery Museum, Royal Albert Dock
desc: By the late 1700s Liverpool was Britain’s leading slaving port. This episode looks at how the city has come to remember that past, including the International Slavery Museum, opened on the waterfront in 2007 for the bicentenary of abolition.

title: The port that made Liverpool, and the warehouses built not to burn
desc: Historian Dan Snow on Liverpool’s docks, which made it Britain’s great Atlantic port. Their showpiece is the Royal Albert Dock, Jesse Hartley’s 1846 ring of iron, brick and stone warehouses built so that nothing in them could catch fire.

title: The world’s first commercial wet dock, buried under a shopping centre
desc: Thomas Steers’s Old Dock opened in 1715 as the world’s first enclosed commercial wet dock, was filled in during the 1820s and rediscovered in 2001 beneath what is now the Liverpool ONE shopping district. National Museums Liverpool tells its story.

title: Bread
creator: Carla Lane
desc: Writer Carla Lane’s BBC sitcom, 1986–91, about the Boswells, a big Catholic family in the Dingle, a working-class district by the south docks, getting by on the dole and small scams in Thatcher’s Britain, all under their mother Nellie’s rule.

title: Brookside
creator: Phil Redmond
desc: Producer Phil Redmond’s soap opera launched with Channel 4 in 1982 and ran 21 years. It was shot in real houses on a new cul-de-sac in Croxteth Park, a suburban estate, and took on strikes, drugs and unemployment.

title: Boys from the Blackstuff
creator: Alan Bleasdale
desc: Writer Alan Bleasdale’s five-part BBC drama about out-of-work tarmac layers in early-1980s Liverpool. Yosser Hughes’s plea “Gizza job” became a national catchphrase. The Royal Albert Dock, now museums and shops, was derelict when they filmed there.

title: The Heart of Belfast: From Humble Beginnings to Shipbuilding Glory
desc: How a small market town on the Lagan grew into one of the world’s great shipbuilding and linen cities, told through the streets of the centre.

title: Belfast’s Maritime Mile: A Walking Tour from City Center to Titanic
desc: Along the river from the old Custom House to the Titanic Quarter, past the docks, cranes and slipways of the city’s shipbuilding past.

title: Boom, Bloodshed, and Belfast’s Remarkable Comeback: A Walking Tour
place: Crown Liquor Saloon, Great Victoria Street
desc: Belfast from Victorian industrial boomtown through the Troubles to today, via the Crown Bar, City Hall and the Grand Opera House.

title: Belfast’s Peace Walls Walking Tour: From Divis Tower to Bobby Sands
desc: A Troubles-history walk through west Belfast, starting at a 1960s tower block once used as an army lookout, following the tall barrier between Catholic and Protestant streets and ending at the mural of a republican hunger striker.

title: Exploring Belfast’s Titanic Quarter
desc: A maritime-heritage walk through the old shipyard district, starting at the marina in Abercorn Basin and passing the restored lighthouse lens known as the Great Light on the way into the land where the Titanic was built.

title: Inside the white parliament on the hill
desc: The Northern Ireland Assembly’s own tour of Parliament Buildings at Stormont, the Portland stone parliament opened in 1932 at the top of a mile-long avenue in east Belfast, now home to the devolved Northern Ireland Assembly.

title: The house of endless books where Narnia began
desc: Lewis scholar Jason Lepojärvi reads from C. S. Lewis’s memoir Surprised by Joy at Little Lea, the east Belfast house the family moved into in 1905, whose rooms of books and attic games fed the boy who later wrote Narnia.

title: Snugs, tiles and gaslight in a Victorian pub
place: Crown Liquor Saloon, Great Victoria Street
desc: Document Belfast looks round the Crown Liquor Saloon, a Victorian gin palace on Great Victoria Street with stained glass, mosaic tiles and carved wooden snugs, owned by the National Trust and still a working pub.

title: The narrow lanes of the old town
desc: Local history channel Document Belfast walks the entries, the narrow alleys running off High Street in the old town, such as Pottinger’s Entry and Winecellar Entry, home to some of the city’s oldest pubs.

title: A night at the most bombed hotel, 1973
desc: BBC Nationwide spends a night in 1973 at the Europa Hotel on Great Victoria Street, opened in 1971 and bombed again and again during the Troubles, the 30-year conflict over Northern Ireland. It was home to the visiting press corps.

title: Families on the decks of Divis Flats, 1980
desc: A 1980 report from the BBC’s Nationwide magazine show hears from tenants of Divis Flats, the damp, overcrowded 1960s deck-access estate in west Belfast. All but Divis Tower was demolished in the 1990s.

title: A wall between neighbours on Cupar Way
desc: A short documentary on one of Belfast’s peace walls, the barriers built between Catholic and Protestant streets during the Troubles. The tallest, on Cupar Way between the Shankill and the Falls, is covered in messages from visitors.

title: Orange sashes and bowler hats on parade
desc: Rick Steves watches an Orange Order parade, the Protestant fraternity’s marches with bands and banners that peak on the Twelfth of July, marking William of Orange’s 1690 victory. Belfast’s main parade passes City Hall.

title: A black cab ride past the Falls Road murals
desc: Travel writer Rick Steves rides a black taxi up the Falls Road, the main street of Catholic, nationalist west Belfast, past political murals and memorials to the Troubles, the 30-year conflict over Northern Ireland’s status.

title: A boss rigger remembers forty years at Harland & Wolff
desc: George McAllister, a rigger at Harland & Wolff from 1948 to 1992, recalls shipyard work in its later decades, the era when the yard put up Samson and Goliath, the yellow gantry cranes that still dominate the Belfast skyline.

title: The firm behind the shipyard’s drawing offices
desc: A history of Harland & Wolff, founded in 1861 by Edward Harland and Gustav Wolff and once the world’s largest shipyard. Titanic was designed in its headquarters drawing offices, now the Titanic Hotel.

title: A Belfast boy grows up to define absolute zero
place: Lord Kelvin’s birthplace, College Square East
desc: William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, was born on College Square East in 1824 and went on to set the absolute temperature scale and help lay the first working transatlantic telegraph cable. A plaque marks the house; his statue stands in Botanic Gardens.

title: Van Morrison’s east Belfast, street by street
desc: In the opening segment of Rick Steves’ radio show, a Belfast guide points out the places that shaped singer Van Morrison, born in 1945 at 125 Hyndford Street in east Belfast, and the streets and parks he named in his songs.

title: A heart doctor puts a defibrillator in an ambulance
desc: In 1966 cardiologist Frank Pantridge of Belfast’s Royal Victoria Hospital launched the world’s first mobile coronary care unit, an ambulance carrying a portable defibrillator run off car batteries. BBC Witness History tells how it started.

title: Shipyard workers win a cup in Vienna
desc: Just before the First World War, a Glentoran FC side of industrial workers from Ballymacarrett, the terraced district by the shipyards, travelled to Vienna and won its cup. Sam Robinson tells the story. Glentoran still plays at The Oval stadium.

title: An orphan from Belfast becomes a society painter
desc: Painter Sir John Lavery, born in Belfast in 1856 and orphaned young, became a leading portraitist of his day, painting Churchill and Michael Collins. He was baptised in St Patrick’s Church on Donegall Street, which holds a triptych he gave it.

title: A city library older than the city hall
place: Linen Hall Library, Donegall Square North
desc: Julie Andrews, director of the Linen Hall Library, talks about Belfast’s oldest cultural institution, founded in 1788 and now in a Victorian linen warehouse facing City Hall. Its first librarian was United Irishman Thomas Russell.

title: Cups of Armada gold come ashore in a museum
desc: Historian Suzannah Lipscomb and Michael B. Barry on the Spanish Armada ships wrecked on Ireland’s coast in 1588. Gold and jewels raised from one of them, the Girona, lost off the Antrim coast, are shown at the Ulster Museum.

title: Belfast radicals start a republican movement
desc: Melvyn Bragg’s In Our Time on the 1798 rising led by the United Irishmen, a society founded by Belfast Presbyterian radicals in 1791. Henry Joy McCracken, hanged in the city that July, is remembered in Clifton Street Cemetery.

title: The man at the door of Europe’s most-bombed hotel
desc: Martin Mulholland, longtime head concierge of the Europa Hotel on Great Victoria Street, talks about decades at a hotel bombed some 30 times in the Troubles, where journalists, presidents and celebrities have stayed.

title: A deal is struck on Good Friday 1998
desc: After all-night talks at Castle Buildings on the Stormont estate, most of Northern Ireland’s parties and the British and Irish governments approved the Good Friday Agreement on 10 April 1998, the deal that largely ended the Troubles.

title: Women talk their way into the peace negotiations
desc: Academic Monica McWilliams co-founded the Northern Ireland Women’s Coalition in 1996, won seats at the peace talks and helped write the 1998 agreement. She went on to sit in the Assembly at Parliament Buildings on the Stormont estate.

title: A Nobel poet’s Belfast years at Queen’s
desc: Comedian Frank Skinner reads and talks through poems by Seamus Heaney, who studied English at Queen’s University Belfast in the 1950s, taught there and joined the Belfast Group of writers before moving south in 1972.

title: A gunman attacks mourners at an IRA funeral
desc: In March 1988, loyalist Michael Stone threw grenades and fired into the crowd at the funeral of three IRA members in Milltown Cemetery on the Falls Road, killing three. BBC Witness History hears from people who were there.

title: A record-shop owner gives Belfast punk somewhere to go
place: Good Vibrations record shop, Great Victoria Street
desc: Terri Hooley opened the Good Vibrations record shop and label in 1976 and released the Undertones’ “Teenage Kicks.” Music writer Stuart Bailie talks about Hooley’s life, and the punk scene that crossed sectarian lines at the height of the Troubles.

title: Twenty IRA bombs go off in an afternoon
desc: On 21 July 1972, during the Troubles (the 30-year conflict over Northern Ireland’s status), the IRA set off about 20 bombs across Belfast in 75 minutes, killing nine. The Belfast Telegraph’s podcast revisits the day and the Oxford Street bus station blast.

title: Walls built as a stopgap in 1969 are still standing
desc: Belfast’s “peace lines” are barriers between Catholic and Protestant streets, first put up after rioting burned Bombay Street in 1969. Roman Mars’s design show 99% Invisible asks why there are more of them now than in 1998.

title: German bombers find a city with almost no shelters
desc: German raids in April and May 1941 killed about 1,000 people in Belfast; the Easter Tuesday raid alone was the deadliest night outside London. Historian Dan Snow covers the attacks, which hit north Belfast’s terraces and mills around York Street.
