title: Victorian Belfast laid out for the dead, divided underground
desc: Tom Hartley, a former Lord Mayor and author of a history of Belfast City Cemetery on the Falls Road, walks its graves of linen barons, shipbuilders and the poor, and the sunken wall said to separate Catholic and Protestant plots.

title: A Catholic family is murdered in their home in 1922
desc: In March 1922, amid the violence that followed Ireland’s partition, gunmen broke into publican Owen McMahon’s house on Kinnaird Terrace off the Antrim Road and killed six men. Historian Edward Burke examines who was behind it.

title: Unionist leaders gather at a mansion to defy Home Rule
desc: Craigavon House in east Belfast, home of unionist leader James Craig, was where Edward Carson rallied crowds against Irish Home Rule in 1911 and where loyalist volunteers drilled. Carol Walker of the Somme Association tells its story.

title: The biggest ship in the world takes shape on the Lagan
desc: Historians Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook begin their series on the Titanic, built from 1909 to 1911 at Harland & Wolff shipyard. Its slipway on Queen’s Island now lies beside the Titanic Belfast museum.

title: A German-born linen baron is hounded out of the city he served
desc: Sir Otto Jaffe, a German-Jewish linen merchant, was twice Lord Mayor of Belfast and built its synagogue, yet anti-German feeling in the First World War drove him out. His family’s memorial fountain now stands in Victoria Square.

title: One of the old town’s first streets, end to end
desc: The Historical Belfast podcast explores North Street, one of the old town’s original thoroughfares, running from the city centre past the Cathedral Quarter, the arts and nightlife district around St Anne’s Cathedral.

title: C.E.A.R.T.A.
place: Cultúrlann McAdam Ó Fiaich, Falls Road
creator: Kneecap
desc: The title means “rights.” West Belfast rap trio Kneecap rhyme in Irish and English about a member refusing to speak English to police. Their Irish-language scene centres on Cultúrlann, an arts centre on the Falls Road.

title: My Lagan Love
creator: Kate Bush
desc: Belfast poet Joseph Campbell wrote the words and Belfast-born composer Herbert Hughes published the air in 1904, a lament for a girl by the River Lagan. Kate Bush recorded it in 1989; the river meets the city at Lagan Weir.

title: The Fall
creator: Allan Cubitt
desc: BBC crime series with Gillian Anderson as a London detective hunting a serial killer (Jamie Dornan) who poses as a family man. A rare Belfast story not about the Troubles. Much of it plays out in the well-off south of the city around Malone Road.

title: Say Nothing
creator: Patrick Radden Keefe
desc: Journalist Patrick Radden Keefe on Jean McConville, a widowed mother of ten taken from her flat by the IRA in 1972 and killed. Her body was found in 2003. Divis Tower is the last surviving block of the Divis Flats estate where she lived.

title: Surprised by Joy
place: C. S. Lewis Square, East Belfast
creator: C. S. Lewis
desc: Novelist C. S. Lewis on his early life, starting in a big, book-crammed house in East Belfast where he and his brother invented imaginary worlds. C. S. Lewis Square, a plaza nearby, has bronze figures from the Narnia books.

title: From Stalin to Skyscrapers: A Walk Around Warsaw’s Palace of Culture
desc: An architecture and politics walk around the Soviet-built tower Stalin gave the city in 1955, crossing the vast parade ground at its foot and ending among the glass office towers that have grown up around it since communism fell.

title: Wilanów Palace: Legacy of King Jan III Sobieski
desc: A royal history tour of the baroque summer palace built by King Jan III Sobieski, who broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna, telling the story of his 1683 victory at the palace on the city’s southern edge.

title: Łazienki Park: Legacy of the Last King
desc: A walk through the royal bathhouse park laid out by Poland’s last king, Stanisław August Poniatowski, taking in the story of the warrior king who beat the Ottomans at Vienna, and the monument to the composer Chopin.

title: Warsaw at War: 1939-1945
desc: A Second World War history of Warsaw from the German invasion of 1939 to the city’s destruction in 1945, passing the musical benches that play the composer Chopin’s works.

title: Krakowskie Przedmieście: The fascinating story of the street
desc: A history of the city’s grandest street, starting at the main entrance of the royal castle and heading south past the statue of the national poet and the old palace that now houses the university, along the old road to Kraków.

title: A Miracle from the Rubble: Warsaw Old Town Walking Tour
desc: A history of the Old Town’s destruction in 1944 and its rebuilding, past the reconstructed royal castle, the Jesuit church and cathedral, the main market square and the city’s brick defensive gate, ending at a lookout over the Vistula river.

title: The ghetto, told by the museum that will house its story
place: Warsaw Ghetto Museum, former Bersohn and Bauman Children’s Hospital
desc: The Warsaw Ghetto Museum’s account of the ghetto, sealed in November 1940, where some 400,000 Jews were confined. The museum is moving into the Bersohn and Bauman Children’s Hospital on Sienna Street, one of the few ghetto buildings left.

title: A café where Warsaw’s poets held court
place: Site of Mała Ziemiańska café, Mazowiecka Street
desc: POLIN, the museum of Polish Jewish history, visits the site of Mała Ziemiańska, the interwar café on Mazowiecka Street where poets such as Julian Tuwim and Antoni Słonimski held court. It was destroyed in 1944.

title: The 1920 battle Poles call a miracle
desc: The History Guy, an American history channel, on the Battle of Warsaw in August 1920, when Polish forces stopped the Red Army near the capital: the ‘Miracle on the Vistula’. Józef Piłsudski, Poland’s head of state, then lived in Belweder Palace.

title: Socialist realism on Constitution Square
desc: Radosław Gajda explains MDM, the Marszałkowska Residential District built in 1950–52 in socialist realism, the Soviet-imposed official style. Its showpiece, Constitution Square, has arcades, giant lamp standards and reliefs of model workers.

title: The last king’s bathhouse palace
place: Palace on the Isle, Łazienki Park
desc: TVP World’s ‘Pulse of Culture’ tours Royal Łazienki, the park of Poland’s last king, Stanisław August Poniatowski. Łazienki means ‘baths’: its Palace on the Isle began as a bathhouse that he turned into a summer palace in the 1780s.

title: Old shop signs saved from the scrapheap
desc: TVP World, Poland’s English-language public broadcaster, talks to David Hill, co-founder of the Neon Muzeum, which rescues cold-war neon signs from Warsaw’s shops and cafés. It fills a former factory hall in the Soho Factory complex in Praga.

title: The tower Stalin gave Warsaw
desc: Megaprojects, an engineering history channel, on the Palace of Culture and Science, Stalin’s ‘gift’ built by Soviet workers in 1952–55. At 237 metres with its spire it was long Poland’s tallest building, and many Varsovians still resent it.

title: Daffodils for the ghetto fighters, eighty years on
desc: In April 1943 Jewish fighters in the Warsaw Ghetto, the walled district where the Nazis confined the city’s Jews, rose against deportation to Treblinka. BBC News reports on the 2023 commemoration at the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes in Muranów.

title: Chopin, and the national spirit
desc: Rick Steves on two Polish passions, vodka and the composer Fryderyk Chopin, who grew up in Warsaw and left for Paris in 1830. The Chopin Museum in the Ostrogski Palace holds his last piano and manuscripts.

title: Monuments to the fighters of 1944
desc: Rick Steves looks at how Warsaw remembers its dead and rebuilt its streets. The Warsaw Uprising Monument on Krasiński Square, unveiled in 1989, shows insurgents climbing down into the sewers they used to move between districts.

title: A city that put its own centre back together
desc: American travel writer Rick Steves on how Warsaw, about 85 per cent destroyed by 1945, rebuilt itself. Castle Square, with King Sigismund III’s column and the reconstructed Royal Castle, is where the rebuilt Old Town begins.

title: Teenage scouts in the 1944 Uprising
desc: A former scout recalls the Warsaw Uprising of 1944, the Home Army’s revolt against German occupation, in which boys and girls ran messages, mail and ammunition. The Little Insurgent statue on Podwale Street honours the child fighters.

title: The plane crash that killed a president
desc: In April 2010 a plane carrying President Lech Kaczyński and 95 others crashed near Smolensk in Russia, on the way to a Katyn massacre commemoration. Radosław Sikorski, then foreign minister, recalls the day. A memorial stands on Piłsudski Square.

title: Students against the censors, March 1968
desc: After the authorities banned a staging of Adam Mickiewicz’s play ‘Forefathers’ Eve’, University of Warsaw students rallied for free speech in March 1968 and were beaten by police. Their protests began at the university’s gate on Krakowskie Przedmieście.

title: A ghetto fighter who led survivors out through the sewers
desc: Simha ‘Kazik’ Rotem, who guided fighters out through the sewers as the Germans crushed the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, tells his story. The mound at Miła 18 marks the bunker where the uprising’s commander, Mordechai Anielewicz, died.

title: Smuggling children out of the ghetto
desc: Irena Sendler, a Catholic social worker, used her pass into the Warsaw ghetto to smuggle out Jewish children for Żegota, the underground aid council, and buried their names in jars. A stretch of the ghetto wall survives in a courtyard off Sienna Street.

title: The Rolling Stones play behind the Iron Curtain
place: Congress Hall, Palace of Culture and Science
desc: Culture.pl’s podcast on the Rolling Stones’ April 1967 concert in Warsaw, one of the first by a Western rock band in the Soviet bloc. Fans without tickets clashed with police outside the Congress Hall, the venue inside Stalin’s Palace of Culture.

title: A republic that elected its kings
desc: Melvyn Bragg and guests on the union of Poland and Lithuania, formalised in 1569, whose nobles elected their kings. One of them, Jan III Sobieski, victor over the Ottomans at Vienna in 1683, built Wilanów Palace as his summer residence.

title: Warsaw’s turning points, with a historian of its ruin
desc: Travel journalist Paul Bloomfield talks to historian Alexandra Richie, author of a history of the 1944 Uprising, on the turning points of Warsaw’s past. The Barbican, a 16th-century gate tower rebuilt after 1945, guards the Old Town’s north side.

title: Moscow signs up its satellites in a Warsaw palace
desc: On 14 May 1955 the Soviet Union and seven Eastern Bloc states signed a military alliance in Warsaw, a reply to West Germany joining NATO. The BBC’s Witness History hears the story; the treaty was signed in what is now the Presidential Palace.

title: Civilians killed street by street in the Uprising’s first week
desc: In early August 1944, days into the Warsaw Uprising, German and collaborating units shot tens of thousands of civilians in the western district of Wola. History Hit’s Warfare show covers the massacre; a memorial now stands on Leszno Street.

title: Sixty-three days of fighting for a city the Red Army watched
desc: On 1 August 1944 the Home Army, Poland’s underground resistance, rose against the German occupiers and held out for 63 days while Soviet forces halted across the Vistula. The Warsaw Rising Museum, in an old tram power station in Wola, tells the story.

title: A city besieged for three weeks in September 1939
desc: Historians Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook on the German siege of Warsaw in 1939, when shelling and bombing set the Royal Castle on Castle Square ablaze, and the city’s surrender on 28 September after nearly three weeks of resistance.

title: A girl from Freta Street becomes the first woman to win a Nobel
desc: Maria Skłodowska was born in 1867 on Freta Street in the New Town, studied at Warsaw’s illegal ‘Flying University’ and left for Paris, where she discovered polonium and radium. Her birthplace is now a small museum to her life.

title: Rebuilding the Old Town from 18th-century paintings
desc: German forces levelled Warsaw’s Old Town after the 1944 Uprising. 99% Invisible, Roman Mars’s design show, tells how it was rebuilt from the 1940s using 18th-century views of the city by the painter Bernardo Bellotto, known as Canaletto.

title: Patointeligencja
place: Stefan Batory High School, Myśliwiecka street
creator: Mata
desc: The title is slang for “pathological intelligentsia”: Mata, a 19-year-old pupil at the elite Stefan Batory High School, rapped about rich Warsaw teenagers’ drugs and boredom. The song set off a national row and topped the Polish charts.

title: Następna stacja
creator: Taco Hemingway
desc: “Next Station,” from Warsaw rapper Taco Hemingway’s EP Umowa o dzieło, borrows the metro announcer’s phrase for a ride across a city of hustle and fatigue. Świętokrzyska is the downtown station where the two Warsaw metro lines meet.

title: Dekalog
creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
desc: Krzysztof Kieślowski’s ten one-hour films, each loosely on one of the Ten Commandments, about people in a single grey 1980s housing estate. Shot on the Stawki estate on the edge of Muranów, built over the ruins of the ghetto.

title: 4 Alternative Street
creator: Stanisław Bareja
desc: Stanisław Bareja’s TV satire, originally Alternatywy 4: a petty building caretaker bullies the tenants of a new tower block. Censors held it back until 1986. It was shot in the big concrete estates of Ursynów, in south Warsaw. Nine episodes.

title: The Pianist
creator: Władysław Szpilman
desc: Pianist Władysław Szpilman’s plain account of surviving the ghetto, then hiding alone in the ruined city, helped at the end by a German officer. Published in 1946, it was reissued only in 1998. A piece of the ghetto wall survives on Sienna Street.

title: The Zookeeper’s Wife
creator: Diane Ackerman
desc: Antonina Żabińska and her husband Jan, director of Warsaw Zoo, hid about 300 Jews in empty cages and their own house during the German occupation. Their villa inside the zoo in Praga, across the Vistula river, is open to visitors.

title: Milan Fashion Tour: A Guide to Quadrilatero della Moda with Context
desc: A walk through the Quadrilatero della Moda, the block of streets where Milan’s fashion houses keep their flagship shops, and how the city became a fashion capital.

title: The Mysteries of Milan: From the Duomo to the Royal Palace
desc: Legends and odd details around the cathedral square, from the Duomo’s spires to the Royal Palace next door.

title: Milan Walking Tour • Duomo and La Scala Secrets with Brera District
desc: From La Scala opera house to the cobbled lanes and galleries of Brera, the old artists’ quarter, with stories of the people who lived and worked there.

title: A tower shaped like a castle keep rises from bomb damage
desc: Torre Velasca, the BBPR studio’s 1958 office and apartment tower, its upper floors jutting out like a medieval castle keep, rose on a bomb-damaged site. Architectural Record, the US architecture magazine, tells its postwar story.

title: A glass-roofed arcade between cathedral and opera
desc: Art historian Rocky Ruggiero on the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, the iron-and-glass shopping arcade built from 1865 to 1877 to link the Duomo square with La Scala, named after Italy’s first king.

title: A duke’s daughter grows up at the Sforza court
desc: Extra History’s animated series on Caterina Sforza, daughter of Galeazzo Maria Sforza, Duke of Milan, starts with her childhood at the ducal court, which lived in the Castello Sforzesco, before marriage took her to Romagna.

title: Two rival clubs, one ageing stadium
desc: San Siro, officially the Stadio Giuseppe Meazza, opened in 1926 and is shared by AC Milan and Inter. BBC Sport looks at the clubs’ plans to replace the stadium and what the city stands to lose.

title: Two apartment towers planted with trees
desc: Architect Stefano Boeri’s Bosco Verticale, two Porta Nuova apartment towers planted with hundreds of trees and finished in 2014. The B1M, a construction channel, asks whether the greenery makes up for the extra concrete and steel needed to carry it.

title: A world’s fair about feeding the planet
desc: Milan hosted the 2015 World Expo, themed “Feeding the Planet, Energy for Life”, on a new site at Rho on the city’s northwest edge. DW’s lifestyle show Euromaxx tours the national pavilions; the grounds are now the MIND science district.

title: Domed concrete igloo homes from the postwar housing crisis
desc: In 1946 engineer Mario Cavallè built a small estate of domed concrete houses in the Maggiolina neighbourhood as quick postwar housing. The Tim Traveller visits the survivors, on and around Via Lepanto, still lived in today.

title: The city’s uprising against Austria, told in a quiet museum
desc: The Risorgimento was the 19th-century drive to unify Italy, and Milan’s Five Days revolt against Austrian rule in March 1848 was a turning point. Rick Steves visits the Risorgimento Museum in Palazzo Moriggia, a mansion in Brera.

title: Glass towers and tree-covered flats on old railway land
desc: Rick Steves visits Porta Nuova, a business district built on former rail yards in the 2010s, with the spired UniCredit Tower above Piazza Gae Aulenti square and Stefano Boeri’s planted apartment towers, the Bosco Verticale (Vertical Forest).

title: A marble middle finger faces the stock exchange
place: Piazza Affari, outside the stock exchange
desc: Artist Maurizio Cattelan’s marble hand, L.O.V.E., with every finger cut off but the middle one, has stood since 2010 in Piazza Affari square, facing the 1930s stock exchange. Rick Steves considers who it is meant for.

title: Walking among the spires on the cathedral roof
desc: Rick Steves climbs onto the marble roof terraces of the Duomo, Milan’s Gothic cathedral, begun in 1386 and worked on for nearly six centuries, where visitors walk among its forest of spires and statues.

title: Painters in love with speed, machines and the modern city
place: Museo del Novecento, Piazza del Duomo
desc: Poet Filippo Tommaso Marinetti launched Futurism in 1909, and its painters, led by Umberto Boccioni, worked in Milan, celebrating speed, machines and war. The Museo del Novecento, the 20th-century art museum on Piazza del Duomo, holds key works.

title: Venetian merchants search Alexandria’s tombs for a saint
desc: Jacopo Tintoretto painted the Finding of the Body of Saint Mark in the 1560s for a Venetian confraternity, with men pulling corpses from tombs in Alexandria down a deep vaulted hall. It now hangs in Milan’s Pinacoteca di Brera gallery.

title: A duke kneels in armour under a hanging ostrich egg
desc: Piero della Francesca’s altarpiece shows Federico da Montefeltro, Duke of Urbino, kneeling in armour before the Virgin, an ostrich egg hanging from the shell-shaped apse. It came from Urbino to the Pinacoteca di Brera gallery in 1811.

title: A young Raphael reworks his teacher’s wedding scene
desc: Raphael was about 21 when he painted the Marriage of the Virgin in 1504 for a church in Città di Castello, reworking a design by his teacher Perugino. It entered the Pinacoteca di Brera art gallery in 1806.

title: A dead Christ seen feet-first
desc: Andrea Mantegna’s Lamentation over the Dead Christ, around 1483, shows the body from the feet in steep foreshortening, mourners squeezed at the edge. It hangs in the Pinacoteca di Brera, the gallery in a former Jesuit college.

title: A Last Supper painted on a monks’ dining-room wall
desc: Leonardo painted the Last Supper around 1495–98 in the refectory of the Dominican convent at Santa Maria delle Grazie church. His experimental paint mix began flaking within his lifetime; Smarthistory looks at what survives.

title: Leonardo applies for a job and barely mentions painting
desc: Around 1482 Leonardo da Vinci wrote to Ludovico Sforza, ruler of Milan, offering bridges, cannon and siege engines, with painting near the end. The draft survives in the Codex Atlanticus, kept at the Biblioteca Ambrosiana library.

title: A bishop’s fourth-century church, rebuilt in Romanesque brick
desc: Ambrose, bishop of Milan, founded this basilica in the 380s and lies in its crypt. Smarthistory looks at the Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio, whose brick Romanesque church and arcaded forecourt date mostly from the 11th and 12th centuries.

title: Why the furniture world descends on Milan each April
desc: Editors at the architecture and design magazine Dezeen explain why Milan design week matters: the Salone del Mobile furniture fair at the Fiera Milano grounds in Rho, plus hundreds of satellite shows around the city known as the Fuorisalone.

title: A poet’s canal and the writers around it
place: Alda Merini’s home, Naviglio Grande canal
desc: A literary walk along the Navigli, Milan’s old canals, starting with poet Alda Merini, who lived for decades on the Ripa di Porta Ticinese beside the Naviglio Grande and wrote about the asylum where she spent years.

title: A fashion editor invents the concept store
desc: Carla Sozzani, former fashion magazine editor, tells how she opened 10 Corso Como in 1990, a gallery, bookshop, boutique and café around a courtyard that is often called the first concept store.

title: A fake apse less than a metre deep
place: Santa Maria presso San Satiro church
desc: Two Renaissance architects in Milan: Filarete, designer of the Ospedale Maggiore hospital, and Donato Bramante. At Santa Maria presso San Satiro church, Bramante painted and modelled a deep choir behind the altar into a wall less than a metre deep.

title: An architect’s flats for a couple of collectors
place: Casa Museo Boschi Di Stefano, Via Jan
desc: Architect Piero Portaluppi shaped interwar Milan. This episode visits his buildings that are open to the public, among them the Casa Museo Boschi Di Stefano, a couple’s flat hung floor to ceiling with 20th-century Italian art.

title: Art nouveau, Milan style, around Porta Venezia
desc: Listen To MI, a podcast from Milan’s house museums, looks at Liberty, the Italian art nouveau of about 1900, in the Porta Venezia district. The style’s best-known building there is Giuseppe Sommaruga’s Palazzo Castiglioni on Corso Venezia.

title: Sculpted family tombs in the city of the dead
desc: History Goes Bump, a podcast on haunted history, tours the Cimitero Monumentale, opened in 1866 and filled with sculpted tombs of Milan’s industrial families. Novelist Alessandro Manzoni is buried in its Famedio, a hall of fame by the main gate.

title: The Argentine coach who taught Inter to defend
desc: Football writers Jonathan Wilson and Rob Draper on Helenio Herrera, the Argentine coach whose Inter won the European Cup in 1964 and 1965 with catenaccio, a defence-first system. Inter play at San Siro stadium, which they share with AC Milan.

title: A fashion heir is shot on his office steps
desc: On 27 March 1995 Maurizio Gucci, former head of the fashion house, was shot dead outside his office on Via Palestro. Rachel Naylor talks to Carmine Gallo, the detective who tied the killing to his ex-wife Patrizia Reggiani and her clairvoyant.

title: Saffron, a prank and a yellow wedding rice
desc: Sauced traces risotto alla milanese, Milan’s saffron rice, from saffron fraud in medieval Nuremberg to the story of a glassmaker’s apprentice on the Duomo cathedral’s windows who, legend says, tinted a 1574 wedding risotto yellow as a joke.

title: Forty minutes in front of the Last Supper
place: Last Supper refectory, Santa Maria delle Grazie
desc: Hosts Phil and Laura take apart Leonardo da Vinci’s Last Supper, painted in the 1490s on the dining-hall wall of the Santa Maria delle Grazie convent in an experimental oil-and-tempera technique that began flaking within decades.

title: An opera house named after the church it replaced
desc: Holly Frey and Tracy V. Wilson’s 2014 episode on the Teatro alla Scala, opened in 1778 on the site of the demolished church of Santa Maria alla Scala. Verdi’s Otello and Puccini’s Madama Butterfly both premiered at the opera house.

title: Leonardo paints a castle hall into a forest
desc: Leonardo da Vinci spent most of his early career serving Ludovico Sforza, “il Moro,” regent and then Duke of Milan. In the Castello Sforzesco, the ducal castle, he painted the Sala delle Asse as an arbour of interlaced mulberry branches.

title: A mercenary becomes duke and builds a hospital for the poor
place: Ca’ Granda, the former Ospedale Maggiore
desc: Mark Rasmussen follows Francesco Sforza, the mercenary captain who became Duke of Milan in 1450, and his dissolute son Galeazzo Maria. Francesco founded the Ospedale Maggiore, the vast hospital now called Ca’ Granda and used by the University of Milan.

title: A family of lords tightens its grip on the city
desc: When Azzone Visconti died in 1339, his uncles Luchino and Giovanni took over Milan and kept expanding it, ending the old self-governing commune. Azzone’s marble tomb is in San Gottardo in Corte, the church of his palace behind the Royal Palace.

title: Milan’s bishop bargains with a usurper
desc: Mike Duncan’s The History of Rome reaches 383, when Milan was an imperial capital and its new bishop, Ambrose, helped negotiate a power-sharing deal with the rebel general Magnus Maximus. Ambrose lies in the crypt of the Basilica of Sant’Ambrogio.

title: Young Fascists dig up Mussolini’s body and hide it for months
desc: Mussolini was buried in an unmarked grave in Milan’s Cimitero Maggiore cemetery. In April 1946 neo-Fascist Domenico Leccisi and friends dug him up and hid the body; it was recovered and later reburied in his home town, Predappio.

title: A blacksmith’s son founds Fascism in a Milan hall
desc: Paul McGann narrates the rise of Benito Mussolini, the socialist editor turned dictator. In March 1919 he founded the Fasci di Combattimento, the first Fascist movement, at a meeting in a hall on Piazza San Sepolcro, a small square near the Duomo.

title: Cara Italia
creator: Ghali
desc: Ghali Amdouni, son of Tunisian parents, grew up in Baggio on Milan’s western outskirts. “Dear Italy” is a love letter to the country that questions who counts as Italian, from a rapper born and raised in Milan.

title: Tran Tran
creator: Sfera Ebbasta
desc: Sfera Ebbasta, real name Gionata Boschetti, comes from Cinisello Balsamo, a commuter town just north of Milan, and built Italian trap there with producer Charlie Charles. The title is slang for the daily grind; the town square is Piazza Gramsci.

creator: Giuseppe Gagliardi
desc: Sky series created by actor Stefano Accorsi, set during Mani Pulite (“clean hands”), the 1992 bribery inquiry by Milan magistrates that brought down Italy’s main parties. The investigators worked from the city’s Palace of Justice.

title: Italian Ways: On and Off the Rails from Milan to Palermo
creator: Tim Parks
desc: English novelist Tim Parks, who has taught in Milan for years, reads Italy through its trains: ticket rules, commuters, strikes and the new fast lines. Much of it starts at Milano Centrale, the vast stone station finished under Mussolini in 1931.

title: Poem Strip
place: Corriere della Sera offices, Via Solferino
creator: Dino Buzzati
desc: Novelist Dino Buzzati retold the Orpheus myth as a comic book set in 1960s Milan: a pop singer follows his dead lover through a door in a city street into the afterlife. Buzzati spent his working life at the Corriere della Sera newspaper on Via Solferino.

title: The Body of Il Duce
creator: Sergio Luzzatto
desc: Historian Sergio Luzzatto follows Benito Mussolini’s corpse after partisans shot him in April 1945. It was hung upside down from a petrol station roof on Piazzale Loreto, now a busy traffic square, then buried, stolen and fought over for years.

title: Calcio: A History of Italian Football
creator: John Foot
desc: Historian John Foot on Italian football: the clubs, the fans, the scandals and the money. Milan has two of the biggest clubs, AC Milan and Inter. They share one ground, the San Siro stadium, which opened in 1926 and holds about 75,000.

title: The Betrothed
place: Casa del Manzoni museum, Via Morone
creator: Alessandro Manzoni
desc: Italy’s great 19th-century novel: two village lovers kept apart by a local lord, with bread riots and the plague of 1630 in Milan. It’s long. Alessandro Manzoni lived and died in the house on Via Morone, now a museum of his life.

title: Confessions
creator: Saint Augustine
desc: Augustine’s account of his own life, written around 400. The turning point comes in Milan: a crisis in a garden in 386, then baptism by the city’s bishop, Ambrose, at Easter 387. Ambrose lies in the crypt of Sant’Ambrogio, the brick church he founded.

title: Eugène Atget’s photographs of old Paris
desc: Atget spent thirty years photographing the streets, shopfronts and courtyards of a Paris that was disappearing, working from his flat in Montparnasse. A look at a rediscovered set of his prints.

title: Monet’s Waterloo Bridge, painted from the Savoy
desc: Around 1900 Monet took a room at the Savoy Hotel and painted Waterloo Bridge again and again through the London fog and smoke. A look at one of the series and what he was after.

title: Frank Auerbach’s Mornington Crescent
desc: For decades the painter Frank Auerbach walked from his Camden studio to paint the same few streets around Mornington Crescent, in thick, heaped-up paint. “This part of London is my world,” he said.

title: How Rembrandt made his etchings
desc: A printmaker shows, step by step, how Rembrandt scratched his drawings into copper plates and printed them. He made many of them in this house, where the museum still demonstrates the press.

title: Canaletto’s Ascension Day at the Molo, with Stephen Fry
desc: Every Ascension Day the Doge sailed out in his golden barge, the Bucintoro, to “marry” Venice to the sea. Stephen Fry looks at Canaletto’s painting of the scene, set right here by the Doge’s Palace.

title: The kidnap and murder of Aldo Moro, 1978
desc: The Red Brigades kidnapped former prime minister Aldo Moro in March 1978 and held him for 55 days. His body was left in a car on this street, between the Christian Democrat and Communist party offices.

title: Rome’s Jews, the gold ransom and the 1943 raid
place: Largo 16 Ottobre 1943, Via del Portico d’Ottavia
desc: In September 1943 the SS demanded 50 kg of gold from Rome’s Jews in return for their safety. Weeks later, on 16 October, over 1,000 were seized in the ghetto and deported to Auschwitz.

title: Life in the Kraków ghetto, 1941
desc: In March 1941 the Nazis forced Kraków’s Jews across the river into a walled ghetto in Podgórze, cleared in 1943 from this square. The episode recalls the move and life inside.

title: Surviving Ireland’s Magdalene laundries
place: Former Magdalene laundry, Seán McDermott Street
desc: Catholic orders ran laundries where women and girls worked unpaid behind locked doors; Dublin’s last closed here in 1996. A woman sent to one as a young girl describes her time inside.

title: The Wannsee Conference, 1942
place: House of the Wannsee Conference, Am Großen Wannsee 56–58
desc: In January 1942 senior Nazi officials met in this lakeside villa to organise the murder of Europe’s Jews. The episode marks 70 years since the meeting and what was decided there.

title: The student revolt of May 1968
desc: In May 1968 students occupied the Sorbonne and fought police behind barricades in the Latin Quarter, and a general strike followed. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook tell how the unrest brought France to a halt.

title: The trial and execution of Louis XVI, 1793
desc: Louis XVI was guillotined on this square in January 1793 after a trial by the National Convention. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook cover the trial, the vote and the execution.

title: Filming The Third Man in occupied Vienna
desc: In 1948 Carol Reed filmed a thriller in a bombed-out Vienna split between four Allied powers. This short episode recalls the shoot, Orson Welles’ Harry Lime and the city the film captured.

title: The fall of Mussolini, 1943
desc: Mussolini ruled from this palace and gave speeches from its balcony. In July 1943 his own Fascist Grand Council voted against him here. The episode explains how his power collapsed and how he died.

title: Garibaldi and the unification of Italy
desc: Garibaldi fought French troops on this hill in 1849 to defend the short-lived Roman Republic. Historians trace his life and the long campaign to unite Italy, which ended with Rome taken in 1870.

title: The 1949 riot over Iceland joining NATO
desc: In March 1949 crowds outside parliament threw stones as MPs voted to join NATO, and police answered with tear gas. The episode tells the story of the riot and why the vote divided Icelanders.

title: Jón Arason, Iceland’s last Catholic bishop
desc: Bishop Jón Arason led resistance to the Lutheran Reformation imposed by the Danish crown, and was beheaded at Skálholt in 1550 with two of his sons. The hosts tell his story and how Iceland turned Lutheran.

title: The assassination of Reinhard Heydrich, 1942
place: Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius, Resslova
desc: Czechoslovak parachutists ambushed the Nazi governor Reinhard Heydrich in 1942, then made their last stand in this church crypt. The episode tells the story of the operation and its aftermath.

title: Jan Hus and the Hussite Wars
desc: Jan Hus preached church reform here in Czech until he was burned as a heretic in 1415. Eleanor Janega and Matt Lewis trace how his death set off decades of revolt and crusades against Bohemia.

title: How Paris moved six million dead into old quarries
place: Catacombs of Paris entrance, Place Denfert-Rochereau
desc: In the 18th century Paris had collapsing limestone mines underfoot and overflowing cemeteries. The hosts explain how the city solved both by moving the bones of some six million people into the tunnels.

title: The Dreyfus Affair and the officer stripped of his rank
desc: In 1895 Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish officer wrongly convicted of spying for Germany, was publicly degraded in this courtyard. Oxford historian Ruth Harris explains how the case split France for a decade.

title: The St Bartholomew’s Day Massacre, 1572
desc: Days after a royal wedding meant to reconcile Catholics and Protestants, Catholic mobs killed thousands of Huguenots across Paris. Historians explain who ordered it and why the killing spread.

title: Westminster Abbey, coronation church since 1066
desc: Monarchs have been crowned here since William the Conqueror on Christmas Day 1066. Historian David Carpenter, who grew up in the abbey, answers listener questions about its long history.

title: The 22 July attacks, 2011
desc: On 22 July 2011 a far-right extremist set off a bomb at the government offices here, then shot dozens of young people at a summer camp on Utøya. A survivor tells her story.

title: The liberation of Dachau, 1945
desc: The first Nazi concentration camp opened at Dachau in 1933. On 29 April 1945 American troops reached it; Mark Felton covers the camp and the day it was liberated.

title: The Beer Hall Putsch ends in gunfire at the Feldherrnhalle, 1923
desc: On 9 November 1923 Hitler’s marchers were stopped by Bavarian police in front of this loggia; the shooting killed 4 police and 16 Nazis. Mark Felton goes through the failed coup.

title: The Atocha lawyers massacre, 1977
desc: In January 1977, as Spain moved toward democracy, far-right gunmen burst into a labour law office here and shot dead five people. The killings and the huge silent funeral march that followed are covered.

title: The Peasants’ Revolt and the death of Wat Tyler, 1381
desc: In June 1381 rebels from Essex and Kent took London, stormed the Tower and met the boy king Richard II at Smithfield, where Wat Tyler was killed. With medievalist Eleanor Janega.

title: Inside Churchill’s underground War Rooms
place: Churchill War Rooms, King Charles Street
desc: Beneath Whitehall, Churchill’s government ran the war from a reinforced basement during the Blitz. The film goes through the map room, cabinet room and the rooms where staff lived and slept.

title: Christopher Wren, the architect of St Paul’s
desc: Wren was an astronomer and anatomist before he rebuilt London after the 1666 fire. Historian Steven Brindle traces his life and how he came to design the cathedral.

title: St Paul’s and the Second Great Fire of London, 1940
desc: On 29 December 1940 German bombs set the City ablaze around St Paul’s. Dan Snow tours the bomb damage with a guide and hears the story behind the famous photo of the dome rising above the smoke.

title: London and the Great Plague of 1665
place: Site of the Bedlam burial ground, Liverpool Street
desc: Plague killed around a fifth of Londoners in 1665. Historian Vanessa Harding describes how it spread, how the city responded and how ordinary people tried to cope.

title: The execution of Charles I, 1649
desc: On 30 January 1649 Charles I stepped out of a window here onto a scaffold and was beheaded in front of a large crowd. The episode explains how it came to that and what it meant for Britain.

title: The Gunpowder Plot, 1605
desc: On 5 November 1605 Guy Fawkes was found with nearly a ton of gunpowder in an undercroft beneath the House of Lords. The episode covers the Catholic plotters, their aims and how the plan was exposed.

title: The history of Westminster Abbey
desc: Every English monarch since 1066 has been crowned here. The film follows the abbey from Edward the Confessor’s church through Henry III’s Gothic rebuild to its coronations and royal tombs.

title: The Tower as a medieval prison, from Flambard to the Princes
desc: Recorded inside the Tower after hours. Two medievalists tell the escape stories of Ranulf Flambard and Roger Mortimer and discuss its best-known prisoners, including the two princes who vanished in 1483.

title: A thousand years at the Tower of London
desc: William the Conqueror’s fortress has been palace, prison, armoury and execution site. Dan Snow walks through its sieges, escapes, beheadings and famous prisoners, from Anne Boleyn onward.

title: The Lisbon Regicide, 1908
desc: On 1 February 1908 gunmen shot King Carlos I and his heir in an open carriage as it turned out of this square. The episode explains the killing and how it led to the end of Portugal’s monarchy in 1910.

title: The Gezi Park Protests, 2013
desc: A 2013 sit-in to save this park’s trees grew into protests across Turkey. The actor and activist Memet Ali Alabora tells how one social media post changed his life.

title: The Soviet Invasion of Finland, 1939–40
desc: The Winter War began on 30 November 1939 with Soviet bombs falling on Helsinki. The video covers the invasion and Finland’s 105-day defence. The national Winter War memorial stands on this square.

title: The Black Death in Boccaccio’s Florence
desc: Boccaccio’s Decameron opens in this church in 1348, as ten young Florentines meet and agree to escape the plague. The episode uses the book to show how people in the city lived through the Black Death.

title: The Union of Scotland and England, 1707
desc: Scotland’s parliament met in this hall until it voted itself out of existence in 1707. A Scottish historian explains what each country wanted from the union and why it went through.

title: The Covenanters and the National Covenant, 1638
desc: In 1638 Scots signed the National Covenant here, rejecting Charles I’s changes to their church. Historians trace the covenants from James VI to the killings of the 1680s.

title: Jonathan Swift’s ‘A Modest Proposal’
desc: Swift was Dean of St Patrick’s for over 30 years and is buried in the nave. In 1729 he wrote this satire suggesting the Irish poor sell their children as food. The episode looks at the pamphlet and its targets.

title: The Great Irish Famine, 1845–52
desc: These gaunt bronze figures face the quay where emigrant ships left during the famine. Historians explain why the potato blight killed a million people and drove two million more out of Ireland.

title: Denmark–Norway and the Atlantic Slave Trade
desc: Sugar, rum and the profits of slavery in the Danish West Indies were stored in this harbourside warehouse. The episode covers how Denmark–Norway ran forts in Ghana, shipped enslaved Africans and held Caribbean colonies.

title: Struensee, the Royal Doctor Who Ran Denmark
desc: In 1772 Struensee, the mentally ill Christian VII’s doctor, de facto ruler and the queen’s lover, was arrested after a masked ball at this court theatre. The episode tells how he rose and fell.

title: Raoul Wallenberg, Budapest’s vanished rescuer
desc: Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg saved thousands of Budapest Jews in 1944 with protective passes. He went to meet Soviet officers in January 1945 and was never seen in public again.

title: The Battle of Waterloo, 1815
desc: On 18 June 1815, Wellington and Blücher defeated Napoleon south of Brussels and ended his rule for good. Dan Snow and his father Peter Snow go through the battle.

title: Queer life in Weimar Berlin
desc: In the 1920s the streets around Nollendorfplatz were the centre of Berlin’s gay and lesbian bars and clubs. Greg Jenner and guests look at queer life in the Weimar Republic and how the Nazis ended it.

title: Frederick the Great of Prussia
desc: Frederick II ruled Prussia from 1740 to 1786, made it a military power and built Sanssouci as his retreat. Melvyn Bragg and guests discuss his wars, his writing and his court.

title: Fighting for Berlin, April–May 1945
desc: In the last weeks of the war the Red Army fought its way into Berlin street by street. A Soviet woman soldier and a German schoolboy who fought on opposite sides describe the battle.

title: Inside Hitler’s bunker, from 1945 to its demolition
desc: Hitler spent his last weeks in a bunker under the Reich Chancellery garden and killed himself there in April 1945. Photographs show the rooms as they were found and what became of them.

title: Kristallnacht, November 1938
desc: On 9–10 November 1938, Nazis attacked Jewish homes, shops and synagogues across Germany. The episode covers how the violence was organised and what followed for German Jews.

title: The storming of parliament and Milošević’s fall, 2000
desc: On 5 October 2000, crowds protesting a stolen election stormed the federal parliament, and Milošević stood down hours later. Otpor student leader Srđa Popović recalls the day.

title: Athens revives the Olympics, 1896
desc: The first modern Olympic Games opened in 1896 in this rebuilt marble stadium. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook start there and follow the Games up to the Second World War.

title: The Athens famine under German occupation, 1941–42
desc: After Germany occupied Greece in 1941, food ran out in Athens and tens of thousands died that winter. A woman who lived through it and historian Mark Mazower describe what happened.

title: How Athenian democracy worked
desc: The citizens’ assembly of ancient Athens met on this hill to debate and vote. Cambridge historian Paul Cartledge explains how the system started and who could take part.

title: The world’s first same-sex weddings, Amsterdam 2001
desc: At midnight on 1 April 2001, four couples married in Amsterdam as the Netherlands became the first country to allow same-sex marriage. One couple recalls the night.

title: Amsterdam’s canals and the Dutch Golden Age
desc: The canal ring was dug in the 1600s to house the merchants who made Amsterdam rich. Part two of the walking tour covers the canals, the Golden Age and the city’s later liberal reputation.

title: Medieval Amsterdam: the 1345 miracle and the Reformation
desc: Amsterdam first drew crowds as a pilgrimage town after a reported miracle in 1345, then broke with Catholic rule in 1578. Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook walk through its early centuries.

title: Anne Frank’s diary reaches the world, 1947
desc: Anne Frank wrote her diary while hiding in the annex behind this canal house until her arrest in 1944. Her cousin recalls the family and how the diary came to be published in 1947.

title: Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear by Vincent van Gogh
desc: A slow, guided look at the portrait Van Gogh painted weeks after cutting off part of his ear in Arles: the bandage, the Japanese print behind him, and what he wanted people to see.

title: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump by Joseph Wright of Derby
desc: A slow, guided look at Wright’s candlelit scene of a travelling scientist pumping the air from a glass bowl with a bird inside, and the faces of the family watching it.

title: The Seagram Murals by Mark Rothko
desc: Dark red and maroon paintings made for a New York restaurant, which Rothko refused to hand over. He gave nine to the Tate, where they fill their own room at Tate Modern.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck
desc: Why a small 1434 double portrait of a Bruges merchant and his wife is so full of riddles, from the mirror to the little dog. At the National Gallery.

title: Yellow-Red-Blue by Wassily Kandinsky
desc: Kandinsky believed colours could sound like music. This 1925 painting is one of his attempts to show it. In the Centre Pompidou’s modern art museum.

title: Bal du moulin de la Galette by Pierre-Auguste Renoir
desc: A Sunday dance in Montmartre, 1876, with sunlight falling through the trees onto the crowd. In the Musée d’Orsay.

title: A Bigger Splash by David Hockney
desc: A California swimming pool, an empty chair and the splash of someone who just dived in, from 1967. In the Tate collection, usually on show at Tate Britain.

title: Potsdamer Platz by Ernst Ludwig Kirchner
desc: Two streetwalkers on a traffic island in Berlin’s busiest square in 1914, painted in jagged, sickly colours. In the Neue Nationalgalerie, a few minutes from the real square.

title: The Cradle by Berthe Morisot
desc: Morisot’s sister watches over her sleeping baby through a gauze veil. It hung in the first Impressionist show in 1874. In the Musée d’Orsay.

title: The Garden of Earthly Delights by Hieronymus Bosch
desc: Bosch’s three-panel vision of paradise, earthly pleasure and hell, crowded with strange creatures. A short tour of its meaning, at the Prado.

title: Jupiter and Io by Correggio
desc: The god Jupiter, disguised as a dark cloud, embraces the nymph Io. A soft, strange painting from the 1530s, in the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck
desc: A Bruges merchant and his wife in 1434, with a mirror on the back wall that reflects two more people. Who are they, and what is going on? At the National Gallery.

title: The Descent from the Cross by Peter Paul Rubens
desc: Rubens’s huge altarpiece of Christ’s body being lowered from the cross, made for Antwerp’s cathedral in 1612 and still there. Antwerp is about 45 minutes from Brussels by train.

title: Portrait of the Journalist Sylvia von Harden by Otto Dix
desc: A monocled writer with a cigarette and a cocktail in 1926 Berlin, painted with cool cruelty. It came to stand for the Weimar era’s new woman. In the Centre Pompidou.

title: The Snail by Henri Matisse
desc: Too ill to paint, Matisse cut shapes from painted paper and had them pinned into a spiral. One of his last big works, from 1953, at Tate Modern.

title: The Alexander Mosaic, from Pompeii’s House of the Faun
desc: A floor of about a million tiny stones showing Alexander the Great charging the Persian king Darius. Found in Pompeii in 1831, now in Naples’ archaeological museum.

title: Portrait of Pope Innocent X by Diego Velázquez
desc: Velázquez’s portrait of a sharp-eyed pope in red silk, from 1650. The pope reportedly called it “too true”. It’s still owned by his family, in their palace gallery on Via del Corso.

title: The Triumphs of Caesar by Andrea Mantegna
desc: Nine huge canvases of a Roman victory parade, painted for the Gonzaga court in Mantua and bought by Charles I. They hang in their own gallery at Hampton Court Palace.

title: Going to the Match by L.S. Lowry
desc: Crowds of Lowry’s “matchstick men” stream toward Bolton Wanderers’ old ground. Owned by the footballers’ union and shown at The Lowry arts centre in Salford.

title: The Jewish Bride by Rembrandt
desc: A couple in an embrace, his hand on her heart, painted thickly in gold and red late in Rembrandt’s life. Van Gogh said he’d give ten years to sit in front of it. In the Rijksmuseum.

title: The Courtyard of a House in Delft by Pieter de Hooch
desc: A quiet Dutch courtyard in 1658: brick paths, a maid, a child, a doorway into the street. A small painting about ordinary life, at the National Gallery.

title: The Great Piece of Turf by Albrecht Dürer
desc: A watercolour of grasses and dandelions from 1503, studied as closely as any portrait. It belongs to the Albertina. Being on paper, it’s only shown now and then, so check before you go.

title: Miss La La at the Cirque Fernando by Edgar Degas
desc: An acrobat hangs from a rope by her teeth, high under a circus dome in 1879 Paris. Degas painted her from below, as the crowd saw her. At the National Gallery.

title: Self-Portrait as Saint Catherine of Alexandria by Artemisia Gentileschi
desc: Artemisia painted herself as a martyred saint, holding the broken wheel she was tortured on. The National Gallery bought it in 2018, its first painting by her.

title: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump by Joseph Wright of Derby
desc: A travelling scientist pumps the air out of a glass bowl while a family watches a bird struggle, lit by one candle. A scene from the Age of Enlightenment, at the National Gallery.

title: Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci
desc: The world’s most famous portrait, taken slowly: who she was, how Leonardo painted that smile, and how a theft in 1911 made her a celebrity. She hangs in the Louvre’s largest room.

title: The Sagrada Família by Antoni Gaudí
desc: Gaudí’s basilica, begun in 1882 and still being built. The episode looks at how one building became a lifelong obsession, and what to look for in its stone forest of columns.

title: Seaport with the Embarkation of the Queen of Sheba by Claude Lorrain
desc: A golden sunrise over an imagined harbour, painted in Rome in 1648. Turner loved it so much he asked to hang beside it, and he still does, in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère by Édouard Manet
desc: Manet’s last big painting: a barmaid at a Paris music hall, with a mirror behind her that doesn’t quite add up. A long, unhurried look at why. It hangs in the Courtauld Gallery at Somerset House.

title: The Taking of Christ by Caravaggio
desc: Caravaggio’s night scene of Judas kissing Christ as soldiers close in, and the story of how the lost painting turned up in 1990 in a Jesuit house in Dublin. In the National Gallery of Ireland.

title: The Milkmaid by Johannes Vermeer
desc: Vermeer’s small painting of a kitchen maid pouring milk: how he made light, bread and plaster wall look so real, and why a plain household task was worth painting in 1650s Delft. In the Rijksmuseum.

title: David by Michelangelo
desc: The marble giant Michelangelo carved in his twenties from a block others had given up on: how he did it, why the proportions look odd up close, and what the figure meant to the Florentine Republic. In the Accademia.

title: The Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci
desc: The longer cut of the channel’s Mona Lisa video: who the sitter was, how Leonardo built up the soft haze on her face over years, and how a 1911 theft made the portrait famous. In the Louvre.

title: The Throne of Weapons, a sculpture from decommissioned guns
desc: A chair made in Mozambique in 2001 from guns handed in after the civil war, and what it says about turning weapons into art after decades of fighting.

title: The Great Wave by Katsushika Hokusai
desc: Hokusai’s print of a huge wave and Mount Fuji, made around 1831 as Japan was closed to the world, and what its Prussian blue ink and Western perspective say about change coming.

title: The Akan Drum, a West African drum
desc: A drum made by the Akan people of West Africa, taken to Virginia on a slave ship and later collected in America, and what it carries of the history of the Atlantic slave trade.

title: The Benin Plaque: The Oba with Europeans, a brass plaque
desc: A 16th-century brass plaque from the royal palace of Benin showing the king with Portuguese traders, and how it came to London after the British looted the city in 1897.

title: The Mechanical Galleon, a clockwork table ornament
desc: A gilded clockwork ship made in Augsburg around 1585 that rolled down banquet tables, fired cannons and played music, and what it says about power and technology in Renaissance Europe.

title: Dürer’s Rhinoceros by Albrecht Dürer
desc: The 1515 woodcut of a rhino Dürer never saw, drawn from a sketch and a letter, and how this wrong picture fixed what Europeans thought a rhino looked like for centuries.

title: The Taíno Ritual Seat, a carved wooden seat
desc: A carved wooden seat made by the Taíno of the Caribbean, used by leaders to speak with spirits, and what happened to the Taíno after Columbus arrived.

title: The Hoa Hakananai’a, an Easter Island statue
desc: A basalt figure taken from Rapa Nui in 1868, the carvings on its back added when the island’s religion changed, and the island’s calls for its return.

title: The Ife Head, a brass portrait
desc: A brass head made in the West African city of Ife around 1400, why its realism stunned Europeans in the 1930s, and what it says about a powerful kingdom.

title: The Statue of Tara, a Buddhist bronze
desc: A gilded bronze of the Buddhist goddess Tara from Sri Lanka, about 1,200 years old, and how statues like this spread Buddhism across Asia.

title: The Hinton St Mary Mosaic, a Roman floor
desc: A 4th-century floor mosaic from a Dorset villa with one of the earliest known pictures of Christ, and how Christianity and pagan myth sat side by side in Roman Britain.

title: The Hoxne Pepper Pot, a Roman silver pot
desc: A silver pepper pot shaped like a Roman lady, from a hoard buried in Suffolk around AD 400, and how pepper from India reached the edge of the empire.

title: The Warren Cup, a Roman silver cup
desc: A Roman silver drinking cup decorated with scenes of male lovers, why it shocked collectors for decades, and what it says about sex and status in the Roman world.

title: The Head of Augustus, a bronze Roman portrait
desc: A bronze head of Rome’s first emperor, cut from a statue and buried under a temple step in Meroë, Sudan, by raiders who wanted it trodden on, and what it says about Roman propaganda.

title: The Rosetta Stone
desc: Neil MacGregor on the stone slab with one decree in three scripts, how it unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs, and why a tax decree became the museum’s most visited object.

title: The Oxus Chariot Model, a Persian gold model
desc: A tiny gold chariot from the Oxus Treasure, made in the Persian Empire around 500 BC, and what it tells us about how that vast empire was held together by roads.

title: The Gold Coin of Croesus
desc: A small gold coin from Lydia in modern Turkey, minted around 550 BC by the famously rich King Croesus, and how pure-metal coins changed trade.

title: The Lachish Reliefs, Assyrian palace carvings
desc: Stone panels from Sennacherib’s palace at Nineveh showing the siege of the Judean city of Lachish in 701 BC, an early piece of war reporting made for a king.

title: The Statue of Ramesses II
desc: The huge granite bust of Egypt’s best-known pharaoh, how it was dragged to London in 1818, and how Ramesses used statues like this to project power.

title: The Mold Gold Cape, a Bronze Age cape
desc: A cape beaten from a single gold ingot about 3,700 years ago, found in a Welsh burial mound in 1833, and what it says about wealth and power in Bronze Age Britain.

title: The Minoan Bull-leaper, a bronze figure
desc: A small bronze from Crete of an acrobat somersaulting over a charging bull, and how the Minoans, and later Victorian archaeologists, shaped our idea of early Greece.

title: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus
desc: An Egyptian scroll of maths problems from about 1550 BC, covering fractions, bread rations and pyramid slopes, and what it shows about how ancient Egypt was run.

title: The Flood Tablet, a cuneiform clay tablet
desc: A clay tablet from Nineveh telling of a great flood long before the Bible’s, how a self-taught scholar decoded it in 1872, and what it says about the world’s oldest stories.

title: The Jade Axe, a Neolithic ceremonial axe
desc: A polished jade axe head found in Kent but quarried high in the Italian Alps 6,000 years ago, and why people carried such a useless, beautiful thing across Europe.

title: The Ain Sakhri Lovers, a stone figurine
desc: A small calcite pebble carved about 11,000 years ago near Bethlehem showing a couple embracing, possibly the oldest image of people making love, and what it says about early farming life.

title: The Swimming Reindeer, an Ice Age carving
desc: Two reindeer carved from a mammoth tusk about 13,000 years ago in France, and what they say about the first art and the minds of Ice Age hunters.

title: The Olduvai Handaxe, a stone tool
desc: A 1.2-million-year-old stone axe from Tanzania’s Olduvai Gorge, and how this all-purpose tool shows early humans planning, sharing skills and starting to spread out of Africa.

title: The Mummy of Hornedjitef, an Egyptian priest’s coffin and body
desc: The first episode: Neil MacGregor on the mummy and painted coffins of a Theban priest from around 240 BC, and what they tell us about Egyptian beliefs about the afterlife.

title: The Haywain Triptych by Hieronymus Bosch
desc: Bosch’s three-panel altarpiece with a huge cart of hay at its centre, everyone from peasants to the pope grabbing at it, between Eden and hell. What the hay stands for. In the Prado.

title: The Deposition by Jacopo Pontormo
desc: Pontormo’s altarpiece of Christ’s body being carried, in pinks and pale blues, with figures that seem to float. Why it looks so strange for the 1520s. Still in its chapel in the church of Santa Felicita.

title: Augustus of Prima Porta, Roman marble statue
desc: A marble statue of Rome’s first emperor, found at his wife’s villa in 1863, posed as a commander with a carved breastplate full of political messages. How to read it. In the Vatican Museums.

title: The Conversion of Saint Paul by Caravaggio
desc: Saul thrown from his horse on the road to Damascus, lying on his back in a burst of light while the horse fills the frame. The episode looks at the story and how Caravaggio staged it.

title: The Calling of Saint Matthew by Caravaggio
desc: Christ points across a dim room at a tax collector counting money at a table, in light that falls like a beam. Which figure is Matthew, and how the scene fits its chapel. Still in the church it was painted for.

title: Salisbury Cathedral from the Meadows by John Constable
desc: Constable’s storm over Salisbury Cathedral with a rainbow breaking through, painted after his wife’s death. What troubled him at the time and what the weather is doing in the picture. Owned by Tate.

title: Ruby Loftus Screwing a Breech-ring by Laura Knight
desc: A young factory worker machining part of an anti-aircraft gun in 1943, painted by Laura Knight for the government’s war artists scheme. Who Ruby Loftus was and what the picture was for.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck
desc: A merchant and his wife in their room in Bruges in 1434, with a small round mirror on the back wall showing two more people. Who they were and what the details may mean. In the National Gallery.

title: The Ambassadors by Hans Holbein the Younger
desc: Two French envoys in London in 1533, with a shelf of instruments between them and a stretched skull across the floor. What the objects mean and where to stand to see the skull. In the National Gallery.

title: The Fighting Temeraire by J.M.W. Turner
desc: An old warship from Trafalgar towed up the Thames by a small steam tug to be broken up, under a blazing sunset. The episode explains the story and what Turner changed. In the National Gallery.

title: Rain, Steam and Speed by J.M.W. Turner
desc: Turner’s steam train charging over a Thames bridge through rain and mist in 1844. What railways meant then, the hare racing the engine, and how loose the paint really is. In the National Gallery.

title: Starry Night over the Rhône by Vincent van Gogh
desc: Van Gogh’s night view of the river at Arles, with gaslights reflected in the water and a couple on the bank, painted in 1888. Discussed with Van Gogh writer Martin Bailey. In the Musée d’Orsay.

title: Whistler’s Mother by James McNeill Whistler
desc: Whistler’s side-on portrait of his mother in black against a grey wall, which he called an arrangement in grey and black. How it was made and how it became an emblem far beyond art. In the Musée d’Orsay.

title: Amor Victorious by Caravaggio
desc: Caravaggio’s grinning, half-grown Cupid stepping over the symbols of music, war and learning, painted for a Roman collector around 1602. Who modelled, and why it caused talk. In the Gemäldegalerie.

title: Virgin and Child with Canon van der Paele by Jan van Eyck
desc: An elderly canon kneels before the Virgin and Child with two saints, painted in close detail down to his wrinkles and spectacles. The episode works through the picture. In Bruges, a day trip from Brussels.

title: The Death of Marat by Jacques-Louis David
place: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
desc: David’s painting of the murdered revolutionary journalist slumped in his bath, made within months of the killing in 1793. How it turned a political murder into something like a religious image. In Brussels.

title: Seated Woman with Bent Knees by Egon Schiele
place: National Gallery Prague, Trade Fair Palace
desc: Schiele’s 1917 picture of a woman sitting with her knees drawn up, looking straight out. The episode looks at how he drew bodies and why his work shocked Vienna. Held by the National Gallery Prague.

title: The Skating Minister by Henry Raeburn
desc: A Church of Scotland minister gliding across a frozen loch just outside Edinburgh, arms folded. Who he was, why the picture became a Scottish icon, and the doubts once raised over who painted it.

title: Bathers at Asnières by Georges Seurat
desc: Seurat’s big canvas of working men resting by the Seine near Paris, painted when he was 24, and how it was rejected by the official Salon before ending up in London.

title: Hermine Gallia by Gustav Klimt
desc: Klimt’s full-length portrait of a wealthy Viennese woman in a white dress, painted just before his gold period, and how it ended up as one of very few Klimts in Britain.

title: The Night Watch by Rembrandt van Rijn
desc: Rembrandt’s group portrait of an Amsterdam civic guard company: who paid for it, why it looks so busy compared with other militia pictures, and what happened when it was cut down to fit a wall.

title: The Hunters in the Snow by Pieter Bruegel the Elder
desc: Tired hunters come home over a frozen valley in Bruegel’s winter scene. The episode walks through the details, the cycle of seasons it belonged to, and how it came to Vienna.

title: Las Meninas by Diego Velázquez
desc: A close look at Velázquez’s painting of the Spanish princess, her maids and the painter himself at work, and why the mirror at the back still has people arguing about who is being painted.

title: The Sutton Hoo Helmet, an Anglo-Saxon king’s helmet
desc: Neil MacGregor on the iron-and-bronze helmet from a 7th-century ship burial in Suffolk, how it was rebuilt from hundreds of fragments, and what it shows about kings in early England.

title: The Lewis Chessmen, walrus-ivory chess pieces
desc: Neil MacGregor on the 12th-century chess pieces found on the Isle of Lewis: where they were probably carved in Norway, how chess travelled from India, and what the glum little figures say about medieval Europe.

title: Guernica by Pablo Picasso
desc: Melvyn Bragg and guests on the bombing of Guernica in 1937, how Picasso turned it into a huge black-and-white canvas, and the painting’s long road to the Reina Sofía.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck
desc: A merchant couple in their room in Bruges, painted in fine detail down to the convex mirror on the back wall. The episode works through those details. In the National Gallery.

title: Mona Lisa by Leonardo da Vinci
desc: Tamar Avishai goes to the Louvre to see Leonardo’s portrait through the crowds and asks why this one small painting became the most famous in the world.

title: The Night Watch by Rembrandt
desc: Rembrandt’s huge group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company caught mid-movement, and how he used light to pull it out of the dark. Hangs in its own gallery at the Rijksmuseum.

title: Judith Slaying Holofernes by Artemisia Gentileschi
desc: The biblical widow and her maid killing an enemy general, painted by a woman who had survived assault and a public trial. The episode reads the painting through her life. In the Uffizi.

title: The Birth of Venus by Sandro Botticelli
desc: Why a goddess arriving on a seashell became the picture of the Florentine Renaissance, and what the myth meant to the Medici circle. In the Uffizi.

title: Las Meninas by Diego Velázquez
desc: A short episode on the Spanish court painter’s puzzle of a picture: the princess, her maids, the painter at his easel and the king and queen in a mirror. Hangs in the Prado.

title: Tree Roots by Vincent van Gogh
desc: The tangle of roots and trunks Van Gogh was likely working on the day he shot himself in 1890, and the recent discovery of the exact spot in Auvers he painted. In the Van Gogh Museum.

title: The Potato Eaters by Vincent van Gogh
desc: Van Gogh’s dark early painting of a peasant family eating by lamplight, made in 1885 before he went to Paris: what he wanted it to say and why critics disliked it. In the Van Gogh Museum.

title: The Scream by Edvard Munch
desc: Munch’s figure clutching its face under a blood-red sky above the Oslo fjord: the experience behind it and why he made several versions. The 1893 painting is in the National Museum; others are at the Munch Museum.

title: The Ambassadors by Hans Holbein the Younger
desc: Holbein’s 1533 double portrait of two French envoys surrounded by instruments and books, with a distorted skull across the floor. Explains the objects and how to see the skull. In the National Gallery.

title: Napoleon Crossing the Alps by Jacques-Louis David
desc: David’s portrait of Napoleon on a rearing horse in an Alpine pass, a picture of a crossing that really happened on a mule. How it was made as propaganda, in five versions. The first is at Malmaison.

title: The Thinker by Auguste Rodin
desc: Rodin’s seated bronze man began as Dante at the top of his Gates of Hell. Explains how it became a standalone figure. The best-known large cast sits in the garden of the Musée Rodin.

title: Water Lilies by Claude Monet
desc: Monet’s late paintings of the pond in his Giverny garden, made while his eyesight failed. The largest of them fill two oval rooms he designed with the state at the Musée de l’Orangerie.

title: The Raft of the Medusa by Théodore Géricault
desc: A huge painting of survivors of an 1816 French shipwreck, adrift on a raft: the scandal behind the disaster, and how Géricault studied corpses and survivors to paint it. In the Louvre.

title: Apollo and Daphne by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
desc: Bernini’s marble of a nymph turning into a laurel tree as the god catches her, carved in his early twenties: how he made stone look like skin, leaves and motion. At the Galleria Borghese.

title: The School of Athens by Raphael
desc: Raphael’s fresco of ancient philosophers gathered in an imagined hall, painted for the pope’s rooms: who is who, including the faces borrowed from Leonardo and Michelangelo. In the Raphael Rooms, Vatican.

title: The Birth of Venus by Sandro Botticelli
desc: Botticelli’s goddess arriving on a shell, painted for the Medici circle: the classical myth behind it, who may have posed, and why a pagan nude was a bold choice in 1480s Florence. In the Uffizi.

title: The Black Paintings by Francisco Goya
desc: The dark murals, Saturn among them, that an aging, deaf Goya painted on the walls of his own house, later moved to canvas. This part covers the paintings and what they suggest about his state of mind. In the Prado.

title: Las Meninas by Diego Velázquez
desc: Velázquez paints himself at work beside the young Spanish princess and her attendants, with the king and queen glimpsed in a mirror. Unpicks who is looking at whom, and why. In the Prado.

title: Guernica by Pablo Picasso
desc: Picasso’s huge black-and-white response to the 1937 bombing of a Basque town: how he made it in weeks, what the bull, horse and lamp might mean, and its long road to Madrid. At the Reina Sofía.

title: The Garden of Earthly Delights by Hieronymus Bosch
desc: Bosch’s three-panel altarpiece moving from Eden to a crowded garden of pleasure to a strange hell, panel by panel, with what its odd details may have meant around 1500. In the Prado.

title: The Hunters in the Snow by Pieter Bruegel the Elder
desc: A winter scene from 1565 of hunters trudging home above a frozen valley, part of a series on the seasons. Explains how Bruegel built the view and what village life it records. In the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

title: The Kiss by Gustav Klimt
desc: Klimt’s gold-leaf painting of an embracing couple, made at the height of his “golden period”: why it looks the way it does and what it says about Vienna around 1900. It hangs in the Upper Belvedere.

title: Apollo in the Forge of Vulcan by Diego Velázquez
desc: Velázquez painted this in Rome in 1630, as Apollo tells Vulcan that his wife Venus is unfaithful. It hangs in the Prado, Madrid’s great picture gallery on the Paseo del Prado.

title: Saturn Devouring His Son by Francisco Goya
desc: One of the “black paintings” Goya painted on the walls of his house outside Madrid around 1820, later moved to canvas. It hangs in the Prado, Madrid’s great picture gallery on the Paseo del Prado.

title: The Death of the Virgin by Andrea Mantegna
desc: A small Mantegna panel from about 1462, made for the Gonzaga court at Mantua, with a view of the lakes outside. It hangs in the Prado, Madrid’s great picture gallery on the Paseo del Prado.

title: The Triumph of Bacchus (Los Borrachos) by Diego Velázquez
desc: Velázquez’s 1628–29 painting puts a pale Bacchus among sunburnt Spanish drinkers. It hangs in the Prado, Madrid’s great picture gallery on the Paseo del Prado.

title: Self-Portrait by Albrecht Dürer
desc: Dürer painted himself in 1498 in fine gloves and a striped cap, a picture of the artist as a gentleman. It hangs in the Prado, Madrid’s great picture gallery on the Paseo del Prado.

title: The Martyrdom of Saint Philip by Jusepe de Ribera
desc: Ribera’s 1639 painting of the apostle Philip being raised for crucifixion, with onlookers in the crowd. It hangs in the Prado, Madrid’s great picture gallery on the Paseo del Prado.

title: The Calling of Saint Matthew by Juan de Pareja
desc: Juan de Pareja worked in Velázquez’s studio, was freed in 1650 and became a painter in his own right. His 1661 canvas, with his self-portrait at the left, is in the Prado, Madrid’s great picture gallery.

title: The Descent from the Cross by Rogier van der Weyden
desc: Painted in the 1430s for a crossbowmen’s guild in Leuven, the panel shows Christ lowered from the cross while Mary collapses in the same pose. It is now in the Prado, Madrid’s royal picture gallery.

title: The Annunciation by Fra Angelico
desc: Fra Angelico’s altarpiece of around 1425–26, made for a convent in Fiesole, with the Expulsion shown in the garden at left. It hangs in the Prado, Madrid’s great picture gallery.

title: The Third of May 1808 by Francisco Goya
desc: Goya painted it in 1814 to recall the executions of Madrid citizens by French troops after the uprising of 2 May 1808. It is in the Prado, Madrid’s royal picture gallery on the Paseo del Prado.

title: Guernica by Pablo Picasso
desc: Picasso painted this huge canvas in 1937 for the Spanish pavilion at the Paris World’s Fair. It only came to Spain in 1981 and now hangs in the Museo Reina Sofía, Madrid’s modern art museum near Atocha station.

title: The Garden of Earthly Delights by Hieronymus Bosch
desc: Bosch’s triptych from around 1500, packed with naked figures, giant fruit and strange machines of punishment. Two art historians look at it panel by panel in the Prado, Madrid’s great picture gallery.

title: The Family of Charles IV by Francisco Goya
desc: Goya’s 1800 group portrait of the Spanish royal family, with the painter himself standing in the shadows at the left. It hangs in the Prado, Madrid’s royal picture gallery on the Paseo del Prado.

title: The Alexander Sarcophagus, a royal tomb from Sidon
desc: A marble sarcophagus of the late fourth century BCE from the royal necropolis of Sidon, still with traces of paint. It is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, beside Topkapı Palace.

title: The Deësis Mosaic of Hagia Sophia
desc: A thirteenth-century mosaic, damaged in its lower half, with soft modelling in tiny glass cubes. It is in the upper south gallery of Hagia Sophia in Sultanahmet.

title: Hagia Sophia, from museum back to mosque
desc: Hagia Sophia was a church for nine centuries, a mosque for nearly five, a museum from 1934, and a mosque again from 2020. Two Byzantine art historians look at what the minarets, mihrab and great calligraphic roundels added to the building.

title: Hagia Sophia by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus
desc: Justinian’s builders raised Hagia Sophia in under six years after riots burned its predecessor in 532. Art historians show how forty windows at the base of the dome make it look weightless, and how the church shaped Byzantine and Ottoman architecture.

title: The Virgin and Child Apse Mosaic of Hagia Sophia
desc: Unveiled in 867, the enthroned Virgin and Child marked the return of religious images after the Iconoclast period. It sits high in the apse of Hagia Sophia in Sultanahmet.

title: The Şehzade Mosque by Mimar Sinan
desc: Süleyman the Magnificent ordered this mosque in 1543 after his son Mehmed died young, and it was Sinan’s first major imperial commission. It stands in the Şehzadebaşı district near the Valens Aqueduct.

title: Little Hagia Sophia, the Church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus
desc: Built in the 520s and turned into a mosque around 1500, its octagonal plan under a dome anticipates Hagia Sophia. It is known as Little Hagia Sophia and stands near the Sea of Marmara shore below Sultanahmet.

title: The Rüstem Pasha Mosque by Mimar Sinan
desc: Rüstem Pasha, Süleyman’s grand vizier and son-in-law, had Sinan raise this small mosque on a platform over rented shops near the Spice Bazaar. Inside, almost every surface is covered in Iznik tiles, including the new tomato-red glaze of the 1560s.

title: The Süleymaniye Mosque by Mimar Sinan
desc: The architect Mimar Sinan finished this mosque for Süleyman the Magnificent in 1558 on the Third Hill above the Golden Horn. Around it he built schools, a hospital, a soup kitchen and baths, and the tombs of Süleyman and his wife Hürrem lie in the garden.

title: The Chora Church, a late Byzantine monastery church
desc: The Chora, a monastery church near the Edirnekapı land walls, was redecorated around 1320 by the statesman Theodore Metochites. Its gold mosaics and the fresco of Christ pulling Adam and Eve from their tombs are among the finest late Byzantine art.

title: The Wise and Foolish Virgins by the Master of Pedret
desc: Wall paintings of around 1100 from a side apse of a small church at Pedret, near Berga; they were removed in 1921. They are in the Museu Nacional d’Art de Catalunya in the Palau Nacional on Montjuïc.

title: The Historiated Capitals of Sant Miquel, Camarasa
desc: Carved capitals from the church of Sant Miquel in Camarasa in the Noguera, Lleida province. They are in the Romanesque galleries of the Museu Nacional d’Art de Catalunya on Montjuïc.

title: The Virgin of Ger, a Romanesque wooden Madonna
desc: A painted Romanesque wood carving from the 12th century, from the village of Ger in the Cerdanya. It is in the Museu Nacional d’Art de Catalunya, in the Palau Nacional on Montjuïc.

title: Les Demoiselles d’Avignon by Pablo Picasso
desc: Picasso’s 1907 canvas of five women takes its title from Carrer d’Avinyó, a narrow street in the Gothic Quarter he knew as a teenager in Barcelona. Smarthistory explains how its masks and splintered space opened the road to Cubism.

title: The Sagrada Família by Antoni Gaudí
desc: Two art historians walk around the basilica and read its façades: the Nativity side Gaudí lived to see built, the stark Passion side added after his death, and the forest of tree-like columns that holds up the nave without flying buttresses.

title: The Mask of Agamemnon, a Mycenaean gold death mask
desc: Heinrich Schliemann found the gold mask in a shaft grave at Mycenae in 1876; it predates the Trojan War era by centuries. It is in the National Archaeological Museum on Patission Street.

title: The Parthenon Marbles and the restitution debate
desc: Greece has asked for decades for the sculptures Lord Elgin removed around 1801. The Acropolis Museum, opened in 2009 below the Acropolis, keeps space for the frieze it hopes to reunite.

title: Nike Adjusting Her Sandal, from the Temple of Athena Nike
desc: A relief of about 410 BCE from the parapet around the Temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis, carved in clinging, wet-looking folds. It is in the Acropolis Museum below the hill.

title: The Erechtheion, a temple on the Acropolis
desc: The Erechtheion on the Acropolis, built in the late 400s BCE beside the Parthenon, sits on uneven rock and shelters older shrines, including the spot of Athena’s sacred olive tree. Its four sides and different levels follow from that.

title: The Antikythera Youth, a bronze from a shipwreck
desc: Most ancient bronzes were melted down for metal; this life-size youth from about 340 BCE survived because the ship carrying it sank. Sponge divers raised it in 1900, and it now stands in the National Archaeological Museum.

title: The Grave Stele of Hegeso
desc: Hegeso’s grave relief, carved around 410 BCE, stood along the Street of Tombs in the Kerameikos cemetery, where a cast now marks its place. The original, showing her seated with a servant, is in the National Archaeological Museum.

title: The Artemision Bronze, Zeus or Poseidon
desc: The Artemision Bronze, cast around 460 BCE and pulled from a shipwreck off Cape Artemision in 1926–28, stands in the National Archaeological Museum. Scholars still argue whether his missing weapon was Zeus’s thunderbolt or Poseidon’s trident.

title: The Kroisos Kouros, an Archaic grave statue
desc: This kouros, about 530 BCE, marked the grave of a young man named Kroisos in the Attic countryside; its base asks viewers to pause for one killed in battle. It is now a centrepiece of the National Archaeological Museum’s Archaic rooms.

title: The Ancient Agora of Athens
desc: The Ancient Agora below the Acropolis was where Athenians shopped, argued, held trials and ran their democracy. The film looks at its law courts, council house and stoas; finds such as ostraka are shown in the rebuilt Stoa of Attalos.

title: The Dipylon Amphora, a Geometric grave marker
