desc: Around 750 BCE this huge amphora stood over a woman’s grave in the Dipylon cemetery at Kerameikos, the potters’ quarter by the city gate. Its bands of meander pattern frame one of the earliest scenes of mourners in Greek art.

title: The Peplos Kore, a painted Archaic statue
desc: The Peplos Kore, a votive statue of a young woman from about 530 BCE, stood on the Acropolis until the Persian sack. Now in the Acropolis Museum’s Archaic gallery, she shows how brightly painted Greek sculpture once was.

title: The Kritios Boy, an early Classical marble youth
desc: The Kritios Boy, carved around 480 BCE and found buried in the debris the Persians left on the Acropolis, is now in the Acropolis Museum. Its relaxed stance, weight on one leg, marks the break from stiff Archaic figures.

title: A Caryatid from the Erechtheion
desc: Two art historians look at one of the caryatids from the south porch of the Erechtheion, the temple on the Acropolis built in 421–407 BCE, and at how a column could be turned into a standing woman without looking like it was carrying a load.

title: The Parthenon by Iktinos and Kallikrates
desc: Two art historians look closely at the temple on the Acropolis rock that Iktinos and Kallikrates built for Athena between 447 and 432 BCE, with sculpture directed by Phidias, and at what Periclean Athens meant it to say about itself.

title: Self-Portrait in a Fur-Collared Robe by Albrecht Dürer
desc: Albrecht Dürer’s 1500 self-portrait, frontal and fur-collared, presents the artist with a gravity once kept for images of Christ. It hangs in the Alte Pinakothek, the Wittelsbachs’ old master gallery in the Kunstareal museum district.

title: The Four Apostles by Albrecht Dürer
desc: Dürer painted the Four Apostles in 1526 as a gift to Nuremberg, inscribed with warnings drawn from Luther’s Bible. Elector Maximilian I took the panels to Munich in 1627; they now hang in the Alte Pinakothek art museum.

title: The Battle of Alexander at Issus by Albrecht Altdorfer
desc: Duke William IV of Bavaria commissioned Albrecht Altdorfer’s 1529 painting of Alexander defeating Darius, with thousands of soldiers under a curving earth and sky. It is now in the Alte Pinakothek, the city’s old master museum.

title: The Barberini Faun, a Hellenistic marble satyr
desc: The Hellenistic marble Barberini Faun sprawls asleep, drunk and openly sensual. Crown Prince Ludwig acquired it from Rome’s Barberini family in the 1810s for the Glyptothek, the sculpture museum he built on Königsplatz.

title: The Aegina Marbles, from the Temple of Aphaia
desc: The pediment figures from the Temple of Aphaia on Aegina show Greek sculpture shifting from Archaic to Classical within a few years. Ludwig I bought them in 1812; they are displayed in the Glyptothek museum on Königsplatz.

title: The House of German Art by Paul Ludwig Troost
desc: Paul Troost designed the House of German Art for Hitler, opened in 1937. Nearby, the Degenerate Art exhibition ridiculed modern works seized from museums. The building on Prinzregentenstrasse is now the Haus der Kunst art museum.

title: The Campanile Reliefs by Andrea Pisano
desc: Reliefs by Andrea Pisano and his workshop from the 1330s for Giotto’s bell tower, showing human labour and the arts. The originals are in the Museo dell’Opera del Duomo, with copies on the tower.

title: The Consequences of War by Peter Paul Rubens
desc: Rubens painted this allegory of the Thirty Years’ War in 1637–38 and explained it in a letter. It hangs in the Palatine Gallery of Palazzo Pitti, the Medici palace on the Oltrarno.

title: The Duke and Duchess of Urbino by Piero della Francesca
desc: Piero’s double portrait of the rulers of Urbino, with their triumphs on the back; the duke is shown from his left after losing his right eye. It is in the Uffizi, Florence’s great picture gallery.

title: The Madonna of the Goldfinch by Raphael
desc: Raphael painted this around 1505–06 as a wedding gift; it broke into pieces in a 1547 house collapse and was repaired. It is in the Uffizi, Florence’s great picture gallery beside the Palazzo Vecchio.

title: The Madonna with the Long Neck by Parmigianino
desc: Parmigianino worked on this altarpiece from 1534 until his death and left it unfinished, with a single column in the background. It is in the Uffizi, Florence’s great picture gallery beside the Palazzo Vecchio.

title: The Venus of Urbino by Titian
desc: Titian’s 1538 painting for Guidobaldo della Rovere, later Duke of Urbino, inspired Manet’s Olympia. It is in the Uffizi, Florence’s great picture gallery beside the Palazzo Vecchio.

title: The Saint Lucy Altarpiece by Domenico Veneziano
desc: Domenico Veneziano painted this around 1445–47 for Santa Lucia dei Magnoli, with a painted courtyard of coloured marble. It is in the Uffizi, Florence’s great picture gallery beside the Palazzo Vecchio.

title: The Presentation in the Temple by Ambrogio Lorenzetti
desc: Lorenzetti’s 1342 altarpiece for Siena Cathedral, set inside a painted church with a gilded dome. It is in the Uffizi, Florence’s great picture gallery beside the Palazzo Vecchio.

title: Madonna and Child with Two Angels by Fra Filippo Lippi
desc: Lippi’s painting from around 1460–65, with a landscape seen through a window behind the young Madonna. It is in the Uffizi, Florence’s great picture gallery beside the Palazzo Vecchio.

title: Eleonora of Toledo and Her Son by Bronzino
desc: Bronzino’s 1545 portrait of the wife of Cosimo I de’ Medici, her brocade gown painted thread by thread. It is in the Uffizi, Florence’s great picture gallery beside the Palazzo Vecchio.

title: Santo Spirito by Filippo Brunelleschi
desc: Brunelleschi designed this Augustinian church in the 1430s on a strict grid of grey stone and white plaster; it was finished after his death. It faces Piazza Santo Spirito in the Oltrarno district.

title: The Old Sacristy by Filippo Brunelleschi
desc: Brunelleschi’s sacristy of the 1420s was built for the Medici, with roundels by Donatello. It is in the basilica of San Lorenzo, the Medici parish church near the central market.

title: The Santa Trinita and Ognissanti Madonnas by Cimabue and Giotto
desc: Cimabue’s altarpiece of about 1280 and Giotto’s of about 1310 hang in the same room, so the shift in weight and space is easy to compare. They are in the Uffizi Gallery, beside Piazza della Signoria.

title: Palazzo Rucellai by Leon Battista Alberti
desc: Designed by Alberti for Giovanni Rucellai around 1450, its façade layers pilasters storey by storey over smooth rusticated stone. It is on Via della Vigna Nuova.

title: Perseus with the Head of Medusa by Benvenuto Cellini
place: Loggia dei Lanzi, Piazza della Signoria
desc: Cellini cast the bronze for Cosimo I de’ Medici and unveiled it in 1554, after a dramatic pour he wrote about in his memoirs. It stands in the Loggia dei Lanzi on Piazza della Signoria.

title: The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden by Masaccio
place: Brancacci Chapel, Santa Maria del Carmine
desc: Masaccio’s fresco of around 1425, one of the most emotional figures of the early Renaissance; fig leaves added later were removed in the 1980s. It is in the Brancacci Chapel in Santa Maria del Carmine, Oltrarno.

title: Fruit and Insects by Rachel Ruysch
desc: Ruysch, court painter to the Elector Palatine, painted it in 1711; her still lifes sold for more than Rembrandt’s did. It is in the Uffizi Gallery, beside Piazza della Signoria.

title: The Façade of Santa Maria Novella by Leon Battista Alberti
desc: Commissioned by the Rucellai family in 1456, the green and white marble façade adds scrolls and a temple pediment to a medieval base. It faces Piazza Santa Maria Novella near the station.

title: The Adoration of the Magi by Gentile da Fabriano
desc: Painted in 1423 for Palla Strozzi, Florence’s richest man, with real gold and raised patterns throughout. It hangs in the Uffizi Gallery, beside Piazza della Signoria.

title: Judith Slaying Holofernes by Artemisia Gentileschi
desc: Artemisia painted this version around 1620 for Cosimo II de’ Medici. It hangs in the Uffizi Gallery, the Medici office building beside Piazza della Signoria.

title: The Birth of Venus by Sandro Botticelli
desc: Botticelli painted it on canvas in the 1480s, a large mythological nude rare for its time. It hangs in the Uffizi Gallery, the Medici office building beside Piazza della Signoria.

title: The Ognissanti Madonna by Giotto
desc: Painted around 1310 for the church of Ognissanti, it shows Mary as a heavy, rounded figure in a Gothic throne. It hangs in the Uffizi, the city’s main picture gallery, beside Cimabue’s and Duccio’s Madonnas.

title: The Annunciation by Simone Martini and Lippo Memmi
desc: Painted in 1333 for Siena cathedral, with the angel’s words raised in gold and Mary drawing back. It was brought to Florence in the 18th century and hangs in the Uffizi, the city’s main picture gallery.

title: The Rucellai Madonna by Duccio
desc: The Sienese painter Duccio made this Virgin and Child in 1285 for a confraternity at Santa Maria Novella. It hangs in the Uffizi, the city’s main picture gallery, beside the big Madonnas of Cimabue and Giotto.

title: The Codex Amiatinus, the oldest complete Latin Bible
desc: The oldest complete Latin Bible, made by monks at Wearmouth-Jarrow in northeast England around 700, and weighing about 34 kilos. It belongs to the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, the Medici library at San Lorenzo.

title: The Santa Trinita Maestà by Cimabue
desc: A tall altarpiece from around 1290 made for the church of Santa Trinita, with Hebrew prophets in arches beneath the throne. It hangs in the Uffizi, the city’s main picture gallery, next to Duccio’s and Giotto’s Madonnas.

title: The Portinari Altarpiece by Hugo van der Goes
desc: A Medici banker in Bruges ordered this huge Nativity in the 1470s and shipped it to Florence, where its rough shepherds and fine detail impressed local painters. It is now in the Uffizi, the city’s main picture gallery.

title: Palazzo Medici Riccardi by Michelozzo
desc: Michelozzo built it for Cosimo de’ Medici from 1444, with rough stone below and smoother floors above. The family lived here for about a century. It stands on Via Cavour and is now Palazzo Medici Riccardi.

title: The Deposition by Pontormo
desc: An altarpiece from the 1520s in bright pinks and blues, with no cross, tomb or landscape to anchor the scene. It is still in the Capponi Chapel of Santa Felicita, a small church just south of the Ponte Vecchio.

title: The Sacrifice of Isaac by Lorenzo Ghiberti and Filippo Brunelleschi
desc: In 1401 the cloth merchants’ guild asked artists for a trial panel of the sacrifice of Isaac. Ghiberti’s won and Brunelleschi’s lost, and both now hang side by side in the Bargello, the city’s sculpture museum.

title: Primavera by Sandro Botticelli
desc: Painted around 1480 for the Medici, with Venus, Mercury, the Three Graces and Flora in an orange grove. It hangs in the Uffizi, the old Medici office building that became one of Europe’s first public galleries.

title: David by Michelangelo
desc: Carved from a block other sculptors had given up on, it stood outside the town hall from 1504 as a symbol of the republic. The original moved indoors in 1873 to the Galleria dell’Accademia on Via Ricasoli.

title: The Penitent Magdalene by Donatello
desc: A painted wooden figure from the 1450s showing the Magdalene as a hermit in the desert, gaunt and covered by her own hair. It is in the Museo dell’Opera del Duomo, the cathedral museum behind the Duomo.

title: Saint Mark by Donatello
desc: Donatello carved this marble figure around 1411–13 for the linen weavers’ niche on Orsanmichele, the guild church. The original is in the museum upstairs at Orsanmichele, with a copy outside.

title: The South Doors of the Baptistery by Andrea Pisano
desc: Andrea Pisano finished the doors in 1336, the earliest of the Baptistery’s three sets. The originals are now in the Museo dell’Opera del Duomo, with copies in the frames on the Baptistery across the square.

title: David by Andrea del Verrocchio
desc: A bronze David made for the Medici around 1470, wiry and pleased with himself, with Goliath’s head at his feet. It stands in the Bargello, the former police headquarters and prison that is now the sculpture museum.

title: The Cavalcanti Annunciation by Donatello
desc: Donatello made this gilded sandstone relief in the 1430s for the Cavalcanti family. It is still set into the right wall of the nave in Santa Croce, the Franciscan basilica on the east side of the centre.

title: Brunelleschi’s Perspective Experiment
place: Duomo central doorway, facing the Baptistery
desc: Around 1420 Brunelleschi stood inside the cathedral doorway and painted the Baptistery opposite, then had viewers compare it with the real building through a hole and a mirror. The demonstration gave painters a working system of linear perspective.

title: The Dome of Florence Cathedral by Filippo Brunelleschi
desc: The cathedral sat with a hole in its roof for decades because no one knew how to span it. Brunelleschi built the dome without wooden centering, using two shells, herringbone brickwork and hoisting machines of his own design, finishing in 1436.

title: Saint George by Donatello
desc: Each guild filled a niche on the outside of Orsanmichele, a grain hall turned church. The armorers chose St George and hired Donatello. The marble original moved to the Bargello museum; a copy stands in the niche on Via dell’Arte della Lana.

title: Four Crowned Saints by Nanni di Banco
desc: The stonemasons’ and woodworkers’ guild picked four Christian sculptors martyred for refusing to make a statue for the Roman emperor. Nanni di Banco carved them as a group of Roman-looking men in conversation for their niche on Orsanmichele church.

title: David by Donatello
desc: Donatello’s bronze David, probably made for the Medici palace courtyard, was the first freestanding male nude since antiquity. It now stands in the Bargello, the former police headquarters and prison that houses the city’s sculpture museum.

title: The Laurentian Library by Michelangelo
desc: Michelangelo designed the Medici family’s library above the cloister of San Lorenzo church. Its tall, cramped vestibule breaks classical rules on purpose, and the staircase seems to pour out of the reading room like a slow flow of stone.

title: The New Sacristy by Michelangelo
desc: The New Sacristy behind San Lorenzo church is a room Michelangelo designed both as architecture and as a setting for his sculpture. Reclining figures of Night, Day, Dawn and Dusk lie on the tombs of two minor Medici dukes.

title: The Tribute Money by Masaccio
place: Brancacci Chapel, Santa Maria del Carmine
desc: In the Brancacci Chapel of Santa Maria del Carmine church, Masaccio painted figures lit from a single direction and standing on solid ground. His weeping Adam and Eve, driven out of Eden, became a school for later artists, Michelangelo among them.

title: The Annunciation by Fra Angelico
desc: Fra Angelico was a Dominican friar at San Marco convent, and he painted this fresco where his brothers would see it each time they climbed to their cells. It is quiet, spare and meant for prayer. The convent is now a museum.

title: The Gates of Paradise by Lorenzo Ghiberti
desc: Lorenzo Ghiberti cast ten gilded Old Testament panels for the east doors of the Baptistery, facing the cathedral. Michelangelo is said to have named them. The originals are now indoors in the cathedral museum; copies hang on the building.

title: The Holy Trinity by Masaccio
desc: Masaccio’s fresco in Santa Maria Novella church, painted around 1427, is one of the first uses of single-point perspective. Below the Trinity, a skeleton on a tomb carries a warning to the living. Two art historians explain how it works.

title: Cut with the Kitchen Knife by Hannah Höch
desc: Höch’s 1919–20 photomontage of cut-up magazine pictures, mixing generals, Dada artists and machines; it was shown at the 1920 Dada Fair. It belongs to Berlin’s Nationalgalerie, shown at the Neue Nationalgalerie at the Kulturforum.

title: The Monk by the Sea by Caspar David Friedrich
desc: Friedrich’s 1808–10 painting puzzled its first viewers with its almost empty composition; the Prussian crown prince bought it. It hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie, the 19th-century art museum on Berlin’s Museum Island.

title: The Abbey in the Oakwood by Caspar David Friedrich
desc: Friedrich painted this winter funeral among bare oaks in 1809–10 as a pair with Monk by the Sea. It hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie, the 19th-century art museum on Berlin’s Museum Island.

title: The Lone Tree by Caspar David Friedrich
desc: Friedrich’s 1822 landscape of a shepherd resting under an old oak with distant mountains behind. It hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie, the 19th-century art museum on Berlin’s Museum Island.

title: Self-Portrait with Death Playing the Fiddle by Arnold Böcklin
desc: Böcklin’s 1872 self-portrait, with Death bowing a single string just behind him. It hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie, the 19th-century art museum on Berlin’s Museum Island.

title: Woman at a Window by Caspar David Friedrich
desc: An 1822 painting of the artist’s wife Caroline at the window of his Dresden studio above the Elbe, seen from behind. It hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie, the 19th-century art museum on Berlin’s Museum Island.

title: In the Conservatory by Édouard Manet
desc: Manet’s 1879 painting of a fashionable couple among potted plants, bought by the Berlin museum in 1896. It hangs in the Alte Nationalgalerie, the 19th-century art museum on Berlin’s Museum Island.

title: Portrait of Georg Gisze by Hans Holbein the Younger
desc: Holbein’s 1532 portrait of a Hanseatic trader at the Steelyard in London, surrounded by scales, coins and a glass vase of carnations. It is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin’s old master gallery at the Kulturforum.

title: The Dormition of the Virgin by Giotto
desc: A Florentine panel from around 1310 by Giotto and his workshop, showing the Virgin laid in her tomb as Christ receives her soul. It is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin’s old master gallery at the Kulturforum.

title: The Monforte Altarpiece by Hugo van der Goes
desc: The central panel of an altarpiece from around 1470, named after the Spanish monastery at Monforte where it stood until 1914. It is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin’s old master gallery at the Kulturforum.

title: The Ideal City by Francesco di Giorgio Martini
desc: A long painted panel from the 1490s, attributed to Francesco di Giorgio Martini, showing an ideal city of colonnades and palaces in perfect perspective. It is in the Gemäldegalerie at Berlin’s Kulturforum.

title: The Madonna in the Church by Jan van Eyck
desc: A small panel from around 1440 in which Mary is taller than the nave around her and sunlight falls through the windows. It is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin’s old master gallery at the Kulturforum.

title: The Glass of Wine by Johannes Vermeer
desc: Vermeer’s interior from around 1660, with a stained-glass window, a lute on a chair and a quiet courtship. It is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin’s old master gallery at the Kulturforum.

title: Netherlandish Proverbs by Pieter Bruegel the Elder
desc: Bruegel’s 1559 panel turns Dutch proverbs into people banging heads against walls and casting roses before swine. It is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin’s old master gallery at the Kulturforum.

title: The Centaur Mosaic from Hadrian’s Villa
desc: A Roman floor mosaic from around 130 CE, found at the emperor Hadrian’s villa at Tivoli, with a centaur defending his mate from big cats. It is in the Antikensammlung at the Altes Museum on Berlin’s Museum Island.

title: Singing Boy with a Flute by Frans Hals
desc: Hals painted this half-length boy around 1623–25 with quick, visible brushstrokes, possibly as a picture of the sense of hearing. It is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin’s old master gallery at the Kulturforum.

title: Malle Babbe by Frans Hals
desc: Hals’s portrait of “Mad Babbe”, a real Haarlem woman of the 1630s, painted in loose, fast strokes with a tankard and an owl. It is in the Gemäldegalerie, Berlin’s old master gallery at the Kulturforum.

title: House Altar of Akhenaten, Nefertiti and Their Daughters
desc: A limestone house altar from Amarna, around 1350 BCE, showing the royal family at ease beneath the sun-disc Aten. It is in the Egyptian Museum in the Neues Museum on Berlin’s Museum Island, near the bust of Nefertiti.

title: The Pergamon Altar, a Greek altar to Zeus
desc: The Hellenistic altar from Pergamon in Asia Minor, about 170 BCE, with its long frieze of the gods’ battle against the giants. It was rebuilt inside the Pergamonmuseum on Berlin’s Museum Island, now closed for renovation.

title: The Head of Queen Tiye, a small yew-wood portrait
desc: A small yew-wood head of Queen Tiye, mother of Akhenaten, from around 1355 BCE; later reworked with a wig and feathered crown. It is in the Egyptian Museum in the Neues Museum on Berlin’s Museum Island.

title: The Ishtar Gate of Babylon
desc: The Ishtar Gate at the Pergamon Museum is among the most awe-inspiring artifacts in any museum in Europe. In this video from Smarthistory, two art historians passionately describe the gate and its role as the entrance to the fortified city of Babylon.

title: The Bust of Nefertiti by Thutmose
desc: The dramatic presentation in the Neues Museum of the iconic bust of Nefertiti makes for an exceptional museumgoing experience. This video from Smarthistory expertly explains details about the sculpture itself and Nefertiti’s influential role in Egypt.

title: The Basilica of Saint-Denis, birthplace of Gothic architecture
desc: Abbot Suger rebuilt the choir of the royal abbey of Saint-Denis in the 1140s with ribbed vaults and tall windows. The basilica, burial place of French kings, is in Saint-Denis on the northern edge of Paris.

title: The Palais Garnier by Charles Garnier
desc: Charles Garnier’s opera house, built 1861–75 under Napoleon III, with its grand staircase and gilded foyer. The Palais Garnier stands on the Place de l’Opéra at the end of the Avenue de l’Opéra.

title: Portrait of the Journalist Sylvia von Harden by Otto Dix
desc: Dix’s 1926 portrait of a journalist became a picture of the Weimar “new woman”. The museum bought it from Dix in 1961. It is in the Musée National d’Art Moderne at the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

title: Composition A XX by László Moholy-Nagy
desc: A 1924 painting by the Hungarian artist who taught at the Bauhaus, testing how light and transparency can be painted. It is in the Musée National d’Art Moderne at the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

title: Mechanical Head (The Spirit of Our Time) by Raoul Hausmann
desc: Hausmann built this Dada head around 1920 from a hairdresser’s dummy and bits of measuring kit. It is in the Musée national d’art moderne at the Centre Pompidou in the Beaubourg area.

title: La Belle Jardinière by Raphael
desc: Raphael painted this Madonna in 1507 in Florence, soon after studying Leonardo’s pyramid-shaped groups. It entered the French royal collection under Francis I and hangs in the Louvre on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: Peasant Family in an Interior by Louis Le Nain
desc: A 1640s painting by one of the Le Nain brothers, showing a rural household with unusual dignity. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: The Victory Stele of Naram-Sin
desc: A pink limestone stele from around 2250 BCE, carried off to Susa as war booty a thousand years later and found there by French archaeologists. It is in the Louvre’s Near Eastern antiquities galleries.

title: The Death of Sardanapalus by Eugène Delacroix
desc: Delacroix’s 1827 painting of an Assyrian king ordering his treasures and women destroyed before his enemies arrive. It shocked the Salon. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: Saint Francis Receiving the Stigmata by Giotto
desc: A tall gold-ground altarpiece of around 1295–1300, signed by Giotto, made for San Francesco in Pisa. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: The Sleep of Endymion by Anne-Louis Girodet
desc: Girodet’s 1791 painting, made as a student in Rome, shows the goddess of the moon visiting Endymion as a beam of light. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: The Dying Slave and the Rebellious Slave by Michelangelo
desc: The Dying Slave and Rebellious Slave were carved around 1513–16 for the tomb of Pope Julius II, then given away. They are in the Louvre, the former royal palace on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: The Intervention of the Sabine Women by Jacques-Louis David
desc: David began this large painting in prison after the Terror and showed it in 1799, charging an entry fee. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: The Death of the Virgin by Caravaggio
desc: Caravaggio’s 1601–06 altarpiece was rejected by the Roman church that ordered it; Rubens advised the Duke of Mantua to buy it. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: The Lictors Bring to Brutus the Bodies of His Sons by Jacques-Louis David
desc: David showed this painting in 1789, just as the Revolution began: Brutus had ordered his own sons’ deaths for treason. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: The Painted Beaker from Susa, with ibex motifs
desc: A thin painted beaker from a cemetery at Susa, about 4200–3500 BCE, its ibex reduced to a few bold shapes. It is in the Near Eastern galleries of the Louvre on the Right Bank.

title: Bathsheba at Her Bath by Rembrandt
desc: Rembrandt’s 1654 painting, probably modelled by his partner Hendrickje Stoffels, shows Bathsheba with the king’s summons in her hand. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace on Paris’s Right Bank.

title: The Bull Capital from Darius I’s Palace at Susa
desc: A colossal column capital of about 510 BCE from the apadana, or audience hall, of Darius I at Susa, in present-day Iran. It is in the Near Eastern galleries of the Louvre.

title: The Crowning with Thorns by Titian
desc: Titian painted this violent scene around 1542–43 for a church in Milan; it was taken to Paris by Napoleon’s armies. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: Pilgrimage to Cythera by Antoine Watteau
desc: Watteau’s reception piece for the Royal Academy in 1717, which created the category of the fête galante. This version is in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: The Avignon Pietà by Enguerrand Quarton
desc: Painted around 1455 for a church near Avignon, probably by Enguerrand Quarton, with a kneeling donor at the left. It is in the French painting galleries of the Louvre.

title: The Lamassu of Khorsabad, Assyrian palace guardians
desc: Human-headed winged bulls from Sargon II’s palace at Khorsabad, carved around 713–706 BCE and dug up by Paul-Émile Botta in the 1840s. They stand in the Assyrian courtyard of the Louvre.

title: The Presentation of the Portrait of Marie de’ Medici by Peter Paul Rubens
desc: Part of the cycle of 24 canvases Rubens painted for Marie de’ Medici’s Luxembourg Palace in the 1620s. The whole series now fills the Galerie Médicis in the Louvre.

title: The Plaque of the Ergastines, from the Parthenon frieze
desc: A slab from the east frieze of the Parthenon, about 445–438 BCE, showing young women who wove Athena’s robe. It is one of the few frieze pieces in Paris, in the Greek galleries of the Louvre.

title: Charles I at the Hunt by Anthony van Dyck
desc: Van Dyck painted Charles I around 1635 in hunting dress beside his horse, relaxed yet commanding. It is in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: The Niobid Krater by the Niobid Painter
desc: An Athenian red-figure krater of about 460 BCE, found at Orvieto, with figures placed at different levels across the surface. It is in the Greek galleries of the Louvre on the Right Bank.

title: Et in Arcadia Ego by Nicolas Poussin
desc: Poussin painted this second version around 1638, with shepherds tracing the words on a tomb in an ideal landscape. It is in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: The Baptistère de Saint Louis by Muhammad ibn al-Zayn
desc: Made in Egypt or Syria around 1320–40 and inlaid with silver and gold, the basin was used for royal baptisms in France. It is in the Islamic art galleries of the Louvre.

title: The Barberini Ivory, a Byzantine imperial panel
desc: A sixth-century ivory from Constantinople, probably showing Justinian, later owned by the Barberini family in Rome. It is in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: The Oath of the Horatii by Jacques-Louis David
desc: David painted it in Rome and showed it at the Paris Salon in 1785, a severe Neoclassical scene a few years before the Revolution. It is in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: Liberty Leading the People by Eugène Delacroix
desc: Delacroix painted it in 1830 after three days of street fighting toppled Charles X; Notre-Dame is visible in the smoke. It is in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: The Code of Hammurabi, a Babylonian law stele
desc: A basalt stele of about 1750 BCE topped by Hammurabi before the sun god, with nearly 300 laws below. Found at Susa in 1901, it is in the Near Eastern galleries of the Louvre.

title: Self-Portrait with Her Daughter Julie by Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun
desc: Vigée Le Brun, painter to Marie Antoinette, showed this tender double portrait at the Salon of 1789. It is in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: Seated Gudea Holding a Temple Plan, a Sumerian statue
desc: Carved in hard black diorite around 2100 BCE, Gudea of Lagash holds a ground plan of the temple he built. It is in the Near Eastern galleries of the Louvre on the Right Bank.

title: The Virgin and Child of Jeanne d’Évreux, a silver statuette
desc: A gilded silver statuette that Queen Jeanne d’Évreux gave to the abbey of Saint-Denis in 1339, with a lily that once held a relic. It is in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: The Lady of Auxerre, an early Greek statuette
desc: A limestone figure of about 650–625 BCE in the early Greek Daedalic style, found in a store of the Auxerre museum in 1907. It is in the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: The Winged Victory of Samothrace
desc: A Hellenistic marble found in pieces on the Greek island of Samothrace in 1863, probably marking a naval victory. It stands at the head of the Daru staircase in the Louvre, the former royal palace.

title: The Harbaville Triptych, a Byzantine ivory altarpiece
desc: A tenth-century Byzantine ivory with Christ, Mary, John the Baptist and rows of saints, small enough for private prayer. It is in the Louvre’s objets d’art department, the former royal palace that became France’s national museum.

title: Bonaparte Visiting the Plague Victims of Jaffa by Antoine-Jean Gros
desc: Painted in 1804 to answer reports that Bonaparte had abandoned his sick soldiers in Palestine. It shows him calmly touching a sore. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace that became France’s national museum.

title: The Seated Scribe, an ancient Egyptian statue
desc: A painted limestone figure from Saqqara, made around 2600 BCE, with eyes of inlaid rock crystal. It is in the Egyptian galleries of the Louvre, the former royal palace on the Right Bank.

title: Women of Algiers in Their Apartment by Eugène Delacroix
desc: Delacroix travelled to North Africa in 1832 and based this 1834 painting on sketches made in a house in Algiers. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace that became France’s national museum.

title: Grande Odalisque by Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres
desc: Ingres painted this harem woman in 1814 for Napoleon’s sister Caroline. Critics complained she had extra vertebrae. It hangs in the Louvre, the former royal palace that became France’s national museum.

title: The Massacre at Chios by Eugène Delacroix
desc: Delacroix showed this canvas at the 1824 Salon, two years after Ottoman troops killed and enslaved thousands on the Greek island of Chios. It hangs in the Louvre’s large-format French paintings galleries.

title: The Red Rock by Paul Cézanne
desc: A Cézanne landscape from around 1895, from the collection of the dealer Paul Guillaume. It hangs in the Musée de l’Orangerie, the gallery in the Tuileries garden best known for Monet’s water lilies.

title: The Argenteuil Bridge by Claude Monet
desc: Monet painted the bridge at Argenteuil, the Seine town where he lived in the 1870s, with quick broken strokes on the water. This 1874 canvas hangs in the Musée d’Orsay on Paris’s Left Bank.

title: The Balcony by Édouard Manet
desc: Manet’s 1868–69 painting includes the painter Berthe Morisot seated at the green railing. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay, the former railway station on Paris’s Left Bank.

title: Portrait of Émile Zola by Édouard Manet
desc: Manet’s 1868 portrait of Zola at his desk, with a print of Olympia and a Japanese woodblock pinned up behind. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay, the former railway station on Paris’s Left Bank.

title: The Bellelli Family by Edgar Degas
desc: Degas painted his aunt’s family in Florence in the late 1850s, the husband turned away from his wife and daughters. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay, the former railway station on Paris’s Left Bank.

title: The Dance by Jean-Baptiste Carpeaux
desc: Carpeaux’s 1869 group for the façade of the Paris Opera was attacked as indecent and once splashed with ink. The original was moved indoors and is in the Musée d’Orsay; a copy stands on the Opera.

title: Luxe, Calme et Volupté by Henri Matisse
desc: Matisse’s 1904 painting of Saint-Tropez in Neo-Impressionist dabs, titled after a line by Baudelaire. It belongs to the national modern art collection and hangs in the Musée d’Orsay on Paris’s Left Bank.

title: The Angelus by Jean-François Millet
desc: Millet’s 1857–59 painting of a couple bowed over a potato field at dusk; later reproduced on countless plates and prints. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay, the former railway station on Paris’s Left Bank.

title: Ploughing in the Nivernais by Rosa Bonheur
desc: Bonheur’s 1849 state commission, a large frieze of oxen made after close study of animals in the field. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay, the former railway station on Paris’s Left Bank.

title: The Gleaners by Jean-François Millet
desc: Millet’s 1857 painting of gleaners, with a big harvest piled up in the distance. Critics saw it as a political picture. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay, the former railway station on Paris’s Left Bank.

title: Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe by Édouard Manet
desc: Rejected by the official Salon, Manet’s painting was the scandal of the 1863 Salon des Refusés. It is in the Musée d’Orsay on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: The Floor Scrapers by Gustave Caillebotte
desc: Caillebotte’s 1875 painting was turned down by the Salon as vulgar and shown instead with the Impressionists. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay, the former railway station on Paris’s Left Bank.

title: Romans of the Decadence by Thomas Couture
desc: Couture’s huge 1847 Salon painting, a warning about moral decline aimed at his own time; the state bought it. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay, Paris’s 19th-century art museum in a former railway station on the Left Bank.

title: The Cradle by Berthe Morisot
desc: Morisot painted her sister Edma with her newborn daughter in 1872 and showed it at the first Impressionist exhibition. It is in the Musée d’Orsay on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: A Burial at Ornans by Gustave Courbet
desc: Courbet painted the townspeople of Ornans, his home in eastern France, life-size in 1849–50, shocking critics used to heroes at that scale. It is in the Musée d’Orsay on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: The Painter’s Studio by Gustave Courbet
desc: A huge canvas from 1855 that Courbet called a “real allegory” of seven years of his life, with friends on one side and society on the other. It is in the Musée d’Orsay on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: Hunting Butterflies by Berthe Morisot
desc: Painted in 1874, the year Morisot showed at the first Impressionist exhibition, it shows her sister Edma and Edma’s daughters. It is in the Musée d’Orsay on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette by Pierre-Auguste Renoir
desc: Renoir painted the crowd at the open-air dance hall by the Moulin de la Galette in 1876, many of them his friends. It is in the Musée d’Orsay on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: The Basin at Argenteuil by Claude Monet
desc: Monet lived in Argenteuil, a short train ride from Paris, and painted this promenade by the Seine in 1872. It is in the Musée d’Orsay on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: The Swing by Pierre-Auguste Renoir
desc: Renoir painted this in 1876 in the overgrown garden of his rue Cortot studio, with dappled light scattered over the figures. It is in the Musée d’Orsay on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: The Gare Saint-Lazare by Claude Monet
desc: One of a dozen views Monet painted of the Saint-Lazare station in 1877. It hangs in the Musée d’Orsay, itself a converted railway station on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: Still Life with Chair Caning by Pablo Picasso
desc: Made in 1912, it is often called the first collage in modern art. It is in the Musée national Picasso, housed in the Hôtel Salé, a 17th-century mansion in the Marais.

title: Notre-Dame de Paris, a Gothic cathedral
desc: Begun in 1163, Notre-Dame was filmed here before the April 2019 fire that brought down its spire; it reopened in December 2024. It stands on the Île de la Cité in the Seine.

title: The Porte Dauphine Métro Entrance by Hector Guimard
desc: Guimard designed the green Art Nouveau entrances for the Paris Métro from 1900. Dozens survive; Porte Dauphine keeps one of the two original glass-roofed pavilions, at the edge of the 16th arrondissement.

title: The Eiffel Tower by Gustave Eiffel
desc: Eiffel’s company put up the 300-metre tower for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, meaning it to stand for only twenty years. It rises over the Champ de Mars on the Left Bank of the Seine.

title: Jupiter and Semele by Gustave Moreau
desc: One of Moreau’s last great paintings, finished in 1895 and crowded with jewel-like detail. It hangs in the Musée Gustave Moreau, the artist’s own house and studio on rue de La Rochefoucauld in the 9th arrondissement.

title: The Arrival of Marie de’ Medici at Marseilles by Peter Paul Rubens
desc: Marie de Medici landed at the old port in November 1600 on her way to marry Henri IV. Two decades later Rubens painted the arrival for her palace in Paris, adding Neptune and naked sea nymphs. Two art historians unpack the political flattery.

title: Viaduct at L’Estaque by Georges Braque
desc: In 1908 Georges Braque painted the hillside village of L’Estaque, on the city’s northern shore, following Cézanne who had worked there before him. Two art historians look at how the viaduct and houses collapse into simple geometric volumes.

title: The Death of Marat by Jacques-Louis David
place: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
desc: Two art historians look closely at Jacques-Louis David’s 1793 painting of Jean-Paul Marat, stabbed in his bath by Charlotte Corday. The canvas hangs in the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, on Rue de la Régence.

title: Still Life with a Silver Ewer by Willem Kalf
desc: Kalf painted luxury objects from Dutch trade, including Chinese porcelain, around 1655–60. It is in the Rijksmuseum, the national museum on Museumplein.

title: The Potato Eaters by Vincent van Gogh
desc: This video from Smarthistory analyzes The Potato Eaters, a memorable canvas at the Van Gogh Museum. The art historians explain Van Gogh’s penchant for painting peasants and how his rough brush strokes evoke the hardscrabble life of the family pictured.

title: Self-Portrait (Les Misérables) by Paul Gauguin
desc: Gauguin painted it in Brittany in 1888 and sent it to Vincent van Gogh in an exchange of portraits. It is in the Van Gogh Museum on Museumplein.

title: Interior of Saint Bavo, Haarlem by Pieter Saenredam
desc: A quick jaunt from Amsterdam, the old town of Haarlem spills out from a lovely square with Saint Bavo Church at its center. This Smarthistory video explains Pieter Saenredamthe’s meticulous 1631 painting of the church during the town’s cultural heyday.

title: The Tempest by Giorgione
desc: Giorgione’s small canvas of a soldier, a nursing mother and a lightning bolt has resisted every attempt at a single meaning. Two art historians look closely at it in the Gallerie dell’Accademia, the city’s main museum of Venetian painting.

title: The Feast in the House of Levi by Paolo Veronese
desc: In 1573 Veronese was questioned over the dogs, dwarfs and drunken soldiers in his Last Supper. Rather than repaint it, he changed the title. The huge canvas, painted for a Dominican refectory, now fills a wall of the Gallerie dell’Accademia museum.

title: The Pesaro Madonna by Titian
place: Frari church (Santa Maria Gloriosa dei Frari)
desc: Jacopo Pesaro, a bishop who led a papal fleet against the Ottomans, paid for this altarpiece and had his relatives kneel in it. Titian moved the Virgin off centre, a bold break. It still hangs on the altar it was made for, in the Frari church.

title: The Tetrarchs, four Roman co-emperors in porphyry
desc: This purple porphyry group of four co-rulers was carved around 300 AD and taken from Constantinople by Venetian crusaders in 1204. It is set into the outer corner of St Mark’s Basilica beside the Doge’s Palace gate. One missing foot was found in Istanbul.

title: The Crucifixion of Saint Peter by Caravaggio
desc: Caravaggio painted this in 1600–01 for the Cerasi Chapel, opposite his Conversion of Saint Paul. It is still in place in Santa Maria del Popolo, the church beside the Piazza del Popolo city gate.

title: Narcissus by Caravaggio
desc: A painting from the late 1590s attributed to Caravaggio, with the youth and his reflection forming a closed circle. It hangs in the Gallerie Nazionali at Palazzo Barberini, the Baroque palace near Piazza Barberini.

title: The Chair of Saint Peter by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
place: Chair of St Peter, St Peter’s Basilica
desc: Bernini’s 1657–66 monument encases a wooden chair said to be Saint Peter’s, held up by four Church Fathers below a window of the Holy Spirit. It fills the apse of Saint Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City.

title: St Peter’s Basilica, from Bramante to Bernini
desc: Bramante began rebuilding Saint Peter’s in 1506; Michelangelo, Maderno and Bernini followed. The basilica stands over the traditional tomb of Saint Peter in Vatican City.

title: Santa Prassede, a ninth-century mosaic church
desc: A 9th-century church built by Pope Paschal I, known for its apse mosaics and the small gold-lined Chapel of San Zeno. It is on a side street near Santa Maria Maggiore on the Esquiline hill.

title: Medusa by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
desc: A marble bust of the snake-haired gorgon from the 1640s, attributed to Bernini, with a look of shock on her face. It is in the Capitoline Museums on Michelangelo’s Piazza del Campidoglio.

title: The Tempietto by Donato Bramante
place: Bramante’s Tempietto, San Pietro in Montorio
desc: Bramante’s little domed shrine of around 1502 stands in a cloister courtyard and set a model for Renaissance architecture. It is at San Pietro in Montorio on the Janiculum hill above Trastevere.

title: The Garden Room of the Villa of Livia
desc: A fresco garden from around 30–20 BCE that once lined a sunken dining room at the villa of Livia, wife of Augustus. The whole room was moved to Palazzo Massimo, the National Roman Museum near Termini station.

title: Saint Stanislas Kostka on His Deathbed by Pierre Legros the Younger
place: Rooms of St Stanislas Kostka, Sant’Andrea al Quirinale
desc: A 1702–03 statue of the Polish novice Stanislas Kostka, with a black marble robe and white face, in the rooms where he died in 1568. It is in the novitiate beside Sant’Andrea al Quirinale.

title: Sant’Andrea al Quirinale by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
desc: A small Jesuit church of 1658–70 that Bernini considered his best work; the oval is entered on its long side, so it feels wide rather than deep. It is on Via del Quirinale, across from the Quirinal Palace.

title: The Boxer at Rest, a Hellenistic bronze
desc: A Greek bronze from the Hellenistic period with a broken nose, cauliflower ears and inlaid copper blood. Found on the Quirinal hill in 1885, it is in Palazzo Massimo, the National Roman Museum near Termini station.

title: The Triumph of Galatea by Raphael
desc: Raphael’s fresco of around 1512 for the banker Agostino Chigi’s riverside villa, with cupids aiming arrows from the sky. It is in the Villa Farnesina in Trastevere, on the west bank of the Tiber.

title: The Glorification of Saint Ignatius by Andrea Pozzo
desc: Pozzo’s 1691–94 nave fresco sends Saint Ignatius into heaven through painted architecture; a marble disc in the floor marks where the illusion works best. It is in the church of Sant’Ignazio near the Pantheon.

title: The Apoxyomenos (Scraper), after Lysippos
desc: A Roman marble copy of a bronze by Lysippos, about 330 BCE, found in Trastevere in 1849. It is in the Vatican Museums, in the Pio-Clementino galleries of ancient sculpture.

title: The Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus
desc: A 3rd-century sarcophagus with a crowded scene of Roman soldiers routing Goths, a calm general on horseback at its centre. It is in Palazzo Altemps, a branch of the National Roman Museum near Piazza Navona.

title: Achilles and Ajax Playing a Game by Exekias
desc: A black-figure amphora signed by the Athenian potter and painter Exekias around 540–530 BCE, found in an Etruscan tomb at Vulci. It is in the Gregorian Etruscan Museum of the Vatican Museums.

title: The Chapel of Saint Ignatius by Andrea Pozzo
place: Chapel of St Ignatius, Church of the Gesù
desc: Pozzo designed this lavish altar chapel in the 1690s, where Saint Ignatius of Loyola is buried. It is in the left transept of the Gesù, the Jesuits’ mother church on Rome’s Piazza del Gesù.

title: The Baldacchino by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
desc: Bernini’s bronze canopy, finished in 1634, stands nearly 30 metres high over the high altar and the tomb of Saint Peter. It is under Michelangelo’s dome in St Peter’s Basilica.

title: The Capitoline Brutus, an ancient bronze head
desc: A bronze head of about 300 BCE traditionally identified as Lucius Junius Brutus, founder of the Republic. It is in the Capitoline Museums on the Campidoglio.

title: The Pantheon
desc: Built under Hadrian around 125 CE, its unreinforced concrete dome is still the world’s largest, with a nine-metre oculus. It became a church in 609 and stands on Piazza della Rotonda.

title: The Basilica of Maxentius and Constantine
desc: Begun by Maxentius around 308 CE and finished by Constantine, it once held a colossal statue of the emperor. The coffered vaults of one aisle still stand on the Via Sacra in the Roman Forum.

title: The Sistine Chapel Ceiling by Michelangelo
desc: Painted for Pope Julius II from 1508 to 1512, with nine scenes from Genesis framed by prophets and sibyls. It is the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican.

title: The Last Judgment by Pietro Cavallini
desc: Cavallini painted this fresco around 1293, and it was only uncovered in 1900 behind later choir stalls. It is in the nuns’ choir of Santa Cecilia in Trastevere.

title: The Last Judgment by Michelangelo
desc: Painted from 1536 to 1541, more than twenty years after the ceiling, with a flayed skin that may be Michelangelo’s self-portrait. It is the altar wall of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican.

title: Trajan’s Markets by Apollodorus of Damascus
desc: Built around 100–110 CE by Apollodorus of Damascus, the curving brick complex held shops and offices over several levels. It rises above Trajan’s Forum on the slope of the Quirinal.

title: The Catacombs of Priscilla
desc: Miles of tunnels used for burials from the second to fifth centuries, with what may be the oldest known painting of Mary. The entrance is on the Via Salaria, north of the centre.

title: The Spoils of Jerusalem Relief on the Arch of Titus
desc: A relief inside the arch built after 81 CE to honour Titus, showing loot from the Temple after Jerusalem fell in 70 CE. The arch stands on the Via Sacra at the edge of the Roman Forum.

title: The Sarcophagus of the Spouses
desc: A painted terracotta coffin of about 520 BCE from Cerveteri, the man’s arm around his wife. It is in the National Etruscan Museum at Villa Giulia, near the Borghese gardens.

title: The Capitoline Venus, a Roman marble copy
desc: A marble copy of a Greek original related to Praxiteles’ Aphrodite of Knidos, found in Rome in the 1660s. It has its own small room in the Capitoline Museums on the Campidoglio.

title: Moses and the Tomb of Julius II by Michelangelo
desc: Planned in 1505 as a huge freestanding monument, Julius II’s tomb ended up a wall tomb decades later, with Moses at its centre. It is in San Pietro in Vincoli on the Esquiline Hill.

title: The Arch of Constantine
desc: Dedicated in 315 CE after Constantine’s victory at the Milvian Bridge, it reuses reliefs taken from monuments of earlier emperors. It stands beside the Colosseum.

title: The Apollo of Veii, an Etruscan terracotta statue
desc: A life-size painted terracotta Apollo of about 510–500 BCE from the temple at Veii, north of Rome. It is in the National Etruscan Museum at Villa Giulia, near the Borghese gardens.

title: Apollo and Daphne by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
desc: Bernini carved it for Cardinal Scipione Borghese in 1622–25, with leaves and roots sprouting from her fingers and toes. It is in the Galleria Borghese, the cardinal’s villa in the Borghese gardens.

title: The Santa Maria Antiqua Sarcophagus, an early Christian coffin
desc: An early Christian sarcophagus of about 270 CE that mixes biblical scenes with pagan imagery. It is kept in Santa Maria Antiqua, a buried and restored church in the Roman Forum.

title: The Conversion of Saint Paul by Caravaggio
desc: Painted in 1601 for the Cerasi Chapel, opposite Caravaggio’s Crucifixion of Saint Peter, with a horse filling most of the canvas. It is in Santa Maria del Popolo, beside Piazza del Popolo.

title: The Rape of Proserpina by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
desc: Bernini carved this abduction for Cardinal Scipione Borghese in 1621–22, when he was in his early twenties. It is in the Galleria Borghese, the cardinal’s villa in the Borghese gardens.

title: The Dying Gaul and the Ludovisi Gaul, Roman marble copies
desc: Marble copies of bronzes made for Pergamon around 220 BCE, showing Celtic warriors in defeat. The Dying Gaul is in the Capitoline Museums; the Ludovisi Gaul is in Palazzo Altemps.

title: Santa Maria Antiqua, a sixth-century church in the Forum
desc: A sixth-century church built into imperial buildings at the foot of the Palatine, sealed by a collapse in 847 and dug out in 1900. It is in the Roman Forum.

title: St Peter’s Square by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
desc: Built from 1656 to 1667, the oval piazza is ringed by four rows of columns topped with saints, with an Egyptian obelisk at the centre. It is in front of St Peter’s Basilica in Vatican City.

title: The Fonseca Bust, a Flavian woman’s portrait
desc: A marble bust of about 90 CE, its towering hairstyle carved with a drill, the fashion of Domitian’s court. It is in the Capitoline Museums on the Campidoglio.

title: The Decemviri Altarpiece by Perugino
desc: Perugino painted this Madonna and saints for the town council of Perugia in 1495–96. French troops took it in 1797, and its main panel never went back. It hangs in the Pinacoteca, the picture gallery of the Vatican Museums.

title: Castel Sant’Angelo, Hadrian’s Mausoleum
desc: Built as Hadrian’s mausoleum in the 130s, later turned into a fortress, prison and refuge for popes, linked to the Vatican by a raised corridor. It stands on the Tiber’s right bank, facing the Ponte Sant’Angelo.

title: The Colosseum
desc: Opened in 80 by Emperor Titus on the site of Nero’s palace lake, with seating for around 50,000. Later it was mined for building stone. It stands at the east end of the Roman Forum.

title: The Arch of Septimius Severus
place: Arch of Septimius Severus, Roman Forum
desc: A triple arch from 203 celebrating Septimius Severus and his sons over the Parthians. One son’s name was later chiselled out after his brother had him killed. It stands at the northwest end of the Roman Forum.

title: The Roman Forum
desc: For centuries this drained valley between the Capitoline and Palatine hills was where Romans voted, traded, heard speeches and worshipped. The ruins are entered from Via dei Fori Imperiali or near the Colosseum.

title: The Augustus of Primaporta
desc: A marble statue found in 1863 at the villa of Livia, Augustus’ wife, north of Rome. Its breastplate shows the return of Roman standards from Parthia. It stands in the Braccio Nuovo of the Vatican Museums.

title: The Ara Pacis, Augustus’s Altar of Peace
desc: An altar to peace dedicated in 9 BCE, carved with the emperor’s family in procession and scenes of plenty. It was pieced back together in the 1930s and sits in Richard Meier’s glass museum beside the Mausoleum of Augustus.

title: The Spinario (Boy with Thorn), an ancient bronze
desc: A bronze of a boy picking a thorn from his foot, on view in Rome since the Middle Ages and much copied in the Renaissance. It is in the Capitoline Museums, in the Palazzo dei Conservatori on the Capitoline Hill.

title: The Church of the Gesù by Giacomo da Vignola and Giacomo della Porta
desc: The Jesuits’ main church, begun in 1568, with a wide open nave for preaching and a painted ceiling where figures seem to spill out of the frame. It stands on Piazza del Gesù, just off Via del Plebiscito.

title: Landscape with the Flight into Egypt by Annibale Carracci
desc: Painted around 1604 for a chapel in the Aldobrandini palace, it helped set the model for the ideal classical landscape. It now hangs in the Galleria Doria Pamphilj, a private palace gallery on Via del Corso.

title: Trajan’s Column
desc: Finished in 113, its frieze winds 23 times around the shaft with scenes of Trajan’s wars in Dacia. The emperor’s ashes were placed in its base. It stands at the edge of Trajan’s Forum, near Piazza Venezia.

title: The Chapel of San Venanzio, lined with seventh-century mosaics
place: Chapel of San Venanzio, Lateran Baptistery
desc: Pope John IV, from Dalmatia, built this chapel in the 640s for relics of martyrs from Salona and covered it in mosaics. It opens off the Lateran Baptistery beside the Archbasilica of St. John Lateran.

title: The Apse Mosaic of Santa Pudenziana
desc: The apse mosaic of this church, from around 400, is one of the oldest in Rome, showing Christ enthroned before a city skyline. The church sits below street level on Via Urbana, near Santa Maria Maggiore.

title: The Mausoleum of Santa Costanza
desc: This round fourth-century mausoleum was built for Constantina, daughter of Constantine, and later became a church. Its vault mosaics of grape harvests survive. It is on Via Nomentana beside Sant’Agnese fuori le Mura.

title: The Lateran Obelisk, made for Pharaoh Thutmose III
place: Lateran Obelisk, Piazza San Giovanni in Laterano
desc: Made for Thutmose III at Karnak, shipped to Rome for the Circus Maximus in 357, then dug up and re-erected by Pope Sixtus V in 1588. It stands in the piazza beside San Giovanni in Laterano.

title: The Mosaics of Santa Maria Maggiore
desc: The nave mosaics date from the 430s, while the golden apse showing Mary crowned in heaven was added in the 1290s. Santa Maria Maggiore is one of Rome’s four papal basilicas, on the Esquiline Hill.

title: The Equestrian Statue of Marcus Aurelius
desc: The only bronze equestrian statue to survive from ancient Rome, spared because it was thought to show Constantine. The original is indoors in the Capitoline Museums; a copy stands on Michelangelo’s piazza outside.

title: Trajan’s Forum by Apollodorus of Damascus
desc: The last and largest of the imperial forums, paid for with plunder from Trajan’s wars in Dacia and finished around 112. Its column and the remains of the basilica stand beside Via dei Fori Imperiali.

title: The Pietà by Michelangelo
desc: Michelangelo carved the marble in his early twenties, around 1498–99. It is the only work he ever signed. It sits behind glass in the first chapel on the right in St. Peter’s Basilica.

title: The Sarcophagus of Junius Bassus
desc: Junius Bassus, prefect of Rome, died in 359 as a new Christian convert. His marble sarcophagus mixes Roman forms with scenes from both Testaments. It is kept in the Treasury museum of St. Peter’s Basilica.

title: The Odyssey Landscapes, Roman wall paintings
desc: These first-century BCE wall paintings were found in a house on the Esquiline Hill in 1848 and show scenes from the Odyssey in sweeping landscapes. They are now in the Vatican Museums.

title: Laocoön and His Sons, an ancient marble group
desc: The sculpture was dug up in a Roman vineyard in 1506, with Michelangelo among those sent to see it. Pope Julius II bought it, and it still stands in the Octagonal Court of the Vatican Museums.

title: The Colossus of Constantine
place: Palazzo dei Conservatori courtyard, Capitoline Museums
desc: The pieces of a seated statue of Constantine, once about twelve metres tall, were found in the Basilica of Maxentius. The head, hand and feet now line the courtyard of Palazzo dei Conservatori, part of the Capitoline Museums.

title: Santa Sabina, an early Christian basilica
desc: Santa Sabina on the Aventine Hill is one of the best-preserved early Christian basilicas: a plain brick outside, rows of reused Roman columns and clear light within. Its carved wooden doors include one of the earliest surviving images of the Crucifixion.

title: The MAXXI Museum by Zaha Hadid
desc: MAXXI, Italy’s national museum of contemporary art and architecture, opened in 2010 in the Flaminio district. Its curving concrete galleries and black stairs overlap and cross each other, built on the site of a former military barracks.

title: The School of Athens by Raphael
desc: Plato and Aristotle stride through a vast vaulted hall surrounded by Greek thinkers, some given the faces of Raphael’s contemporaries. The fresco covers a wall of the Stanza della Segnatura, one of the Raphael Rooms in the Vatican Museums.

title: The Temple of Portunus
desc: This compact temple to Portunus, god of harbours, stood beside Rome’s river port and cattle market, the Forum Boarium. It survived largely intact because it was turned into a church, and it shows Romans pairing Greek columns with an Etruscan-style podium.

title: The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
place: Cornaro Chapel, Santa Maria della Vittoria
desc: Bernini built the Cornaro Chapel as a complete stage set, with hidden windows lighting the marble saint and an angel holding an arrow. Cornaro family members watch from carved boxes on the walls of Santa Maria della Vittoria, a small church near Termini.

title: The Loves of the Gods (Farnese Ceiling) by Annibale Carracci
desc: Annibale Carracci, helped by his brother Agostino, filled the gallery of Palazzo Farnese with the loves of the gods, painted as if they were framed pictures hung on the vault. The palace is now the French embassy and opens only for booked tours.

title: David by Gian Lorenzo Bernini
desc: Bernini was in his mid-twenties when he carved this David for Cardinal Scipione Borghese. Unlike Michelangelo’s calm hero, his figure twists in the instant before the stone flies. It stands in the Galleria Borghese, the cardinal’s villa museum.

title: The Calling of Saint Matthew by Caravaggio
desc: Caravaggio’s first big public commission still hangs where he painted it, in the Contarelli Chapel of San Luigi dei Francesi, the French national church. Christ points at a group of men counting money in a dim room, and one of them is about to be chosen.

title: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane by Francesco Borromini
place: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane church
desc: Borromini’s first church fits on a cramped crossroads plot about the size of one of St Peter’s piers. Its walls ripple in and out and its oval dome is coffered with crosses, octagons and hexagons that shrink as they rise toward the lantern.

title: The Flagellation of Christ by Caravaggio
desc: Caravaggio painted it in 1607 after fleeing Rome on a murder charge, for a chapel in San Domenico Maggiore. It now hangs in the Museo di Capodimonte, the former Bourbon palace on the hill above the city.

title: Woman with Wax Tablets and Stylus, a Pompeian fresco
desc: A small round fresco found in a house in Pompeii, showing a woman holding wax tablets and a stylus. It is in the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, which holds most of the finds from the buried towns.

title: The Doryphoros (Spear Bearer), after Polykleitos
desc: Polykleitos’s bronze spear bearer, made around 450 BCE, was meant to embody perfect proportion. The best surviving copy, carved in marble, came out of a sports ground in Pompeii and stands in the National Archaeological Museum.

title: The Farnese Hercules, after a bronze by Lysippos
desc: A giant Roman marble copy of a lost bronze by Lysippos, found in Rome’s Baths of Caracalla in the 1540s. It passed from the Farnese family to the Bourbon kings, and so to the National Archaeological Museum in Naples.

title: The Alexander Mosaic, from Pompeii’s House of the Faun
desc: This floor mosaic of Alexander the Great routing the Persian king Darius was dug up in Pompeii’s House of the Faun in 1841 and moved to Naples two years later. It now fills a wall of the National Archaeological Museum.

title: Imperial War Museum North by Daniel Libeskind
place: Imperial War Museum North, Salford Quays
desc: Daniel Libeskind designed the museum, opened in 2002, as three curved fragments of a shattered globe. It stands on the Manchester Ship Canal at Salford Quays, opposite the Lowry arts centre.

title: Work by Ford Madox Brown
desc: Ford Madox Brown spent more than a decade on this crowded picture of Victorian society, finished in 1865. It is in Manchester Art Gallery on Mosley Street, near St Peter’s Square.

title: All Saints, Margaret Street by William Butterfield
desc: Butterfield’s Gothic Revival church of 1850–59, built in red and black brick with a richly decorated interior and tall spire. It is on Margaret Street, a short walk north of Oxford Circus.

title: The Black George, a Russian icon of Saint George
desc: A late 14th-century Russian icon of Saint George on horseback, named for the black paint that covered it before cleaning. It is in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: The Triumph of Orthodoxy, a Byzantine icon
desc: A Byzantine icon from around 1400 marking the restoration of icon veneration in 843, after the Iconoclasm. It is in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: Adam and Eve by Lucas Cranach the Elder
desc: Cranach’s 1526 panel of the Fall, with Adam scratching his head and a stag in the Eden thicket. It is in the Courtauld Gallery at Somerset House on the Strand.

title: Nevermore by Paul Gauguin
desc: Gauguin painted this in Tahiti in 1897, naming it after Edgar Allan Poe’s poem The Raven. It is in the Courtauld Gallery at Somerset House on the Strand.

title: Girl at a Window by Rembrandt
desc: Rembrandt’s 1645 painting, once said to have been put in a window to fool passers-by. It hangs in Dulwich Picture Gallery, England’s first public art gallery, in south London.

title: Still Life with Plaster Cupid by Paul Cézanne
desc: Cézanne’s 1894 still life combines a studio cast with paintings leaning against the wall. It is in the Courtauld Gallery at Somerset House on the Strand.

title: Emanuele Filiberto of Savoy by Anthony van Dyck
desc: Van Dyck painted the Viceroy of Sicily in Palermo in 1624, shortly before he died of plague. It hangs in Dulwich Picture Gallery, England’s first public art gallery, in south London.

title: Metamorphosis of Narcissus by Salvador Dalí
desc: Dalí’s 1937 painting, with a poem of his own, which he took with him to meet Sigmund Freud in London in 1938. It is in Tate Modern, the gallery in the former Bankside power station.

title: Standing by the Rags by Lucian Freud
desc: Freud’s large 1988–89 painting uses the pile of paint rags in his studio as a backdrop for the figure. It is in the Tate collection, shown at Tate Britain at Millbank.

title: The Vale of Rest by John Everett Millais
desc: Millais’s 1858 painting of a nun digging in a convent graveyard while another watches, with an ominous cloud overhead. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art on the Thames at Millbank.

title: Triptych – August 1972 by Francis Bacon
desc: Bacon painted this triptych after the death of George Dyer in Paris in 1971, the night before a big Bacon retrospective opened. It is in the Tate collection, shown at Tate Britain at Millbank.

title: King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid by Edward Burne-Jones
desc: Burne-Jones’s 1884 painting of the legend of a king who fell in love with a poor girl, set in a dark, rich interior. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art at Millbank.

title: Claudio and Isabella by William Holman Hunt
desc: Hunt’s scene from Shakespeare’s Measure for Measure, painted 1850–53, shows Claudio asking his sister to give up her honour to save him. It hangs in Tate Britain at Millbank.

title: Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose by John Singer Sargent
desc: Sargent painted this in the Cotswold village of Broadway in 1885–86, working only a few minutes each evening as the light faded. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art at Millbank.

title: Chatterton by Henry Wallis
desc: Wallis’s 1856 painting of Thomas Chatterton, who died at 17 in 1770; the model was the writer George Meredith. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art on the Thames at Millbank.

title: Titania and Bottom by Henry Fuseli
desc: Fuseli’s dreamlike scene from Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, painted around 1790. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art on the Thames at Millbank.

title: Thoughts of the Past by John Roddam Spencer Stanhope
desc: Stanhope’s 1859 Pre-Raphaelite painting of a woman by a window on the Thames, with coins and flowers scattered at her feet. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art at Millbank.

title: An Athlete Wrestling with a Python by Frederic Leighton
desc: Leighton’s 1877 bronze, the painter’s first full sculpture, launched the New Sculpture movement. It is in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art on the Thames at Millbank.

title: The Golden Stairs by Edward Burne-Jones
desc: Burne-Jones’s 1880 painting, with no story at all, was meant to be like music. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art on the Thames at Millbank.

title: Our English Coasts (Strayed Sheep) by William Holman Hunt
desc: Hunt painted this 1852 view at Fairlight near Hastings, with intense colour and sunlight through the sheep’s ears. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art on the Thames at Millbank.

title: Christ in the House of His Parents by John Everett Millais
desc: Millais’s 1849–50 painting of the holy family as working people was savaged by Charles Dickens. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art on the Thames at Millbank.

title: Mariana by John Everett Millais
desc: Millais’s 1851 painting is based on Tennyson’s poem about a woman waiting for a man who does not come. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art on the Thames at Millbank.

title: Portrait of Pope Julius II by Raphael
desc: Raphael’s 1511 portrait of the pope who hired Michelangelo for the Sistine ceiling; the beard was a vow he took during his wars. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Virgin and Child with Saints Dominic and Aurea by Duccio
desc: A gold-ground triptych by the Sienese painter Duccio, around 1315, with prophets in the side panels. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: Corner of a Café-Concert by Édouard Manet
desc: Manet painted this scene of a café-concert in 1878–80, cut down from a larger canvas. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Burlington House Cartoon by Leonardo da Vinci
desc: A large drawing of the Virgin, Saint Anne and the infants Jesus and John, around 1500. It was bought for the nation in 1962 and was shot at in 1987. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Baptism of Christ by Piero della Francesca
desc: Piero’s panel of the 1440s, made for a church in his home town of Sansepolcro, with a Tuscan landscape behind. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Supper at Emmaus by Caravaggio
desc: Caravaggio’s 1601 painting shows a young, beardless Christ revealed at supper, with a fruit basket balanced on the table edge. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Awakening Conscience by William Holman Hunt
desc: Hunt’s 1853 painting of a young woman in a London villa, full of clues such as a cat with a bird. It hangs in Tate Britain, the gallery of British art on the Thames at Millbank.

title: Rain, Steam and Speed by J.M.W. Turner
desc: Turner’s 1844 painting of the Great Western Railway crossing Maidenhead Bridge, with a small hare running ahead. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: Lady Cockburn and Her Three Eldest Sons by Joshua Reynolds
desc: Reynolds’s 1773 portrait of Augusta Cockburn and her sons, borrowed from an old master idea of Charity. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: A Man with a Quilted Sleeve by Titian
desc: Titian’s portrait of around 1510, once thought to be the poet Ariosto, with the sitter turning over his shoulder. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: Bacchus and Ariadne by Titian
desc: Titian painted this for the Duke of Ferrara in 1520–23, with Bacchus’s noisy procession and cheetahs pulling his chariot. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Virgin and Child with Saints and Donor by Gerard David
desc: Gerard David’s panel of around 1510, with the donor Richard de Visch van der Capelle and saints in a garden. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: Bathers at Asnières by Georges Seurat
desc: Seurat’s first big painting, rejected by the 1884 Salon, shows men and boys on a riverbank west of Paris. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Family of Darius before Alexander by Paolo Veronese
desc: Veronese’s wide 1565–67 painting shows Darius’s family kneeling before Alexander and his friend, in Venetian costume. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: Cupid Complaining to Venus by Lucas Cranach the Elder
desc: Cranach’s painting of the 1520s shows Venus in a big hat beside Cupid holding a honeycomb, a lesson about pleasure and pain. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Origin of the Milky Way by Tintoretto
desc: Tintoretto’s painting of around 1575 shows Jupiter putting the baby Hercules to Juno’s breast, with milk spraying up into stars. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: Christina of Denmark, Duchess of Milan by Hans Holbein the Younger
desc: Holbein painted the young Duchess of Milan in mourning dress in 1538 when Henry VIII was looking for a new wife; she did not marry him. The portrait is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: Marriage A-la-Mode by William Hogarth
desc: Six paintings from about 1743 that Hogarth turned into best-selling prints, mocking a match between a broke earl’s son and a merchant’s daughter. They hang in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: Noli me Tangere by Titian
desc: An early Titian of around 1514, showing the risen Christ telling Mary not to touch him, with a Venetian landscape behind. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Vision of Saint Helena by Paolo Veronese
desc: Veronese painted the mother of Constantine asleep by a window, around 1570, as angels bring her a vision of the cross. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Battle of San Romano by Paolo Uccello
desc: One of three panels Uccello painted around 1438–40 of a Florentine victory over Siena; the others are in Florence and Paris. This one, with Niccolò da Tolentino leading the charge, is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Wilton Diptych
desc: A small folding altarpiece made around 1395–99 for Richard II, who kneels with his patron saints; the angels wear his white hart badge. It is in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Lion Hunt of Ashurbanipal, Assyrian palace reliefs
desc: Carved reliefs from the palace of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, around 645 BCE, show the king killing lions released from cages. They line a gallery in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: The Book of the Dead of Hunefer
desc: A painted sheet from the Book of the Dead of Hunefer, a royal scribe around 1275 BCE, showing his judgement before Osiris. It is in the Egyptian galleries of the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: The Palace of Westminster by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin
desc: After fire destroyed the old palace in 1834, Charles Barry planned the new building and Augustus Pugin drew its Gothic detail, down to the clock tower. It is the seat of Parliament beside the Thames.

title: The Lullingstone Busts, Roman marble portraits
desc: Two second-century marble busts, probably ancestors of a villa’s owners, were found in a cellar room at Lullingstone in Kent in 1949. They are now in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: Portrait of a Man in a Red Turban by Jan van Eyck
desc: Painted in 1433, the original frame carries Van Eyck’s motto, “As I can”, which is why many see a self-portrait. It hangs in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: An Allegory with Venus and Cupid by Bronzino
desc: Bronzino painted this cool, crowded allegory in Florence around 1545, probably as a gift from Cosimo de’ Medici to the French king. It hangs in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Parthenon Sculptures, also called the Elgin Marbles
desc: Pediment figures, metopes and frieze slabs carved under Phidias in the 440s–430s BCE, removed by Lord Elgin’s agents around 1801. They fill a long gallery in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère by Édouard Manet
desc: Manet’s last major painting, from 1882, sets a Paris music-hall barmaid before a mirror that does not quite add up. It is in the Courtauld Gallery at Somerset House on the Strand.

title: The Virgin and Child from the Pisa Altarpiece by Masaccio
desc: The central panel of an altarpiece Masaccio painted for a Pisa church in 1426, later broken up and scattered across Europe. It hangs in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Hay Wain by John Constable
desc: Constable painted this view of Flatford Mill in 1821; it was snubbed in London before winning a gold medal in Paris. It hangs in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Annunciation, with Saint Emidius by Carlo Crivelli
desc: Crivelli painted this Annunciation in 1486 for a church in Ascoli Piceno, packing a busy town street with carpets, birds and fruit. It hangs in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.

title: The Henry VII Lady Chapel, Westminster Abbey
place: Henry VII Lady Chapel, Westminster Abbey
desc: Henry VII built this Lady Chapel from 1503 as his own burial place, under a fan-vaulted ceiling with stone pendants. It sits at the east end of Westminster Abbey, where monarchs are crowned.

title: The Symmachi Panel, a late Roman ivory
desc: An ivory leaf carved around 400 CE for a Roman family that kept faith with the old gods, showing a priestess at an altar. It is in the V&A, the South Kensington museum of art and design.

title: The Sutton Hoo Ship Burial
desc: Dug from an East Anglian field in 1939, the seventh-century ship burial held a helmet, gold buckle and silver from as far as Byzantium. The finds are in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: The Archangel Michael Ivory, a Byzantine panel
desc: A large ivory panel from around 525, likely made in Constantinople, showing Michael holding an orb and staff at the top of a flight of steps. It is in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: The Lindisfarne Gospels
desc: A gospel book made on Holy Island around 700, credited to Bishop Eadfrith, with a later Old English translation squeezed between the lines. It is kept at the British Library on Euston Road, next to St Pancras station.

title: The Rosetta Stone
desc: A priests’ decree from 196 BCE written in hieroglyphs, demotic and Greek, found by French soldiers in 1799 and taken by the British in 1801. It is in the British Museum in Bloomsbury, in the Egyptian sculpture gallery.

title: The Swing by Jean-Honoré Fragonard
desc: A small Rococo painting from around 1767 of a young woman on a swing above a man in the bushes. Fragonard took the job after another painter refused. It hangs in the Wallace Collection, Hertford House on Manchester Square.

title: The Standard of Ur, a Sumerian inlaid box
desc: A small wooden box inlaid with shell, red limestone and lapis lazuli, found in a royal grave at Ur in Iraq and dating to about 2500 BCE. It is in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: The Holy Thorn Reliquary
desc: Made around 1400 for Jean, Duke of Berry, to hold a thorn said to come from Christ’s crown. It came to the museum in the Waddesdon Bequest and is on show in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: Chiswick House by Lord Burlington
desc: Lord Burlington designed this Palladian villa in the 1720s as a place for art, books and entertaining rather than living. The house and its gardens are open to visitors in Chiswick, west London.

title: Ophelia by John Everett Millais
desc: Millais painted the riverbank outdoors in Surrey and the figure in his studio, with model Elizabeth Siddal lying in a bath. The 1852 painting is one of the best-known works in Tate Britain on Millbank.

title: Pegwell Bay, Kent by William Dyce
desc: Dyce painted his family gathering shells under ancient chalk cliffs, with Donati’s comet faint in the evening sky. The painting is in Tate Britain, the national gallery of British art on Millbank.

title: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III
desc: A black limestone monument from Nimrud, about 825 BCE, listing the campaigns of Shalmaneser III. One panel shows King Jehu of Israel kneeling with tribute. It stands in the British Museum in Bloomsbury.

title: La Loge by Pierre-Auguste Renoir
desc: Renoir showed this 1874 picture of a fashionable woman and her opera-glass-wielding companion at the first Impressionist exhibition. It belongs to the Courtauld Gallery in Somerset House on the Strand.

title: The David Vases, Chinese porcelain dated 1351
desc: A pair of Chinese porcelain temple vases whose inscription dates them precisely, making them key to the history of blue-and-white ware. They are in the British Museum’s Chinese galleries in Bloomsbury.

title: The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck
desc: Van Eyck’s 1434 portrait of a Bruges merchant and his wife, signed on the wall above the convex mirror. Two art historians look closely at it in the National Gallery on Trafalgar Square.
