desc: The title is a girl’s name meaning ‘rose-pink’ — an elegy for a childhood friend who died young. Barış Manço, the mustachioed uncle of Turkish rock, lived in this Moda mansion, now a museum devoted to him.

title: Suspus
creator: Ceza
desc: The title means ‘Dead Silent.’ Ceza, born across the water in Üsküdar, raps in rapid-fire Turkish and helped found the country’s hip-hop. His home district on the Asian shore is stamped through his work.

title: Şehnaz Longa
creator: Selim Sesler
desc: A ‘longa’ is the fast instrumental finale of the fasıl suite. Selim Sesler, the Roma clarinet master who came to Istanbul from Thrace, was the sound of the rakı tables — nowhere more than the fish-and-meyhane square of Kumkapı.

title: Cemalım
creator: Erkin Koray
desc: The title means ‘My Cemal,’ a village name dragged through eight minutes of fuzzed-out Anatolian psych. Erkin Koray, born in Kadıköy, started Turkey’s first rock band on this Asian shore of Moda.

title: Bir Teselli Ver
creator: Orhan Gencebay
desc: The title means ‘Give Me Some Consolation,’ the record that invented arabesk — Arabic-tinged laments for a city filling with migrants. The İMÇ blocks at Unkapanı housed the labels and studios that pressed the whole genre.

title: Manolyam
place: Site of the Maksim Gazino, Taksim
creator: Zeki Müren
desc: The title means ‘My Magnolia.’ Zeki Müren — the sequined ‘Sun of Art,’ the most beloved singer the country has known — descended to the Maksim gazino stage on a swing and reigned over Beyoğlu’s nightclub era.

title: Benzemez Kimse Sana
creator: Müzeyyen Senar
desc: The title means ‘No One Is Like You.’ Müzeyyen Senar, the grande dame of Turkish art music, ruled the airwaves from İstanbul Radyosu and the Beyoğlu gazinos for half a century. Bursa-born, wholly of the city.

title: Çeçen Kızı
creator: Tanburi Cemil Bey
desc: The title means ‘Chechen Girl,’ a dazzling instrumental for tanbur and kemençe. Cemil Bey, born and died in Istanbul, was the last great virtuoso of the Ottoman capital; his world lay along the Bosphorus shore at Kadıköy.

title: Aziz İstanbul
creator: Münir Nurettin Selçuk
desc: The title means ‘Dear Istanbul,’ setting Yahya Kemal’s poem that gazes down on the city from its seven hills. Selçuk, born here, was the father of the modern sanat concert. The view is best from the ramparts of Rumeli Hisarı.

title: Tavus Havası
creator: Baba Zula
desc: The title means ‘Peacock Melody.’ Baba Zula built their electric saz-and-dub sound in the Beyoğlu clubs below the Galata Tower, and carried it into Fatih Akın’s film portrait of the city’s music.

title: Ab-ı Rû
creator: Mercan Dede
desc: The title, roughly ‘water of the face,’ means dignity or grace. Mercan Dede laces the Mevlevi ney flute through electronica; the Galata dervish lodge is the living Istanbul home of that whirling Sufi music. He works from the diaspora.

title: Tchikita
creator: Jul
desc: A sugar-rush ode to a girl, and the song that turned Jul into a phenomenon — now the best-selling rapper in French history. He grew up on the Cité Louis-Loucheur in Saint-Jean-du-Désert, in the city’s east.

title: Cosmo
creator: Soprano
desc: Soaring pop-rap about reaching for the stars, from the city’s biggest crossover star. Of Comorian family, Soprano and his group Psy 4 de la Rime came up on the Plan d’Aou estate in the far northern 15th.

title: Marseille
creator: Patrick Fiori
desc: A full-throated variété love letter to the city by the Marseille-born singer — all sun and salt and homesickness. Pinned to the Corniche Kennedy, the seafront road that is the city’s long balcony onto the Mediterranean.

title: Balkan Qoulou
creator: Watcha Clan
desc: Diaspora electronica that stitches Balkan brass, Arabic vocals and dub into one caravan. Watcha Clan are pure Mediterranean Marseille; pinned to the Noailles market, the ‘belly of Marseille’ where every shore of the sea trades.

title: La rage
creator: Keny Arkana
desc: The title means ‘The Rage’ — furious, conscious rap from an activist of Argentine family who came up in Noailles. Keny Arkana’s world is La Plaine, the militant, multicultural square at the city’s heart.

title: Ma ville est malade
creator: Massilia Sound System
desc: The title means ‘My City Is Sick’ — a tough-love lament from the band that fused Jamaican sound-system reggae with the Occitan language. Massilia are inseparable from the bohemian Cours Julien and La Plaine.

title: Art de rue
creator: Fonky Family
desc: The title means ‘Art of the Street.’ Fonky Family were IAM’s fierce younger cousins; their founders came up in Le Panier, Marseille’s steep, ancient old town rising above the port.

title: Cane… Cane… Canebière
creator: Alibert
desc: Music-hall Marseille at full throttle — a strutting ode to the great central boulevard. Vincent Scotto, born in the city, wrote hundreds of these tunes; the 1935 operetta made the Canebière shorthand for Marseille swagger the world over.

title: Mademoiselle Marseille
creator: Moussu T e lei Jovents
desc: Bluesy, accordion-warmed song in Occitan and French, reviving the 1930s Marseille of the operettas. Moussu T are rooted in L’Estaque, the northern fishing-village quarter that Cézanne painted again and again.

title: Je danse le Mia
creator: IAM
desc: IAM invented Marseille rap, and this disco-sampling smash — ‘le Mia’ was ’80s local slang for a poser — was their breakout. ‘La planète Mars’ looks out over the Vieux-Port, the old harbour at the city’s heart.

title: Strange Entity
creator: Oscar and the Wolf
desc: Sleek, sensual electropop with a falsetto ache, from Max Colombie’s Oscar and the Wolf, born in the Brussels commune of Jette. One of Belgium’s biggest festival draws of the 2010s.

title: Dilemme
creator: Lous and the Yakuza
desc: The title means ‘Dilemma’ — spare, wounded R&B in French. Lous and the Yakuza (Marie-Pierra Kakoma), Belgian-Congolese, rose through Brussels’ underground; her world edges Matonge at the Porte de Namur.

title: Formidable
creator: Stromae
desc: The title means ‘wonderful,’ sung by a man falling apart. Stromae filmed himself acting blind-drunk with hidden cameras at the Louise tram stop — passers-by really tried to help him. Raised in Laeken, he is Brussels’ biggest modern star.

title: Moskow Diskow
creator: Telex
desc: Deadpan, robotic synth-pop about a train to Moscow, from a Brussels trio who were among Europe’s electronic pioneers. Marc Moulin was also a jazzman and radio voice; Flagey was Belgium’s grand old broadcasting house.

title: Headhunter
creator: Front 242
desc: ‘One: you lock the target…’ — the coldwave stomp that made Belgium the world capital of EBM, the harsh electronic body music that fed techno and industrial. Front 242 formed just outside the city; this pin is the Molenbeek club Plan K.

title: Do You Read Me?
creator: Ghinzu
desc: Widescreen, piano-driven art-rock with a paranoid edge, from one of Brussels’ biggest bands of the 2000s. Pinned to Le Botanique, the greenhouse-turned-venue at the heart of the city’s rock scene.

title: Accouplés
creator: Marka
desc: The title means ‘Coupled Together.’ Marka — Serge Van Laeken, raised in Molenbeek — is a wry Brussels chanson-rocker, and, as it happens, the father of two later stars on this very list: Angèle and Roméo Elvis.

title: Nah Neh Nah
creator: Vaya Con Dios
desc: A brassy, foot-stomping singalong with a nonsense title, from Dani Klein’s Brussels band. Their smoky lounge-swing suits the antique-dealer cafés around the Place du Grand Sablon.

title: Ça plane pour moi
creator: Plastic Bertrand
desc: The title means roughly ‘this is going great for me’ — gibberish-joy Euro-punk that outlived every band around it. A Brussels novelty that conquered the world; pinned to the Ancienne Belgique, the city’s great music hall.

title: Dominique
creator: Sœur Sourire
desc: The impossibly wholesome ode to St Dominic that made a Belgian nun a US number one in 1963, outselling Elvis. Jeanne Deckers was born in Laeken; her later life turned tragic. Pure, strange early-60s pop.

title: Bluesette
creator: Toots Thielemans
desc: A featherlight waltz for whistling and harmonica that became a jazz standard. Toots Thielemans was born above a café on the rue Haute in the Marolles, the earthy old working-class quarter around the Jeu de Balle flea market.

title: Bruxelles
creator: Jacques Brel
desc: A giddy waltz remembering the Brussels of his grandparents’ courtship, trams and bustles and all. Brel, the towering Belgian chansonnier, was born here in Schaerbeek before conquering Paris; the song aches for a city already vanishing.

title: Motivé
creator: Xen & EAZ
desc: The title means ‘motivated.’ Streetwise drill in Zurich slang from Xen, who reps Dietikon just up the Limmat. Its world is the Langstrasse, the neon nightlife spine of Kreis 4.

title: Bruxelles je t’aime
creator: Angèle
desc: The title means ‘Brussels, I Love You’ — a bittersweet hometown serenade, half proud, half exasperated. Angèle, daughter of Marka, became a Franco-Belgian pop phenomenon; the Grand-Place stands in for the whole city she addresses.

title: Brotherlove
creator: Crimer
desc: Pure 1980s pastiche — big hair, bigger synths — delivered with a wink. Crimer, born in St. Gallen but a Zurich creation, made the city’s stages, like the grand Kaufleuten, his glam playground.

title: Le Vent Nous Portera
creator: Sophie Hunger
desc: The title means ‘The Wind Will Carry Us,’ her hushed cover of a French rock song. Bern-born but Zurich-launched, Sophie Hunger rose through the indie clubs of Zürich-West, the old industrial quarter turned music hub.

title: White Creatures
creator: Black Sea Dahu
desc: Six minutes of hushed, swelling indie-folk from Black Sea Dahu, led by Janine Cathrein. The band came up on Zurich’s intimate acoustic circuit, in small rooms like El Lokal down by the Sihl river.

title: Ain’t You
creator: Kleenex / LiLiPUT
desc: Zurich’s Kleenex — soon forced by the tissue giant to rename themselves LiLiPUT — were among Europe’s first all-women punk bands, snarling and joyful at once. Their world was Kreis 4 around Helvetiaplatz, the district of squats and protest.

title: The Captain of Her Heart
creator: Double
desc: A jazz-cool one-hit wonder — the first Swiss record to crack the US Top 40. The Zurich duo Double distilled the moneyed calm of the lakefront at Bürkliplatz into three minutes of late-night sophisti-pop.

title: Tubel Trophy
creator: Baby Jail
desc: The title means roughly ‘Idiot of the Year.’ Baby Jail’s gleeful dialect fun-punk was a fixture of the Rote Fabrik, the lakeside factory that Zurich’s youth won as a culture house in the 1980 riots.

title: Rosalie
creator: Bligg
desc: Bligg helped push Züridütsch — Zurich German — into the pop mainstream. This tender rap ballad points back at the working-class Kreis 4 around the Bäckeranlage park where the city’s hip-hop grew up.

title: Karawane
creator: Hugo Ball
desc: The title means ‘Caravan,’ though the poem is pure invented nonsense-sound. In 1916, in a cabaret on this alley, Ball chanted it in a cardboard costume — the night Dada was born. No recording of him survives; hear it through later sound-poets.

title: O mein Papa
creator: Paul Burkhard
desc: The title means ‘Oh, My Papa,’ a daughter’s tribute to her late clown father. Zurich composer Paul Burkhard wrote it for a musical that premiered at the Schauspielhaus; it became a worldwide hit in the 1950s.

title: Träume (Wesendonck Lieder, No. 5)
creator: Richard Wagner
desc: The title means ‘Dreams.’ Exiled in Zurich, Wagner fell for Mathilde Wesendonck and set her poems while living beside her family’s villa — now the Museum Rietberg. This song became a study for Tristan und Isolde.

title: Litania
creator: Tomasz Stańko
desc: The title means ‘Litany.’ Trumpeter Tomasz Stańko, who studied here and founded one of Europe’s first free-jazz groups in the city, devoted this album to Komeda. Pinned to the Academy of Music where he trained.

title: HUTA (gasną światła)
creator: Szaran
desc: The title means ‘Steelworks (the lights go out).’ Szaran raps his home turf of Nowa Huta, the socialist-realist steel town grafted onto Kraków after the war. Pinned to its monumental Central Square.

title: Nikt nam nie zrobił nic
creator: Hańba!
desc: The title means ‘No One Did Anything to Us.’ Hańba! play furious 1930s-style protest punk on banjo and megaphone; their world is Plac Nowy, the ragged nightlife heart of Kazimierz.

title: Zacznij od Bacha
creator: Zbigniew Wodecki
desc: The title means ‘Start with Bach’ — sunny advice to cure heartbreak with music. Zbigniew Wodecki, a Kraków-born pop showman and trained violinist of the city’s Philharmonic, turned it into a national singalong.

title: Naprawdę nie dzieje się nic
creator: Grzegorz Turnau
desc: The title means ‘Really, Nothing Happens.’ Grzegorz Turnau, born in Kraków, spent years at the piano of the Piwnica pod Baranami, carrying its literate cabaret song into the 1990s.

title: Krakowski spleen
creator: Maanam
desc: The title means ‘Kraków Spleen’ — a grey martial-law mood where ‘the awning won’t roll up, the day won’t begin.’ Maanam, Kora’s new-wave band, formed in the city; the fog sits heaviest over the Main Square.

title: Man of the Light
creator: Zbigniew Seifert
desc: Kraków-born Zbigniew Seifert reinvented the jazz violin, playing it like Coltrane’s saxophone before dying at 32. This soaring title track is his testament; pinned to U Muniaka, the city’s legendary basement jazz club.

title: Dni, których nie znamy
creator: Marek Grechuta
desc: The title means ‘The Days We Don’t Know,’ a gentle hymn to living now. Grechuta studied architecture here and founded his band Anawa in Kraków; he belongs to the sung-poetry world of old cafés like Jama Michalika.

title: Threnody to the Victims of Hiroshima
creator: Krzysztof Penderecki
desc: Fifty-two strings shrieking, sliding, clustering into pure dread — Penderecki’s requiem terrified and thrilled the postwar world. He built his life at Kraków’s Academy of Music, which now bears his name.

title: Es brent
creator: Mordechai Gebirtig
desc: The title means ‘It’s Burning’ — a prophetic cry that the Jewish town is in flames. Gebirtig, a carpenter-poet of Kazimierz, was murdered in the ghetto in 1942; a plaque marks the tenement where he lived and worked.

title: Amerika
creator: Lucie
desc: The title means ‘America.’ Lucie were one of the biggest Czech rock bands of the 1990s, all widescreen hooks and yearning. Pinned to the Holešovice exhibition grounds, a great Prague concert stage of their heyday.

title: Higher
creator: NobodyListen, Emma Smetana & Jordan Haj
desc: A sleek electronic-pop collaboration by the Prague producer NobodyListen with Emma Smetana and Jordan Haj. Pinned to Forum Karlín in Karlín, the flood-ravaged district reborn as the city’s creative quarter.

title: Veronika’s Dream
creator: Floex
desc: Floex — Tomáš Dvořák, no relation to Antonín — folds clarinet into warm electronica; he also scores Prague’s dreamlike Amanita Design video games. Pinned to DOX, the contemporary-art centre in post-industrial Holešovice.

title: Praha
creator: PSH
desc: The title simply means ‘Prague.’ PSH — Vladimir 518 and Orion — founded Czech hip-hop, and this is their love letter to the city. Pinned to the Palác Akropolis, the Žižkov culture-house that was the scene’s home.

title: Modlitba pro Martu
creator: Marta Kubišová
desc: The title means ‘A Prayer for Marta.’ Kubišová recorded this hymn as Soviet tanks rolled in in 1968; the regime then banned her for twenty years. Crowds sang it again beneath the Wenceslas statue during the 1989 Velvet Revolution.

title: Lady Karneval
creator: Karel Gott
desc: The bubbly signature of Karel Gott, ‘the Golden Voice of Prague,’ who ruled Czech pop for half a century. Born in Plzeň, he made his throne here at the Lucerna, the Art Nouveau pleasure-palace off Wenceslas Square.

title: Bugatti Step
creator: Jaroslav Ježek
desc: A giddy jazz sprint named for the race car. Ježek scored Prague’s satirical Liberated Theatre through the 1930s and composed in this flat, its walls painted deep blue to spare his failing eyes — now a tiny museum in the old Jewish Quarter.

title: Stříhali dohola malého chlapečka
creator: Vladimír Mišík
desc: The title means ‘They Shaved the Little Boy’s Head,’ a Josef Kainar poem about the loss of childhood. Mišík, a Prague rock elder, gave it a renaissance-tinged melody. Pinned to Vinohrady, the leafy district long tied to the city’s musicians.

title: Songs My Mother Taught Me (Gypsy Songs, Op. 55)
creator: Antonín Dvořák
desc: A grown child remembering a mother’s tears over old melodies. Prague’s other national composer worked just blocks from this Baroque summer villa, now the little museum that keeps his name.

title: Želva
creator: Olympic
desc: The title means ‘Tortoise.’ Olympic, ‘the Czech Beatles,’ were the house band at the Rokoko theatre on Wenceslas Square, turning British beat into something wholly Prague at the height of the 1960s thaw.

title: Vltava (Má vlast, No. 2)
creator: Bedřich Smetana
desc: The title is the Czech name for the river that curls through the city. Smetana, by then deaf, traced it in music from mountain springs down to Prague — the melody every Czech knows. The museum sits right on its bank beside Charles Bridge.

title: New Gods
creator: Withered Hand
desc: Wry, tender, faith-haunted anti-folk from Dan Willson, a long-standing fixture of the city’s scene. Portobello, Edinburgh’s seaside suburb, stands in as a representative pin for his home ground.

title: Don Giovanni, K. 527: Overture
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
desc: Mozart finished this opera in Prague and conducted its premiere here in 1787, the ink reportedly still wet. ‘My Praguers understand me,’ he said of the city that adored him when Vienna cooled. The Baroque house still stages it.

title: Get Up
creator: Young Fathers
desc: Percussive, gospel-edged art-rap from the trio who won the 2014 Mercury Prize for ‘Dead.’ Graham Hastings is from Drylaw; Bannerman’s on the Cowgate anchors the grassroots scene they rose from.

title: Stay Out
creator: Nina Nesbitt
desc: Bright, early acoustic-pop from the singer-songwriter raised in this village on Edinburgh’s south-western edge, years before her later synth-pop reinvention.

title: Default
place: Edinburgh College of Art, Lauriston Place
creator: Django Django
desc: Kaleidoscopic, motorik-driven art-rock. The four members met as students at the College of Art, though the band came together formally later in London — an Edinburgh-met rather than Edinburgh-founded act.

title: Roygbiv
creator: Boards of Canada
desc: Warm, woozy, half-remembered synth textures from the reclusive duo who built their Hexagon Sun studio in the hills southwest of the city. The title is the schoolroom mnemonic for the colours of the rainbow.

title: Sunshine on Leith
creator: The Proclaimers
desc: A soaring love song that became a Hibernian FC hymn, from the bespectacled twins Craig and Charlie Reid. The Shore is the cobbled old harbour street at the heart of the district they made famous.

title: Roseability
place: Site of The Venue, Calton Road
creator: Idlewild
desc: Ragged, literate indie rock that name-checks Gertrude Stein, from the band that formed in Edinburgh in 1995. The pin is The Venue on Calton Road (1986–2006), the central room that anchored the late-90s scene.

title: Sorry for Laughing
creator: Josef K
desc: Wiry, anxious guitar-pop from one of the great lost Edinburgh bands, cut for Glasgow’s Postcard label. Singer Paul Haig grew up in the Oxgangs scheme in the city’s southwest.

title: Golden Eagle
creator: Tommy Smith
desc: The opener of ‘Beasts of Scotland,’ a suite by the Blue Note saxophonist who first picked up the horn at twelve in this southwest housing scheme, before cutting his debut album at sixteen.

title: Top of the Pops
place: Edinburgh College of Art, Lauriston Place
creator: The Rezillos
desc: A gleeful punk swipe at the BBC chart show — which promptly invited them on to play it. The band formed among students at the art college on Lauriston Place, with Fay Fife and Eugene Reynolds trading vocals.

title: Shang-a-Lang
creator: Bay City Rollers
desc: The tartan-scarf teen frenzy that briefly made Edinburgh the pop capital of the world. Formed by the Longmuir brothers of Dalry; Ryrie’s at Haymarket carries the band’s city plaque and was Alan Longmuir’s local.

title: Flower of Scotland
creator: The Corries
desc: Now roared before every Scotland rugby match, it was written by Edinburgh-born Roy Williamson, who met his bandmate Ronnie Browne at the city’s College of Art. Sandy Bell’s is the pub at the heart of the folk revival that raised them.

title: The Freedom Come-All-Ye
place: School of Scottish Studies, George Square
creator: Hamish Henderson
desc: Scotland’s great unofficial anthem, written in dense Scots by the folklorist who spent decades in this university building archiving the tradition. Sung here by the Leith-raised Dick Gaughan.

title: Auld Lang Syne
creator: Robert Burns
desc: Burns was an Ayrshire man, but his fame was made across his 1786–87 Edinburgh seasons, and the words were printed here in Johnson’s Scots Musical Museum. The museum celebrating him sits in this narrow close off the Lawnmarket.

title: I Wanna Be Adored
creator: The Stone Roses
desc: Swagger uncoiling from a slow-building bassline — the opening of the album that made Manchester the centre of the world for about two years. Ian Brown and John Squire were schoolboys together in Timperley.

title: One Day Like This
creator: Elbow
desc: The string-swelling, arms-aloft anthem that has soundtracked every northern summer since. Elbow formed in Bury, and Guy Garvey has been Manchester’s warmest public voice ever since.

title: Voodoo Ray
creator: A Guy Called Gerald
desc: Manchester acid house in one wobbling, euphoric record, built by Gerald Simpson on borrowed machines in a Moss Side bedroom. The stray vocal sample was meant to say ‘voodoo rage’ — the tape ran out.

title: Step On
creator: Happy Mondays
desc: Baggy at its loosest and most gleeful, Shaun Ryder gurning over a 1971 cover. The Mondays came off the Little Hulton estates in Salford, seven miles and a whole world from the Haçienda they colonised.

title: Live Forever
creator: Oasis
desc: Noel Gallagher’s deliberate rebuke to grunge misery, written in Burnage bedsit-land. The brothers grew up on Cranwell Drive, a mile from Sifters, the record shop Noel immortalised in another song.

title: Blue Monday
place: Site of the Haçienda club, Whitworth Street West
creator: New Order
desc: The best-selling 12-inch single in history, and the sound of a city learning to dance. New Order bankrolled the Haçienda with it — the club that stood on this spot until 2002, now flats called, inevitably, the Hacienda Apartments.

title: Totally Wired
creator: The Fall
desc: Amphetamine yelp and scratchy garage-funk from Mark E. Smith, the most cussed man in English music. The Fall formed in Prestwich, and Smith barely left the suburb across forty years and sixty-odd line-ups.

title: Dirty Old Town
creator: Ewan MacColl
desc: Written in 1949 about Salford’s docks and gasworks, and so good that half the world assumes it’s Irish. MacColl was born James Miller in Broughton; the Pogues’ famous version is a cover of a Salford man’s song.

title: Love Will Tear Us Apart
place: Ian Curtis memorial stone, Macclesfield Cemetery
creator: Joy Division
desc: The bleakest great pop song ever made, cut at Strawberry Studios in Stockport weeks before Ian Curtis died at twenty-three. His memorial stone in Macclesfield is carved with this very title.

title: Ever Fallen in Love (With Someone You Shouldn’t’ve)
creator: Buzzcocks
desc: Punk’s most perfect lovesick two minutes. Buzzcocks promoted the two 1976 Sex Pistols shows in the Lesser Free Trade Hall — the gigs credited with detonating almost everything that follows on this list.

title: Sally
place: Gracie Fields’ birthplace, Molesworth Street, Rochdale
creator: Gracie Fields
desc: The signature song of ‘Our Gracie,’ the mill girl from Rochdale who became Britain’s biggest star and its highest-paid film actress. She was born above her grandmother’s fish-and-chip shop on this street.

title: Bus Stop
creator: The Hollies
desc: Umbrella-sharing sunshine pop from Manchester’s biggest beat group. Allan Clarke and Graham Nash met as boys at school in Ordsall — and Graham Gouldman, later of 10cc, wrote it.

title: Tammurriata Nera
creator: Nuova Compagnia di Canto Popolare
desc: The title means ‘Black Tammurriata,’ after the folk drum-dance. Written in 1944 about the mixed-race babies born of the Allied occupation — matter-of-fact and tender. The centro storico around Gesù Nuovo is its world.

title: Nove Maggio
creator: Liberato
desc: The title means ‘Ninth of May,’ a date of teenage heartbreak. The masked, anonymous Liberato remade Neapolitan pop for the streaming age; his videos haunt the fishing cove of Marechiaro on the Posillipo cliffs.

title: Tienatè
creator: Nu Genea
desc: The title means roughly ‘hold on to it.’ Nu Genea’s sun-warm Neapolitan disco, sung by Fabiana Martone, belongs to the Lungomare — the seafront promenade where the whole city walks at dusk with Vesuvius behind.

title: Salvamm’ o munno
creator: Enzo Avitabile & Bottari
desc: The title means ‘Let’s Save the World.’ Avitabile, from the northern Piscinola–Marianella edge, fuses gospel-soul with the thundering barrel-drums of the Bottari; here Cameroon’s Manu Dibango guests on saxophone.

title: Figli di Annibale
creator: Almamegretta
desc: The title means ‘Sons of Hannibal’ — a wink at the notion that Hannibal’s African army left southern Italians part-Black. Almamegretta’s dub manifesto for a mixed Mediterranean Naples, at home in the Quartieri Spagnoli.

title: Curre curre guagliò
creator: 99 Posse
desc: The title means ‘Run, run, boy.’ Ragamuffin rap in dialect from 99 Posse, born inside Officina 99, the occupied social centre in gritty Gianturco that gave the band its name and its politics.

title: Napule è
creator: Pino Daniele
desc: The title means ‘Naples is.’ Pino Daniele’s aching hymn — ‘Naples is a thousand colours, a bitter voice’ — written in his twenties in the old-town alleys. The city’s unofficial anthem, mournful and proud at once.

title: Funiculì Funiculà
creator: Luciano Pavarotti
desc: Written to celebrate the 1880 opening of the railway that climbed Mount Vesuvius — some call it the world’s first advertising jingle. The little cable car is long gone, but the volcano and its song still tower over the bay.

title: Tu vuo’ fa’ l’americano
creator: Renato Carosone
desc: The title means ‘You want to play the American.’ Carosone’s swinging jab at postwar Naples kids in blue jeans chasing rock ‘n’ roll and whisky while their mothers’ money ran out. He grew up near the old Piazza del Mercato.

title: Malafemmena
place: Totò’s birthplace, Via Santa Maria Antesaecula
creator: Totò
desc: The title means ‘wicked woman.’ The comic-tragic prince Totò — born in a tenement on this Sanità street — wrote this bitter serenade after his marriage broke apart. It remains his most enduring song.

title: ‘O Sole Mio
creator: Enrico Caruso
desc: The title means ‘My Own Sun.’ The most famous Neapolitan song ever written, sung here by Caruso, the tenor born a mile inland. Its dazzling light and blue water are those of the Santa Lucia seafront below Pizzofalcone.

title: Santa Lucia Luntana
creator: Massimo Ranieri
desc: The title means ‘Faraway Santa Lucia,’ the anthem of the emigrants who watched the lights of Naples sink below the horizon from the decks of the ocean liners. Ranieri, born in the Santa Lucia borgo, carries it.

title: ‘O Zappatore
creator: Mario Merola
desc: The title means ‘The Ploughman,’ a 1920s tearjerker about a farmer who paid for his son’s law degree only to be disowned at a fancy wedding. Merola, king of the sceneggiata, made it a ritual at the Trianon in Forcella.

title: Buleríâ del aire acondiçionao (Versión Maxi)
creator: Califato ¾
desc: The Andalusian-spelled title means ‘Bulería of the Air Conditioning.’ This Seville collective rebuilds flamenco palos as club music, writing lyrics in phonetic Andaluz. Place-less, so it sits at the symbolic centre.

title: Aliento de Dragón
creator: Derby Motoreta’s Burrito Kachimba
desc: The title means ‘Dragon’s Breath,’ the breakout single of Seville’s psychedelic ‘kinkidelia’ scene. It names no place, so it sits at Plaza Nueva, the city’s symbolic centre.

title: S.e.v.i.l.l.a.
creator: SFDK
desc: An ode to the city spelled out letter by letter by rap duo SFDK — Zatu and Acción Sánchez — who grew up in Pino Montano, the working-class barrio on the northern edge that raised them.

title: Mili Kk
creator: Reincidentes
desc: The title mocks the old compulsory military service, ‘la mili.’ A 100-second blast from Seville’s veteran punk band; it names no place, so it lands at Plaza Nueva, the symbolic centre.

title: Al Este del Edén
creator: Silvio y Luzbel
desc: The title means ‘East of Eden.’ The cult title track of Seville’s patron saint of rockers and misfits, who held court in the bars of the Alameda de Hércules for decades.

title: Macarena
creator: Los del Río
desc: Named for the Virgen de la Macarena, whose basilica anchors the pin. This is the original Spanish cut, by a duo from Dos Hermanas in the Seville metro — years before the English remix conquered the planet.

title: Echo de menos
creator: Kiko Veneno
desc: The title means ‘I miss (you),’ the wry heart of Échate un cantecito. Kiko wrote ‘Volando voy’ for Camarón; born in Figueres and raised partly in Cádiz, he became a sevillano by adoption, settling in Nervión.

title: Todo es de color
creator: Lole y Manuel
desc: The title means ‘Everything Is Colour.’ The couple who dragged flamenco into the modern age — reputedly the first Mellotron on a flamenco record — came up in Triana, Lole from a Sevillian Roma family of the barrio.

title: Pasa la Vida
creator: Pata Negra
desc: The title means ‘Life Goes By.’ The Amador brothers, gitanos of Triana, fused flamenco with electric blues on a landmark album recorded steps from the Triana Bridge (the song itself was penned by Pascual González).

title: Marinero de Luces
creator: Isabel Pantoja
desc: The title means ‘Sailor of Lights,’ the José Luis Perales copla that became her signature. Pantoja was born into a Roma flamenco family in Triana, just off the Plaza del Altozano gateway to the barrio.

title: La Salvaora
creator: Manolo Caracol
desc: The title is a woman’s nickname, ‘the one who saves.’ A flamenco-copla titan born right on the Alameda at Calle Lumbreras; here he trades verses with Lola Flores. His statue stands near Pastora’s on the same square.

title: Abre la puerta
creator: Triana
desc: The title means ‘Open the Door,’ the ten-minute epic that launched Andalusian prog rock. Despite the band’s name, this was a citywide phenomenon, so it sits at Plaza Nueva, the civic heart under the statue of Saint Ferdinand.

title: El Adiós (Algo se muere en el alma)
place: Feria de Abril fairground, Los Remedios
creator: Amigos de Gines
desc: The refrain means ‘something dies in the soul when a friend goes away.’ Seville’s universal farewell, written by Manuel Garrido and sung and danced every April across the vast Feria fairground in Los Remedios.

title: Canción del Ole (Bulerías)
creator: Niña de los Peines
desc: The greatest woman’s voice of flamenco’s golden age, born a few streets off in the Puerta Osario. Her bronze bust now presides over the Alameda, the leafy square where the old cantaores lived and sang.

title: Jugoslovenka
creator: Lepa Brena
desc: The title means ‘Yugoslav Woman.’ The biggest star the country ever produced sang it alongside a Bosnian, a Montenegrin and a Croat — weeks before the federation began to come apart. It is heard now as pure Yugonostalgia.

title: Moji drugovi
creator: Bajaga i Instruktori
desc: The title means ‘My Friends’ — a kafana anthem for lost companions, tarabuka drum and all. Bajaga came up through Riblja Čorba before building one of Belgrade’s most durable bands.

title: In corpore sano
creator: Konstrakta
desc: The Latin means ‘in a healthy body,’ from the tag about a sound mind. Konstrakta — Ana Đurić, a trained architect — turned a Eurovision stage into a deadpan conceptual performance about health care, beauty and the female body.

title: Moving on Up
creator: M People
desc: Big-lunged house-soul that carried Manchester’s dancefloor into the national top three. M People were built around Mike Pickering, the Haçienda’s resident DJ, with Heather Small — a Londoner — out front.

title: Cine iubește și lasă
creator: Maria Tănase
desc: The title means ‘Whoever Loves and Abandons’ — a curse-song of heartbreak. Maria Tănase, the Piaf of Romania, was born in this southern mahala and turned the lăutar tradition into high art.

title: Va Bene
creator: L’Algérino
desc: The title is Italian for ‘all good’ — sunny, cruising pop-rap from the ‘Taxi 5’ soundtrack, name-checking Marseille at every turn. L’Algérino, a Marseillais of Algerian family, made it a summer anthem.

title: Ochii tăi
creator: Holograf
desc: The title means ‘Your Eyes.’ Holograf are Bucharest’s enduring pop-rock institution, all polished hooks and stadium warmth, going strong since the late 1970s.

title: Pe aripi de vânt
creator: Delia
desc: The title means ‘On Wings of Wind.’ Delia, Bucharest-born, is one of Romania’s biggest pop voices — theatrical, restless, everywhere at once. A glossy dance-pop showcase from her imperial phase.

title: Majesty
creator: Madrugada
desc: Smouldering, noir-tinged alt-rock. Madrugada began in far-northern Stokmarknes but made their name after moving to Oslo in the mid-90s; guitarist Robert Burås later died young in his Oslo flat.

title: Beggin’
creator: Madcon
desc: The Four Seasons cover, rebuilt with their own rap verses, that became a worldwide smash long before TikTok found it. Madcon’s Tshawe Baqwa and Yosef Wolde-Mariam grew up in Oslo’s eastern estates.

title: Lovers
creator: Anna of the North
desc: Wistful, frost-bright Scandinavian electropop. Gjøvik-born Anna Lotterud based her Anna of the North project in Oslo; this is the title track of her debut, made in the city.

title: Garden Party
creator: Mezzoforte
desc: The unlikely hit that first put Iceland on the pop map — a slinky jazz-funk instrumental that cracked the UK Top 20. Mezzoforte were Reykjavík schoolfriends barely out of their teens.

title: Angel Numbers
creator: Hamish Hawk
desc: Literary, baritone-crooned art-pop from one of the city’s finest contemporary voices. The album was recorded and produced by Idlewild’s Rod Jones at this Leith studio — a neat handing-on of the torch.

title: Czerwiec
creator: Rycerzyki
desc: The title means ‘June.’ Rycerzyki are a Kraków indie quartet who spin bittersweet, brass-flecked sophisti-pop out of the city’s songwriting tradition, at home in the clubs off the Old Town’s eastern edge.

title: Filandia
creator: Świetliki
desc: A woozy, funny-sad anthem of small-hours defeat, sung with the actor Bogusław Linda. Świetliki formed around the Kraków poet Marcin Świetlicki and became the house band of the city’s literary underground, at bars like Piękny Pies.

title: Muchomůrky bílé
creator: The Plastic People of the Universe
desc: The title means ‘White Toadstools.’ The Plastic People played illegally for a decade; their 1976 trial so outraged the country it helped spark the Charter 77 dissident movement. The pin marks the Prague courthouse.

title: Oh Yeah
creator: Yello
desc: You know it from every 1980s movie: that leering ‘oh yeah… chika chika.’ Yello — Dieter Meier, millionaire dandy, and studio wizard Boris Blank — built sample-pop in a Zurich studio and conquered the world from the lakeside.

title: Circle of the Tyrants
creator: Celtic Frost
desc: Out of the Zurich underground, Celtic Frost half-invented extreme metal — the grunts, the riffs, the death-black theatrics that spawned whole genres. Frontman Tom G. Warrior came from Nuolen, just up the lake.

title: Ein guter Tag
creator: Klaus Johann Grobe
desc: The title means ‘A Good Day.’ Klaus Johann Grobe are a Zurich duo who make hypnotic, organ-drenched krautrock sung in German — motorik grooves for a Swiss afternoon. A cult name abroad, quietly local at home.

title: Italia
creator: Undergrunn
desc: Self-produced Oslo-dialect pop-rap from a six-piece collective who came up around Tøyen and Gamlebyen — the warm, unbothered sound of the current young city.

title: Poroci Beograda
creator: Beogradski Sindikat
desc: The title means ‘The Vices of Belgrade’ — a tour of the city’s appetites and self-destructions. The collective formed in 1999 from two crews and has always defined itself by neighbourhood first: Dorćol, the old riverside quarter.

title: Nu am chef azi
creator: Vama Veche
desc: The title means ‘I Don’t Feel Like It Today’ — slacker rock with a wink. Vama Veche were a fixture of the smoky Bucharest club scene after the revolution; Control Club stands in for that whole rowdy world.

title: Krvn
creator: Uzi
desc: The title stylizes ‘kervan’ — caravan. Uzi, raised in working-class Güngören on the western edge, became the biggest Turkish trap star of the 2020s and the first Turkish act to chart on Billboard’s global list.

title: Kiša u Beogradu 1981
creator: Sajsi MC
desc: The title means ‘Rain in Belgrade, 1981’ — the year she was born. Sajsi MC is the sharpest woman in Serbian rap, a poet who writes the city as weather and memory rather than as territory.

title: The Age of Pamparius
creator: Turbonegro
desc: Oslo’s self-styled ‘deathpunk’ kings — leather, denim, and knowing sleaze — formed in the city in 1988. A downtown nightlife square stands in for their rowdy hometown scene.

title: Bande organisée
creator: 13 Organisé
desc: The title means ‘Organized Gang’ — the six-minute posse cut where Jul’s collective lined up the whole city’s rappers and broke the internet in 2020. Fittingly watched over by Notre-Dame de la Garde, ‘la Bonne Mère’ on her hill.

title: Petrouchka
creator: Soso Maness
desc: Melancholy, string-laced rap with PLK, its title borrowed from the Stravinsky puppet. Soso Maness, of Algerian family, reps Cité Font-Vert, a housing estate in the northern 14th.

title: Macarena
creator: Damso
desc: Not the party song — a brooding, melodic trap confession, its title marked with a Greek theta on the album ‘Ipséité.’ Damso, born in Kinshasa, grew up around Matonge, the Congolese quarter of Ixelles that shaped him.

title: Life
creator: Hamza
desc: Woozy, auto-tuned Brussels trap that helped define the Belgian sound. Hamza, from Laeken, threads French, English and melody into something silky and sad. Pinned to Place Bockstael, his northern home turf.

title: Kokalero
creator: Yzomandias
desc: Trap in Prague slang from Yzomandias, ringleader of the Milion+ crew that rewired Czech rap. Born in Karlovy Vary, he built his empire here; pinned to the Žižkov TV tower rising over the district his scene claimed.

title: Otto
creator: SCH
desc: Cold, cinematic mafia-rap named for a gangster; SCH built a whole ‘Julius’ saga around this menace. He grew up between the creative old quarter of La Belle de Mai and nearby Aubagne.

title: Taste (Make It Shake)
creator: Aitch
desc: Bouncy, deadpan north-Manchester rap that went to number two. Aitch made his Moston accent the whole point, carrying a UK-wide audience back to the streets above Rochdale Road.

title: Om bun
creator: Sfinx
desc: The title means ‘Good Man.’ Sfinx were Romania’s great progressive-rock band, spinning Anglo prog through Carpathian folk under the Communist censors. Dan Andrei Aldea’s aching melody is a quiet classic of Bucharest rock.

title: Bernabeu
creator: Șatra B.E.N.Z.
desc: Named for Real Madrid’s stadium, an autotuned flex in Romanian trap. Șatra B.E.N.Z. dragged the sound into the Bucharest mainstream; ‘șatra’ means a Roma encampment, worn here as a badge.

title: The Secrets of the Life Tree
creator: Kroke
desc: Kroke — the Yiddish name for Kraków — are three Academy graduates who revived klezmer from the Kazimierz quarter. This brooding piece later haunted a David Lynch film; Szeroka street is their festival home.

title: The Swedish Theory of Love
creator: Erik Gandini
desc: Documentary on Sweden’s ideal of self-sufficiency, in a society so independent that many people now live, and die, alone. Uneasy viewing. Sergels torg, the modernist concrete plaza in the city centre, stands for the welfare-state capital.

title: Joy
creator: Sudabeh Mortezai
desc: A plain drama about Nigerian women trafficked into sex work in Vienna, and the debts that trap them. Praterstern, a station and square, and the Leopoldstadt streets around it are the migrant red-light Vienna tourists rarely see.

title: Rembetiko
creator: Costas Ferris
desc: Musical drama about rembetiko, the Greek blues. It follows a singer from the 1922 Smyrna catastrophe through refugee Athens to ruin. Kaisariani, a district settled by refugees from Asia Minor, is one of the quarters where the music took root.

title: Dead City (Ciutat morta)
place: Carrer de Sant Pere més Baix
creator: Xavier Artigas & Xapo Ortega
desc: Documentary on the 4F case: a 2006 arrest, tortured suspects, and a young woman who later took her life. It describes a Barcelona that clears its streets of the inconvenient. The case began on Carrer de Sant Pere més Baix, a street in the old town.

title: Metello
creator: Mauro Bolognini
desc: From Vasco Pratolini’s novel: a bricklayer comes of age in a hardening Florence, from orphanhood to the great 1902 building strike. The working-class city tourists don’t see. Its labourers lived in the Oltrarno, the artisan quarter across the Arno.

title: Las bicicletas son para el verano (Bicycles Are for the Summer)
creator: Jaime Chávarri
desc: From Fernán Gómez’s well-loved play: a middle-class Madrid family’s ordinary life slowly starves and cracks through the 1936–39 siege. Argüelles, a western district, was shelled from front lines that ran through the university and Casa de Campo.

title: Devil’s Island (Djöflaeyjan)
place: Site of Camp Knox barracks, Vesturbær (area)
creator: Friðrik Þór Friðriksson
desc: A family scrapes by in the American army barracks that became a Reykjavík slum after the war. Friðriksson’s crowded family epic. The ‘braggar’ huts stood in the old camp districts of west Reykjavík, such as Camp Knox in Vesturbær.

title: Jan Palach
creator: Robert Sedláček
desc: The final months of the student who set himself on fire in January 1969 to protest the Soviet crushing of the Prague Spring. A true story. He burned at the top of Wenceslas Square, in front of the National Museum, where a memorial now marks the spot.

title: Fires Were Started
creator: Humphrey Jennings
desc: Humphrey Jennings’ wartime docudrama uses real firemen to show one day and night of the Blitz. Propaganda, made with a poet’s eye. The crews fight warehouse fires in the London Docks, the East End port area around Wapping.

title: Ballymun Lullaby
creator: Frank Berry
desc: Documentary about a music teacher who writes a song cycle with children from Ballymun while the estate’s last tower blocks come down. Hopeful, not grim. Ballymun is a high-rise housing estate on the north side of Dublin.

title: Stella
creator: Michael Cacoyannis
desc: Michael Cacoyannis’s film, Melina Mercouri’s first: a free-living taverna singer refuses to be tamed by the man who loves her, heading for a Carmen-like end. It moves through Plaka, the old quarter of tavernas and bouzouki nights.

title: Toward Nowa Huta (Richtung Nowa Huta)
creator: Dariusz Krzeczek
desc: Documentary wandering through Nowa Huta, the Stalinist steel town, decades on: its avenues, its mill and ageing believers who still hold to a lost utopia. The whole town was built to serve the steelworks, a huge plant east of Kraków’s centre.

title: Bäckerei Zürrer
creator: Kurt Früh
desc: Kurt Früh’s ‘poetic realist’ portrait of a widowed master baker and his wayward sons in 1950s Zurich, a working-class city since gone. His bakery is in the Langstrasse quarter, the rough district of immigrants and vice in Kreis 4.

title: Budapest Noir
creator: Éva Gárdos
desc: A hard-boiled reporter takes up a dead girl’s case in 1936, as Hungary drifts toward fascism after its prime minister’s death. More style than depth. The nightlife is on Nagymező utca, the theatre street of interwar Pest.

title: Agora (From Democracy to the Market)
creator: Yorgos Avgeropoulos
desc: Documentary filmed over four years of Greece’s crisis, from mass protests to shuttered lives, asking how markets and debt remake a democracy. The anti-austerity movement massed in Syntagma Square, in front of the parliament building.

title: Hunger (Sult)
creator: Henning Carlsen
desc: From Knut Hamsun’s novel. A proud young writer starves in 1890 Kristiania, refusing food and pity as he comes apart. Per Oscarsson plays him. He paces Karl Johans gate, the main boulevard through central Oslo, too vain to beg.

title: In Diamond Square (La plaça del Diamant / The Time of the Doves)
creator: Francesc Betriu
desc: From Mercè Rodoreda’s novel. Natàlia, nicknamed Colometa, marries, loses her husband to the Civil War and nearly starves under Franco. A bronze statue of her now stands in Plaça del Diamant, a small square in Gràcia.

title: Wasted Youth
creator: Argyris Papadimitropoulos & Jan Vogel
desc: Two parallel days in crisis-era Athens, one with a drifting teenage skater, the other with a burnt-out cop. Inspired by the 2008 police killing of Alexis Grigoropoulos in Exarcheia, the central district where he was shot and the riots began.

title: El Garrotín
creator: Smash
desc: A garrotín is a flamenco palo, and this psychedelic Seville band welded it to blues-rock, with Triana’s own Manuel Molina on flamenco guitar. Cut it by Calle Betis, the riverbank tavern strip facing the old town.

title: This Charming Man
creator: The Smiths
desc: Johnny Marr’s chiming guitar, Morrissey’s arch misery — the moment English indie found its template. The brick doorway of Salford Lads Club, shot for ‘The Queen Is Dead’ sleeve, is Manchester’s great music pilgrimage.

title: primabalerina
creator: Coals
desc: Glassy, melancholy electropop about performing happiness. Coals — Silesian by roots, Kraków by home — are fixtures of the city’s live scene, not least the AGH campus club that named their tour.

title: Pastel colours and pictograms for a cheerful Olympics
desc: Designer Otl Aicher’s team gave the 1972 Games soft blues and greens, no red or black, and the sport pictograms still copied today, to present a new, open West Germany. Mark Holt co-wrote the book on Aicher’s department.

title: Letters from the Jewish president who built FC Bayern
desc: Kurt Landauer led FC Bayern to its first German title in 1932, was forced out in 1933 as a Jew and survived in Swiss exile. He returned as president after the war. The club museum at the Allianz Arena stadium now tells his story.

title: Litres, visitors and records at the world’s biggest beer festival
desc: DW’s lifestyle show runs through the numbers behind Oktoberfest: millions of visitors, litre steins carried by the armful and the vast temporary beer tents built each summer on the Theresienwiese fairground.

title: After the king flees, Bavaria tries a revolution of its own
desc: In November 1918 Kurt Eisner toppled the Wittelsbach monarchy. His murder on this street in February 1919 led to a short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic, crushed by Freikorps troops in May. A pavement outline marks the spot.

title: US Army engineers blow up the Nazis’ temples of honour
desc: The Nazis reburied their sixteen putsch dead in two open-air temples beside Königsplatz square, guarded day and night. In 1947 the US Army demolished them; the overgrown stone bases still stand by Arcisstrasse.

title: Live television turns a hostage siege into a global broadcast
desc: In September 1972 Palestinian gunmen took Israeli athletes hostage at Connollystraße 31 in the Olympic Village. Cameras broadcast police positions live, which the attackers could watch. All eleven hostages were killed.

title: The beer festival’s uncomfortable chapters
desc: Oktoberfest began with a horse race celebrating a royal wedding in 1810. DW History looks at the darker side of its two centuries. The festival still fills the Theresienwiese meadow, named after the bride, Princess Therese.

title: Surfers ride a standing wave in the middle of the city
desc: Where the Eisbach channel emerges under a bridge at the edge of the Englischer Garten park, a standing wave lets surfers ride in place all year. Locals have surfed it since the 1970s, long before the city made it legal.

title: From the town hall glockenspiel to the city’s open-air food market
desc: Rick Steves walks from Marienplatz and the New Town Hall’s glockenspiel to the Viktualienmarkt, the open-air food market held here since 1807, with its maypole, butchers, cheese stalls and small beer garden.

title: Room after room of Wittelsbach splendour in the royal palace
desc: For four centuries the Wittelsbach family ruled Bavaria from the Residenz. Rick Steves tours its Antiquarium hall and state rooms, much of it rebuilt after wartime bombing, in the palace by Odeonsplatz.

title: Eight centuries of a city that kept reinventing itself
desc: Paul Bloomfield and Munich guide Christine Lehner walk through the city’s past, from its founding as a market town to its rulers, writers and Christmas markets. Marienplatz, the main square, was the medieval salt market and is still the city’s centre.

title: Germany locks Hitler’s book away in a library’s poison cabinet
desc: German libraries kept dangerous books in a Giftschrank, or poison cabinet, open only to scholars. After 1945 Mein Kampf went in too, with Bavaria holding its copyright until 2016. A well-known cabinet sits in the Bavarian State Library on Ludwigstraße.

title: A Cold War radio editor tells his wife he has been spying for the KGB
place: Former Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty building, Englischer Garten
desc: Svetlana’s husband Oleg ran the Russian service of Radio Liberty, the US-funded station broadcasting to the USSR from Munich. He confessed to years of spying for the KGB, then resurfaced in Moscow in 1986. The station stood by the Englischer Garten park.

title: Chamberlain flies to meet Hitler and comes home waving a piece of paper
place: Führerbau, now the University of Music and Performing Arts
desc: In September 1938 Britain, France, Italy and Germany handed Hitler the Sudetenland without asking Czechoslovakia. Did Chamberlain buy time or sell out? The deal was signed in the Führerbau on Arcisstraße, now a music school.

title: Three seconds are replayed until the Americans lose a gold medal
desc: The US had never lost an Olympic basketball game until the 1972 final, when officials twice reset the clock and the Soviets scored at the buzzer. The Americans still refuse their silver medals. The hall in Sendling-Westpark was built for the Games.

title: A basement studio under a tower block invents the sound of the future
desc: Donna Summer, Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte made “I Feel Love” in 1977 with a Moog synthesiser in Munich, where Summer then lived. The track seeded house and techno. Moroder’s Musicland Studios sat in the basement of the Arabella tower in Bogenhausen.

title: A snowbound takeoff destroys a great young football team
desc: On 6 February 1958 a plane carrying Manchester United home from Belgrade crashed on its third attempt to leave slushy Riem airport; 23 died, eight of them players. A granite plaque stands near the site in Trudering, where the old airport was.

title: Hitler’s own exhibition of the art he wanted the public to sneer at
desc: In July 1937 the Nazis hung some 650 confiscated modernist works in cramped rooms beside the Hofgarten park, with mocking labels. About a million people came in six weeks, far more than visited the official Great German Art show across town.

title: Students scatter leaflets in a university atrium and pay with their lives
desc: Dominic Sandbrook tells the story of Hans and Sophie Scholl and their friends, who wrote anti-Nazi leaflets in Munich. In February 1943 the siblings were caught throwing copies into the atrium of the university’s main building and executed four days later.

title: An unknown agitator storms a beer hall and stumbles into a myth
place: Site of the Bürgerbräukeller beer hall
desc: On 8 November 1923 Hitler fired a pistol into the ceiling of the Bürgerbräukeller and declared a revolution that collapsed by noon the next day. Frank McDonough explains what he learned from it. The beer hall in Haidhausen was demolished in 1979.

title: A mad king’s money gets Wagner’s strangest opera onto the stage
desc: Joshua Weilerstein, long a Wagner sceptic, takes apart the Prelude and Liebestod. Tristan und Isolde, once called unperformable, premiered in 1865 at the National Theatre on Max-Joseph-Platz with Ludwig II paying the bills.

title: An Irish dancer posing as a Spaniard costs a king his throne
desc: Lola Montez arrived in Munich in 1846 and soon had Ludwig I making her a countess, outraging ministers and students until riots forced his abdication in 1848. Her portrait still hangs in his Gallery of Beauties at Nymphenburg Palace.

title: A castle-building king is deposed and found dead in a lake
desc: Ludwig II, builder of fairy-tale castles, was declared insane and deposed in 1886, then found dead in Lake Starnberg days later. Dana Schwartz weighs murder against suicide. He lies in the crypt of St Michael’s, the Jesuit church on Neuhauser Straße.

title: Death at La Fenice
place: Venice police headquarters (Questura), Fondamenta San Lorenzo
creator: Donna Leon
desc: The first of Leon’s crime novels about Commissario Brunetti: a German conductor is poisoned at the opera. The series is really about how Venetians live and eat. Brunetti works from the Questura, the police headquarters, by a canal in Castello.

title: The Stones of Venice
place: Ca’ d’Oro palazzo on the Grand Canal
creator: John Ruskin
desc: Ruskin’s argument that Venice’s Gothic buildings show a moral, working culture. It’s long, so J.G. Links’s one-volume abridgement is the way in. In 1845 Ruskin drew the Ca’ d’Oro, a gilded palazzo, while workmen were smashing its old stone.

title: Sonata pian’ e forte
creator: Giovanni Gabrieli
desc: The title means “soft and loud”: published in 1597, it is among the first pieces to mark dynamics in the score. Gabrieli was organist at St Mark’s Basilica, writing for brass choirs set in its facing galleries.

title: A floating city filmed as one living heritage site
place: St Mark’s Basin (Bacino di San Marco)
desc: Venice and its lagoon were listed as a World Heritage Site in 1987, the city and its 118 islands counted together with the water around them. This short NHK film for UNESCO surveys both.

title: Roman stones hidden in a city that claims it was never Roman
desc: Venice liked to say it was born free on empty islands, but its lagoon had Roman villas and roads, and its builders reused Roman stone. Refugees from the mainland town of Altinum settled Torcello, the island whose cathedral is the lagoon’s oldest building.

title: The needle lace of Burano, filmed in 1935
desc: Burano’s needle lace was prized across Europe’s courts and revived by a lace school founded in 1872. This newsreel shows the island’s women at work. The old school building on Piazza Galuppi is now the Museo del Merletto, the lace museum.

title: A painter covers a whole confraternity in his canvases
desc: Over more than two decades Tintoretto painted some 60 canvases for the Scuola Grande di San Rocco, a brotherhood devoted to the plague saint Roch. The walls and ceilings of its two great halls are almost all his, with a vast Crucifixion upstairs.

title: Tintoretto’s miracles of St Mark, painted for a brotherhood’s hall
desc: Tintoretto’s cycle of miracles of Venice’s patron saint was painted for the Scuola Grande di San Marco, a wealthy lay confraternity whose marble façade still stands on Campo Santi Giovanni e Paolo. The building is now the city’s hospital.

title: Day-trippers outnumber the people who live here
desc: The historic centre has fallen below 50,000 residents while visitors run into the millions. Venetians argue over cruise ships, holiday flats and how to cap the crowds. The crush is thickest on the Rialto Bridge, the old commercial heart.

title: The world’s first ghetto, five storeys high
desc: In 1516 Venice confined its Jews to a former foundry island in Cannaregio. The word ghetto comes from the Venetian getto, a casting. Short of space, residents built upwards, and five synagogues survive, tucked into the upper floors around the campo.

title: Why the water keeps rising through St Mark’s Square
desc: St Mark’s Square is the lowest part of the city, so acqua alta, the seasonal high tide, reaches it first, bubbling up through the drains. Raised walkways go out across the paving. The worst flood since 1966 came in November 2019.

title: Steel gates rise from the seabed to hold back the Adriatic
desc: MOSE is a line of 78 hollow steel gates lying on the seabed at the three lagoon inlets. When a high tide threatens, air is pumped in and they swing up to seal off the sea. They were first raised in 2020, after decades of delays and a corruption scandal.

title: Out across the lagoon to the islands of glass and lace
desc: The Venetian lagoon is a shallow basin dotted with islands that each had a job: glassmaking on Murano, lace on Burano, the first cathedral on Torcello, the dead on San Michele. Rick Steves takes a boat out from the city to see them.

title: Small plates and small glasses in the bars around the Rialto
place: Bacari wine bars near the Rialto market
desc: Cicchetti are Venice’s bar snacks: salt cod on polenta, sardines in saor, tiny sandwiches, eaten standing with an ombra, a small glass of wine. The old bacari, or wine bars, cluster in the lanes by the Rialto market where traders once drank.

title: A city survives the plague and thanks it with a church
desc: The Senate vowed a church to the Virgin during the plague of 1630, which killed about a third of the city. Baldassare Longhena’s domed Santa Maria della Salute now marks the mouth of the Grand Canal. Every November a pontoon bridge is built to reach it.

title: A cathedral glittering with loot from Constantinople
desc: St Mark’s Basilica was built to hold relics of the evangelist smuggled out of Alexandria in 828. Its gold mosaics and onion domes look east to Byzantium, and much of its treasure arrived after the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204.

title: Councils, courts and cells under one gilded roof
desc: For centuries the Doge’s Palace held the Republic’s councils, courts and cells under one roof. Rick Steves walks through its gilded halls, from the vast Great Council chamber to the Bridge of Sighs leading to the prisons across the canal.

title: A spritz and a meatball at the bar are a Venetian ritual
desc: Drinks writer Susan L. Schwartz talks about her guide to drinking in Venice, from traditional bàcari, small wine bars serving cicchetti, to coffee and cocktails. Cantina Do Mori, near the Rialto market, is one of the oldest bàcari.

title: Brothers in a Murano workshop carve glass layer by layer
desc: The Ferro brothers, trained by their father Paolo, cut coloured glass on spinning wheels in their Murano workshop, La Moleria, in work that can take weeks per piece. Fondamenta dei Vetrai is the island’s glassmakers’ quay.

title: Venice’s first female gondolier takes on a closed guild
place: Squero di San Trovaso, gondola boatyard
desc: Reporters meet Alex Hai, hailed by the press as the city’s first woman gondolier, and find a tangled story about identity and a thousand-year-old trade. Gondolas are still built and repaired at the San Trovaso boatyard.

title: A conductor is found poisoned between acts at the opera house
desc: John Yorke looks at Donna Leon’s 1992 novel, which introduced Commissario Guido Brunetti. A famous conductor dies during “La Traviata” at La Fenice, the opera house that burned down in 1996 and reopened in 2003.

title: A walk through Venice from island huts to mass tourism
desc: Travel writer Paul Bloomfield and historian Elizabeth Horodowich walk the canals and alleys, from the first island settlements through the trading empire to today’s pressures. The Rialto Bridge marks the old commercial heart of the city.

title: A writer on holiday falls fatally in love on the Lido
place: Grand Hotel des Bains, Lido di Venezia
desc: Thomas Mann’s 1912 novella follows the writer Aschenbach into an obsession that ends in his death during a cholera outbreak. Mann stayed at the Hotel des Bains, the beachfront hotel on the Lido where the story is set.

title: Napoleon ends a republic that lasted eleven centuries
place: Museo Storico Navale, naval history museum
desc: Roger Crowley, author of “City of Fortune”, tells Dan Snow how a navy and its shipyards made Venice rich, and how Ottoman pressure and Napoleon brought it down in 1797. The naval museum by the Arsenal holds models of the Republic’s ships.

title: A mask maker explains what Venetians hid behind papier-mâché
place: Tragicomica mask workshop, Calle dei Nomboli
desc: Venetian host Monica Cesarato talks with Tobia Dall’Osto of Tragicomica about the history of masks in the city and how they are still made by hand. The workshop is in Calle dei Nomboli, a lane in San Polo near Goldoni’s house.

title: Carnival once meant bull-baiting and human towers
desc: The old Republic’s carnival had animals loose in the alleys, mock castles smashed with maces and acrobats on ropes. Many of its biggest spectacles took place in St Mark’s Square, which is still the centre of the festival today.

title: A charming adventurer leaves a trail of scandal across Europe
desc: Dan Snow and Kate Lister look past the legend of Giacomo Casanova to the scams, spying and abuse in his memoirs. He was born in 1725 in Calle Malipiero, a lane in San Samuele parish; a plaque marks the spot. Contains adult themes.

title: A pupil of Vivaldi’s orphanage orchestra becomes his rival
place: La Pietà church, Riva degli Schiavoni
desc: The Ospedale della Pietà took in abandoned baby girls and hired Antonio Vivaldi to teach them music. Suzannah Lipscomb and novelist Harriet Constable tell the story of his star violinist, Anna Maria. The Pietà church stands on the waterfront.

title: A Christian fleet built in Venice sinks the Ottoman navy at Lepanto
desc: In 1571 the Holy League, led by Venice and Spain, defeated the Ottomans off Greece after the loss of Venetian Cyprus. Many of its galleys came from the Arsenal, whose gateway was given a statue of St Justina to mark the victory.

title: A printer with a mid-life crisis invents the pocket book
desc: Aldus Manutius set up his press in Venice in the 1490s and gave Europe small portable books and italic type. A plaque near Campo Sant’Agostin in San Polo marks the house where the Aldine Press worked.

title: Venice’s Jews are locked into the world’s first ghetto
desc: Marking 500 years since 1516, historian Jerry Brotton visits Cannaregio to tell how the Republic confined its Jewish residents to a former foundry island, the origin of the word “ghetto”. Its square, Campo del Ghetto Novo, still has three synagogues.

title: A doge is beheaded and painted out of the palace’s portrait gallery
place: Hall of the Great Council, Doge’s Palace
desc: Marino Faliero plotted a coup against the Republic in 1355 and was executed. In the Doge’s Palace, where portraits of the doges line the Hall of the Great Council, his place is still painted as a black shroud.

title: A Venetian merchant’s son spends decades at the court of Kublai Khan
place: Corte del Milion, Marco Polo’s family home
desc: Greg Jenner, historian Sharon Kinoshita and comedian Ria Lina follow Marco Polo to China and back. The Polo family house stood in the courtyard now called Corte del Milion, named after his book “Il Milione”, behind the Malibran theatre.

title: A wall-less city runs an empire from the Adriatic to the Black Sea
desc: Melvyn Bragg and guests explain how Venice built a trading empire stretching to Crete, Cyprus and the Black Sea. The Fondaco dei Turchi, a Grand Canal palazzo leased to Ottoman merchants from 1621, shows how close its business ties to the East ran.

title: Crusaders sack Constantinople and ship the loot home to Venice
place: Horses of St Mark, St Mark’s Basilica
desc: In 1204 a crusade steered by the Venetian doge Enrico Dandolo turned on Christian Constantinople. The four bronze horses on the front of St Mark’s Basilica are the most famous of the treasures carried back across the sea.

title: Refugees on a muddy lagoon build a city out of nothing
desc: Patrick Wyman traces how people fleeing the mainland after Rome’s fall settled the lagoon islands and grew rich on trade. Torcello, whose cathedral was founded in 639, was one of the earliest and busiest of those island settlements.

title: Romania Joins the Allies
desc: On August 23, 1944, twenty-two-year-old King Michael had dictator Ion Antonescu arrested inside this palace and switched Romania from the Axis to the Allies overnight, a move historians credit with shortening the war in Europe by months.

title: An army football club wins Europe in a country that has nothing
desc: Football writer Craig McCracken explains how Romania’s clubs were remade under communism, with the army’s Steaua and the police’s Dinamo dominating, and how Steaua, based at the Ghencea stadium, won the European Cup in 1986.

title: A British diplomat watches Romania starve itself to clear its debts
desc: Colin Munro was head of chancery at the British Embassy on Strada Jules Michelet in 1981–82, as Ceaușescu set out to repay the whole foreign debt. He describes the austerity that emptied shops and wore down the economy.

title: A young British lecturer teaches under the Securitate’s gaze
desc: Ron Mackay came to Bucharest in 1967 as a young British lecturer, when the city’s university district around University Square was full of curious students. He recalls shortages, travel restrictions and the secret police who watched foreigners.

title: A Reuters correspondent dodges gunfire to cover a revolution
desc: Former Reuters and BBC reporter Mark Brayne talks his way through roadblocks into Bucharest in December 1989, when the streets around University Square were contested by protesters and gunmen, and reflects on how it changed his life.

title: Belle époque boulevards meet the bulldozers of the 1980s
desc: Rick Steves walks through Bucharest’s mix of 19th-century boulevards, the restored Old Town around Lipscani street and the Civic Centre that replaced the historic core, then sketches the 1989 revolution and the city’s life inside the EU.

title: A TV detective is said to calm a restless communist nation
desc: A story told for decades claims Peter Falk once addressed Romanians on state television after the country ran out of Columbo episodes. Willa Paskin sets out to find whether it happened. TVR, the state broadcaster, is based on Calea Dorobanților.

title: A dictator’s palace swallows a fifth of the old city
desc: Ceaușescu’s Palace of the Parliament took thousands of workers and much of Romania’s marble and timber in the 1980s. Whole neighbourhoods, churches and a hill’s worth of streets were cleared to make room for the building and its boulevard.

title: An earthquake brings down the city’s grand apartment blocks
desc: On 4 March 1977 a magnitude 7.2 earthquake killed about 1,500 people, most of them in Bucharest. Interwar blocks along Magheru boulevard collapsed, and this archive footage shows rescuers working through the rubble in the days after.

title: A centuries-old market still feeds the city’s northeastern edge
desc: Piața Obor, the sprawling market hall and stalls on the city’s northeastern side, has been a cornerstone of Bucharest life for centuries. Monocle’s Laura Kramer walks the aisles of produce, butchers and snack counters where locals still do their shopping.

title: A translator secretly dubs thousands of banned Hollywood films
desc: Irina Nistor translated programmes for Romanian state television, whose headquarters stand on Calea Dorobanților. From 1985 she also voiced smuggled VHS films at night, four to six a sitting, and her voice became known in homes across the country.

title: Teenagers string their own internet across the tower blocks
desc: In the late 1990s, Bucharest teenagers ran cables between the rooftops of communist-era apartment blocks to share a connection. The homemade neighbourhood networks grew big enough to worry telecom firms and helped give Romania fast, cheap broadband.

title: A dictator’s balcony speech turns into his downfall
desc: How Nicolae Ceaușescu went from Western-courted maverick to hated despot, ending with the jeering crowd below the Central Committee building on what is now Revolution Square in December 1989.

title: Svefn-g-englar
creator: Sigur Rós
desc: The title means ‘Sleepwalkers’ — ten minutes of bowed-guitar drift and Jónsi’s falsetto ‘Vonlenska’ (hopelandic) nonsense-tongue. Recorded at Sundlaugin, the band’s studio in a converted swimming pool at Álafoss.

title: A government committee decides what parents may call their baby
desc: Iceland keeps an approved list of about 4,000 first names, and new ones must pass a three-person committee. Its chair, a professor at the University of Iceland, explains the rules; former mayor Jón Gnarr recalls his 25-year fight to change his name.

title: A hilltop church takes four decades to build
desc: State architect Guðjón Samúelsson modelled Hallgrímskirkja, the white concrete church on Skólavörðuholt hill, on basalt columns. Work began in 1945 and it was consecrated only in 1986. The episode also covers the poet it honours and its huge Klais organ.

title: Wine and vodka are legal but beer stays banned until 1989
desc: Strong beer stayed illegal in Iceland until 1 March 1989, long after wine and spirits returned, so people spiked weak legal ale with vodka. The host asks Helga Vollertsen, ethnology curator at the National Museum of Iceland, how the rule lasted so long.

title: Reagan and Gorbachev arrive at a small white house by the sea
desc: Archive footage from the Reagan Library of the October 1986 summit: arrivals in the rain, handshakes on the steps and the grim faces at the end. The talks took place in Höfði, a 1909 wooden house on the shore that the city uses for official receptions.

title: An office-block school teaches the lore of Iceland’s hidden folk
desc: The Elf School, Álfaskólinn, runs classes on elves and other hidden people from a building on Síðumúli, a street of offices in eastern Reykjavík. The host sits in on a lesson with headmaster Magnús Skarphéðinsson.

title: A column of light rises every autumn from a small island
desc: Yoko Ono’s own film about the Imagine Peace Tower, a beam of searchlights on Viðey, an island in the bay off Reykjavík. It is lit each year on 9 October, John Lennon’s birthday, and the white base is engraved with “imagine peace” in 24 languages.

title: An artist wraps a concert hall in thousands of glass bricks
desc: Ólafur Elíasson talks through the façade he designed with Henning Larsen Architects for Harpa, the concert hall on Reykjavík’s old harbour, where geometric glass cells catch the low northern light. The 2008 crash nearly halted construction.

title: Neighbours settle the day’s news in a steaming hot pot
desc: Geothermal water keeps Reykjavík’s public pools warm all year, and their hot tubs work as the city’s meeting places. Laugardalslaug, the largest, sits in the Laugardalur valley. BBC Reel asks whether this daily soak explains Icelanders’ contentment.

title: Two superpowers nearly scrap their nukes in a seaside house
desc: In October 1986 Reagan and Gorbachev met in Höfði, a white wooden house on the Reykjavík shore. US arms control chief Ken Adelman recalls the talks that came close to abolishing nuclear weapons, then broke down over missile defence.

title: Nine in ten women walk out and the whole country stops
desc: On 24 October 1975 Icelandic women stopped work and housework, shutting banks and factories, and about 25,000 gathered at Lækjartorg, the square in central Reykjavík. Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, later the first woman elected president, recalls the day.

title: Women walk off work and fill the square in the centre of town
desc: On 24 October 1975 about 90% of Iceland’s women stopped work, at home and in offices, for a day. Around 25,000 of them rallied at Lækjartorg, the square at the heart of old Reykjavík, in a country of only 220,000 people.

title: A rainbow-painted street climbs to a concrete church
desc: Skólavörðustígur runs uphill from the main shopping street to Hallgrímskirkja, with a rainbow painted along its lower stretch since Pride 2015. It is lined with galleries, wool shops and cafés in central Reykjavík.

title: A small fishing capital in the 1950s, on archive film
desc: Archive footage from the Huntley Film Archives shows Reykjavík and Iceland in the 1950s, when the capital was still a modest town of low houses around the harbour and Lækjartorg, the square at the heart of the old centre.

title: A polite invasion catches a neutral nation off guard
desc: British marines landed here before dawn on May 10, 1940, and the British consul reportedly asked a local police officer to move the crowd back so soldiers could disembark. Iceland, with no military of its own, formally protested but offered no resistance.

title: British troops sail into a neutral harbour without asking
desc: On 10 May 1940 British forces landed at Reykjavík’s harbour to keep Germany out of Iceland, and American troops later took over. The occupiers built the city’s airport, and their army huts housed Reykjavík families for years after the war.

title: Fermented shark and whale meat test a visitor’s nerve
desc: Hákarl is Greenland shark cured by fermenting and then hanging it to dry for months, a traditional Icelandic food with a strong ammonia smell. Old-style dishes like this are still served in central Reykjavík near the old harbour.

title: Bands from a tiny capital play every bar and gallery for a week
desc: A documentary about Iceland Airwaves, the music festival that since 1999 has filled downtown clubs, churches and museums with local and visiting bands each autumn. Hafnarhús, the art museum in a former harbour warehouse, is a longtime venue.

title: A reclusive American challenges the Soviet champion in a sports hall
desc: A 1972 BBC film on the world chess championship between Bobby Fischer and Boris Spassky, a Cold War duel full of demands and walkouts. It was played at Laugardalshöll, the city’s sports arena in the Laugardalur valley.

title: A teacher sets out to collect the penis of every Icelandic mammal
desc: A look inside the Icelandic Phallological Museum, begun in 1974 by teacher Sigurður Hjartarson and now run by his son. It holds hundreds of specimens from whales to mice, displayed in a museum at Hafnartorg by the old harbour.

title: A country lets its banks fail and puts bankers on trial
desc: In October 2008 Iceland’s three big banks collapsed within days. Instead of rescuing them, the state let them fail, protected domestic savers and later prosecuted senior bankers. Landsbanki’s old head office stands on Austurstræti, the downtown street.

title: A government treats policy like a design problem
desc: Built in 1822 as the seat of Russian-era government, this neoclassical palace now houses an office that tests laws like design prototypes, running small-scale trials before rolling policies out nationwide, a practice Finland had to legalize first.

title: A city gives itself a library as a birthday present
desc: Oodi, the central library facing Parliament across Kansalaisaukio square, opened in 2018 for Finland’s centenary. Its timber wave holds sewing machines, 3D printers and studios below a top-floor reading room the city calls its living room.

title: A public sauna on the shore looks like a slab of rock
desc: Löyly, a public sauna on the Hernesaari waterfront, was built in 2016 by Avanto Architects on a former industrial shore. Thermally treated pine slats wrap the saunas, and bathers climb down a ladder straight into the Baltic between rounds.

title: A country decides homeless people should get a flat first
desc: Finland is the only EU country where homelessness has kept falling, after it swapped hostels for permanent flats with support under the Housing First policy from 2008. In Helsinki the big hostel at Alppikatu 25 in Kallio became supported homes.

title: Inside the studio where Alvar Aalto drew his late masterpieces
desc: Studio Aalto, the architect’s office on Tiilimäki in leafy Munkkiniemi, was built in 1955 around a sunken courtyard that doubled as an outdoor theatre. Finlandia Hall and much of his later work were drawn here, and it is still open for tours.

title: A postwar textile firm prints Finland’s bright self-image
desc: Marimekko, founded in 1951 by Armi Ratia, still prints fabric at its factory and headquarters in Herttoniemi in east Helsinki. Its bold poppies and stripes, worn by Jacqueline Kennedy, turned simple cotton dresses into a national calling card.

title: A city’s bomb shelters double as gyms and swimming pools
desc: Helsinki has dug hundreds of civil defence shelters into its granite, enough for everyone. In peacetime they serve as gyms, car parks and play halls, like the cavern swimming pool at Itäkeskus, built to be emptied and turned back into a shelter.

title: A student writes an operating system in his Helsinki bedroom
desc: In 1991 Linus Torvalds, a 21-year-old computer science student at the University of Helsinki, posted a hobby kernel online. This episode retells his memoir Just for Fun, from a Swedish-speaking Helsinki childhood to the birth of Linux.

title: A Lutheran church rises over the tsar’s new capital
desc: Helsinki Cathedral, the white domed church at the top of Senate Square’s steps, was designed by Carl Ludvig Engel and finished in 1852 after his death. Built for Russian-ruled Finland, it became the defining shape of the city skyline.

title: A sea fortress turns into a neighbourhood with a ferry commute
desc: Suomenlinna, the island fortress fifteen minutes by ferry from Market Square, lost its military role and is now home to residents, artists’ studios, a prison work camp and summer picnickers. Monocle visits to see how Helsinki uses it today.

title: An old bus station hides an art museum under its square
desc: Amos Rex, the art museum by JKMM Architects, opened in 2018 beneath the yard of Lasipalatsi, a 1930s functionalist pavilion. Its galleries sit underground, and their skylight domes rise from the square, where children climb and slide on them.

title: A theatre on a park slope becomes a modernist landmark
desc: Helsinki City Theatre, a long white building set into the slope of Eläintarha park, was designed by Timo Penttilä and opened in 1967. It is counted among Finland’s best postwar modernist buildings and still stages the city’s big productions.

title: A Swedish island fortress guards the harbour for two centuries
desc: Suomenlinna, the sea fortress spread over islands at the harbour mouth, was begun by Sweden in 1748 to hold off Russia. Russia took it anyway in 1808. Today it is a UNESCO site and a neighbourhood of about 800 people, reached by city ferry.
