title: Granite bears and forest myths creep onto city facades
desc: Around 1900 Helsinki’s architects built a national style from rough granite, animals and Finnish legend. Eliel Saarinen’s railway station, with its four lantern-carrying giants, is the best-known example in the city centre.

title: A 1914 brick market hall reopens after five years shut
desc: Hakaniemi’s red-brick market hall opened in 1914 to feed the working-class north side of the bridge. It closed for a full renovation in 2018 and reopened in 2023, with fishmongers, bakers and cafés back on two floors.

title: A newly independent country splits into Reds and Whites
desc: Weeks after declaring independence, Finland fell into civil war. In January 1918 a red lantern lit in the tower of Paasitorni, Helsinki’s workers’ hall, signalled the Red Guards’ takeover of the capital. Wesley Livesay traces how the split began.

title: The Soviet Union joins the Olympics in a small Nordic capital
desc: The Olympic Stadium, with its white functionalist tower, finally hosted the Games in 1952 after the 1940 edition was cancelled by war. The Soviet Union competed for the first time, housed in its own village, and Emil Zátopek won three golds.

title: A Czech soldier wins three golds in eight days
desc: At the 1952 Games in Helsinki’s Olympic Stadium, Emil Zátopek won the 5,000m, the 10,000m and then the marathon, his first ever race at that distance. Author Richard Askwith talks about the runner and how communist Czechoslovakia later turned on him.

title: A forest grows to print books no one has read yet
desc: One thousand spruce trees were planted here in 2014 to eventually print a single anthology in 2114, containing manuscripts by authors like Margaret Atwood that no living person will read, sealed away in an Oslo library room until the forest matures.

title: A prime minister recalls building a fund to outlast the oil
desc: Jens Stoltenberg, twice Norway’s prime minister and later head of NATO, talks with the oil fund’s chief about the political choices behind it, many argued out in the Storting, the parliament building on Karl Johans gate, and the rule limiting spending.

title: A teenager’s murder brings tens of thousands onto the streets
desc: In 2001, 15-year-old Benjamin Hermansen was killed by neo-Nazis near his home in Holmlia, a suburb in south Oslo. The march that followed was called the city’s biggest crowd since liberation in 1945. A childhood friend remembers him.

title: A sloping marble roof invites the whole city to walk on the opera
desc: Snøhetta’s opera house opened in 2008 on the Bjørvika waterfront, its white stone roof rising from the fjord like an ice floe. This explainer walks through the idea of a public building people can climb on freely, and how its form was worked out.

title: A politician’s surname becomes a word for traitor
desc: Vidkun Quisling urged Hitler to occupy Norway, then led the puppet government from 1942. He lived at Villa Grande on Bygdøy, a mansion he renamed Gimle, now the Norwegian Holocaust Center. He was shot for treason at Akershus Fortress in 1945.

title: Two women are buried in a ship that survives eleven centuries
place: Museum of the Viking Age (Viking Ship Museum)
desc: The Oseberg ship was dug out of a burial mound near Tønsberg in 1904, with the remains of two women, a cart, sledges and carved animal heads. It now sits on the Bygdøy peninsula at the Museum of the Viking Age, the rebuilt Viking Ship Museum.

title: A girl from Oslo wins three Olympics, then conquers Hollywood
desc: Sonja Henie grew up in Oslo and trained on the ice at Frogner Stadium, where a statue of her now stands. She won Olympic gold in 1928, 1932 and 1936, then moved to America to star in skating films and ice revues, which made her rich and divisive at home.

title: One sculptor fills a city park with 200 naked figures
desc: Gustav Vigeland spent decades on the granite and bronze figures in Frogner Park, from bawling babies to the old, ending at a monolith of 121 tangled bodies. Rick Steves walks the main axis and explains what the sculptor was trying to say about life.

title: A Viking museum is rebuilt around ships too fragile to move far
place: Museum of the Viking Age (Viking Ship Museum)
desc: The 1920s Viking Ship Museum on Bygdøy is being expanded into the Museum of the Viking Age, and its thousand-year-old ships had to stay on site while builders worked around them. Oslo guide Pål gets an early look behind the hoardings.

title: A ski jump towers over the city that made skiing a sport
desc: Ski jumping has been held on the Holmenkollen hill since 1892, and the current steel jump, rebuilt in 2010, is visible from much of Oslo. Pål goes up the jump tower and through the ski museum in its base, which covers four thousand years of skiing.

title: Office workers take a sauna break and jump into the fjord
desc: In the last decade Oslo’s harbour has filled with wood-fired saunas, many floating on rafts beside the Bjørvika quays near the opera house. Pål tries one and then the cold plunge into the Oslofjord that locals do even in midwinter.

title: A polar hero becomes a champion for stateless refugees
desc: This ship carried Nansen to a record-setting Arctic latitude, and a third of Oslo turned out to welcome him home. He later won the Nobel Peace Prize for repatriating half a million WWI prisoners and inventing a passport for stateless refugees.

title: A nation’s art collections move under one enormous roof
desc: The National Museum opened in 2022 beside the old Vestbanen rail station, merging four collections of art, architecture and design, including Munch’s The Scream. The museum’s own film shows the slate building and its glowing alabaster-glass hall on top.

title: Old farmhouses and a stave church are rebuilt on a city peninsula
desc: The Norwegian Folk Museum on Bygdøy collected log farmhouses, barns and a medieval stave church from across the country and reassembled them as an open-air village, showing how rural Norwegians lived before industry.

title: A container port is turned into a city on the water
desc: Since the 1980s Oslo has cleared roads and docks from its harbour edge under the Fjord City plan, building Aker Brygge, Tjuvholmen and the Barcode towers in Bjørvika. Urban researcher Heidi Bergsli explains how the plan came together.

title: Secret talks run by Norwegian diplomats lead to a Middle East handshake
desc: In 1993 Norway quietly hosted Israeli and PLO negotiators. Mona Juul, a diplomat at the foreign ministry at Victoria Terrasse, helped arrange the meetings that ended in the Rabin–Arafat handshake at the White House.

title: A seafaring nation keeps its famous vessels in one harbourside row
desc: Bygdøy’s museum quarter holds the polar ship Fram, which carried Nansen and Amundsen into the ice, alongside Thor Heyerdahl’s rafts and Norway’s maritime museum. The Fram Museum is built around the ship itself.

title: A capital pulls the cars out of its downtown streets
desc: Oslo removed most parking spaces and through traffic from its centre and handed the space to benches, bike lanes and cafés. The report looks at how shops and residents in the centre, around Karl Johans gate, took the change.

title: Fjäriln vingad syns på Haga
creator: Carl Michael Bellman
desc: The title means “the winged butterfly appears at Haga.” Bellman, Stockholm’s beloved 18th-century troubadour, set this song in Haga Park, the royal grounds north of the city. Most Swedes still know it by heart; a nearby carillon chimes it hourly.

title: A leaning tower opens to hold one painter’s life’s work
desc: The MUNCH museum opened in 2021 on the Bjørvika waterfront, a 13-storey tower with a bent top built to hold the thousands of paintings, prints and drawings Edvard Munch left to the city of Oslo.

title: Old trams and buses rest in a depot in Majorstuen
desc: The Sporveismuseet keeps Oslo’s public transport history, from horse trams to early metro cars, in an old tram depot. It is run by volunteers and sits in Majorstuen, on the west side of the city centre.

title: A toboggan run races the metro back down from the forest
desc: Korketrekkeren, the Corkscrew, is a 2 km sledging run built for the 1952 Winter Olympics. Sledgers ride the Holmenkollen line up to Frognerseteren station, in the forest above the city, and slide back down to Midtstuen.

title: Emmylou
creator: First Aid Kit
desc: First Aid Kit are sisters Klara and Johanna Söderberg, from the Stockholm suburb of Enskede, who taught themselves close-harmony Americana. This 2012 song, name-checking country legends, is their tender breakthrough — Swedes channelling the old west.

title: The Final Countdown
creator: Europe
desc: Before the synth riff conquered every stadium on earth, Europe were a glam-metal band from Upplands Väsby, a commuter town north of Stockholm. This 1986 monster — all hair, keyboards, and drama — remains one of Sweden’s biggest global exports.

title: Somliga går med trasiga skor
creator: Cornelis Vreeswijk
desc: The title means “some walk in worn-out shoes.” Cornelis Vreeswijk, the Dutch-born bard of Stockholm’s 1960s café scene, sang this tender lament for the down-and-out. Picture it up on Söder’s Mosebacke, long a haunt of the city’s poets and singers.

title: Välkommen till förorten
creator: The Latin Kings
desc: The title means “welcome to the suburbs.” The Latin Kings, from the immigrant estates of Alby in Botkyrka, were among the first to rap in Swedish — in the multi-ethnic slang of the suburbs. Their 1994 debut gave Stockholm’s concrete outskirts a voice.

title: Staten och kapitalet
creator: Ebba Grön
desc: The title means “the state and capital.” Ebba Grön, four kids from the concrete suburb of Rågsved, made this snarling 1980 cover the anthem of Swedish punk — a working-class roar against power that Swedes still shout back word for word.

title: Levels
creator: Avicii
desc: Avicii — Tim Bergling, from Stockholm’s Östermalm — became the face of the global EDM boom before his death in 2018. This 2011 track, built on a sampled Etta James wail, is his euphoric calling card; the city’s old Globe arena now bears his name.

title: 163 För Evigt
creator: Cherrie
desc: The title means “163 forever” — 163 is the postcode of Rinkeby, the Somali-Swedish suburb where Cherrie grew up. Her 2017 R&B hit, a love letter to the neighborhood’s overlooked youth, went viral far beyond Sweden without a word of English.

title: Ginseng Strip 2002
creator: Yung Lean
desc: Yung Lean, a teenager from Stockholm’s Södermalm, became an unlikely global cult figure — a founder of woozy internet “cloud rap.” This raw 2013 track, half-joking and strangely moving, spread worldwide from a bedroom and shaped a generation of sound.

title: Dancing On My Own
creator: Robyn
desc: Robyn, born and raised in Stockholm, reinvented herself as pop’s queen of the crying-on-the-dancefloor anthem. This 2010 masterpiece — heartbreak set to euphoric synths — is her signature, and the spirit of Södermalm’s nightlife distilled.

title: Dancing Queen
creator: ABBA
desc: ABBA formed in Stockholm in 1972 and became the biggest pop group the world had ever seen. This 1976 disco anthem is their shimmering peak. Their whole story now fills the ABBA Museum on the green island of Djurgården, where you can sing along yourself.

title: A herding call once meant to summon cows across valleys
desc: For centuries, Swedish herdswomen used kulning, a piercing, wordless singing style, to call cattle home across mountain valleys. Folk scholar Susanne Rosenberg, who teaches the technique at this conservatory, keeps a nearly lost rural tradition alive.

title: A prime minister is shot walking home from the movies
desc: Palme dismissed his bodyguards, as he often did, and was walking home from a cinema with his wife when a gunman shot him on this sidewalk in 1986. Nearly forty years and over a hundred confessions later, the case remains formally unsolved.

title: A laureate crosses the stage and spots his daughter crying
desc: Every December 10th, this hall hosts the ceremony for five of the six Nobel categories, laureates receiving medals from the King of Sweden. Chemistry laureate Morten Meldal recalls crossing this stage and glimpsing his daughter crying a few rows back.

title: Death challenges a knight to one final chess game
desc: Bergman directed here for decades before and after making the 1957 film that opens with Death challenging a Crusader to chess on a plague-ridden beach. The 1000th edition of this show unpacks how one haunting image made a Swedish director world-famous.

title: Lush Life
creator: Zara Larsson
desc: Zara Larsson, a Stockholm girl who won Sweden’s got-talent show at ten, grew up into a global pop star. This bright, brass-flecked 2015 single was her international breakthrough — the polished, radio-ready end of the Stockholm hit machine.

title: Young Folks
creator: Peter Bjorn and John
desc: Peter Bjorn and John, a Stockholm indie trio, built this 2006 worldwide hit around one of pop’s most famous whistled hooks and a boy-girl duet. Impossibly catchy, it became the sound of late-2000s indie and put Swedish indie-pop on the map.

title: Cobrastyle
creator: Teddybears
desc: Teddybears, a Stockholm band who began in hardcore punk, struck global gold with this 2004 dancehall-rock romp — later inescapable in games, ads, and clubs. Brash, playful, and a showcase of the city’s knack for a monster hook.

title: Sakta vi gå genom stan
creator: Monica Zetterlund
desc: The title means “slowly we walk through town.” Monica Zetterlund, Sweden’s great jazz voice, turned an American standard into the definitive Stockholm night-song — a hushed stroll through the old city, best pictured across Gamla stan’s lamplit lanes.

title: A whole country swaps sides of the road before dawn
desc: On 3 September 1967 Sweden switched from driving on the left to the right, despite a referendum that had rejected it. Traffic paused nationwide at dawn. The best-known photos of the day were taken on Kungsgatan, the central shopping street.

title: A young queen is crowned king, then gives up the throne
desc: Christina of Sweden was crowned king at Storkyrkan, the cathedral in Gamla stan, in 1650. Learned, unmarried and restless, she abdicated four years later, converted to Catholicism and moved to Rome. Suzannah Lipscomb sorts fact from legend.

title: A sunken warship is hauled up from the harbour after 333 years
desc: In 1961 divers and pontoons lifted the Vasa, lost on her maiden voyage in 1628, back to the surface of Stockholm’s harbour. The museum’s own film tells the salvage story; the ship now sits restored inside the Vasa Museum on Djurgården.

title: A Cold War bunker under a park becomes a server hall
desc: Pionen, a civil-defence shelter blasted into the bedrock under Vitabergsparken on Södermalm, was rebuilt as a data centre with greenhouse plants, fake waterfalls and submarine engines. The internet provider that runs it gives the tour.

title: Two young architects turn a gravel pit into a forest of the dead
desc: Gunnar Asplund and Sigurd Lewerentz won the 1915 competition for Skogskyrkogården, the Woodland Cemetery in southern Stockholm, and spent decades on its pines, chapels and open hill. It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1994.

title: A royal island retreat keeps its 18th-century theatre working
desc: Drottningholm Palace on Lovön, west of the city, is the royal family’s home. Its grounds hold a Chinese pavilion and a 1766 court theatre whose original wooden stage machinery still runs. The whole estate is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

title: The medieval island where Stockholm began
desc: Gamla stan, the old town, packs narrow lanes, merchant houses and the royal palace onto one small island. At its centre is Stortorget, the square where the painted gabled houses face the old Stock Exchange, now the Nobel Prize Museum.

title: The town hall where Nobel laureates dine each December
desc: Stockholm City Hall, the brick tower on the tip of Kungsholmen finished in 1923, hosts the Nobel banquet every 10 December. Guests eat in the Blue Hall, then dance upstairs in the Golden Hall under walls covered in gold mosaic.

title: Old farmhouses from across Sweden rebuilt on one hill
desc: Skansen, opened on Djurgården in 1891 by Artur Hazelius, was the world’s first open-air museum. Farmsteads, churches and workshops were moved here from all over Sweden, with costumed staff showing old crafts and rural life.

title: White ferries thread through thousands of islands
desc: The Stockholm archipelago spreads around 30,000 islands and skerries east of the city, many dotted with red summer cottages. Old steamers and commuter boats still leave from Strömkajen, the quay facing the Grand Hôtel.

title: A king flees his palace hours before Nazi tanks arrive
desc: King Haakon VII was woken in this palace before dawn on April 9, 1940, and fled with his government just hours ahead of the German invasion. He spent the war broadcasting to Norway from exile in London, refusing every demand to abdicate.

title: A king dies after a feast of cream-filled buns
desc: King Adolf Frederick died at the Royal Palace in 1771 after a huge Shrove Tuesday dinner capped with semlor, cardamom buns filled with almond paste and cream. Max Miller bakes the 18th-century version and explains how the bun became a Swedish obsession.

title: Unarmed bombers fly ball bearings out of neutral Sweden
desc: During the Second World War, BOAC flew stripped-down Mosquito bombers between Scotland and Bromma airport, carrying ball bearings, diplomats and passengers in the bomb bay. Mark Felton tells the story of the risky night run over occupied Norway.

title: A tangle of traffic between lake and sea is rebuilt for people
desc: Slussen, the lock and road junction between Gamla stan and Södermalm, holds back Lake Mälaren from the Baltic. The city’s own film explains why the 1930s cloverleaf was torn down and what the new bridges, quays and squares are meant to become.

title: Old working ships retire along a promenade full of joggers
desc: Stockholm is built on 14 islands joined by about 50 bridges, and much of its shoreline is given over to walkers rather than cars. Rick Steves strolls the waterfront promenades, where old steamers and working boats are moored below grand apartment facades.

title: Sweden’s national art collection reopens in its 1860s palace
desc: Nationalmuseum, the waterfront art museum on Blasieholmen, holds Sweden’s national collection of painting, sculpture and design, from Rembrandt to Carl Larsson. Its 1866 building by Friedrich August Stüler reopened in 2018 after a five-year renovation.

title: The joy and anxiety of Søren Kierkegaard
desc: In a leafy square outside the Royal Library sits a statue of Søren Kierkegaard, the Copenhagen-born philosopher. This fun and lucid video from the School of Life explains how his suggested antidote to anxiety was to “laugh defiantly at life’s horrors.”

title: Hostages come to trust the man holding them captive
desc: Bank robber Jan-Erik Olsson held four employees hostage here for six days in 1973, and by the end they trusted him more than the police outside. Psychiatrist Nils Bejerot coined a new term to explain it, one that escaped the original crime entirely.

title: A bank robbery gives the world a name for loving your captor
desc: In August 1973 a robber held four bank employees for six days in the vault of Kreditbanken on Norrmalmstorg. The hostages came to side with their captors, and a psychiatrist’s comment gave ‘Stockholm syndrome’ its name.

title: A brief history of the world at Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek
desc: Graciously donated by beer magnates, the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek houses an impressive art collection spanning several millennia of human history. In this video, guidebook author Rick Steves points out a few highlights. Pro tip: Don’t miss the Rodin room.

title: Small jokes and details built into the metro’s trains
desc: Stockholm’s tunnelbana opened in 1950 and now has three colour-coded lines and about 100 stations, many of them decorated by artists. All lines meet at T-Centralen, the hub beneath the main railway station.

title: New thinking on old coffee traditions
desc: April is an acclaimed coffee roaster in Copenhagen with a small café in Inner Østerbro. In this podcast episode, Benjamen Walker visits April as he journeys through Paris, Copenhagen, and Nairobi to learn about the burgeoning business of artisanal coffee.

title: Creating the world’s first carbon-neutral capital
desc: On the northern tip of the industrial-cool Refshaleøen area is a massive power plant, converted from coal to cleaner biomass in 2016. This video from B1M explains many other technologies and policies Copenhagen uses to meet its carbon neutrality goal.

title: Feelings of food and family
desc: Milton Abel II is the pastry chef of Hart Bageri, a beloved bakery in Copenhagen. In this poignant and cinematic short film, he reflects on how his work to become an all-star chef at The French Laundry and Noma mirrors his father’s journey as a musician.

title: Hygge and what it means to be Danish
desc: This piece from The Guardian opens with jaded gripes about the trendiness of hygge—the Danish word for convivial coziness—but unfolds into a fascinating exploration of broader cultural issues. (For a decidedly hygge part of Copenhagen, try Jægersborggade.)

title: The Prophet Mohammad and the right to publish freely
desc: In 2010, police dogs searched the Cophenhagen office of Jyllands-Posten newspaper after a bomb threat. This report from Witness History explains the global controversy that erupted in 2005 after the paper published cartoons depicting the Prophet Mohammed.

title: The vote (and re-vote) to form the European Union
desc: In May 1993, irate Danes gathered in St. Hans Square in Nørrebro to protest Denmark joining 11 other countries to form the European Union. They had reason to be angry — Denmark had voted “no” a year earlier. This episode of Witness History tells the story.

title: Twisting above the treetops
desc: Located an hour south of Copenhagen by car, Camp Adventure is a nature-oriented park that features a stunning tower with a walkway that spirals dramatically above the trees. This report from CBS Sunday Morning offers a look at the unique structure.

title: Feast your eyes at Torvehallerne Food Market
desc: This quick video from Condé Nast Traveler shares fleeting glimpses of the food available at the chic and modern Torvehallerne Food Market. The video itself isn’t anything special, but it will make you want to visit the market for a tasty smørrebrød or two.

title: Getting a taste for Danish licorice
desc: Lakrids by Bülow makes artisanal licorice that can shock tastebuds outside Scandinavia. In this jokey report from CBS Sunday Morning, Conor Knighton meets the founder Johan Bülow and tours the factory. (There is a Lakrids shop in Illum department store.)

title: Copenhagen’s contribution to medical science
desc: The modern ventilator was invented by the desperate staff at Copenhagen University Hospital as they fought to save lives during the polio epidemic of 1952. This episode of Witness History relays the firsthand account of a medical student who was there.

title: Studying the stars with Tycho Brahe
desc: The Tycho Brahe Planetarium has a small exhibit about its namesake Danish astronomer. This well-made episode of Noble Blood offers a catchy introduction to Brahe, a leading scientist in 16th-century Europe who died just before the telescope’s invention.

title: Staying grounded at a “kolonihave”
desc: Founded in 1892, Kolonihaven Vennelyst is one of Copenhagen’s many community garden allotments called “kolonihave.” This quick episode of The Urbanist paints a picture of the slower pace and idyllic lifestyle associated with the sought-after gardens.

title: Pizza under the influence
desc: Restauranteur Christian Puglisi owns Bæst, a pizza-focused restaurant that blends the acclaimed chef’s Italian roots with other European influences. He talks about pizza and sustainability in an interview halfway through this episode of The Europeans.

title: Voices from inside Herstedvester prison
desc: In Copenhagen, a prison houses dozens of men deemed too dangerous to stay in their native Greenland, a former Danish colony. This episode explains the controversies and challenges caused by the situation, then shares somber interviews with several inmates.

title: Cold beer and warm vibes
desc: This video from Visit Copenhagen shares the story of Microbrewery Ølsnedkeren. The owner and brewer, Simon Toft Hansen, shares the story of how he slowly transformed used brewing equipment into a cozy neighborhood pub serving unique artisanal beers.

title: The turnaround of Carlsberg brewery
place: Home of Carlsberg brewery visitor centre
desc: This half-hour report from Bloomberg details the many efforts taken by a new Dutch CEO who helped revitalize and reinvigorate the Danish brewery after it struggled in the market in the mid-2010s. Carlsberg’s Copenhagen brewery offers tours and tastings.

title: Alliances across Scandinavia
desc: At Ved Stranden 18 is the global headquarters of Nordic Council, a cooperative group between nearby countries that acts almost like a mini-EU within Scandinavia — or, kind-of-Scandinavia. This fun video from CGP Grey explains the regional terminology.

title: A city in pursuit of livability
desc: This meditative video from Denmark.dk focuses on how architecture, urban planning, and city infrastructure can create a more livable city. Many of Copenhagen’s most bold projects are featured, including Superkilen Park and the residential complex 8 House.

title: Scandi Noir and Danish films of the future
desc: This video from Culture Trip’s “Beyond Hollywood” series visits Stockholm and Copenhagen to learn about Scandi Noir, a style of moody drama films made by Scandinavian directors. The Copenhagen part features Huset cultural center and Super 16 film school.

title: Getting a lay of the land in Christianshavn and Christiania
place: Church of Our Saviour (Vor Frelsers Kirke)
desc: In this video, American travel writer Rick Steves visits two central neighborhoods: trendy Christianshavn and communal Christiania. He suggests climbing the beautiful twisting spire of the Church of Our Savior for sweeping views over Copenhagen.

title: Champagne Galop
creator: Hans Christian Lumbye
desc: Hans Christian Lumbye, the “Strauss of the North,” was the house composer of the Tivoli Gardens. He wrote this fizzing 1845 galop — complete with a popping champagne cork — for the pleasure garden in the heart of the city, where his music still plays.

title: A bar that caters to regulars
desc: Gensyn is a pleasant cocktail bar in the Frederiksberg neighborhood. In this video from VisitCopenhagen, the co-owner Terkel Kleist explains his delightfully simple vision for the convivial and cozy neighborhood bar, whose name means “to see you again.”

title: 7 Years
creator: Lukas Graham
desc: Lukas Forchhammer grew up in Freetown Christiania, the car-free “free town” commune in the heart of Copenhagen. This aching 2015 ballad about ageing and ambition became a worldwide number one — and put his unconventional childhood on the map.

title: Sun of a Gun
creator: Oh Land
desc: Oh Land — Nanna Øland Fabricius — trained as a ballet dancer in Copenhagen until an injury turned her to music. This shimmering 2011 art-pop single launched her dreamlike sound, made near the city’s creative harbour island of Holmen.

title: My Little Anna
creator: Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen
desc: Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen — “NHØP,” the greatest of Danish jazz musicians — became house bassist at Jazzhus Montmartre at fifteen. There he backed the American greats who made 1960s Copenhagen a jazz haven; this is one of his own warm tunes.

title: A half-century of life in Freetown Christiania
desc: In the 1970s, squatters took over a former military base to create Freetown Christiania, a self-governed commune. In this episode, part of a series about utopias, people who grew up there recount their experiences and share bittersweet feelings on change.

title: Tidligt Op
creator: Gilli
desc: The title means “up early.” Gilli — from Rødovre, by way of the Nørrebro B.O.C. crew — turned melodic trap into the defining sound of Danish rap. This 2016 number one helped make him the most-streamed Danish artist of his generation.

title: I Danmark er jeg født
creator: Poul Schierbeck
desc: The title means “in Denmark I was born.” Hans Christian Andersen wrote these words as a love poem to his homeland; Poul Schierbeck’s 1926 melody made it a national favorite. Andersen lived for years on the colorful canal quay of Nyhavn.

title: Midt om natten
creator: Kim Larsen
desc: The title means “in the middle of the night.” After Gasolin’ split, frontman Kim Larsen became Denmark’s best-loved troubadour, a working-class poet born in Copenhagen. This 1983 anthem, from a film of the same name, is sung at every Danish party.

title: Kvinde min
creator: Gasolin’
desc: The title means “my woman.” Often called the finest Danish-language song ever, this 1975 power-pop ballad ends with a soaring guitar solo. Gasolin’, the country’s greatest rock band, were four friends from the canals of Christianshavn.

title: The rescue of the Danish Jews
desc: This report from Witness History explains how Jews fled by boat from occupied Denmark to neutral Sweden once the Nazis invaded in April 1940. The small Danish Jewish Museum has more on the valiant efforts that saved 95% of Danish Jews from the Holocaust.

title: Still Counting
creator: Volbeat
desc: Volbeat fuse heavy metal with rockabilly and a Johnny Cash twang, a sound built by frontman Michael Poulsen in Copenhagen. This thundering 2008 single, with its cynical chorus about a crooked world, became their international breakthrough.

title: Sleeping My Day Away
creator: D-A-D
desc: D-A-D — once “Disneyland After Dark,” until the lawyers called — were a Copenhagen cowboy-rock band who broke out worldwide with this 1989 hit, riding a galloping riff and a deadpan Danish swagger all the way to a major US record deal.

title: Barbie Girl
creator: Aqua
desc: The Danish-Norwegian group Aqua turned bubblegum Europop into a global phenomenon with this 1997 smash — a candy-coloured “life in plastic” satire that became one of the best-selling and most divisive pop songs ever made. They formed here in Copenhagen.

title: The ambitious aims of New Nordic Cuisine
desc: Claus Meyer founded the New Nordic Cuisine movement and co-founded the acclaimed Copenhagen restaurant Noma with Chef René Redzepi. This piece from The Guardian explains the aspirational intent and tangible outcomes of the movement’s 2004 food manifesto.

title: Overcoming a mid-life crisis with the help of a Danish chef
desc: After a painful divorce, New York Times food writer Jeff Gordinier got an unexpected invitation to meet Noma’s legendary chef René Redzepi for coffee. This delightful story from Outside shares how the two became fast friends who often adventured together.

title: Getting into the mind of Søren Kierkegaard
desc: In the atmospheric Assistens Cemetery is the grave of Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard. This slightly puzzling academic panel discussion from BBC’s In Our Time explores his theories and influences, from his hero Socrates to his Christian faith.

title: Maskarade (ouverture)
place: Royal Danish Theatre (Old Stage), Kongens Nytorv
creator: Carl Nielsen
desc: Carl Nielsen, Denmark’s greatest composer, set this beloved comic opera in 18th-century Copenhagen, where young lovers escape into a masked ball. Its sparkling overture still raises the curtain at the Royal Danish Theatre, where Nielsen once conducted.

title: The beheading of The Little Mermaid
desc: In 1998, mysterious vandals decapitated the statue of The Little Mermaid, a famous attraction on Copenhagen’s waterfront. This report from Witness History interviews Peter Jensen, the charmingly annoyed bronze specialist tasked with re-attaching the head.

title: Quiet pioneers of gay marriage
desc: At Copenhagen’s city hall in 1989, Ivan Larsen and Ove Carlsen became one of the first same-sex couples in the world to get a civil union. Witness History describes how the ceremony took place as a homophobic culture was rapidly becoming more tolerant.

title: A king’s summer house still guards the crown jewels
desc: Rosenborg Castle was built by Christian IV in the early 1600s as a summer retreat in what is now the King’s Garden. Its rooms keep royal furniture and tapestries, and the basement treasury holds the Danish crown jewels.

title: An army of Santas hands out a department store’s stock
place: Magasin du Nord department store, Kongens Nytorv
desc: In December 1974 about a hundred people dressed as Santa, from the theatre group Solvognen, gave away goods off the shelves of Magasin du Nord on Kongens Nytorv until police arrived. The stunt inspired today’s SantaCon.

title: Molly Malone
desc: Dublin’s unofficial anthem: a 19th-century ballad of a fishmonger crying “cockles and mussels, alive, alive-oh” through the streets until fever takes her. Her buxom bronze statue on Suffolk Street is rubbed for luck by every passing tourist.

title: Painted walls tell a nation’s story where the peace prize is given
desc: Oslo City Hall’s main hall is covered in murals of farmers, workers, occupation and resistance. The clip then crosses to Akershus Fortress, where a small museum recounts how Norwegians resisted the Nazi occupation of 1940–45.

title: British rockets set a neutral capital on fire
desc: In September 1807 Britain shelled Copenhagen for three nights to seize the Danish fleet. Hundreds of civilians died and the Church of Our Lady, the city’s cathedral, burned down; the neoclassical church there now replaced it.

title: Nelson’s fleet fights moored Danish hulks outside the harbour
desc: In April 1801 a British fleet attacked Danish ships moored as floating batteries off Copenhagen. The Trekroner sea fort, still on its artificial island at the harbour mouth, fired on the British line during the battle.

title: Gay couples sign the world’s first registered partnerships
desc: On 1 October 1989 Denmark became the first country to let same-sex couples register a legal partnership. Eleven couples signed at Copenhagen City Hall that day, among them activists Axel and Eigil Axgil.

title: Generating energy with a ski hill
desc: The first part of this BBC Travel episode showcases Amager Bakke—also known as CopenHill—an unlikely combination of trash incinerator, power plant, and recreational ski hill. In this video, reporter Cat Moh takes a behind-the-scenes tour. (Starts at ~1:15)

title: A waste-burning power plant with a ski slope on its roof
desc: Bjarke Ingels’ Amager Bakke, or CopenHill, opened in 2019: it burns the city’s rubbish for heat and power while skiers use the artificial slope on top. It stands in the industrial harbour area of Amager, east of the centre.

title: Nothing Compares 2 U
creator: Sinéad O’Connor
desc: Sinéad O’Connor, raised in the Dublin suburb of Glenageary, turned a little-known Prince song into one of the most devastating vocals ever recorded. The 1990 video — her shaven head, a single tear — made her a global, uncompromising icon.

title: I Will Follow
creator: U2
desc: Four teenagers from a Northside school became the biggest band on earth. This urgent 1980 debut single, from their album Boy, is where it began — recorded around Windmill Lane, whose graffitied studio wall became a pilgrimage site for U2 fans.

title: Raglan Road
creator: Luke Kelly / The Dubliners
desc: The poet Patrick Kavanagh set these verses of doomed love on a real Dublin street in Ballsbridge; Luke Kelly of The Dubliners gave them their definitive, aching voice — a ballad of a walk down a quiet road, and a heart given away too easily.

title: Whiskey in the Jar
creator: Thin Lizzy
desc: Thin Lizzy electrified this old highwayman ballad in 1972, and Dublin’s Phil Lynott became Ireland’s first great rock star — a mixed-race kid from Crumlin fronting a hard-rock band. His statue stands just off Grafton Street, on Harry Street.

title: Take Me to Church
creator: Hozier
desc: Hozier, from Bray just south of Dublin, wrote this smouldering 2013 anthem — a swipe at the church’s grip on Irish life, wrapped in gospel and blues — in his attic. It became one of the biggest songs on earth, from an Irish unknown.

title: I Have a Love
creator: For Those I Love
desc: David Balfe, from Coolock on Dublin’s Northside, made this 2021 elegy for a close friend he lost — spoken-word grief over shimmering electronics. Raw, local, and universal, it turned working-class Dublin sorrow into something transcendent.

title: Crazy World
creator: Aslan
desc: Aslan came out of working-class Finglas on Dublin’s Northside, fronted by the beloved, troubled Christy Dignam. This 1993 anthem of love and struggle is a Dublin singalong staple, roared back at the band by crowds who claim it as their own.

title: The Blower’s Daughter
creator: Damien Rice
desc: Damien Rice, from Celbridge on Dublin’s western edge, recorded his hushed debut O largely himself. This 2002 heartbreak ballad — “I can’t take my eyes off you” — reached the world through the film Closer, all whispered intimacy and slow ache.

title: Falling Slowly
creator: Glen Hansard & Markéta Irglová
desc: Glen Hansard busked for years on Grafton Street before this song won an Oscar. Written with Markéta Irglová for the tiny Dublin film Once — a love story between two street musicians — it’s the sound of the city’s buskers made luminous.

title: Boys in the Better Land
creator: Fontaines D.C.
desc: Fontaines D.C. led a roaring revival of Dublin post-punk, Grian Chatten snarling the city’s contradictions. This 2019 track from Dogrel careens through a taxi ride across town — jangling, restless, unmistakably Dublin. Picture it in the old Liberties.

title: I Wanna Be a Cowboy, Baby!
creator: CMAT
desc: CMAT — Ciara Mary-Alice Thompson, from Dunboyne outside Dublin — is Ireland’s brightest new pop star, all glamour and self-deprecating wit. This 2022 country-pop stomp about small-town longing announced a singular, hilarious, heartbroken voice.

title: Rat Trap
creator: The Boomtown Rats
desc: Before Live Aid made him Sir Bob, Geldof led The Boomtown Rats, new-wave upstarts from the seaside suburb of Dún Laoghaire. This sprawling 1978 song of dead-end working lives was the first by an Irish band to top the UK chart.

title: Vikings found a port that still shapes Dublin
desc: Vikings established a trading settlement on the Liffey here around 841 AD, and archaeologists later found over a hundred of their houses when 1970s excavations briefly halted a planned civic office block. The port they founded still shapes the city.

title: Rebels hold the post office for a week
desc: Rebels seized this building at Easter 1916 and held it for a week against a massive British military response. Simon Watts brings together eyewitness accounts of the doomed rising that nonetheless set Irish independence in motion.

title: Go Dig My Grave
creator: Lankum
desc: Lankum, four Dubliners steeped in the city’s folk sessions, reinvent old ballads as vast, droning, almost unbearable beauty. This 2023 reworking of a traditional song of grief opens their acclaimed False Lankum. Their trad lives at the Cobblestone.

title: Married women banned from Irish civil service jobs
desc: Until 1973, Irish law forced women out of civil service jobs the moment they married. Bernie Flynn postponed her wedding to become one of the first married women allowed to keep working, in one of the longest-lasting marriage bars in the world.

title: Ireland becomes first to legalize gay marriage by vote
desc: Crowds packed this courtyard in May 2015 to watch results confirm Ireland as the first country to legalize same-sex marriage by popular vote. Comedian Shane Daniel Byrne marks the tenth anniversary with the campaigners who made it happen.

title: Former allies shell each other at the Four Courts
desc: Free State artillery, borrowed from the British, opened fire on this building in June 1922 to dislodge anti-Treaty forces occupying it, opening a civil war that would claim Michael Collins himself within weeks.

title: Readers are locked in cages at Ireland’s first public library
desc: Archbishop Narcissus Marsh opened his library beside St Patrick’s Cathedral in 1707. Its dark oak bookcases are largely unchanged, and readers of rare books were once locked into wire alcoves so nothing walked out the door.

title: A prison tour looks for the queer lives behind Kilmainham’s walls
desc: Kilmainham Gaol, the jail that held Irish rebels from 1796 to 1924, is usually told through the 1916 executions. This tour by the state heritage body follows its LGBTQ+ stories instead, from an Ireland where gay sex stayed illegal until 1993.

title: Former tenement residents remember working life on Henrietta Street
desc: Number 14 Henrietta Street was built in the 1740s as a mansion for the Georgian elite; by 1911 more than 100 people lived in its rooms. Former residents of the street’s tenements recall the jobs that kept their families going.

title: A round tower for ‘the Liberator’ rises over Glasnevin’s graves
desc: Daniel O’Connell won Catholic emancipation and founded Glasnevin Cemetery in 1832 so Catholics could bury their dead freely. His crypt lies beneath this 55-metre round tower, damaged by a bomb in 1971 and later reopened to climbers.

title: A city’s meeting place is blown up and remembered on film
desc: For generations Dubliners arranged to meet at Nelson’s Pillar on O’Connell Street, until a bomb brought it down in 1966. This 1967 short about the city was nominated for an Oscar; the steel Spire now stands where the Pillar did.

title: A Valentine’s disco fire becomes a 43-year fight for answers
place: Site of the Stardust nightclub, Artane
desc: The Stardust nightclub in Artane, north Dublin, burned in the early hours of 14 February 1981, killing 48 young people. Survivor Antoinette Keegan, who lost two sisters, recalls the night and the 2024 inquest verdict of unlawful killing.

title: Brick terraces and fanlights line the city’s Georgian squares
desc: In the eighteenth century Dublin was the second city of the British Empire, and its gentry built uniform brick terraces around green squares. Rick Steves walks St Stephen’s Green, the city-centre park, and looks inside a Georgian townhouse.

title: Swimmers brave the Irish Sea every morning off a rocky point
desc: The Forty Foot, a rocky promontory below the Martello tower at Sandycove, has drawn year-round sea swimmers for more than two centuries. Joyce set the opening of Ulysses here, and it was once a men-only bathing spot.

title: A mining millionaire leaves his treasures to Ireland
desc: American-born mining magnate Alfred Chester Beatty moved to Dublin in 1950 and left his collection of Islamic, East Asian and biblical manuscripts to the nation. The museum now sits in the Clock Tower building in the grounds of Dublin Castle.

title: A walk through the Elizabethan college at the heart of the city
desc: Founded by Elizabeth I in 1592, Trinity College is Ireland’s oldest university. The clip crosses its cobbled squares to the Old Library, whose barrel-vaulted Long Room holds some 200,000 of the college’s oldest books.

title: Only Shallow
creator: My Bloody Valentine
desc: My Bloody Valentine formed in Dublin before perfecting their vast wall of guitar noise. This 1991 track opens Loveless, the album that defined “shoegaze” — beauty buried under distortion, and one of the most influential records ever made.

title: The jewels of an order of knights vanish from a castle safe
desc: In 1907 the jewelled insignia of the Order of St Patrick disappeared from a safe in Dublin Castle’s Office of Arms, days before a royal visit, and were never found. The Bedford Tower, where the safe stood, faces the castle’s Upper Yard.

title: A countess trades her ballgowns for a rebel’s uniform
desc: Born into a landed family, Constance Markievicz fought in the 1916 Rising and became the first woman elected to Westminster. During the Rising she was second in command at St Stephen’s Green, where a bust of her now stands.

title: What a pastry says about Balkan identity
desc: A surreal audio comedy wrapped around a real question: what does the flaky, meat-or-cheese pastry sold at markets like this one say about Balkan identity? Burek, the episode argues, is food, life, culture, and politics at once.

title: Hunyadi holds Belgrade against an Ottoman army
desc: Three years after Constantinople fell, Sultan Mehmed II turned his army on this fortress. János Hunyadi held the walls; church bells worldwide still ring at noon to mark the victory that stalled the Ottoman advance into Europe.

title: A bombed army headquarters waits to learn its fate
place: Former Yugoslav Army HQ (Generalštab), Kneza Miloša
desc: Nikola Dobrović’s twin red-stone blocks on Kneza Miloša street were hit by NATO missiles in 1999 and left as ruins. Guy de Launey looks at the building’s design, its long decay and the arguments over what should happen to the site.

title: Yugoslav rock defines itself against both blocs
desc: Music historian Petar Janjatović talks Yugoslav rock over coffee and rakija in this cobblestone quarter of taverns and poets, tracing a scene confident enough to define itself against both Western pop and Soviet control.

title: A Tito-era tower greets everyone arriving from the airport
desc: The Western City Gate in New Belgrade, two concrete towers joined by a bridge and a revolving restaurant, was built in 1977 for the Genex trading company. Andrew Tuck asks why such a striking building has never quite become the icon it could be.

title: An old riverside quarter becomes the city’s place to eat
desc: Dorćol, the old neighbourhood sloping from the fortress down to the Danube, was long liked for its streets and cafés. Guy De Launey and chef Lars Ekberg walk through it to show how it also became a destination for food.

title: American bombs strike China’s embassy in the middle of a war
place: Chinese Cultural Centre (site of 1999 embassy bombing)
desc: On 7 May 1999, during NATO’s Kosovo campaign, five US bombs hit China’s embassy in New Belgrade, killing three people and souring relations with the West. A Chinese businessman who was among the first on the scene recalls the night.

title: An architect makes the case for Belgrade as a concrete capital
desc: An architect’s walk through the raw-concrete buildings that went up across Belgrade under socialist Yugoslavia, many of them in New Belgrade, the planned district of housing blocks and government buildings laid out on marshland across the Sava.

title: Gay Serbians march again after four years of cancelled parades
desc: VICE News followed members of Belgrade’s gay community through the 2014 Pride march, the first in four years after earlier ones were banned or attacked. Heavy police cordons sealed off the city centre around the government buildings on Nemanjina street.

title: American bombs hit the Chinese embassy in the middle of a war
place: Chinese Cultural Centre (site of 1999 embassy bombing)
desc: In May 1999, during NATO’s bombing of Yugoslavia, US missiles struck China’s embassy in New Belgrade and killed three Chinese journalists. A Chinese cultural centre, with a statue of Confucius outside, now stands on the site.

title: A football rivalry that brings the whole city to a halt
desc: Red Star and Partizan, both founded in 1945, play the “Eternal Derby” a few hundred metres apart in Belgrade’s south. COPA90 follows the flares, chants and loyalties around Partizan Stadium, the black-and-white side’s home ground.

title: Yugoslavia’s last great team wins Europe as the country breaks
desc: Red Star Belgrade beat Bayern Munich in a frantic semi-final at their Marakana stadium, then won the 1991 European Cup against Marseille. Within months war had scattered the squad. Jonathan Wilson tells how the team came together and came apart.

title: An inventor’s ashes rest in a golden sphere in a Belgrade villa
desc: Melvyn Bragg and guests discuss Nikola Tesla, the Serbian-American pioneer of alternating-current power. His ashes, brought from New York in 1957, sit in a gold-plated sphere at the Nikola Tesla Museum, a villa in the Vračar district.

title: Penalties in Bari crown the last great Yugoslav club side
desc: In May 1991 Red Star beat Marseille on penalties with Prosinečki, Savićević and Pančev, weeks before Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. A history of the run and the squad’s break-up, centred on the Marakana, the club’s stadium.

title: A capital of over a million people waits decades for its metro
desc: Belgrade has planned a metro since the 1920s and is one of Europe’s largest cities without one. The closest it came is the deep-level Vukov Spomenik station, a city-rail stop opened in 1995 under the boulevard beside the Vuk Karadžić monument.

title: Sea baths on stilts teach Istanbul to swim in public
desc: In the 19th century, wooden sea baths were built out over the water along the Bosphorus, at shores like Salacak and Moda. They sat halfway between the private, gender-segregated hamam and the mixed public beaches that came later.

title: The neighborhood bathhouse maps an empire’s politics
desc: Historian Nina Ergin maps Istanbul’s mid-18th-century hamams: who owned them, who worked in them and where the workers came from. Pinned at Çemberlitaş Hamamı, a Sinan-designed bathhouse from 1584 that is still open on Divanyolu.

title: Tanks and civilians face off on the bridge between two continents
desc: On the night of 15 July 2016, rogue soldiers tried to overthrow President Erdoğan. The fiercest fighting was on the Bosphorus Bridge, where crowds faced down troops; the suspension bridge has since been renamed for those killed.

title: A quiet edge of town becomes Istanbul’s holiest quarter
desc: Eyüp grew up around the tomb of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, a companion of the Prophet, at the top of the Golden Horn. Geographer Timur Hammond traces how the district was remade over centuries, deliberately and by accident, as an Islamic space.

title: Subway diggers hit a lost harbor full of Byzantine ships
desc: Excavations for the Marmaray rail tunnel at Yenikapı uncovered the silted-up Harbor of Theodosius and dozens of wrecked ships from the 5th to 11th centuries. Nautical archaeologists explain how eight of the vessels were recorded and what they reveal.

title: Three lines of stone hold off invaders for a thousand years
desc: Built under Theodosius II in the 5th century, the land walls ran about six kilometres from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn, with a moat, an outer wall and a towered inner wall. Long stretches still stand beside Topkapı gate and the old city edge.

title: Sixteen million people wait for the fault under the sea
desc: The North Anatolian Fault runs beneath the Sea of Marmara, a few kilometres off Istanbul’s shore, and seismologists expect a major quake within decades. DW follows how the city prepares. Kandilli Observatory, on the Asian shore, monitors it.

title: The longest-reigning sultan builds an empire and a skyline
desc: Süleyman ruled for 46 years, pushing Ottoman power to Vienna’s walls and reshaping law and culture. His architect Sinan crowned the city’s third hill with the Süleymaniye Mosque, where the sultan is buried in a tomb in the garden.

title: A novelist builds a real museum for the lovers in his book
desc: Orhan Pamuk wrote his novel The Museum of Innocence and stocked this red wooden house in Çukurcuma at the same time. Its vitrines hold the cigarette butts, earrings and salt shakers of a 1970s Istanbul love affair, as if the characters had lived.

title: Designers take over an old Greek schoolhouse to imagine the future
desc: Monocle visits the second Istanbul Design Biennial in 2014, themed “The Future Is Not What It Used To Be.” Its hub was the Galata Greek Primary School in Karaköy, a 19th-century school building that now serves as an exhibition space.

title: A chariot-racing riot nearly topples an emperor
desc: Rival chariot-racing factions, the Blues and Greens, united here in 532 after a botched execution and nearly overthrew Justinian. Empress Theodora reportedly talked him out of fleeing; troops then killed an estimated 30,000 people trapped inside.

title: Rice, spoons and strict etiquette at the Ottoman sultan’s table
desc: Max Miller cooks acem pilav, a Persian-style rice dish served at the Ottoman court, and explains how people ate in the empire: from shared trays, with spoons and the right hand. Topkapı Palace’s vast kitchens fed that court.

title: One roof, four thousand shops, five centuries of haggling
desc: Mehmed the Conqueror founded this covered market soon after he took the city in 1453, when merchant guilds fixed prices and even banned advertising here. Now over 4,000 shops across 61 streets, its centuries of gold and intrigue get a darker retelling.

title: An Egyptian obelisk still marks the old chariot racetrack
desc: The Hippodrome was Constantinople’s chariot-racing arena; today it is Sultanahmet Square. Theodosius I set up an obelisk from Karnak here in 390, beside a bronze Serpent Column brought from Delphi.

title: Thousands of shops crowd under the domes of a covered market
desc: The Grand Bazaar grew from a 15th-century Ottoman warehouse into a covered maze of around 60 streets and thousands of shops. It sits in the old city between Beyazıt Square and the Nuruosmaniye Mosque.

title: Byzantine domes and Ottoman minarets share one peninsula
desc: The listing covers the old peninsula between the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara: Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque, Topkapı Palace, the Süleymaniye and the land walls. Sultanahmet Square, on the site of the Byzantine Hippodrome, is at its centre.

title: A Levantine family builds the café life of Pera
desc: Three generations of the Vallaury family shaped 19th-century Pera: a café on the Grande Rue, now İstiklal Avenue, then Café Lebon, then architect Alexander Vallaury’s buildings, including the Archaeology Museum and the Imperial Ottoman Bank.

title: A long shopping street carries the crowds of the European side
desc: İstiklal Avenue, once the Grande Rue de Péra, runs about 1.4 km from Taksim Square to Tünel, lined with 19th-century facades, churches and arcades. A red heritage tram still runs its length in Beyoğlu.

title: Ferries cross between Europe and Asia on a busy strait
desc: The Golden Horn is the inlet that splits European Istanbul, and the Bosphorus is the strait that divides Europe from Asia. Boats leave from Eminönü, at the foot of the Galata Bridge.

title: Sultans rule an empire from courtyards above the Bosphorus
desc: Topkapı was the Ottoman sultans’ main residence for nearly 400 years, a sequence of courtyards, kiosks and a harem rather than a single building. It occupies Seraglio Point at the tip of the historic peninsula.

title: Six minarets and 20,000 blue tiles face the old cathedral
desc: Sultan Ahmed I built this mosque between 1609 and 1616, its interior lined with Iznik tiles that give it its nickname. It stands across Sultanahmet Square from Hagia Sophia, still in use for daily prayer.

title: Crusaders desecrate the church they came to save
desc: Fellow Christians, not Muslim invaders, first ransacked this cathedral, smashing icons and looting its treasures during three days of violence in 1204. The wound never fully healed, deepening the East-West schism and leaving Byzantium too weak to survive.

title: A confectioner’s shop and the soft sweets it made famous
desc: Lokum is made from starch and sugar, flavoured with rosewater, mastic or nuts. Hacı Bekir, said to have opened in 1777, is often credited with popularising it. Its original shop is in Bahçekapı, by the Spice Bazaar in Eminönü.

title: A shoestring sci-fi film borrows its space battles from Hollywood
desc: Director Çetin İnanç made The Man Who Saves the World in 1982 on a tiny budget, splicing in stolen Star Wars footage. It came out of Yeşilçam, the Beyoğlu street that gave its name to Turkey’s whole popular film industry.

title: The Attaché Guide to Lisbon
desc: This handy travel guide to Lisbon from Attaché offers tips for making the most of a visit to the city. Among other places, host Alex Hunter visits restaurants Frangasqueira Nacional for piri-piri chicken and Cantinho do Aziz for east African curry.

title: A cult sci-fi film stitched together from borrowed footage
desc: Dünyayı Kurtaran Adam (1982) reused real Star Wars footage and pirated soundtracks on a tiny budget. Turkey’s film industry is nicknamed Yeşilçam after Yeşilçam Sokak, the Beyoğlu side street where its studios and producers once clustered.

title: Fishing for gooseneck barnacles for a celebrity chef
desc: In this video from BBC Travel Show, prolific chef Nuno Mendes sends the host to gather ingredients at Mercado da Ribeira, then on a dangerous fishing adventure in search of gooseneck barnacles. They finish with a meal at BAHR, his luxury restaurant.

title: Shining a spotlight on a Michelin 2-Star chef
desc: Having opened 20 restaurants in a decade, chef Jose Avillez is prolific. This video from CNA visits his restaurants Belcanto and Beco Cabaret, describing his theatrical approach to Portuguese cuisine and how Portugal’s former colonies influence it.

title: Three culinary standouts in Lisbon
desc: This video from Booking.com recommends three places to eat in Lisbon. They stop by the classic Pastéis de Belém for their eponymous custard tarts, Cervejaria Ramiro for seafood, and Palacio Chiado, an upscale restaurant housed in an 18th-century palace.

title: Shopping for uniquely Portuguese products
place: Feira da Ladra flea market, Campo de Santa Clara
desc: This quick video from Booking.com points out three of the best places in Lisbon to find Portuguese products. For the most variety and fun, check out the recommended Campo Santa Clara flea market, which magically materializes every Tuesday and Saturday.

title: Cocktails mixed with history at Pavilhão Chinês
desc: This video from Booking.com takes us on a quick outing with a local Lisboeta named Tiago to see some of his favorite places in town. Most unexpected was Pavilhāo Chinês, a museum-like cocktail bar filled with antique toys from World War I and II.

title: Restful and rousing places to visit in Lisbon
desc: In this video from Booking.com, Lisbon couple Joao and Filipa show off their favorite places in town. They relax in the serene Jardim de Estrella park before visiting lively LX Factory, an artsy complex filled with restaurants, galleries, and shops.

title: An unlikely path to becoming a celebrity chef
desc: How does an aspiring professional basketball player become the chef of a Michelin 2-Star restaurant? This video from CNA stops by Alma, where chef Henrique Sá Pessoa recounts his journey to becoming a restauranteur, cookbook author, and cooking show host.

title: A tour of three culinary treats in Lisbon
desc: This video from Culture Trip showcases a trio of cheap Lisbon dishes. After enjoying a ubiquitous pastel de nata, we visit Bifanas do Alfonso for a bifana stuffed with juicy pork. Finally, we stop by Lucimar to try a sloppy and caloric francesinha.

title: Safeguarding the secret recipe of Pastéis de Belém
desc: There is no Portuguese pastry more well-known than the tasty pastel de nata, an egg custard tart. This video from Great Big Story goes behind the scenes—almost—at the famous pastry shop in Belem that serves tens of thousands of the sweet treats per day.

title: New perspectives of Lisbon from a boat on the Tagus River
desc: In this video from Lonely Planet, travel writer Marika McAdam climbs aboard a sailboat and reflects upon Lisbon’s long and symbiotic relationship with the open sea. “It’s the most peaceful way of experiencing this magnificent seaside city.”

title: Riding the waves at Carcavelos Beach
desc: Towns along Portugal’s coast like Ericeira are famous for their epic surfing conditions, but it’s also possible to surf near the big city. In this video, Lonely Planet writer Marika McAdam learns to surf at Carcavelos Beach just outside central Lisbon.

title: Big surfing in a small town
desc: Less than an hour from Lisbon, Ericeira has become a focal point for surfing in Portugal. This video from Monocle Films thoughtfully chronicles the flourishing surfing scene and how its international appeal has shaped the town’s economy and culture.

title: Repairing and restoring dolls at the Hospital de Bonecas
desc: Since 1830, Hospital de Bonecas has been fixing Lisbon’s damaged and deteriorating dolls. In this video from Great Big Story, the “head doctor” in charge of patching up the neglected toys shows us around the delightfully unusual 200-year-old hospital.

title: Summers spent slurping snails by the seashore
desc: Snails are a seasonal dish in Lisbon, best enjoyed with a cold beer on a hot summer day. This video from Portugal Daily View visits restaurant Júlio dos Caracóis to explain cultural norms around snail-eating and offers a handy primer for snail novices.

title: Five ways to order coffee in Portugal
desc: Although lattes and flat whites are easy to find, it’s helpful to know how local Lisboetas drink their coffee. This video from Portugal Daily View takes a trip to historic Café Martinho da Arcada to explain five common ways to order coffee in Portugal.

title: Music that makes magic out of melancholy
place: Café Luso fado house, Bairro Alto
desc: Fado exemplifies the Portuguese notion of “saudade,” a kind of melancholy or longing. In this video, Portugal Daily View visits several Fado houses: cavernous Café Luso in Bairro Alto and cozier Mesa de Frades and Bela Vinhos e Petiscos in Alfama.

title: Historic technology to help the city ascend
desc: Lisbon is notoriously hilly. This video from Portugal Daily View shows how Lisboetas have tamed some of the city’s most daunting hills with the Gustave Eiffel-inspired Santa Justa elevator and a trio of mighty funiculars: Lavra, Gloria, and Bica.

title: Manueline architecture at the Jerónimos Monastery
desc: In this video, travel writer Rick Steves offers a quick primer on the nautical motifs and astonishingly intricate patterns of Manueline architecture. He focuses on the remarkable Jerónimos Monastery, built in 1500 using taxes from the pepper trade.

title: “A Tribute” to the longtime residents of Mouraria
desc: Lining many walls in the Mouraria neighborhood near Beco das Farinhas Street are dozens of beautiful silver emulsion photographs of nearby residents. This video from Portugal Daily View highlights Camila Watson’s moving public artwork called “A Tribute.”

title: Collecting the creations of a country
desc: A Vida Portuguesa is a boutique shop that houses artisanal Portuguese products that are a far cry from typical touristy trinkets. This video from Portugal Daily View interviews sweet and optimistic owner Catarina Portas about the idea behind the store.

title: The human cost of Portugal’s trading empire
desc: Ribeira das Naus is now a lively riverfront promenade, but it was once a hub for unloading human cargo during the horrific Atlantic Slave Trade. This video from TedEd describes the escalating brutality and racist ideologies embedded in trade at the time.

title: Understanding Portugal’s pioneering nautical voyages
desc: Portugal spearheaded the Age of Discovery for two centuries, personified by famed explorers like Vasco de Gama and Ferdinand Magellan. This video from travel writer Rick Steves focuses on Lisbon’s Maritime Museum, which carefully chronicles the era.

title: A century of royal carriages in one place
desc: The National Coach Museum in Belém showcases dozens of ornate horse-drawn carriages used by Portuguese royalty, collected and stored by a preservation-minded queen. In this video, travel writer Rick Steves gives us a fun and informative look around.

title: Fleeing war in Angola before becoming a Lisbon chef
desc: Batala Doce is a cozy Afro-Portuguese restaurant in the Santos neighborhood. This Washington Post video relays owner Isabel Manuel Jacinto’s harrowing journey as she left her childhood home in Angola during the 1965 war of independence against Portugal.

title: Drawing inspiration from Lisbon’s azulejo tiles
desc: Ceramic tiles are one of the elements that make Lisbon a magical city. In this video from Lonely Planet, travel writer Marika McAdam reflects on the long tradition of hand-painted azulejo tiles, then visits Sedimento ceramics studio to create her own.

title: The inverted tower of Quinta da Regaleira
desc: A popular place to visit in Sintra is the dramatic Initiation Well, an inverted tower that plummets 30 meters deep. This slightly-too-speedy video from BBC Reel explains how the entire complex is brimming with Pagan, Templar, and Christian symbolism.

title: The last upscale glove shop in Lisbon
desc: Established in 1925, Luvaria Ulisses is a tiny shop that sells handmade and custom-tailored gloves. This video from CNA shows how the family business has thrived in a century of changing fashion. “If there is quality, there will always be customers.”

title: Moments of modernity mixed into Lisbon
desc: Lisbon has a rich history, but it’s a thriving modern city too. This video from Monocle recommends of-the-moment places to stay, see, shop, and eat, including the seafood restaurant Sea Me Peixaria Moderna and colorful tile shop Cortiço & Netos.

title: Surviving the Lisbon earthquake of 1755
desc: The vast interior of São Domingos Church was left partially destroyed as a moving memorial to the earthquake that struck while many Lisboetas were at church for All Saints’ Day. This episode of Witness History relays firsthand accounts of survivors.

title: The multicolored castle of Sintra
desc: Perched on a hillside northwest of Lisbon stands Pena Palace, a castle with more colors and styles of architecture than seem possible in one building. This woefully short video by Great Big Story offers a fleeting glimpse of the 1830s royal summer home.

title: Cherry liqueur at a hole-in-the-wall bar
place: A Ginjinha bar, Largo de São Domingos
desc: Ginjinha is a sour cherry liqueur enjoyed throughout Lisbon. In this video, we visit A Ginjinha, a venerable hole-in-the-wall that has served shots of the drink since 1840. The employee’s charmingly nonchalant origin story of ginjinha is delightful.

title: The violent spectacle of Portuguese-style bullfighting
desc: Campo Pequeno is Lisbon’s lovely Moorish-inspired bullring. This wordless short film shows the part of a bullfight featuring forcados, eight men who face-off against a bull completely defenseless. The result is as violent and chaotic as you might expect.

title: Reviving traditions after the darkness of dictatorship
desc: Praça Luís de Camões is one of many atmospheric plazas in Lisbon with lively outdoor kiosks. In this episode of Kitchen Sisters, the owner of nearby A Vida Portuguesa shares her efforts to reopen dilapidated kiosks and revive nearly-extinct products.

title: Inventing a way to tame the Waterwolf
desc: Northeast of Amsterdam is Afsluitdijk, a giant dike built after World War I. In this fun episode of The Omnibus, Ken Jennings and John Roderick banter about how the inventive Dutch have tamed the North Sea with an array of dams, windmills, and dikes.

title: Baruch Spinoza: A pioneer of the Enlightenment
desc: An eye-catching statue roughly marks where the 17th-century philosopher Baruch Spinoza lived in Amsterdam. This episode of In Our Time contains a discussion and light debate about the lasting legacy of Spinoza’s skeptical view of traditional religion.

title: Asserting the right to think, speak, and write freely
desc: On April 25, 1974, army officers toppled Portugal’s half-century fascist regime in a bloodless coup known as the Carnation Revolution. This episode of Witness History shares how the events culminated at Largo do Carmo, a charming plaza in central Lisbon.

title: Circumnavigating the globe with Ferdinand Magellan
desc: Magellan’s sixth-row position on the Monument to the Discoveries is a nod to Portugal’s bittersweet relationship with him — the Portuguese explorer first circled the globe flying Spain’s flag. Witness History shares a riveting account of the 1519 journey.

title: Seeing through the eyes of Ace & Tate
place: Ace & Tate eyewear shop, Nine Streets
desc: Starting from a small shop in the 9 Streets area, Ace & Tate has expanded its eyewear empire to 65 locations across Europe. In the first part of this episode of The Entrepreneurs, founder Mark de Lange chats about the shop’s past and post-pandemic future.

title: Protesting the Vietnam War from the comfort of bed
desc: In March 1969, the press flocked to the Amsterdam Hilton based on a cryptic invitation from newly-married Yoko Ono and John Lennon. This episode of Retropod describes their Bed-In for Peace, an unorthodox war protest that garnered global attention.

title: The Dutch painter who conned the art world
desc: In 1943, the man who lived at the townhouse at Keizersgracht 321 had a secret: he had swindled art collectors out of millions of dollars by forging a series of Vermeer paintings. The first part of this episode of Futility Closet describes his brazen con.

title: Quietly exploring Amsterdam’s hidden hofjes
desc: This charming video from Amsterdam Calling takes a peek into many publicly accessible hofjes—“little courtyards” in Dutch—hidden just off the street in the Jordaan neighborhood. The video’s YouTube description has names and addresses of places visited.

title: The fearlessness of Freddie Oversteegen
desc: The Dutch Resistance Museum offers a gripping look at the thousands of regular people who risked their lives to defy Nazi occupation of the Netherlands. This episode of Retropod tells the story of a brave 14-year-old girl who became a reluctant assassin.

title: Surviving a famine during the Hunger Winter
desc: This episode of Witness History shares a sorrowful firsthand story of Dutch starvation as the Nazis tried to keep their grip on the Netherlands in 1944. For more, the fascinating Dutch Resistance Museum has an exhibit about the famine that killed 20,000.

title: Daring to be caring about herring
desc: Jonk Volendammer Haringhandel is one of a few remaining stands where you can nosh Amsterdam-style herring, marinated in saltwater brine with pickles and onions on the side. This fun video from Great Big Story describes the Dutch fondness for the fish.

title: Making souvenir houses come to life
desc: This earnest and endearing video from Half-Asleep Chris has a great premise: he visits Amsterdam to find four buildings his parents had souvenir statues of when he was a kid. One stop on his journey was Herengracht 81, the oldest residence in Amsterdam.

title: Where we’re going, we don’t need roads
desc: A few hours northeast of Amsterdam is the quaint village of Giethoorn, where residents get around by bike, boat, or on foot — the town is devoid of roads. This charming video from Great Big Story makes life in the canal-lined hamlet seem delightful.

title: Fishing for bicycles
place: Amstel canal junction north of Rembrandtplein
desc: Several of Amsterdam’s 165 canals converge north of Rembrandtplein, so it’s a handy spot to see Waternet employees hoist bikes out of the water with a crane arm. This entertaining video from Great Big Story explains why there are so many submerged bikes.

title: Building emotional intelligence at the School of Life
desc: Founded in London, the School of Life has a branch in Amsterdam that holds events, convenes classes, and sells books about living a better life. In this video, founder Alain de Botton explains the purpose of the unique community gathering space and shop.

title: Some like it sour
desc: Thull’s is a deli and shop in East Amsterdam with a focus on pickling and fermenting vegetables. In this brief video from Monocle Films, owner Simone van Thull explains how she revives old pickling traditions for today’s receptive adventurous eaters.

title: The simmering debate over Zwarte Piet
desc: Each November, Amsterdam kicks off the world’s largest Saint Nicholas celebration as “Sinterklaas” arrives at the Maritime Museum by boat. This video from Vox takes an even-keel look at a tense debate about his sidekick Black Pete, a racial stereotype.

title: At the heart of the global flower trade
desc: On the southwestern edge of Amsterdam is Aalsmeer Flower Auction, the largest in the world. This video from Monocle Films takes a compelling and multifaceted look at the Dutch flower trade, visiting a grower, the auction, and a florist along the way.

title: Inside an opulent Art Deco cinema
desc: Theater Tuschinski is a stunning Art Deco cinema built in 1921. In this video, Sander from Amsterdam Calling excitedly points out ornate details throughout the stylish space. It’s worth a stop to admire the lobby, see a movie, or go on the morning tour.

title: Three of Amsterdam’s most unusual hotels
desc: In this video, Sander from Amsterdam Calling tours three unusual hotels in the city. He visits Lloyd Hotel’s many unique rooms, a hostel inspired by Japanese pod hotels, and hotel rooms installed in huts that formerly housed canal bridge tower operators.

title: Tea and brunch at the smallest house in Amsterdam
place: Het Kleinste Huis tea shop, Oude Hoogstraat
desc: The upscale tea shop Het Kleinste Huis is housed in “the smallest house in Amsterdam.” In this video from Amsterdam Calling, host Gessell links up with Dutch travel blogger Anne to visit the shop and try brunch in its tiny reservation-only dining room.

title: Primary colors with Piet Mondrian
desc: Housed in an evocative 1930s building, Kunstmuseum is a modern art museum in The Hague with a vast collection of Piet Mondrian paintings. This video from Amsterdam Calling doesn’t tell much of a story but shows plenty of examples of artwork on display.

title: Celebrating flavors at Foodhallen Amsterdam
desc: Foodhallen is an indoor food hall with 21 stands around a convivial communal dining area. In this 2016 video, Jessica, Vicky, and Gessell from Amsterdam Calling try dishes from five newly-opened eateries. Foodhallen’s website lists what’s on offer today.

title: Exploring the Dutch wetlands by canoe
desc: Wetlands Safari is a highly-rated tour company that picks up tourists at Amsterdam Noord station and takes them by canoe through wetlands and quaint waterside villages. The charming owner Majel Tromp guides the group in this video from Amsterdam Calling.

title: A cacophony of color at the Dutch flower parade
desc: Every April, a flower parade glides from town to town between Noordwijk and Haarlem. This video from Amsterdam Calling captures floats slathered with blooming flowers in Sassenheim. The clip is scant on details, but the parade itself looks delightful.

title: A hotel emblematic of the Amsterdam School style
desc: In this video, Amsterdam Calling explores the cozy yet ornate interior of the Grand Hotel Amrath, a canonical example of the Amsterdam School style. The hotel is visitable on an organized tour, or try your luck at entering with a smile and confident wave.

title: Picking your own fruit at Fruittuin van West
desc: Fruittuin van West is a sustainability-focused urban farm that offers guided tours, cheesemaking workshops, and pick-your-own fruits and vegetables. In this earnest and upbeat video, Valerie from Amsterdam Calling visits the farm to chat with the owner.

title: A riding school with a history
desc: Founded in 1744, De Hollandsche Manege is an equestrian school and museum tucked into a neighborhood near Vondelpark. In this video, Gessell from Amsterdam Calling visits the venerable school, where she watches an equestrian performance and rides a horse.

title: The Netherlands in miniature
desc: An hour by train from Amsterdam is Madurodam, a charming park in The Hague filled with impressive miniatures of real-life landmarks from across the Netherlands. In this video, Gessell from Amsterdam Calling has fun with the playful and interactive models.

title: A museum for things too small to see
desc: Opening a museum dedicated to microscopic organisms may sound like an absurd idea, but that didn’t stop Micropia from trying. In this video, Shoshannah from Amsterdam Calling explores the interactive and highly-rated museum and chats with the curators.

title: A small distillery tucked away in the Red Light District
place: Wynand Fockink distillery and tasting room
desc: Although renovated in 2013, Wynand Fockink Distillery can trace its lineage way back to 1679. In this video, Elysia from Amsterdam Calling takes a peek inside to see the convivial atmosphere in the jenever distillery, liquor shop, and tasting room.

title: Creativity and curiosity in Amsterdam Noord
desc: In this lo-fi video from Amsterdam Calling, a trio of guides visit the trendy and thriving Amsterdam Noord neighborhood. Along the way, they stop at Blom & Blom, a unique shop that harvests and recycles old lamps from defunct factories in East Germany.

title: Relaxing in a 400-year-old botanical garden
desc: Founded in 1638, Hortus Botanicus is among the oldest botanical gardens in the world. In this video, Sander from Amsterdam Calling excitedly explores the lush outdoor spaces, greenhouses, beehives for honey production, pleasant cafe, and upscale shop.

title: Organic ice cream on a stick
desc: Ijsmanschap Popsicle Bar aims “to make the tastiest ice creams in the Netherlands.” In this video, Gessell from Amsterdam Calling meets the owner and explains the flavors offered, including unexpected Vietnamese iced coffee or champagne and raspberry.

title: Museums of mutation and morbidity
desc: In this video, Gessell from Amsterdam Calling visits two morbid museums in Amsterdam. She starts with a look at Museum Vrolik’s unsettling jars containing human and animal deformities, then digs deep into Dutch funeral traditions at Museum Tot Zover.

title: Apartments where density and nature coexist
desc: Parkrand is a dense and modern housing complex set alongside a leafy park. In this video from Dezeen, architect Jacob van Rijs explains the design’s intent. The playful elements in the outdoor areas—like tiny elephants and giant flowerpots—are surreal.

title: The clock at Schipol Airport with a man inside
place: Maarten Baas ‘Real Time’ clock, Schiphol Airport
desc: On the ground floor of the international terminal is a clock that appears to have a man inside, painting the clock hands minute-by-minute. This video from Dezeen shows a chunk of the delightfully creative 12-hour video installation by artist Maarten Baas.

title: Building to meet diverse needs and lifestyles
desc: Silodam is an unusual building in Amsterdam that resembles a stack of mismatched shipping containers. In this video from Dezeen, architect Nathalie de Vries describes the ambitious building’s diverse housing types and strong connection to the water.

title: How to print a bridge
desc: The Amsterdam-based robotics company MX3D created one of the world’s first 3D-printed steel bridges, highlighted in this video from Dezeen. Once in place, the technological marvel will span the Oudezijds Achterburgwal canal in the Red Light District.

title: A study in brick and glass
