desc: The beginning of this wordless timelapse video is concerning: a historic building gets dismantled brick-by-brick for a new Chanel flagship store. What happens next is surprisingly magical — it gets beautifully put back together with an unexpected twist.

title: Living below sea level
desc: At four meters below sea level, Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport is the lowest major airport on earth. This thoughtful report from Singapore-based CNA describes how the Netherlands has kept low-lying areas called “polders” dry through innovative technology.

title: The last of a dying breed
desc: In 1883, a zebra-like animal called a “quagga” passed away at Amsterdam’s Artis Zoo. Although all zoo animals inevitably die, this time was different — it was the last quagga left on earth. This Day in History shares details of the animal’s extinction.

title: Art and food in the Dutch Golden Age
desc: This clever and unusual video sheds light on the Dutch Golden Age by recreating a still-life painting using modern food. A careful look at the Clara Peeters canvas—on view at Mauritshuis in The Hague—will make you see still-life paintings in a new way.

title: In pursuit of sustainable denim
desc: Denim City is a shop in De Hallen with a mission that goes way beyond selling jeans. In this video, travel vlogger Eileen Aldis explains how the shop is a front for House of Denim, a non-profit working to make the production of denim more sustainable.

title: A primer on Dutch politics with Pieter Gerrit Kroeger
desc: The Binnenhof is a complex in The Hague that houses the Netherlands parliament. This episode of Here in Holland begins with some dated newsy bits, but quickly delves into a broad and engaging explanation of Dutch history through the lens of politics.

title: Cycling in Amsterdam and beyond
desc: A great place to see the surreal rhythm of cyclists in Amsterdam is across the canal from the Rijksmuseum on Weteringshans street. In this episode of Here in Holland, a member of Amsterdam’s Urban Cycling Institute explains cycling culture in the city.

title: A Night Like This
creator: Caro Emerald
desc: Caro Emerald was born in Amsterdam and trained at its conservatory on the waterfront. Her 2010 retro-swing hit — all film-noir glamour and Bond-movie cool — was the most-played song in the country that year, and its video was shot around the city.

title: Bijlmermeer: A futuristic city from the past (Part 2)
desc: This second episode in a two-part series from 99% Invisible describes how an inhumane design left the Bijlmermeer nearly vacant. Dutch migrants from colonial Suriname filled the gaps, creating tensions as architect fantasies clashed with real human needs.

title: Geef mij maar Amsterdam
creator: Johnny Jordaan
desc: The title means “just give me Amsterdam.” Johnny Jordaan, uncrowned king of the sentimental Jordaanlied, made this 1955 hit a citywide singalong, still belted out when Ajax win. Statues of him and fellow singers stand on Johnny Jordaanplein.

title: Aan de Amsterdamse grachten
creator: Pieter Goemans
desc: The title means “on the Amsterdam canals.” Goemans dreamed up this waltz in 1949 on the bridge where the Leidsegracht meets the Prinsengracht; a plaque now marks the spot. Wim Sonneveld’s version became the city’s unofficial anthem.

title: Bijlmermeer: A futuristic city from the past (Part 1)
desc: This excellent two-part series from 99% Invisible describes Bijlmermeer, a futuristic modernist neighborhood concocted by utopian-minded architects in the 60s and 70s. This first part tells how dreams collided with reality as the initial buildings arose.

title: Zij gelooft in mij
place: André Hazes statue, Albert Cuyp Market
creator: André Hazes
desc: The title means “she believes in me.” André Hazes, beloved voice of the levenslied, grew up in De Pijp and was discovered singing at the Albert Cuyp market as a boy. His statue stands there now; 48,000 mourners filled the ArenA when he died.

title: Origineel Amsterdams
creator: Osdorp Posse
desc: The title means “originally Amsterdam.” Osdorp Posse invented Nederhop — rap in Dutch — out in the Osdorp estates on the city’s western edge from 1989 on. This was their first real chart hit: hard-edged, fast, and proudly local.

title: In the Dutch Mountains
creator: The Nits
desc: An ironic ode to a flat country’s imaginary peaks. The Nits, an Amsterdam art-pop band, recorded their 1987 signature live in an old gym in the city; singer Henk Hofstede grew up in the eastern Watergraafsmeer district, which features in the video.

title: Watskeburt?!
creator: De Jeugd van Tegenwoordig
desc: The title is Amsterdam street slang for “what’s happening?!” De Jeugd van Tegenwoordig, three goofball rappers from Amsterdam-Noord, turned it into an inescapable 2005 number one. They played their first release show in a café just off the Zeedijk.

title: Animals
creator: Martin Garrix
desc: Martin Garrix was a teenager in Amstelveen, just outside Amsterdam, when this 2013 big-room banger made him the youngest DJ ever to top Beatport. It’s a flagship of Amsterdam’s reign as the world’s dance capital, home of the Amsterdam Dance Event.

title: Welterusten, Meneer de President
creator: Boudewijn de Groot
desc: The title means “good night, Mr. President.” De Groot’s 1966 anti-war song became the anthem of a restless Dutch youth — the same generation whose Provo pranksters gathered around the little Lieverdje statue on the Spui.

title: Vluchtstrook
creator: Kris Kross Amsterdam, Antoon & Sigourney K
desc: The title means “hard shoulder,” the motorway emergency lane. Built around Amsterdam DJ duo Kris Kross Amsterdam, this 2022 smash with Antoon and Sigourney K was the year’s most-streamed single in the Netherlands — the city’s stadium-pop era.

title: Zing, Vecht, Huil, Bid, Lach, Werk en Bewonder
creator: Ramses Shaffy
desc: The title means “sing, fight, cry, pray, laugh, work and admire.” Ramses Shaffy, the great bohemian of Amsterdam’s theater world around the Leidseplein, turned this 1971 chanson into a defiant, life-affirming anthem of solidarity.

title: Lazy days at the Vondelpark
desc: Dotted with pleasant outdoor cafes nestled among greenery, Amsterdam’s Vondelpark feels intimate, cozy, and wild relative to parks in other big European cities. This slightly dated video from Lonely Planet offers a quick primer for a visit to the park.

title: The world’s first multinational corporation
desc: Starting in 1603, the Oost-Indisch Huis was the Amsterdam hub of the mighty Dutch East India Company for 200 years. Despite the combative host’s behavior in the opening minutes, this academic panel discussion is a solid primer on the country-like company.

title: Trading everything for a tulip bulb
desc: Bloemenmarkt is a flower market in central Amsterdam where fresh flowers are scant, but many tulip bulbs are on offer. In this podcast episode, economist Tim Harford explains how the bulb trade was central to the area’s intense “tulip mania” of the 1630s.

title: Repairing the baroque organ at Oude Kerk
desc: Completed in 1306, Amsterdam’s oldest building is now both a church and a modern art space. In the first part of this podcast episode, the church’s organist explains the 2019 restoration of the 18th-century organ after its last repair way back in 1870.

title: Mein junges Leben hat ein End
creator: Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck
desc: The German title means “my young life has come to an end.” Sweelinck, the “Orpheus of Amsterdam,” played the Oude Kerk organ for over 40 years, giving daily recitals in the city’s oldest building, where these folk-tune variations still ring out.

title: Jordaan neighborhood walk with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Walking from Dam Square to the charming and atmospheric Jordaan neighborhood, this tour meanders through one of Amsterdam’s loveliest areas. Rick’s commentary is fun and engaging, making this a delightful and mellow stroll. Allow at least 90 minutes.

title: Red Light District walk with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Starting at Dam Square, this slightly tricky-to-follow walk takes a clear-eyed and even-keel look at Amsterdam’s infamous Red Light District. The area is unpleasant late at night, so Rick suggests starting in the late afternoon. Allow at least 90 minutes.

title: Hocus Pocus
creator: Focus
desc: Focus formed in Amsterdam in 1969, and this 1971 instrumental — all furious guitar riffs broken up by manic yodelling — became their unlikely worldwide hit, one of the strangest songs ever to storm the charts.

title: A new life for a Syrian refugee in the Netherlands
desc: In 2016, filmmaker Thaeer Muhreez arrived at Amsterdam’s Centraal Station after a harrowing journey across Europe as he fled the Syrian war. This moving episode of Here in Holland tells his story of survival, separation, and a new life in the Netherlands.

title: Amsterdam city walk with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Walking from Centraal Station to Leidseplein, this engaging tour is an excellent introduction to Amsterdam’s core. The lively commentary covers an impressive variety of topics, adding nuance, joy, and surprise to the touristy area. Allow at least 2 hours.

title: Four art deco gems in central Amsterdam
desc: This video from Amsterdam Calling showcases Art Deco interiors in the city’s heart: Grand Café Brasserie at Centraal Station, the former stock exchange at Beurs van Berlage, the venerable tobacco shop P.G.C. Hajenius, and the city archives at De Bazel.

title: Brushstrokes that speak of anguish
desc: Although the painting central to this video from The Nerdwriter is not housed at Amsterdam’s Van Gogh Museum, the video offers a compelling take on the artist, arguing that Van Gogh’s choices of color and composition often mirrored his inner turmoil.

title: Shedding light on The Night Watch
desc: Rembrandt’s monumental masterpiece The Night Watch is arguably the most famous and beloved painting in the Rijksmuseum. This video from The Nerdwriter has a fascinating analysis of the artwork’s subject matter, formal composition, and subtle details.

title: The solemn respect of Johannes Vermeer
desc: The Milkmaid by Johannes Vermeer is among the most iconic paintings in the Rijksmuseum. This strangely serene video from School of Life explains how Vermeer’s paintings redefined glamor by depicting people doing mundane chores with dignity and admiration.

title: Using art as therapy for the mind
desc: In 2014, writer Alain de Botton appended captions to paintings at the Rijksmuseum, inviting visitors to consider each artwork’s potential therapeutic benefits. He explains the idea in this video from Monocle and expands upon it in his book Art as Therapy.

title: A real prison houses a fictional revenge story
desc: This real 16th-century fortress held Huguenots and political prisoners for centuries, though the wrongly imprisoned hero Dumas set here, Edmond Dantès, never existed. His actual inspiration was a Parisian shoemaker jailed in a different fortress.

title: A visiting king is shot in his open car minutes after landing
place: La Canebière at the Palais de la Bourse
desc: In October 1934 King Alexander I of Yugoslavia came ashore at the Old Port and was killed on La Canebière, the city’s main avenue, by a Macedonian nationalist. Newsreel cameras filmed it, and France’s foreign minister died too.

title: A concrete ship of flats becomes Le Corbusier’s model of modern living
desc: The Unité d’Habitation on Boulevard Michelet, finished in 1952, stacks 337 flats, a shopping street and a rooftop school into one raised slab. This architecture essay asks whether the building worked, and why it was copied so badly elsewhere.

title: A Greek navigator sails from here to the edge of the known world
desc: Around 325 BC Pytheas left Massalia, the Greek colony that became Marseille, and sailed round Britain and perhaps to Iceland. The stones of its ancient harbour survive in the Jardin des Vestiges, a garden behind the Centre Bourse.

title: Ice Age painters leave penguins on a cave wall now under the sea
desc: The Cosquer cave’s entrance lies 37 metres underwater in the Calanques, found by a diver in 1985. Rising seas are erasing its horses, seals and stencilled hands, so a full-scale replica was built in the Villa Méditerranée beside the old port.

title: Julia Child makes the fish stew of a city she once called home
place: Quai des Belges fish market, Old Port
desc: Julia Child lived in Marseille in the 1950s and here makes its signature dish on The French Chef. The rockfish for a real bouillabaisse still come from the fishermen’s stalls on the Quai des Belges, the harbour’s inner quay.

title: An American journalist smuggles Europe’s artists past the Nazis
desc: In 1940 Varian Fry arrived at the Hôtel Splendide, on the boulevard below the station, and began getting Chagall, Arendt and others out of Vichy France. Writer Dara Horn admires him but asks how he chose whose lives to save.

title: The French Connection’s old port becomes a teenage gang war zone
desc: Corsican mobsters once ran heroin from here to New York. Today the trade belongs to street gangs fighting over dealing spots in northern estates like La Castellane, hiring teenagers on Telegram for contract killings.

title: Marching volunteers from Marseille give the anthem its name
desc: The song was written in Strasbourg in 1792, but volunteers from Marseille sang it as they marched to Paris, and it took their name. A plaque at 25 rue Thubaneau, in the Belsunce district, marks where it was first sung in the city.

title: Police empty the old quarter behind the port in a single weekend
place: Site of the old Saint-Jean quarter (area)
desc: In January 1943 French police and German troops rounded up thousands in the Saint-Jean quarter beside the Old Port, then dynamited the neighbourhood. Survivors and historians recall a crime the city long preferred to forget.

title: Bourdain eats his way through France’s oldest and least polished city
desc: Anthony Bourdain roams Marseille, France’s oldest city, eating with locals to show how centuries of arrivals through the Old Port harbour shaped the way the city cooks and lives.

title: Marseille’s ultras carry their flares and chants to a European final
desc: Olympique de Marseille’s supporter groups, among them the South Winners founded in 1987, are known as some of the loudest in France. Their home is the Stade Vélodrome, the club’s big bowl of a stadium in the south of the city.

title: Workers occupy a closing McDonald’s and turn it into a food bank
desc: When McDonald’s moved to close its Sainte-Marthe branch in Marseille’s northern housing estates, staff and neighbours occupied it and ran it as a food bank during the pandemic. It later reopened as L’Après M, a community-run fast-food restaurant.

title: An opera performance sparks a revolution
desc: A performance of the opera La Muette de Portici here on August 25, 1830 turned an anti-Dutch crowd into a mob mid-show; the riot that spilled into the street that night grew into the revolution that created Belgium.

title: Iron and glass bend into vines and a new style is born
desc: A short film on how Victor Horta’s Brussels town houses of the 1890s launched Art Nouveau architecture. Hôtel Tassel, the house on Rue Paul-Émile Janson finished in 1894, is usually counted as the first.

title: A European Cup final turns deadly before kick-off
desc: In May 1985, 39 fans died when a wall collapsed at the Heysel Stadium before Liverpool played Juventus. Journalist Tony Evans recalls the day and its long fallout for football. The rebuilt ground is now the King Baudouin Stadium.

title: An architect’s own home becomes his manifesto in glass and steel
desc: Art historian Paul Greenhalgh talks with Benjamin Zurstrassen, director of the Horta Museum, about Victor Horta and Brussels around 1900. The museum is Horta’s former house and studio on Rue Américaine in Saint-Gilles.

title: A Brussels instrument maker survives one disaster after another
desc: Adolphe Sax grew up in his father’s instrument workshop in Brussels and survived falls, a gunpowder blast and poisoning before making his name with the saxophone. Early Sax instruments are in the Musical Instruments Museum, in the Old England building.

title: Angels and monsters tumble out of Bruegel’s crowded heaven
place: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
desc: A 360-degree film made by the museum that drops the viewer inside Pieter Bruegel the Elder’s The Fall of the Rebel Angels (1562), full of hybrid creatures. The painting is in the Old Masters galleries of the Royal Museums of Fine Arts.

title: A giant iron crystal is built for the world’s fair and never leaves
desc: The Atomium, a steel model of an iron crystal magnified 165 billion times, was put up on the Heysel plateau for Expo 58 and meant to be temporary. This episode covers how it was designed, built and kept.

title: The world’s fair of 1958 promises a bright atomic future
desc: Newsreel footage from Expo 58, the first world’s fair after the Second World War, held on the Heysel plateau north of the centre. Its centrepiece, the Atomium, a steel model of an iron crystal enlarged billions of times, still stands there.

title: British tanks roll in and four years of occupation end
desc: Newsreel of the liberation of Brussels on 3 September 1944, when the Guards Armoured Division drove in and crowds took to the streets. As they left, the Germans set fire to the dome of the Palace of Justice, the vast courthouse above the Marolles.

title: A borough tries to shake off its name after the Paris attacks
desc: A France 24 report from Molenbeek-Saint-Jean, the canal-side borough where several of the 2015 Paris attackers grew up. Residents, youth workers and officials describe what has changed since. Place Communale is the borough’s main square.

title: A boy reporter is drawn into propaganda before going global
desc: Anita Anand and William Dalrymple trace Hergé from anti-Soviet cartoons to wartime controversy and a friendship that changed his work. The Belgian Comic Strip Center, in a Horta-designed warehouse, tells the story of the art form he shaped.

title: Puppets on iron rods play the old city’s stories in local dialect
desc: Brussels marionettes are worked from above on a single iron rod, and shows were long played in Brusseleir, the city’s old Flemish-French vernacular. The Théâtre Royal de Toone keeps them going in an alley off the Rue du Marché aux Herbes.

title: Enjoying a classic French bistro at Chez Dumonet
desc: This video from Bon Appétit stops by Chez Dumonet in the Montparnasse neighborhood. The style of this video is fun — it’s like we’re eavesdropping on regulars while they chat about why they like the restaurant so much. The food looks fantastic too.

title: Gabled guildhalls ring a square rebuilt after a bombardment
desc: A short UNESCO/NHK heritage film on the Grand Place, the market square framed by the Gothic town hall and the ornate guild houses rebuilt after the French bombardment of 1695. It became a World Heritage Site in 1998.

title: A city replays a 1549 parade for an emperor every summer
desc: The Ommegang began as a religious procession and is now staged as a re-creation of the 1549 parade held for Emperor Charles V. Guilds, giants and horsemen end up on the Grand-Place, the city’s guildhall-lined main square.

title: Hundreds of thousands of begonias cover the main square for a weekend
desc: Every other August, volunteers lay a carpet of begonias across the Grand-Place in a few hours. The tradition dates from 1971 and the design changes each time; it lasts only a few days in Brussels’ central square.

title: A peek into the hip-hop dance community in Paris
desc: This video from Google stops by Gare de Lyon train station to interview Mufasa, an award-winning Parisian hip-hop dancer. She describes how her mesmerizing movements are inspired by the energy of the city around her, forming a symbiotic relationship.

title: On the roof with an urban beekeeper
desc: Perched above the military and history museums at Les Invalides lies something unexpected: beehives. This video from Atlas Obscura tells the story of Audric de Campeau, a jovial urban beekeeper who harvests honey atop several famous landmarks in Paris.

title: The creative chocolate of Patrick Roger
place: Patrick Roger chocolate shop, Boulevard Saint-Germain
desc: Artisanal chocolate maker Patrick Roger transformed his passion into an empire of seven chocolate boutiques in Paris. In this jokey video from CBS Sunday Morning, we meet the chocolatier to see his creations — from tiny morsels to life-size sculptures.

title: The baker behind the best baguette in Paris
desc: The baguettes at Boulangerie 2M are so tasty that they were declared the Best Baguette in Paris in 2018 and 2019. This video from Great Big Story interviews the shop’s owner and baker Mahmoud M’Seddi about the elements needed to make a great baguette.

title: Shopping for food with a touch of extravagance
place: La Grande Épicerie de Paris, Rue de Passy
desc: Exploring an unfamiliar grocery store is one of the best free cultural experiences, especially in a city known for its love of quality food. In this slightly highfalutin video from Monocle Films, we visit the newest branch of upscale La Grande Epicerie.

title: The multiplying Statues of Liberty
place: Statue of Liberty replica, Île aux Cygnes
desc: Southwest of the Eiffel Tower in the middle of the Seine is Île aux Cygnesa, a skinny artificial island topped with a 1/4 scale replica of the Statue of Liberty. This engaging video from Half-Asleep Chris explains how it is one of many replicas in Paris.

title: Zen and the art of umbrella maintenance
place: La Maison Pep’s umbrella shop, Passage de l’Ancre
desc: Thierry Millet is the charming proprietor of the 50-year-old shop La Maison Pep’s, the only boutique in Europe that repairs umbrellas. This video from Great Big Story showcases the serenity, joy, and meaning that he has found in his work.

title: A chocolate croissant by any other name
desc: In this video from Great Big Story, we stop by pastry shop La P’tite Boulangerie to hear about a playful debate sweeping France: what’s the correct name for a chocolate croissant? Whether you’re on Team Pain au Chocolat or Team Chocolatine, we all win.

title: Inside the mind of a passionate breadmaker
place: Du Pain et des Idées bakery
desc: Du Pain et des Idées—Bread and Ideas in English—is an award-winning bakery run by Christophe Vasseur. In this video from Monocle Films, he shares his heartfelt thoughts about the importance of fresh and high-quality bread to Parisians.

title: Rethinking security in a freedom-loving city
desc: The bulky tree-filled planter boxes lining the Tuileries Garden entrance from Place de la Concorde are ram-resistant barriers in disguise. This video from Monocle Films contemplates modern security challenges that are forcing cities like Paris to adapt.

title: The namesake of Bar Hemingway
desc: The Ritz Paris renamed their bar after Ernest Hemingway, the author, war journalist, and notorious boozehound who frequented the bar. This video from PBS describes a long-lost story by Hemingway set at the Ritz after the liberation of Paris from the Nazis.

title: A taste of Africa at Marché Barbès
desc: Every Wednesday and Saturday, a colorful bazaar of people from all around the world emerges at Marché Barbès. In this video from Sonia’s Travels, she visits the bustling ethnic market to enjoy a bit of French-speaking North and West Africa in Paris.

title: A law to fight food waste
place: La Maison du Zéro Déchet shop
desc: La Maison du Zéro Déchet is a retail boutique promoting innovative eco-friendly products. This video from PBS interviews the shop’s owner as a part of a broader look at a pioneering law to connect soon-to-be-wasted food with charities and people in need.

title: La Petite Ceinture: The lost railway of Paris
desc: Starting at a defunct train station—now La Recyclerie restaurant—this video from The Tim Traveller explores the past, present, and future of a rail line that once encircled Paris. In 1900, the line had 38 million passengers but rapidly fell out of favor.

title: The pipe organ of Saint-Sulpice
desc: In this quick video, travel writer Rick Steves shares a favorite little joy in Paris: hearing the 18th-century pipe organ at the Saint-Sulpice Church, which he says is “arguably the greatest in Europe.” The behind-the-scenes tour looks unusually intimate.

title: Hints of colonialization and immigration
desc: In the late 1800s, France forcibly colonized vast swaths of West Africa, including Morocco and Algeria. In this video, travel writer Rick Steves visits the Grand Mosque of Paris and the Arab World Institute to reflect on the city’s connection with Africa.

title: When a building is not a building at all
desc: At 29 Rue Quincampoix near the Pompidou Centre stands a building with a secret — its facade is painted on, fake windows and all. This video from The Tim Traveller reveals many facades in Paris that cleverly hide unsightly railway ventilation shafts.

title: Rethinking a zoo for the modern era
desc: Starting in 2011, Paris spent three years completely revamping its zoo. In this video from the Telegraph, people involved in the project explain their focus on animals from specific regions of the world housed in more expansive and unobtrusive enclosures.

title: A pillow fight with John, Paul, George, and Ringo
desc: After performing in Paris, the Beatles returned to Hotel George V and had an impromptu pillow fight. The moment was captured beautifully by photographer Harry Benson, who shares great stories about touring with the band in this video from Time Magazine.

title: How to (literally) make money in Paris
desc: Monnaie de Paris has been producing coins for 1150 years, making it the world’s oldest continuously-running mint. This video from Quartz takes us inside to see the fascinating inner-workings of a mint that produces coins for countries around the globe.

title: In the heart of the Marais district
desc: In this video, guidebook author Rick Steves celebrates the joyful street life of the inviting Marais neighborhood. He starts at Place des Vosges, built in 1605 to be “the centerpiece of the finest neighborhood in town.”

title: African culture is just a metro ride away
desc: The streets buzz near Château Rouge metro stop in Little Africa, where a mix of cultures infuses with remnants of France’s colonial era. In this video, Kevin Frazier introduces the neighborhood. Pro tip: Le Paris Noir and Little Africa offer guided tours.

title: A tradition of craftsmanship at Hermès
place: Hermès flagship store, Rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré
desc: Founded in 1837, upscale luxury brand Hermès originally manufactured horse saddles, a tradition they continue above their flagship store in Paris. This video from CBS Sunday Morning shows the elaborate work behind their sought-after handbags and scarves.

title: Conveying a feeling with a building
desc: Completed in 2014, The Fondation Louis Vuitton is an art museum housed in a gorgeous undulating building by famed architect Frank Gehry. In this great video from Nowness, he reflects on his approach to creating unique shapes and forms inspired by nature.

title: Creating costumes for the Moulin Rouge
desc: Maison Février has been fabricating feathery outfits for dancers at the Moulin Rouge since 1929. The show itself may be tacky and touristy, but this video from Great Big Story reveals the beauty, creativity, and skill that goes into the handmade costumes.

title: The cafe culture of the Latin Quarter
desc: The Latin Quarter is named after the neighborhood’s university-educated academics who long-ago spoke Latin in the streets. In this quick video, travel writer Rick Steves ignores the area’s touristy bits to enjoy the historic streets and cafe culture.

title: The rise and fall of Napoleon Bonaparte
desc: Beneath the gilded dome of Hôtel des Invalides is the tomb of Napoleon. In this video, travel writer Rick Steves recounts the Emperor’s triumph as he calmed and united a tumultuous France before leading disasters like Waterloo or the invasion of Russia.

title: Quiet contemplation at Père Lachaise Cemetery
desc: In this video, travel writer Rick Steves explores Père Lachaise Cemetery, “a vast garden of permanent Parisians.” Beyond seeing famous people’s resting places—Édith Piaf, Jim Morrison, Gertrude Stein, Oscar Wilde—the cemetery is a lovely place to wander.

title: Taking a duel to new heights
desc: In 1808, two jealous men were enamored with the same dancer at the Paris Opera. This video from Atlas Obscura describes their unconventional approach to conflict mediation — they took off from the Tuileries Gardens in two hot-air balloons and had a duel.

title: The birthplace of the Bloody Mary
desc: A favorite of hungover brunch-eaters worldwide, the Bloody Mary was invented at Harry’s New York Bar in Paris. This fun video from CBS Sunday Morning tells the story of the bar—dismantled and shipped to Paris from New York—and the cocktail it spawned.

title: The ghosts of Le Chemin des Dames
desc: Ninety miles northeast of Paris is a World War I battleground clustered around abandoned chalk mines. In this video from PBS, Richard Rubin searches through trenches and caves looking for what the young soldiers left behind. His discoveries are poignant.

title: The family that created France’s largest bell
desc: Next to the gleaming white dome of the Sacré-Cœur is a tower holding France’s largest bell. This video from Great Big Story takes a trip to the foothills of the Alps to visit Foderie Paccard, the family-owned bell foundry that created it in 1891.

title: Outside the walls of the Palace of Versailles
desc: The gaudy gilded grandeur of the Palace of Versailles can be a bit overwhelming. In this video, travel writer Rick Steves shares some things to see beyond its walls and contextualizes their history. Pro tip: Consider renting a bike to explore the grounds.

title: The Rodin Museum: In the presence of a master
desc: Housed in his former studio, the fantastic Rodin Museum is small enough to avoid museum fatigue. In this video, Rick Steves tours the mansion and gardens of this “modern Michelangelo” and shares his iconic work. Pro tip: Don’t miss The Burghers of Calais.

title: Gawking at the dead at the public morgue
place: Site of the old Paris Morgue, Square de l’Île-de-France
desc: Tucked behind the Notre Dame was a longstanding public morgue that displayed the unidentified dead in public view. This modestly macabre episode of Paname shares stories of the morgue and describes how it was a big draw for curious tourists of the day.

title: The spectacular stained glass of the Sainte-Chapelle
desc: Completed in 1248 after only six years, the Sainte-Chapelle church has arguably the world’s most beautiful stained glass. In this video, travel writer Rick Steves steps inside to be awed by what he calls “the most dazzling gothic interior anywhere.”

title: Remembering the flood of 1910
desc: Clinging to the side of Pont de l’Alma bridge is a statue of a soldier called the Zouave. In this episode of Paname, host Amber Minogue shares how the figure has become an informal flood marker in Paris, and how in 1910, Zoave was a harbinger of bad news.

title: A less-than-magic start for Disneyland Paris
desc: The fraught opening of Euro Disney in 1992 was an emotional rollercoaster for Bob Fitzpatrick, the person in charge of launching the first Disney park outside the United States. In this episode of BBC Witness History, he shares behind-the-scenes stories.

title: The battle outside Saint Roch Church
desc: In October 1795, an uprising threatened the newly-formed revolutionary government. This episode of Paname relays how a young Napoleon Bonaparte led the army’s violent response, killing hundreds of rebels, uplifting Napoleon into a heroic figure in France.

title: The Egyptian obelisk in Place de la Concorde
place: Luxor Obelisk, Place de la Concorde
desc: Once marking the entrance to Luxor Temple, the 3,000-year-old obelisk in Paris was gifted to France by Egypt in the 1830s. In this episode of Paname, host Amber Minogue vividly describes the nightmarish complexity of moving the massive pillar to Paris.

title: The King of England moves to Paris
place: Windsors’ former house, Bois de Boulogne
desc: In 1936, a scandal engulfed Britain as King Edward VIII abdicated the throne, abruptly making Elizabeth II the new queen. This episode of Witness History relays how Edward, ostracized from the royal family, led a bittersweet life as a socialite in Paris.

title: The abduction of a Moroccan dissident
desc: Medhi Ben Barka was the outspoken leader of Morocco’s left-wing anti-colonialist movement. In October 1965, two plainclothes policemen abducted him outside Brasserie Lipp in Paris. He was never seen again. BBC’s Witness History podcast tells his story.

title: Tapestries symbolic of a renewal of humanism
place: Cluny Museum (Museum of the Middle Ages)
desc: The Cluny Museum celebrates European culture as it emerged from the Dark Ages. In this video, travel writer Rick Steves explains the museum’s highlight, a remarkably preserved set of tapestries from the 15th century called The Lady and the Unicorn.

title: Nazis on the doorstep
desc: On 14 June 1940, the German army marched into Paris and hung a huge swastika flag from the Arc de Triomphe. This episode of Witness History shares the firsthand account of one of the 8 million Parisians who fled their homes when the Nazis invaded France.

title: ​​Assisting artists who fled their home countries
desc: Agency of Artists in Exile is an organization that supplies refugee artists in Paris with equipment, workspaces, and a supportive community of people in a similar situation. This video from Culture Trip quickly shares stories from a few refugee artists.

title: On the verge of liberating Paris from the Nazis
desc: In August 1944, a band of French resistance fighters occupied the Hôtel de Ville, using it as a makeshift headquarters as they were on the cusp of retaking Paris from the Nazis. Witness History relays riveting firsthand accounts of those victorious days.

title: The contest that forever changed the wine world
place: Site of Les Caves de la Madeleine wine shop, Cité Berryer
desc: In 1976, the British owner of La Cave de la Madeleine wine shop organized a rigorous blind tasting of top wines from France and California. This episode of Witness History explains the longlasting impact of the showdown known as “The Judgement of Paris.”

title: The Tennis Court Oath and the revolutions to come
desc: At an indoor tennis court in Versailles in May 1789, ordinary French people rose up against the clergy and aristocracy to assert their power. This video from Crash Course is an engaging look at the many revolutions that followed the Tennis Court Oath.

title: ​​A bakery with an irreverent twist
desc: ​​This video from Culture Trip showcases Legay Choc, a gay-friendly patisserie in the Marais neighborhood famous for its penis-shaped baguettes. Fourth-generation baker Richard Legay describes how they symbolize the openness and irreverence of Parisians.

title: Drawing hungry crowds Holybelly
desc: Chef Sarah Mouchot and her partner Nico Alary run two wildly popular restaurants on the same street: Holybelly 5 and Holybelly 19. In this episode of The New Paris, the insightful owners chat about the complexity and joy of running a hit restaurant.

title: The legacy of sourdough at Poilâne Bakery
desc: Apollonia Poilâne is a contemplative third-generation baker who took over her family’s business after her parents died in a tragic helicopter accident. She describes the 90-year history of Poilâne, which has flourished and expanded under her leadership.

title: A massacre on the road to Algerian independence
desc: On the northeastern edge of Pont Saint-Michel is a plaque: “To the memory of the Algerians, victims of the bloody repression of a peaceful demonstration.” This episode of Witness History explains the grisly 1961 killing of Algerian independence activists.

title: Shopping for dinner on a typical market street
desc: In this video, travel writer Rick Steves visits Rue Cler, the spine of a neighborhood recommended in his guidebooks for its workaday charm. Parisian tour guide Delphine Prigent joins him to shop for a complete meal using specialty shops along the street.

title: A palace fit for the Sun King
desc: The extravagant Palace of Versailles is an icon of France’s years as a world superpower under the reign of Louis XIV around 1700. In this video, guidebook author Rick Steves shares how the massive baroque palace symbolized and enhanced the king’s power.

title: The battle of the pyramid
desc: Now widely adored, the Louvre’s iconic pyramid entrance was hugely controversial when architect I.M. Pei proposed the design. In this episode of BBC’s Witness History, an architect on the team describes how they navigated the contentious design process.

title: The mistresses of King Louis XV
desc: In this video from Google, art historian Emilie Jean gives a behind-the-scenes tour of the tucked-away apartments at the Palace of Versailles used by the two most important mistresses of King Louis XV: Madame de Pompadour and Madame du Barry.

title: Louvre Museum tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Starting inside the pyramidal atrium, this whirlwind tour through the highlights of the Louvre is a great way to kick off a visit — see the famous masterpieces in this structured tour, then explore what interests you. Allow at least 2 hours for the tour.

title: Searching for what remains of the Bastille
desc: After revolutionaries stormed and destroyed the Bastille in 1789, little remained of the once-imposing fortress. This video from The Tim Traveller visits the Bastille metro station and six other spots where scant remnants of the prison can still be found.

title: The turbulent life of Marie Antoinette
desc: An obligatory stop on any tour of the Palace of Versailles is Marie Antoinette’s bedroom. In this irreverent and banter-filled episode of You’re Wrong About, author Dana Schwartz shares vivid stories about the extravagant and much-maligned queen.

title: Palace of Versailles tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Starting in front of the palace, this spirited tour rapidly moves through the chateau’s series of grand and gaudy rooms before heading outside to see the sprawling palace grounds. Allow at least 2 hours for the tour, plus more time to explore the grounds.

title: Rue Cler neighborhood tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Rick explains everyday Parisian living to his (mostly American) audience in this fun two-block walk along Rue Cler, a characteristic market street. Allow at least an hour, go on a Tuesday-Saturday morning, and slowly assemble a picnic lunch along the way.

title: The accidental destruction of a chateau
place: Site of the Château de Saint-Cloud, Saint-Cloud
desc: Just west of Paris, Château de Saint-Cloud was a vast manor owned by three icons of French history: Marie Antoinette, Napoleon Bonaparte, and Napoleon III. This video from The Tim Traveler explains the events that led to its accidental destruction in 1870.

title: The train line that transformed into a park
place: Viaduc des Arts and Coulée Verte park
desc: Although overshadowed by The High Line in New York, the Viaduc des Arts in Paris was its predecessor and partial inspiration. This delightfully nerdy and fun from The Tim Traveller explains the history of the rail viaduct that is now a leafy linear park.

title: The little delights of Montmartre
desc: This fast-paced video from The Tim Traveller describes several overlooked curiosities in the Montmartre area. Along the way, he points out one of the only remaining original metro canopies and the “ridiculously picturesque” dead-end street Villa Léandre.

title: Political rebellion and revolution in bohemian Belleville
desc: A hammer-and-sickle adorns the sign for the restaurant La Bellevilloise, founded in 1877 as a food cooperative after the Paris Commune uprising. This video from Messy Nessy Chic shares how left-wing politics shaped the offbeat Belleville neighborhood.

title: Rocky Horror’s underground subculture
desc: Twice weekly, Studio Galande cinema plays the cult classic film Rocky Horror Picture Show to a raucous crowd. In this video, Nessy visits the theatre after viewing the movie in a secret subterranean screening room in the Paris Catacombs. (Mild nudity)

title: The mushrooms growing beneath our feet
desc: Champignonnière Les Carrières produces mushrooms in underground caves and tunnels in the northwestern outskirts of Paris. This video from Messy Nessy Chic ventures below the streets to meet the grower Angel Moïoli and learn about the Parisian fungi trade.

title: Salvaging historical home goods at Feau & Cie
desc: Five blocks north of the Arc de Triomphe is Feau & Cie, a massive shop crammed with mirrors, frames, and period plaster panels salvaged from old buildings. In this video, Nessy excitedly explores the “architectural dreamworld” found in the unique showroom.

title: Shop signage from the 14th-century hidden in plain sight
desc: At 42 Rue Galande is a carved stone sign dating from around 1380. In this episode of Paname podcast, charming host Amber Minogue points out the medieval sign, shares the myth of St. Julien it depicts, and offers a history of the nearby St. Julien Church.

title: A long legacy of luxury fans at Maison Duvelleroy
desc: Since 1827, Maison Duvelleroy has made upscale hand-fans for fashionistas, flirters, and people who simply need to cool down in a sweltering summer. This video from Messy Nessy Chic stops by for a look at the shop’s many elaborate designs.

title: Exploring a Parisian ghost town
desc: Thirty minutes north of Paris, the once-idyllic village of Goussainville has had an unfortunate half-century. This video from Messy Nessy Chic describes the horror and abandonment that resulted from Charles de Gaulle Airport being built next door in 1974.

title: Learning the art of fencing
desc: Salle D’armes Coudurier is the oldest fencing club in Paris, one of the few remaining swordsmanship schools in the city. In this video, Nessy tries the sport with the club’s alluring owner, then heads to nearby bistro Roger La Grenouille for frog’s legs.

title: Where classic Parisian cafe chairs come from
desc: Maison Gatti has been producing iconic Parisian cafe chairs for a century. This video from Messy Nessy Chic stops by the family-run business for a behind-the-scenes look at how dexterous artisans still assemble the woven bistro chairs by hand.

title: Using models and maps to plan for war
desc: Musée des Plans-Reliefs houses remarkably detailed scale models of cities used for military planning in the 17th century. In this video, Nessy admires the collection and goes behind-the-scenes to see the museum’s archives and digital preservation efforts.

title: Antiques and adventure at Les Puces
desc: One of the world’s largest flea markets is Les Puces — “The Fleas” — a labyrinthian patchwork of markets on the city’s northern edge. This fun video from Messy Nessy Chic takes us exploring market stalls and for lunch at the kitschy eatery Chez Louisette.

title: A whirlwind food and drink tour of Paris
desc: This fun video from Topjaw takes us on an energetic and jam-packed 48-hour journey through food and cocktails in Paris, including a stop at Marché des Enfants Rouges for a bevy of street food choices. They eat and drink an astounding amount in two days.

title: An insider look at an outsider artist
desc: Maïssa Toulet is an outsider artist who makes playful and peculiar sculptures from figurines and other intriguing bric-a-brac. In this 60-second video from Messy Nessy Chic, we see inside the artist’s jam-packed studio, visitable by appointment only.

title: Going underground at the Liberation of Paris Museum
desc: The Liberation of Paris Museum explains how French citizens secretly led a resistance against their Nazi occupiers during World War II. This video from Messy Nessy Chic shows how the museum weaves technology into its exhibits to bring the story to life.

title: Exploring new French cuisine at Au Passage
desc: In this video from Bon Appétit, we visit the trendy 11th Arrondissement neighborhood that is off the radar of a typical tourist in Paris. The sweet and charismatic owner Audrey explains her down-to-earth mentality, which has created many happy regulars.

title: How to rob an art museum
place: Paris Museum of Modern Art (Musée d’Art Moderne)
desc: In 2010, Vjeran Tomic broke into the Museum of Modern Art in Paris and stole $70 million worth of paintings by Picasso, Matisse, Braque, Modigliani, and Léger. This story from The New Yorker offers a fascinating peek into the world of a professional thief.

title: The attack on Charlie Hebdo
place: Former Charlie Hebdo offices, Rue Nicolas-Appert
desc: In 2015, two Islamist extremists burst into the offices of the satirical weekly newspaper Charlie Hebdo and killed 12 people. This even-keel video from Vox explains the tension underpinning the attack and describes its relationship secularism in France.

title: Unexpected architecture in a uniform city
desc: Orgues de Flandre is a set of unusual hi-rise buildings in northeast Paris that jut out over the sidewalk at jaunty angles. This report from Monocle examines how the playful and peculiar structures interact with the city’s more traditional architecture.

title: Giving injured soldiers a new lease on life
place: Site of Anna Coleman Ladd’s studio, 70 Rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs
desc: The horrors of World War I inspired sculptor Anna Coleman Ladd to craft prosthetic masks for soldiers returning home with gruesome facial injuries. This video from Vox shows how she transformed disfigured men in her studio at 70 Rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs.

title: Marie Antoinette behind bars
desc: In the heart of central Paris stands the Conciergerie, a former prison where Marie Antoinette spent her last years before her brutal beheading at the guillotine. This engrossing episode of Noble Blood tells the story of the queen’s “second death.”

title: A portrait of Berthe Morisot
desc: Berthe Morisot was one of the only women in the tight-knit gang of Impressionists who upended the art world in the late-1800s. This episode of The Land of Desire is a sweet tribute to the painter, whose work is often shown at the Musée Marmottan Monet.

title: The Parisians who ate a zoo
desc: This episode of The Land of Desire vividly describes how Prussian troops surrounded the city during the Siege of Paris in 1870. Once the food supply ran out, starving Parisians got desperate: they ate the zoo animals at Ménagerie du Jardin des Plantes.

title: An informal approach to French cuisine
desc: Cookbook author Trish Deseine is an unlikely star in the French culinary scene — she is from Northern Ireland. This episode of The Food Programme visits Librairie Gourmande, the largest culinary bookstore in the world, to understand her appeal in France.

title: Mona Lisa’s rising stardom
place: Salle des États (Mona Lisa room), Louvre Museum
desc: The Mona Lisa is probably the most famous painting in the world, but it wasn’t always that way. This video from Vox describes the series of events that led millions of tourists to flock to Leonardo da Vinci’s enigmatic 16th-century portrait.

title: Curating art to celebrate a vibrant urban culture
place: 25hours Hotel Terminus Nord, opposite Gare du Nord
desc: Alex Toledano has a unique job: he runs a consultancy that helps companies tell a compelling story with art. In this episode of The New Paris, he shares the fascinating process of curating art for the 25 Hours Hotel across the street from Gare du Nord.

title: An in-depth look at the Mona Lisa
place: Salle des États (Mona Lisa room), Louvre Museum
desc: In this inaugural episode Art History for All, self-proclaimed “art nerd” Allyson Healey examines Leonardo da Vinci’s most famous painting — its composition, subject matter, critical reaction, theft, parodies, and iconic status in our collective culture.

title: The painting in Mona Lisa’s watchful gaze
place: Salle des États (Mona Lisa room), Louvre Museum
desc: Every day, overwhelming crowds gawk at the underwhelming Mona Lisa, without realizing the largest painting in the Louvre is right behind them. In this video from Google, Tom Scott shares insights about The Wedding Feast at Cana, Veronese’s epic canvas.

title: Paroles, paroles
creator: Dalida
desc: The title means “words, words” — empty promises. In this 1973 duet, Dalida sings while actor Alain Delon murmurs flattery she no longer believes. She lived in Montmartre, where Place Dalida now has a bust of her that visitors rub for luck.

title: The rise and fall of Joan of Arc
place: Joan of Arc statue, Place des Pyramides
desc: Overlooking the Rue de Rivoli is a striking golden statue of Joan of Arc. This episode of You’re Dead to Me pairs a comedian and a historian to chat about the teen who led downtrodden French troops during the Hundred Years War before her sorrowful fate.

title: A triple-murder that captivated 19th-century Paris
desc: In 1887, someone brutally murdered three courtesan women and left their bodies on Rue Montaigne. In this lengthy episode of Most Notorious, the author of a book about the case explains the investigation and shares lucid tidbits about late 1800s Paris.

title: Feeling invisible as a French-Asian person
desc: The 13th Arrondissement has one of the largest Asian communities in Paris. In this episode of The Europeans, Grace Ly sheds light on how French culture often overlooks French-Asian people or is even outright racist toward them. (Segment starts at ~15:15)

title: The remarkable life of Josephine Baker
desc: In the 1920s, African-American dancer Josephine Baker was a mainstay at the Folies Bergère in Paris. This animated video by Culture Trip offers a woefully brief look at her life as a risqué dancer, Nazi resister, unabashed bisexual, and adoptive mother.

title: Changing the world with Josephine Baker
desc: The dancer Josephine Baker had an astounding life. This fun and chatty episode of You’re Dead To Me explains her American roots, French megastardom, wartime heroism, and equality activism. (She often headlined the Folies Bergère in the 1920s and 1930s.)

title: For the love of print
place: Magazine kiosk near Le Bon Marché
desc: A half-block southwest of Le Bon Marche stands a small kiosk packed with obscure periodicals from all over the world. In this short interview with Monocle Films, the owner’s enthusiasm for beautifully-designed magazines is palpable.

title: La Bohème
creator: Charles Aznavour
desc: The title refers to the “bohemian” life of poor young artists. Charles Aznavour’s 1965 song looks back fondly on the painters who once filled Montmartre. Artists still work in Place du Tertre, the square at the heart of that old neighborhood.

title: Paris sous les bombes
creator: Suprême NTM
desc: The title means “Paris under the bombs,” but the “bombs” are spray paint — the group started out as graffiti artists. This 1995 track is a landmark of French rap. NTM came from Seine-Saint-Denis, the working-class area north of Paris.

creator: Phoenix
desc: Phoenix’s 2009 hit is a dreamy look back at Paris around the year 1901, when the city felt like the center of the world. The band comes from Versailles, the town outside Paris famous for its palace — and, oddly, home to Daft Punk and Air too.

title: One More Time
creator: Daft Punk
desc: Daft Punk’s joyful 2000 dance hit helped define “French touch,” the electronic-music wave that came out of Paris. That scene grew up around clubs like the Rex Club, a Grands Boulevards basement central to the city’s dance music since the 1990s.

title: Je t’aime… moi non plus
place: Maison Gainsbourg, 5 bis Rue de Verneuil
creator: Serge Gainsbourg
desc: The title means “I love you… me neither.” Serge Gainsbourg’s breathy 1969 duet with Jane Birkin shocked listeners and became a French pop landmark. He bought the house at 5 bis Rue de Verneuil that year; it’s now a graffiti-covered museum.

title: Nuages
place: La Chope des Puces bar, Saint-Ouen flea market
creator: Django Reinhardt
desc: Nuages means “clouds.” Django Reinhardt’s dreamy 1940 instrumental, written in wartime Paris, is the heart of the city’s gypsy jazz. His style still plays at the Saint-Ouen flea market north of town, in bars like La Chope des Puces.

title: Clair de Lune
creator: Claude Debussy
desc: The title is French for “moonlight,” and the music sounds like it — soft, slow, and calm. It’s one of the most famous pieces of French classical piano. Its composer, Claude Debussy, is buried in Passy Cemetery, a quiet spot near the Eiffel Tower.

title: The origins of chef Eric Ripert
desc: Top-ranked chef Eric Ripert started his career at La Tour d’Argent, a fine-dining restaurant serving Parisians since 1582. In this fun interview with Bon Appétit, the chef shares stories from his culinary career in Paris, Washington DC, and New York City.

title: La Vie en Rose
place: Édith Piaf’s grave, Père Lachaise Cemetery
creator: Édith Piaf
desc: The title describes seeing life through rose-colored glasses — how things look when you’re in love. It’s Édith Piaf’s most famous song and a symbol of Paris itself. Fans still leave flowers at her grave in Père Lachaise Cemetery, in Division 97.

title: J’ai deux amours
creator: Joséphine Baker
desc: The title means “I have two loves” — her country and Paris. Joséphine Baker was an American-born singer who became a French hero. In 2021 she became the first Black woman honored in the Panthéon, France’s memorial to its great figures.

title: Market meandering at Marché d’Aligre
desc: Marche D’Aligre is a delightful and untouristy food market to explore. In this video from Messy Nessy Chic, Nessy hunts through the indoor-outdoor market for a Parisian version of fast food, then stops by the quirky nearby garden Le Jardin Nomade to eat.

title: Conserving the treasures of the Louvre
desc: In a warehouse at the edge of Paris are molds and plaster casts of thousands of the Louvre’s masterpieces, tended by skilled artisans and conservationists. In this quick video, Nessy visits Ateliers d’Art de la Réunion des Musées Nationaux to take a peek.

title: Cherishing a crumbling chateau
desc: In a village 27 miles outside of Paris, Chateau du Duc d’Epernon is an abandoned manor house slowly succumbing to nature and decay. This video from Messy Nessy Chic is a contemplative and poetic plea for an intervention to save the dilapidated chateau.

title: Haussmann remakes a city in flux
desc: This episode of The Land of Desire explains how the urban planner Baron Haussmann razed the city’s squalid medieval lanes and built modern Paris during a time of political turmoil. For more, Musée Carnavalet offers a detailed look at the history of Paris.

title: A brutal end for the Paris Commune
desc: In 1871, nearly 150 members of the revolutionary Paris Commune government were brutally executed against a wall at Père Lachaise Cemetery, now a memorial. In this episode, an academic panel discusses the complex set of events that led up to the massacre.

title: Djadja
creator: Aya Nakamura
desc: “Djadja” is slang for a guy who spreads lies about a woman — and Aya Nakamura’s 2018 hit shuts him down. She’s France’s most-streamed artist. At the 2024 Olympics she performed it on the Pont des Arts, a bridge fans now call the “Pont d’Aya.”

title: Sous le ciel de Paris
creator: Yves Montand
desc: The title means “under the Paris sky.” This 1951 song, recorded by Yves Montand and many others, mentions real landmarks like the Seine and Notre-Dame. The cathedral stands on the Île de la Cité, the island at the center of the city.

title: Scenes from the Paris Exhibition in 1937
desc: Looking out over Paris from Place du Trocadero is one of the world’s most awe-inspiring views. This historic video reel from British Pathé shows the area’s role as the hub of an international expo in 1937. The footage of the German pavilion is jarring.

title: The spark that started the French Revolution
desc: In July 1789, commoners rose up against their regal government to loot and destroy the Bastille, a prison that symbolized royal authority. This video from Ted-Ed is an easily digestible introduction to the event’s role in the broader French Revolution.

title: Oxygène, Pt. 4
creator: Jean-Michel Jarre
desc: Jean-Michel Jarre was a pioneer of electronic music, and this 1977 instrumental is his best-known piece. On Bastille Day 1979 he performed at the Place de la Concorde for about a million people — at the time, the biggest concert crowd ever.

title: Père Lachaise Cemetery tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: This excellent tour sheds light on the “permanent Parisians” buried in the cemetery and provides context for the many memorials commemorating nation-altering tragedies. It starts near the Gambetta metro stop and ends on Rue de la Roquette. Allow 2 hours.

title: A lone tower so hated the city banned any more
desc: The 210-metre Tour Montparnasse went up above the rebuilt Montparnasse station in 1973. The backlash was so strong that Paris capped building heights in the centre soon after. A full makeover is now under way.

title: A river vanishes under the streets of the Left Bank
place: Buried course of the Bièvre river (area)
desc: The Bièvre once ran past tanneries and the Gobelins tapestry works before joining the Seine. Polluted and stinking, it was buried in sewers by 1912; its old bed runs beneath today’s 13th arrondissement.

title: Hitler orders the city wrecked and his general drags his feet
place: Le Meurice hotel, Rue de Rivoli
desc: General Dietrich von Choltitz commanded Paris in August 1944 and later claimed he refused Hitler’s order to destroy it. His headquarters was the Hôtel Meurice on the Rue de Rivoli, where he was arrested on the day of the surrender.

title: Au DD
creator: PNL
desc: PNL are one of the biggest names in French rap. For this 2019 song, the two brothers filmed a music video at the very top of the Eiffel Tower — the first band ever allowed to do it, rapping high above the city.

title: Göring shops for stolen art in a Tuileries gallery
place: Jeu de Paume gallery, Tuileries Garden
desc: During the occupation, art seized from Jewish families was sorted at the Jeu de Paume, a former royal tennis court in the Tuileries Garden. Hermann Göring visited again and again to pick works for his own collection.

title: Il est cinq heures, Paris s’éveille
creator: Jacques Dutronc
desc: The title means “It’s 5 a.m., Paris is waking up.” Jacques Dutronc’s 1968 song describes exactly that — bakers starting work, the last partiers heading home. It mentions the Eiffel Tower, which makes the tower a natural place to play it.

title: Historic Paris tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Unfortunately, this tour through the historic heart of Paris begins at the Notre Dame. If the area is still closed, start near Pont Saint-Louis and consider jumping ahead to 21:00 where the tour curls behind the damaged church. Allow at least 2 hours.

title: Craftspeople rebuild a cathedral after the fire
desc: Fire destroyed Notre-Dame’s roof and spire in April 2019. Carpenters, stonemasons and roofers rebuilt the oak frame and lead spire largely to the old design, and the cathedral on the Île de la Cité reopened in December 2024.

title: Musée d’Orsay tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: This fun chronological tour starts in the main gallery, where European art begins to veer from academic tradition. Next, Rick goes upstairs to see Impressionism in bloom: Monet, Renoir, Van Gogh, and more. For a relaxed pace, double his suggested 2 hours.

title: Culture and context surrounding Impressionism
desc: The Musée d’Orsay is the world’s best place to see Impressionism emerge from its more conservative academic roots. This fast-paced video from The Art Assignment is a fantastic and detailed look at the art movement and the culture that surrounded it.

title: Olympia versus the art world
desc: In the mid-1800s, the Academy of Fine Arts was the gatekeeper of what was considered “good” in the art world. This excellent video from Vox explains how Olympia, the reclining nude by Édouard Manet, threatened to upend the stodgy establishment in Paris.

title: Living as a woman during the Belle Époque
desc: Marie van Goethem was a ballet dancer who modeled for the iconic Edgar Degas sculpture “Little Dancer of 14 Years,” on view at the Musée d’Orsay. This episode of The Land of Desire shares stories of Marie and other Parisian women during the Belle Époque.

title: Inspirational impressionism at Musée de l’Orangerie
desc: Overshadowed by the Musée d’Orsay nearby, the l’Orangerie is an underrated delight. In this video, travel writer Rick Steves showcases some pieces from the collection, including the unquestionable highlight: two oval rooms of Water Lilies by Claude Monet.

title: The life and work of Claude Monet
desc: Displayed in purpose-built oval rooms at Musée de l’Orangerie, the paintings of water lilies by Claude Monet are a must-see art experience. This video from Biography describes Monet’s painting career and his role in the burgeoning Impressionism movement.

title: A close look at The Turkish Bath by Ingres
desc: Painted late in his life, Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres considered The Turkish Bath to be his greatest painting. This video from The Canvas explains how the meaning behind the sensual artwork depicting dozens of nude women may have been sensuality itself.

title: The weighty meaning behind The Raft of the Medusa
desc: Théodore Géricault’s epic painting of the few desperate survivors of a boat crash is one of the most well-known in the Louvre. This video from The Canvas explains Géricault’s obsessive study of a real event that sparked political controversy in his time.

title: Théâtre de la Mode: A beacon of hope for postwar France
desc: Shortly after World War II, fashion houses in Paris staged an exhibition at the Louvre to save the struggling industry. This episode of Articles of Interest brilliantly describes how the exhibition’s unique collection ended up in a museum in rural Oregon.

title: The theft of the Mona Lisa
desc: In 1911, a sly thief named Vincenzo Peruggia walked out of the Louvre with the Mona Lisa tucked underneath his coat. This episode of BBC’s Witness History explains how the investigation itself propelled Leonardo’s painting into worldwide fame.

title: Fact and fiction in The Phantom of the Opera
desc: The opera house in Paris is the setting for Gaston Leroux’s book The Phantom of the Opera, later adapted into many other versions. In this delightfully nerdy video from Bookworm History, Daniel Thurber shares the true stories that inspired the author.

title: Lifestyles of the rich and famous in the Belle Époque
desc: In this video from travel writer Rick Steves, we get two looks at the lives of upper-crust Parisians in the late 1800s. We see the stately Palais Garnier opera house and then visit a globetrotting couple’s former mansion, now the Jacquemart-André Museum.

title: Getting around the city by lamppost
desc: In the 1880s, as Paris debated its transit network’s future, the public was shocked by a plan to run an elevated train alongside their beloved opera house. This fun video from The Tim Traveler explains the debate and the perplexing invention it inspired.

title: Police lead soccer executives out in sheets at dawn
desc: Swiss police raided this five-star hotel at dawn on May 27, 2015, arresting seven FIFA officials in their beds on US racketeering and bribery charges. Porters tried shielding the men with sheets as they were led to police cars, images seen worldwide.

title: An exile boards a train that ends an empire
desc: Lenin left this station in April 1917 aboard a German-arranged train, insisting it count as extraterritorial so no one could accuse him of collaborating with the enemy. Eight days later he stepped off in Petrograd and began steering a revolution.

title: Thousands of addicts gather openly in a park behind the museum
desc: From 1987 to 1992 the Platzspitz, a riverside park behind the Swiss National Museum, was Europe’s largest open drug scene. Its closure and the chaos that followed pushed Switzerland toward prescribing heroin to severe addicts.

title: Le Corbusier’s last building is a steel-and-glass pavilion by the lake
desc: Gallery owner Heidi Weber persuaded Le Corbusier to design this house of colour panels in 1960 and paid for it herself. It opened in 1967 at the Zürichhorn park. A walk-through after its 2019 restoration, with the pavilion’s director.

title: Two brothers turn old truck tarpaulins into a cult messenger bag
desc: Markus and Daniel Freitag stitched their first bag from a lorry tarp, bike inner tubes and a seatbelt in 1993. The Museum für Gestaltung, Zurich’s design museum, gave the company its first retrospective, with prototypes and archive films.

title: A patent-office genius first learns his physics in Zurich
desc: Einstein trained as a teacher of physics at the Zurich Polytechnic, now ETH, from 1896 and later returned as a professor. Melvyn Bragg and guests trace how a middling student became the man who rewrote space, time and gravity.

title: Church bells ring through an empty new art museum before it opens
desc: Before the art went in, choreographer William Forsythe filled David Chipperfield’s extension to the Kunsthaus, the city art museum on Heimplatz square, with deconsecrated church bells that visitors set off as they walked the bare galleries.

title: Zurich’s old red-light district gets a buyer’s once-over
desc: Kreis 4, the district around Langstrasse just west of the main station, was long Zurich’s working-class and red-light quarter, packed with bars and immigrant shops. Monocle’s property series sizes it up as a place to live.

title: A city where a quarter of homes are run by co-operatives
desc: Non-profit housing co-operatives own a large share of Zurich’s flats, and newer projects such as Kalkbreite, built over a tram depot in Kreis 4, mix homes, shops and shared space. Monocle looks at how the model keeps city living affordable.

title: A sculptor spends decades filling a hillside with mosaic beasts
desc: On the city’s western edge above Dietikon, artist Bruno Weber built a sculpture park of towers, winged dogs and giant mosaic-covered creatures around his home. Laura Kramer walks through the garden for Monocle.

title: Zurich honours the Irish exile who wrote Ulysses there
desc: Joyce wrote much of Ulysses in Zurich during the First World War and died in the city in 1941. This 1966 RTÉ radio tribute marked the unveiling of his statue beside his grave in Fluntern cemetery, on the Zürichberg hill.

title: Office workers float home down the river after work
desc: In summer the Limmat river becomes a commute and a lido at once, with public river baths like the Oberer Letten. Monocle’s Matt Alagiah reports on a city where jumping into the current is ordinary daily life.

title: From the luxury shops of Bahnhofstrasse to Chagall’s glowing windows
desc: A walk from Zurich’s banking street, Bahnhofstrasse, into the cobbled old town, ending at the Fraumünster, the medieval abbey church whose choir got five stained-glass windows by Marc Chagall in 1970.

title: An airport sets the tone for a well-run country
desc: Zurich Airport, just north of the city at Kloten, is Switzerland’s main gateway. Monocle’s Jessica Bridger lands there and makes the case for how an airport should greet arrivals, Swiss style.

title: Campaigners save a lakeside factory and turn it into a culture hub
desc: The Rote Fabrik, a red-brick former silk factory built in 1892 on the shore of Lake Zurich in Wollishofen, was slated for demolition in the 1970s. Local campaigners saved it, and it now hosts concerts, theatre, studios and a restaurant.

title: Guildsmen ride circles round a burning snowman to end winter
desc: At Sechseläuten each April, Zurich’s guilds parade in costume, then light a pyre under the Böögg, a cotton-wool snowman stuffed with fireworks. The faster his head bursts, the better the summer. It happens on Sechseläutenplatz by the opera house.

title: A raw concrete wing grows out of a castle-like museum
desc: Basel architects Christ & Gantenbein added a folded concrete wing to the Swiss National Museum, Gustav Gull’s 1898 turreted building beside the main station. This short architecture film follows light and visitors through the new galleries.

title: Karuzela z Madonnami
creator: Ewa Demarczyk
desc: The title means ‘Carousel with Madonnas.’ Ewa Demarczyk, the ‘dark angel’ of Polish song, sang it like a woman possessed in the candlelit cellar of the Piwnica pod Baranami, the cabaret beneath the Main Square.

title: Rick Steves walks the old royal capital from square to castle
desc: A short Rick Steves segment on why Kraków, Poland’s capital until 1596, kept its medieval core intact. It starts in Rynek Główny, the main market square around the Cloth Hall, one of the largest medieval squares in Europe.

title: A science-fiction writer predicts the internet from a Kraków desk
desc: Stanisław Lem settled in Kraków after the war and wrote Solaris and dozens of other books here, anticipating the internet in the 1960s. He is buried in Salwator Cemetery, on the hill above the Vistula on the city’s western edge.

title: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook go down Poland’s salt mine
desc: A tour of what the hosts call Poland’s seven wonders, from the legend of Krakus the dragon-slayer to the Wieliczka Salt Mine, the underground workings just outside Kraków whose miners carved chapels and chandeliers out of rock salt.

title: A historian walks the streets of Poland’s old royal capital
desc: Travel writer Paul Bloomfield and Oxford historian Natalia Nowakowska trace Kraków from medieval trading hub to Jagiellonian royal seat, with its centuries-old Jewish community. The Cloth Hall, the market’s old trading arcade, sits at its centre.

title: Stalin’s planners build a steel town to outnumber the professors
desc: Nowa Huta was built from 1949 as a model socialist town for steelworkers, partly to dilute conservative, Catholic Kraków. Rick Steves walks its broad avenues from Central Square, the hub of the radiating plan.

title: Miners carve chapels and chandeliers out of solid salt
desc: Salt was dug at Wieliczka from the 13th century until 1996. Over 700 years miners left behind chambers, lakes and the Chapel of St Kinga, where the floor, altar and chandeliers are all salt. A UNESCO/NHK film from inside the mine.

title: A royal capital comes through the war with its old town intact
desc: A short UNESCO/NHK film on the Old Town, Wawel Hill and Kazimierz, one of the first places put on the World Heritage list in 1978. It centres on the Main Market Square, the largest medieval town square in Europe.

title: Leonardo paints a duke’s teenage mistress holding a white stoat
desc: Cecilia Gallerani was about sixteen when Leonardo painted her in Milan around 1490. Prince Adam Czartoryski bought the portrait in 1800, and it now hangs in the Czartoryski Museum, part of the National Museum in Kraków.

title: Conservators spend six years cleaning a 500-year-old wooden altar
desc: Veit Stoss carved the limewood altarpiece in St Mary’s Basilica between 1477 and 1489; its figures stand almost three metres tall. This film covers the 2015–2021 restoration that won a European Heritage Award.

title: A fourth-generation craftsman builds glittering churches from foil
place: Adam Mickiewicz Monument, Main Market Square
desc: Kraków’s szopki are glittering nativity cribs modelled on the city’s own churches and towers. Every December makers bring them to the Mickiewicz monument on the Main Market Square for a contest that UNESCO lists as intangible heritage.

title: A medieval king invites Jews to settle beside his new town
desc: Kazimierz was founded as a separate town in 1335 by King Casimir III and became a centre of Jewish life for five centuries. Rick Steves’ classroom clip looks at Szeroka Street, the long square lined with synagogues.

title: A girl is crowned king of Poland and leaves her jewels to a university
desc: Jadwiga was crowned in Wawel Cathedral in 1384, aged about ten, with the title king rather than queen. Her marriage to Lithuania’s Jogaila founded the Jagiellonian dynasty, and she is buried in the cathedral on the castle hill.

title: A king’s 13-tonne bell rings out for its 500th birthday
desc: King Sigismund the Old had the Zygmunt bell cast in 1520. Now nearly 13 tonnes, it hangs in the Sigismund Tower of Wawel Cathedral, on the castle hill, and is rung by hand by a team of bell-ringers only on major holidays and national occasions.

title: A medieval town lies four metres under the market square
desc: Excavations under Rynek Główny, the main market square, uncovered old trading stalls, paving and graves. The Rynek Underground museum now runs beneath the Cloth Hall, with glass walkways over the remains of the medieval market.

title: Tinfoil churches compete for a prize beside a poet’s statue
desc: Kraków’s szopki are nativity scenes built as glittering miniatures of the city’s churches. Each December makers carry them to the Main Market Square for a contest at the Mickiewicz monument, and the best go on show at the city museum.

title: Synagogues and courtyards return to life in the old Jewish town
desc: Kazimierz was a separate town for centuries and the heart of Jewish Kraków until the Second World War. Its synagogues, Szeroka Street and café-filled squares lie just south of the Old Town, near the Vistula.

title: A Nobel poet from Kraków asks who really likes poetry
desc: Wisława Szymborska spent most of her life in Kraków and lived for years in the writers’ house on Krupnicza Street. Frank Skinner reads two of her poems, ‘Some Like Poetry’ and ‘Plato, or Why’, and unpicks their dry wit. She won the Nobel Prize in 1996.

title: A boy from the Płaszów camp grows up to hunt its commandant
desc: Josef Lefkowitz was 13 when Germany invaded Poland and was sent to the Kraków-Płaszów camp, now a grassy hillside with a stone memorial. He survived Auschwitz and Mauthausen, then hunted Nazis for the US Army and helped capture Amon Göth.

title: Hungary’s Renaissance king and his golden age
desc: In this episode of Anthology of Heroes, the rise of János Hunyadi and his son Matthias Corvinus unfolds — the Renaissance warrior-king whose golden age crowned medieval Hungary, remembered at the Buda church that bears his name.

title: Farmers sell pickles, cheese and berries at an old city market
desc: Stary Kleparz has been a market square since the 14th century and still sells fresh produce, smoked cheese and flowers from covered stalls. It sits just north of Kraków’s Old Town, near the Barbican.

title: The Budapest school that raised a generation of geniuses
desc: In this episode of Stuff You Missed in History Class, the hosts profile John von Neumann — computing and game-theory pioneer, and one of the Budapest-born “Martians” educated at the legendary Fasori Gimnázium, a highly-regarded secondary school.

title: Kraków grows rich on trade and survives the Mongols of 1241
desc: In the Middle Ages Kraków was a royal capital and a trading crossroads of Central Europe, until Mongol armies sacked it in 1241. Rebuilt under a new town charter in 1257, it gained the Main Market Square that still anchors the old town.

title: The escape artist Budapest gave the world
desc: In this episode of Stuff You Missed in History Class, the hosts conjure the life of Harry Houdini — escape artist and showman, born Erik Weisz in Budapest, the city that now honors him at the House of Houdini museum.

title: The doctor who begged everyone to wash their hands
desc: In this episode of Sawbones, the jokey duo Sydnee and Justin McElroy tell the tragic, infuriating story of Ignaz Semmelweis — the handwashing pioneer born in Buda, where his birthplace is now the Semmelweis Medical History Museum.

title: The Csárdás Princess
creator: Imre Kálmán
desc: A csárdás is a fast, whirling Hungarian folk dance. This 1915 operetta — a light romantic musical — is the most loved of its kind, full of sparkle and heartbreak. Imre Kálmán’s works still play at the Budapest Operetta Theatre.

title: Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2
creator: Franz Liszt
desc: Franz Liszt was the most famous Hungarian musician of the 1800s and a rock-star pianist of his day. This dramatic, folk-flavored piece is his most famous. He founded the school that still carries his name, the Liszt Academy in central Budapest.

title: Most múlik pontosan
creator: Quimby
desc: The title roughly means “now it ends, exactly now.” Quimby’s haunting 2005 song about letting go is a Hungarian sing-along staple. Their alt-rock scene fills riverside venues like the A38, a concert ship moored on the Danube.

title: Allegro Barbaro
creator: Béla Bartók
desc: Béla Bartók roamed the countryside recording villagers’ songs, then forged them into bold modern music. This short, pounding 1911 piano piece captures that fierce style. His last home in Budapest, up in the Buda hills, is now a museum.

title: Háry János
creator: Zoltán Kodály
desc: Háry János is a folk tall-tale hero — a boastful old soldier who claims he beat Napoleon single-handedly. Zoltán Kodály’s 1926 orchestral suite tells it with humor. A Budapest square, Kodály körönd, is named for the composer.

title: Szomorú Vasárnap (Gloomy Sunday)
creator: Rezső Seress
desc: This mournful 1933 ballad became world-famous and earned a grim nickname — “the Hungarian suicide song” — through years of dark legend. Its writer, Rezső Seress, played piano nightly at Budapest’s Kispipa restaurant.

title: Introvertált dal
creator: Azahriah
desc: The title means “introvert’s song.” Azahriah, born in Budapest in 2002, became the country’s biggest star almost overnight. In May 2024 he sold out the 60,000-seat Puskás Aréna three nights running — a first for any Hungarian artist.

title: Kedvesem
creator: ByeAlex
desc: Kedvesem means “my darling.” ByeAlex’s soft, catchy 2013 tune represented Hungary at Eurovision and won over a generation. Acts like his fill the stages of Sziget, the giant summer festival on Óbuda Island in the Danube.

title: Szerelem, szerelem
creator: Márta Sebestyén
desc: The title means “love, love.” This old Hungarian folk song, sung by Márta Sebestyén, reached the world through the film The English Patient. You can hear living folk music at a táncház, or “dance house,” like the Fonó in Buda.

title: Himnusz
creator: Ferenc Erkel
desc: Himnusz simply means “anthem” — this is Hungary’s national anthem, a solemn 1844 prayer for a country that had endured centuries of hardship. Its composer, Ferenc Erkel, was the first music director of the Hungarian State Opera House.

title: The 1956 uprising that defied Soviet tanks
desc: In this episode of We Didn’t Start the Fire, the hosts interview an Eastern Europe expert Eric Halsey revisit Budapest’s 1956 uprising against Soviet rule — the revolt remembered today at the House of Terror on Andrássy Avenue.

title: How a herdsman’s stew became Hungary’s pride
desc: In this video from Tasting History, Max Miller simmers the story of goulash — the herdsman’s paprika stew that became Hungary’s national dish, sold in cauldrons and spice-stalls at Budapest’s Great Market Hall.

title: The team that humbled England at its own game
