desc: In this episode of These Football Times, the hosts and author David Bailey celebrate the Mighty Magyars — Hungary’s revolutionary national football team of the 1950s, led by Puskás, Kocsis and Hidegkuti and honored today at Budapest’s Puskás Aréna.

title: The bloodless revolution that began on the museum steps
desc: In this episode of Mike Duncan’s Revolutions, Hungary’s 1848 revolution unfolds — the bloodless uprising, sparked by the poet Sándor Petőfi at Budapest’s National Museum, that won Hungarians their own government.

title: The Budapest boy who dreamed up a nation
place: Hungarian Jewish Museum (site of Herzl’s birthplace)
desc: In this episode of Origin Story, Dorian Lynskey and Ian Dunt trace how Theodor Herzl founded modern political Zionism — the writer born in 1860 beside Budapest’s Dohány Street Synagogue, now the site of the Hungarian Jewish Museum.

title: The boy from Budapest who became war’s greatest photographer
desc: In this episode of The FujiCast, the hosts and a war photographer celebrate Robert Capa — born Endre Friedmann in Budapest, now honored at the city’s Robert Capa Contemporary Photography Center. The story starts 23 and a half minutes into the episode.

title: The composer who turned folk songs into modern art
desc: In this episode of Sticky Notes, conductor Joshua Weilerstein explores Bartók’s life-affirming Concerto for Orchestra — the masterwork of the folk-song collector whose last Budapest home, on Csalán Road, is now the Bartók Memorial House.

title: Classical music’s first rock star, a proud Hungarian
desc: In this episode of the BBC’s The Forum, a panel explores Franz Liszt — the 19th-century piano superstar and proud Hungarian who founded the music academy in Budapest that still bears his name.

title: A TV detective becomes a bronze folk hero on a Budapest street
desc: Since 2014 Peter Falk’s Columbo, raincoat and basset hound included, has stood on Falk Miksa utca, a street near Parliament. The show aired on communist-era TV, and Hungarians liked to think Falk was kin to the journalist the street honours.

title: Paprika and pickles under one iron roof
desc: The Great Market Hall, a steel-framed hall with a Zsolnay tile roof at the Pest end of Liberty Bridge, opened in 1897. Butchers, paprika sellers and pickle stalls fill the ground floor, with hot food counters on the gallery above.

title: A hanged prime minister gets a state funeral thirty years late
desc: Imre Nagy led Hungary in the 1956 uprising and was executed in 1958. On 16 June 1989 his coffin lay in Heroes’ Square, the city’s great monument plaza, before a vast crowd. The day’s master of ceremonies recalls how it signalled communism’s end.

title: A Scottish engineer’s bridge finally joins Buda and Pest
desc: The Széchenyi Chain Bridge, opened in 1849 and designed by William Tierney Clark, was the first permanent crossing of the Danube here. Above it rises Castle Hill, the walled ridge of the royal palace, Matthias Church and the old Buda quarter.

title: Seven chieftains and a thousand years of Hungary in one square
desc: Heroes’ Square was laid out for the 1896 millennium celebrations, with the Magyar tribal leaders around a tall column and kings and statesmen in the colonnades. Behind it lies City Park, home to Vajdahunyad Castle and the Széchenyi baths.

title: Divers explore a flooded cave system beneath a Budapest hillside
desc: Warm spring water has carved a maze of passages under Rózsadomb, the hill on the Buda side. The Molnár János Cave, entered beside the Lukács baths, is one of the largest thermal water caves known, with kilometres of flooded tunnels mapped by divers.

title: Where Budapest sent its unwanted Lenins and Marxes
desc: After 1989 the city removed its communist monuments and gathered dozens of them in Memento Park, an open-air museum on the southwestern edge of Buda. Soldiers, workers and Marx and Engels stand together, alongside a replica of Stalin’s boots.

title: Europe’s largest synagogue and the garden behind it
desc: The Dohány Street Synagogue, finished in 1859 in a Moorish style, seats nearly 3,000. Its courtyard holds a mass grave from the wartime ghetto and the weeping willow memorial whose metal leaves carry the names of Hungarian Jews killed in the Holocaust.

title: The Andrássy Avenue house that served two dictatorships
desc: Andrássy út 60, a grand townhouse on the city’s main boulevard, was headquarters of the fascist Arrow Cross in 1944 and then of the communist secret police. Since 2002 it has been the House of Terror museum, with cells preserved in the basement.

title: Soaking in hot spring water inside a neo-baroque palace
desc: Budapest sits on more than a hundred thermal springs. The Széchenyi baths in City Park, opened in 1913, are among Europe’s largest, with steaming outdoor pools where locals play chess on floating boards year round.

title: Building a parliament big enough for a thousand-year-old nation
desc: Imre Steindl’s Gothic Revival Parliament on the Pest riverbank took from 1885 to 1904 to build and was inaugurated in 1896 for the millennium of the Hungarian state. This film from the Parliament’s own studio follows how it was designed and built.

title: A castle hill and a parliament line the same stretch of river
desc: The World Heritage listing covers the Danube banks between Buda and Pest, the hilltop Castle Quarter, and Andrássy Avenue with the old metro line beneath it. The view from Buda Castle takes in the Parliament and the bridges below.

title: Architects compete to design a permanent home for parliament
desc: An 1880 law ordered a permanent parliament building in Pest, and a design contest followed; Imre Steindl’s Gothic Revival plan won. The building stands on the Danube bank at Kossuth tér. In Hungarian with English subtitles.

title: The Parliament becomes a headquarters of terror in 1919
desc: During the 133-day Hungarian Soviet Republic of 1919, a political police unit was based in the Parliament building, and prisoners were held and beaten there. The building is on Kossuth tér by the Danube. In Hungarian with English subtitles.

title: A wartime prime minister is shot at home as the war ends
desc: István Tisza, Hungary’s prime minister for much of the First World War, was killed at his villa on Hermina út on 31 October 1918; who was behind it is still unclear. The street runs along City Park in Zugló. In Hungarian with English subtitles.

title: A marshy riverside lot becomes the nation’s main square
desc: In the early 1800s Tömő tér was an empty, waterlogged plot on the Pest riverbank. Chosen as the site for Parliament, it grew into Kossuth Lajos tér, the square in front of the building. In Hungarian with English subtitles.

title: A bronze Lieutenant Columbo and his dog stand on a Pest street
desc: The statue of Peter Falk as the rumpled TV detective went up in 2014, nodding to a claimed family link to Hungary. He stands with his dog on Falk Miksa utca, a street of antique shops near Parliament, named for a different Falk.

title: Tiny bronze figures hide on bridges and railings across the city
place: Kermit the Frog statue, Liberty Bridge
desc: Since 2016 the sculptor Mihály Kolodko has fixed dozens of palm-sized bronzes around Budapest, often without asking first. One of the best known is Kermit the Frog, perched on Liberty Bridge, the green iron bridge below Gellért Hill.

title: Glazed tiles from Pécs give the city its shimmering roofs
desc: The Zsolnay factory in Pécs developed frost-proof ceramics and iridescent eosin glazes in the late 1800s. Its patterned roof tiles cover Matthias Church, the Gothic church on Castle Hill beside the Fishermen’s Bastion.

title: Fluidum
creator: The Ecstasy of Saint Theresa
desc: Shimmering dream-pop from Prague’s Ecstasy of Saint Theresa, who bent shoegaze into early Czech electronica just after 1989. Pinned to the Roxy on Dlouhá, the Old Town club at the centre of the city’s 1990s alternative nights.

title: The Power of the Powerless
place: Theatre on the Balustrade (Divadlo Na zábradlí)
creator: Václav Havel
desc: The essay that armed a generation of dissidents: Havel argues that living within a lie sustains tyranny, and ordinary truth can break it. Written under surveillance. His theatre home, Na zábradlí, is where the future president learned the stage.

title: A general builds an imperial palace, then loses everything
desc: Wallenstein raised a private army of tens of thousands and built this Baroque palace as a monument to his power in the 1620s. Declared a traitor for negotiating with the enemy, he was assassinated in Cheb, far from the palace that outlived him.

title: A thrown stone turns a sermon into a massacre
desc: A stone thrown at a Hussite priest during a protest march enraged the crowd into storming this town hall and throwing council members from its windows, the original defenestration that gave the word its meaning, nearly two centuries before the famous one.

title: Prague loves this composer more than his hometown does
desc: Mozart conducted the world premiere of Don Giovanni at this theatre in 1787, one stop on a European tour this live episode traces from child prodigy to working musician. Prague alone held a memorial performance of his Requiem after his death.

title: Women rule from a rival fortress, then lose everything
desc: Legend holds that after Princess Libuše died, warrior Vlasta led women against the men ruling from this hilltop fortress, founding a rival castle before dying in the counterattack. The myth has shaped Czech ideas about gender and power for centuries.

title: A playwright addresses 300,000 people from a balcony
desc: Havel spoke to a crowd of 300,000 from this balcony on November 24, 1989, six days into protests that ended four decades of one-party rule. Twenty-one years after Soviet tanks crushed reform in this same square, jingling keys finally rang the Party out.

title: An astronomer with a metal nose ends his days at the emperor’s court
place: Church of Our Lady before Týn
desc: Tycho Brahe came to Prague in 1599 as Rudolf II’s imperial mathematician and died here in 1601. He is buried in the Church of Our Lady before Týn on Old Town Square, where his tomb was opened in 2010 to test old rumours that he was poisoned.

title: An English princess holds the Bohemian crown for a single winter
desc: Elizabeth Stuart, daughter of James I, moved into Prague Castle in 1619 when her husband Frederick was elected King of Bohemia. Defeat at White Mountain in 1620 sent them into exile. Every British monarch since George I descends from her.

title: Doorless lifts loop endlessly through the old office buildings
desc: Prague still runs a few paternosters, open cabins that circle nonstop and that riders hop on and off. The one in the New City Hall on Mariánské Square is open to visitors, while others have been threatened by safety rules.

title: An Art Nouveau poster artist’s work comes home to Prague
desc: Alfons Mucha made his name in Paris designing posters for Sarah Bernhardt, then returned to serve the new Czechoslovak state. The Mucha Museum on Panská street gathers his posters, drawings and studio photographs.

title: Learning to read a medieval clock that tracks sun and moon
desc: The astronomical clock on the Old Town Hall dates from 1410. Its dials show Old Bohemian and Babylonian hours, the zodiac and the moon’s phase. A Prague local walks through how to read them, which few onlookers ever learn.

title: Newsreel cameras catch the city the year before the Spring
desc: British Pathé footage of Prague in 1967, a year before Dubček’s reforms and the Warsaw Pact invasion. A short archive view of the streets and squares of the Old Town as they looked under late-1960s communism.

title: The largest stadium ever built sits half forgotten on a hill
desc: The Great Strahov Stadium was built for the Sokol movement’s mass gymnastics displays, with a field big enough for tens of thousands of performers at once. Today it is used as a training ground and has no clear future.

title: Six synagogues and a hall of names in the old Jewish Town
desc: Josefov was Prague’s walled Jewish ghetto; its synagogues survive inside a grid of 1900s apartment blocks. The Pinkas Synagogue walls carry the names of nearly 80,000 Czech Jews killed in the Holocaust.

title: Twelve layers of graves crowd a small walled cemetery
desc: Used from the 15th century until 1787, the Old Jewish Cemetery in Josefov had no room to expand, so new graves were laid over old ones. Some 12,000 tombstones lean together, including that of Rabbi Loew. Artist Mark Podwal’s film.

title: Monks build a painted hall for philosophy and theology
desc: The Premonstratensian monastery at Strahov keeps two great library halls, the Theological and the Philosophical, with frescoed ceilings and walnut shelving. Radio Prague’s English service visits the collection and its keepers.

title: A Jesuit college shelves the nation’s books under frescoes
desc: The Clementinum, a former Jesuit college beside Charles Bridge, is now home to the Czech National Library. Its Baroque library hall and astronomical tower, where weather has been recorded since 1775, are the highlights.

title: A thousand years of kings, presidents and saints on one hill
desc: Prague Castle has been the seat of Bohemian princes, Holy Roman emperors and Czech presidents since the 9th century. A local guide explains how St Vitus Cathedral, the Old Royal Palace and Golden Lane fit together.

title: The rebels who broke away to reinvent art
desc: In this slightly highfalutin episode of In Our Time, Melvyn Bragg and guests trace how Klimt and friends broke away to found the Vienna Secession — the movement whose golden-domed Secession Building still crowns the city’s avant-garde.

title: A Gothic stone bridge carries a gallery of Baroque saints
desc: Charles IV laid the first stone of this bridge in 1357, and for centuries it was the only crossing of the Vltava in Prague. The 30 statues along its parapets were added mostly around 1700; most are now copies.

title: A chemist makes the first soft contact lens on his kitchen table
desc: Otto Wichterle, sidelined by the communist authorities, built a lens-spinning machine from his son’s Merkur construction set at Christmas 1961. He founded and ran the Institute of Macromolecular Chemistry in Petřiny, Prague 6.

title: Gothic towers and Baroque domes on both banks of the Vltava
desc: Prague’s historic centre was listed in 1992: the Old and New Towns on the right bank, the Lesser Town and the castle on the left, joined by the Charles Bridge. Old Town Square, with its astronomical clock, is the usual starting point.

title: A long sloping square where Czechs gather to make history
desc: Wenceslas Square is a boulevard-like square in the New Town, topped by the National Museum and a statue of St Wenceslas. Crowds filled it in 1968 and again in the Velvet Revolution of 1989.

title: Where Beethoven composed as his hearing faded
desc: In this episode of In Our Time, Melvyn Bragg and guests trace how Beethoven flourished after moving to Vienna — the city where, in rooms like the Pasqualati House on the Mölker Bastei, he composed as his deafness grew.

title: The melancholy empress behind the glitter
desc: In this episode of Noble Blood, Dana Schwartz tells the lonely, glittering story of Empress Elisabeth “Sisi” — whose world of corsets and melancholy now fills the Sisi Museum inside Vienna’s Hofburg palace.

title: The Third Man Theme
creator: Anton Karas
desc: Anton Karas played this haunting melody on a zither — a plucked Alpine string instrument — for the 1949 film noir The Third Man, set in postwar Vienna. Its most famous scene plays out on the Riesenrad, the giant Ferris wheel at the Prater, a historic park.

title: Heite grob ma Tote aus
creator: Voodoo Jürgens
desc: The dialect title means “today we dig up the dead.” A former gravedigger, Voodoo Jürgens revives the old Wienerlied with morbid wit and a raspy Vienna drawl. No place fits better than the Zentralfriedhof, where he once worked.

title: The circle that tried to banish nonsense
desc: In this episode of In Our Time, Melvyn Bragg and guests examine Logical Positivism and the Vienna Circle — the thinkers who met near the University of Vienna to decide which ideas were truly meaningful.

title: Rise Like a Phoenix
creator: Conchita Wurst
desc: This soaring, Bond-style ballad won the 2014 Eurovision Song Contest for Conchita Wurst — the bearded drag persona of Tom Neuwirth — as a statement for tolerance. The win brought Eurovision 2015 to Vienna’s Stadthalle arena.

title: Bologna
creator: Wanda
desc: Wanda are the cheeky kings of today’s Viennese guitar rock — songs of love, wine, and longing for Italy in a thick local accent. This 2014 breakout pines for the city of Bologna, but the band and their boozy charm are pure Vienna.

title: High Noon
creator: Kruder & Dorfmeister
desc: Kruder & Dorfmeister invented the laid-back “Vienna sound” of the 1990s — hazy, slow-motion electronic grooves. They recorded their 1993 breakthrough, including this track, in Kruder’s flat on Grundsteingasse in the 16th district.

title: Rock Me Amadeus
creator: Falco
desc: Falco’s 1985 smash about Mozart made him the only Austrian to top the US chart, blending German rap with new-wave pop. Vienna’s biggest pop star is buried in an honorary grave at the Zentralfriedhof, the city’s vast, star-studded cemetery.

title: Tauben vergiften
creator: Georg Kreisler
desc: The title means “poisoning pigeons.” Georg Kreisler’s gleefully morbid cabaret song turns a romantic date in the park into exactly that — Viennese black humor at its finest. Picture it in a leafy spot like the Stadtpark.

title: Wien, du Stadt meiner Träume
creator: Rudolf Sieczyński
desc: The title means “Vienna, city of my dreams.” This 1914 tune is the definitive Wienerlied — Vienna’s own kind of bittersweet local song. You’ll still hear them over wine in the Heurigen, the rustic taverns of villages like Grinzing.

title: The Merry Widow
creator: Franz Lehár
desc: Franz Lehár’s 1905 operetta — a frothy comedy about a rich widow and the men chasing her fortune — became a worldwide sensation. It premiered at the Theater an der Wien, the historic home of Viennese operetta.

title: Symphony No. 5 (Adagietto)
creator: Gustav Mahler
desc: Gustav Mahler’s aching, slow Adagietto — later the sound of the film Death in Venice — is one of music’s great love letters. Mahler ran the Vienna Court Opera, today the State Opera, turning it into the finest opera house in Europe.

title: The Blue Danube
creator: Johann Strauss II
desc: Officially “On the Beautiful Blue Danube,” this 1866 waltz by Johann Strauss II is Vienna’s unofficial anthem. His gilded statue, violin in hand, stands in the Stadtpark — one of the most photographed monuments in the city.

title: Radetzky March
creator: Johann Strauss I
desc: Johann Strauss the Elder wrote this jaunty military march in 1848. Every New Year’s Day it closes Vienna’s famous concert at the Musikverein, where the whole audience claps along in time.

title: Ave Maria
creator: Franz Schubert
desc: Schubert’s tender 1825 melody is one of the most beloved sacred songs anywhere. Vienna’s own composer was born in a modest flat on Nussdorfer Straße, now a small museum you can visit in the north of the city.

title: Eine kleine Nachtmusik
creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
desc: The title means “a little night music.” Mozart’s bright, instantly familiar 1787 serenade is pure Vienna. He wrote some of his greatest works at the Mozarthaus on Domgasse — the only one of his Vienna apartments still standing, now a museum.

title: Symphony No. 9 (“Ode to Joy”)
creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
desc: Beethoven wrote his triumphant final symphony — its “Ode to Joy” now Europe’s anthem — while almost completely deaf. Years earlier, in the Vienna wine village of Heiligenstadt, he despaired over that deafness; his house there is now a museum.

title: The raw, electric genius Vienna couldn’t ignore
desc: In this episode of The Lonely Palette, Tamar Avishai gets up close with Egon Schiele’s raw, electric self-portraits — the Expressionist whose largest trove of work lives at Vienna’s Leopold Museum.

title: The stolen Klimt and the fight to reclaim it
desc: In this episode of ArtCurious, Jennifer Dasal follows Klimt’s “Woman in Gold” (Adele Bloch-Bauer I) — looted by the Nazis, hung for decades at Vienna’s Belvedere, and reclaimed in a landmark restitution battle.

title: The opera born in Mozart’s Vienna apartment
desc: In this episode of Aria Code, Rhiannon Giddens unpacks “Dove sono” from Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro — the opera he wrote at the Mozarthaus on Domgasse, his only surviving Vienna apartment.

title: The philosopher who built logic into a house
desc: In this episode of Philosophize This, Stephen West breaks down Ludwig Wittgenstein’s life and logic — the Viennese thinker who even designed a severe modernist mansion for his sister, the Haus Wittgenstein in the 3rd district.

title: The couch where Freud reinvented the mind
desc: In this episode of The History of Literature, Jacke Wilson revisits Sigmund Freud — the father of psychoanalysis who saw patients at Berggasse 19, now Vienna’s Freud Museum, and reshaped how we read minds and books.

title: The grand cafés where Vienna slows down
desc: In this episode of 5THWAVE, the World Coffee Portal team explores Vienna’s UNESCO-listed coffee-house culture — the marble-table world of grand cafés like Café Central, where writers lingered for hours over a single cup.

title: The chocolate cake Vienna still fights over
desc: In this video from Tasting History, Max Miller traces the legend of the Sachertorte — the chocolate-and-apricot cake born in 1832 and still guarded as “the original” at Vienna’s Hotel Sacher.

title: The maestro who reigned at Vienna’s opera
desc: In this episode of Sticky Notes, Joshua Weilerstein explores Mahler’s epic First Symphony and the turbulent life of the composer who once ruled the podium at the Vienna Court Opera, today’s Vienna State Opera.

title: The requiem Mozart didn’t live to finish
desc: In this episode of Sticky Notes, conductor Joshua Weilerstein dives into Mozart’s unfinished Requiem — the music shadowing his mysterious death in Vienna, the city whose St. Stephen’s Cathedral held his funeral rites.

title: The golden kiss that became Vienna’s icon
desc: In this episode of Art Detective, Janina Ramirez unpacks Gustav Klimt’s gold-drenched “The Kiss” — the swooning, shimmering masterpiece that hangs in Vienna’s Upper Belvedere and became the face of Viennese Art Nouveau.

title: Workers move into palaces built by a socialist city
desc: Between 1919 and 1934 the city’s Social Democrats built tens of thousands of council flats with courtyards, laundries and kindergartens. The kilometre-long Karl-Marx-Hof in Heiligenstadt is the best known of these housing estates.

title: Night falls and the city gathers at the sausage stand
desc: A DW film follows Viennese after dark, from late-night coffee houses to the Würstelstand, the sausage kiosk where opera-goers and cab drivers share mustard and beer, such as the stand beside the Albertina museum.

title: Diplomats redraw Europe between banquets and balls
desc: After Napoleon’s defeat in 1814–15, monarchs and ministers met in Vienna to settle the continent’s borders. Metternich ran the talks from the Austrian chancellery on Ballhausplatz while the city laid on endless dances.

title: An Ottoman army surrounds the city and a cavalry charge breaks it
desc: Historian Martyn Rady explains the summer of 1683, when Ottoman forces besieged the Habsburg capital until a relief army under Jan Sobieski came down from the Kahlenberg, the hill above the Danube with a church marking the spot.

title: A Gothic spire and a patterned roof above the old town
desc: St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna’s Gothic mother church, rises over Stephansplatz with its 136-metre south tower and a roof of glazed tiles laid out in zigzags and the double-headed imperial eagle.

title: The crowns and relics of a thousand-year empire
desc: The Schatzkammer, the treasury inside the Hofburg palace, holds the Holy Roman Empire’s 10th-century crown, the Habsburg imperial crown, coronation robes and relics the dynasty used to claim its authority.

title: An emperor tears down the walls and builds a boulevard
desc: In 1857 Franz Joseph ordered the old fortifications razed and replaced with a ring road lined with parliament, opera, museums and town hall. The Greek-temple Parliament building is one of its grandest stops.

title: Winemakers pour this year’s vintage under a pine bough
desc: Vienna is a working wine city, and its growers may sell their own new wine in a Heuriger, a tavern marked by a hanging bundle of branches. Grinzing, a village on the city’s northern edge, is the best known cluster.

title: Vienna’s grand cemetery and its love of a good funeral
desc: The Viennese are known for a fondness for ‘a beautiful corpse’. The Zentralfriedhof, the vast 1874 cemetery holding Beethoven, Schubert and Brahms, also houses a funeral museum with reusable coffins and other relics of that culture.

title: Cheering crowds greet Hitler as Austria disappears overnight
desc: In March 1938 German troops crossed into Austria and Hitler announced its annexation to a vast crowd on Heldenplatz, the square in front of the Hofburg palace. The hosts also examine Austria’s postwar claim to be Hitler’s first victim.

title: An heir to the empire falls for a 17-year-old baroness
desc: Crown Prince Rudolf, a restless outsider in his own family, met Baroness Mary Vetsera in 1880s Vienna. In 1889 both were found dead at his hunting lodge at Mayerling. Rudolf lies in the Imperial Crypt beneath the Capuchin church.

title: White stallions dance under a Baroque riding-hall ceiling
desc: The Spanish Riding School has trained Lipizzaner horses in classical dressage since the 16th century. Its performances take place in the Winter Riding School, a chandeliered hall built in the 1730s inside the Hofburg palace.

title: A century of council flats that still shape the city
desc: Monocle looks at the lasting legacy of Vienna’s Gemeindebau, the city-owned apartment blocks begun in the 1920s and still being built. The Karl-Marx-Hof, a kilometre-long housing estate in Döbling, is the best-known example.

title: Inside the opera house at the heart of musical Vienna
desc: The State Opera on the Ringstrasse opened in 1869 and stages a different production almost every night of the season. Bombed in 1945, its reopening in 1955 was a national event. Rick Steves visits the house.

title: Habsburg collectors fill a palace with Bruegel and Raphael
desc: Vienna’s fine arts museum opened in 1891 to house the Habsburg collections, with the world’s largest group of Bruegels. It faces its twin, the Natural History Museum, across Maria-Theresien-Platz on the Ringstrasse.

title: The Habsburgs’ summer palace and its 1,441 rooms
desc: Schönbrunn was the Habsburg family’s summer residence, remodelled under Maria Theresa in the 18th century. Mozart played here as a child, and Franz Joseph was born and died here. Rick Steves tours its state rooms and gardens.

title: Olives, kebabs and tiny open sandwiches on the market lanes
desc: The Naschmarkt, Vienna’s biggest food market, runs along two parallel lanes above the covered Wien river. Rick Steves samples its stalls, then stops at Buffet Trześniewski for the city’s classic small open sandwiches.

title: A draughtsman’s nightmares fill the print rooms of a palace
desc: Alfred Kubin drew monsters, plagues and dread in ink around 1900, and was also a novelist. The Albertina, the graphic-art museum in a Habsburg palace on the old city wall, holds one of the largest collections of his work.

title: A new town for 25,000 people rises around an old airfield lake
desc: Seestadt Aspern is being built on a former airfield on Vienna’s eastern edge, laid out around an artificial lake and linked to the centre by the U2 metro. It is one of Europe’s largest urban developments.

title: Medieval lanes, Baroque palaces and a boulevard where the walls stood
desc: Vienna’s centre was listed in 2001 for three layers: the medieval core around St Stephen’s Cathedral, the Baroque palaces and churches, and the 19th-century Ringstrasse built where the city walls once ran.

title: One coffee buys an afternoon with the newspapers
desc: Vienna’s coffeehouse culture, on UNESCO’s intangible heritage list since 2011, means marble tables, waiters in black tie and no rush to leave. Café Central, in the Palais Ferstel on Herrengasse, is among the best known.

title: A Habsburg palace holds Dürer’s hare and modern masters
desc: The Albertina palace was remodelled for Duke Albert of Saxe-Teschen and holds one of the great collections of drawings and prints, including Dürer’s Young Hare. It sits on a bastion at the back of the Hofburg, beside the Opera.

title: An old court grocer serves tiny sandwiches at its bar
desc: Zum Schwarzen Kameel has traded on Bognergasse since 1618 and once supplied the imperial court. Its Art Nouveau bar is known for small open sandwiches, in the old town near the Graben.

title: Mozart’s last weeks and the supper some blame for his death
desc: Mozart died in December 1791, aged 35, while working on his Requiem, and the cause has been argued over ever since. His last home stood at Rauhensteingasse 8 in the Innere Stadt, a few steps from St Stephen’s Cathedral.

title: A breaded veal cutlet and the legends about where it came from
desc: Austrian law reserves the name Wiener Schnitzel for veal, pounded thin, breaded and fried. A popular story credits Field Marshal Radetzky with bringing it from Milan. Figlmüller on the Wollzeile, near St Stephen’s, is one of its best-known homes.

title: Bringing an iconic New York sandwich to Berlin
desc: Housed in a Jewish girl’s school built in 1927, Mogg & Melzer is a deli serving tasty-looking pastrami and rye sandwiches. In this video from the New York Times, the owners and chefs describe their challenges procuring uniquely American ingredients.

title: West Berlin’s techno scene in the 1980s
desc: Westbam was a pioneering DJ in West Berlin’s burgeoning techno music scene in the 1980s. In this video from Vice, he visits his old stomping grounds like the Metropol (now Neues Schauspielhaus) to reflect on techno’s joy and positivity in uncertain times.

title: Concealing the Reichstag to see it anew
desc: Artists Christo and Jean-Claude are famous for their ambitious temporary transformations that help people see familiar places in a new way. This video from Tate shows how they wrapped the massive Reichstag in 1995 to acclaim from critics and the public.

title: The fight to save a longstanding punk bar
place: Site of Syndikat punk bar, Weisestraße
desc: In 2018, the beloved punk bar Syndikat received an eviction notice after 30 years in the Neukölln neighborhood. This video from Vice follows their defiant battle against the secretive shell company that owns the building. Their determination is admirable.

title: Where books are burned
desc: In the center of Bebelplatz is an understated yet haunting memorial to the burning of “subversive” or “un-German” books in the square in May 1933. This video from the Holocaust Memorial Museum in the US describes how it foreshadowed the horrors to come.

title: At work with a modern-day hatmaker
desc: Moritz Wolfgruber makes modern one-of-a-kind hats at Captn-Crop, his shop in Berlin. In this video from Culture Trip, he forages for unusual fabrics at a flea market, then transforms his haul into a new hat. His calm and casual creativity is inspiring.

title: Russians atop the Reichstag
desc: Symbolizing their victory over Germany in World War II, the Soviet Union placed its flag atop the Reichstag — a moment captured in an iconic photo. This video from Vox explains how the Russians carefully doctored the image to control what it communicated.

title: Claudia Skoda: An icon of fashion subculture in Berlin
desc: Claudia Skoda is a pioneering fashion designer with a shop in the Mitte neighborhood in Berlin. In this video from Vice, she tells the story of Berlin’s underground fashion scene in the 1980s, centered around her commune in Kreuzberg called Fabrikneu.

title: Scenes from a destroyed Berlin
desc: This understandably smug 1945 newsreel from British Pathé shows the surreal amount of debris and destruction in Berlin only a month after Germany’s defeat. Amazingly, the German people in the film seem calm and unfazed.

title: Inside the former Stasi prison in East Berlin
desc: In this video from NBC News, Tom Brokaw interviews a man who was imprisoned by the East German secret police for attempting to escape the country via Czechoslovakia. The prison will remain as-is to teach future generations about dictatorial governments.

title: The Olympics that put Hitler in the global spotlight
desc: Built for the 1936 Olympics in Berlin, the massive oval Olympiastadion still exists today. This video from the Holocaust Memorial Museum in the US describes how the “Nazi Olympics” is better known for controversy, propaganda, repression than for sports.

title: The downfall of East German leader Erich Honecker
place: Site of the Palace of the Republic (now Humboldt Forum)
desc: In October 1989, increasing unrest led the GDR politburo to oust their longtime leader Erich Honecker during a parliamentary session at East Berlin’s Palace of the Republic, demolished in 2006. This episode of Witness History explains Honecker’s demise.

title: The Bauhaus: A movement on the move
desc: Its unadorned typefaces, judicious color, and abstract forms may lead people to see the Bauhaus as merely an aesthetic style, but its roots are ideological and political. This video from Quartz is a handy primer for a visit to the Bauhaus Archiv museum.

title: The fight to preserve a piece of Berlin’s history
desc: The East Side Gallery is the longest remaining stretch of the Berlin Wall. This 2013 report from PBS NewsHour describes the controversy and debate that erupted as the city removed a few chunks of the gallery to make way for a new apartment building.

title: The kiss that symbolized Soviet influence
place: Fraternal Kiss mural, East Side Gallery
desc: Few paintings on the Berlin Wall are more iconic than “My God, Help Me to Survive This Deadly Love” by Dmitri Vrubel, which features East German leader Honecker kissing Soviet premier Brezhnev. This video from The Story Behind explains its significance.

title: Germania: An unrealized fascist utopia
desc: This engaging episode of Nice Try describes Hitler’s dream to raze and rebuild much of Berlin. Most planned buildings in his imagined “Germania” were never built, like the gigantic Volkshalle dome. A few others—notably Templehof Airport—still exist today.

title: Architecture with a nod toward Moscow
desc: The blocky-yet-palatial Russian Embassy rose along Unter den Linden street just after the Allies partitioned Berlin. This video from Panorama-b Sightseeing describes how its form was a harbinger of Soviet-influenced architecture to come in East Germany.

title: Seeking fulfillment at The School of Life
desc: The School of Life is “built to help us find calm, self-understanding, resilience, and connection.” In this fun animated video, the London-based company tells their new neighbors about their unique shop and classroom, opened in Prenzlauer Berg in 2017.

title: Under den Linden: A street in perpetual flux
desc: Under den Linden’s continual reinvention is a microcosm of changes in Berlin more broadly. This quick video from Panorama-b travels through time to see the street’s residential origins, commercial heydey, wartime destruction, and postwar resurrection.

title: How to curate a museum about East Germany
desc: The DDR Museum aims to explain everyday life in the former East Germany. In this episode of the Radio GDR podcast, the museum’s director explains his challenge: candidly describe East German experiences in a way that rings true for people who lived there.

title: A taste of Scandinavia at Okay Café
desc: Marie-Louise Crona is the charming owner of Okay Café, a cafe in Neukölln inspired by “fika” coffee-and-cake traditions in her native Stockholm. In this Berlin Belly podcast episode, she reflects on the joys and struggles of running a café in Berlin.

title: A repeatedly reinvented war memorial
desc: Neue Wache is a neoclassical building on Unter den Linden street that houses a moving war memorial. This video from Panorama-b describes the building’s metamorphosis from an unusually elegant guardhouse to a string of three tributes to the war dead.

title: The East German uprising of 1953
desc: In June 1953, thousands of East German factory workers protested new laws to increase productivity without raising wages. This episode of Witness History describes the scene at Potsdamer Platz, where Soviet tanks rolled in to quell the protests violently.

title: Words from the east, words from the west
desc: The DDR Museum takes a vivid look at the many curiosities of life in East Germany. This episode of the Allusionist shares anecdotes from Berliners about one — the lingering linguistic quirks between East and West Germans caused by 30 years of separation.

title: In the studio with Olafur Eliasson
desc: Olafur Eliasson is known for colossal art installations that are highly imaginative, deceivingly simple, and technically innovative. This video peeks inside his Berlin studio, where his team aims to transform feelings into something tangible and concrete.

title: A small mistake with a big impact on the world
desc: At 11:30 pm on November 9, 1989, Bornholmer Straße became the first border crossing to open between East and West Berlin. This clear and concise video from Vox explains the press conference slip-up that led 20,000 people to amass at the gate that night.

title: The Berlin Conference and the scramble for Africa
desc: In 1884, at his now-destroyed palace at 77 Wilhelmstrasse, Otto von Bismarck convened Europe’s leaders to carve up Africa. This expert panel explains how European powers hid their murderous imperialist ambition under a veil of humanitarian do-goodery.

title: Foreign flavors in Neukölln
desc: In this short episode of The Menu, Jad Salfiti provides tasty-sounding food suggestions in the Neukölln neighborhood. He mentions shisha bar Café Fairuz, Syrian fried chicken at Aldimashqi, msabaha at Yasmin Alsham, and upscale desserts at CODA.

title: New housing for people living in a divided Berlin
desc: In report from Monocle, Hester Underhill describes plattenbautens, blocky postwar apartment towers built in East and West Berlin after the destruction of World War II. A small museum at Hellersdorfer Straße 179 faithfully recreates a 1980s plattenbauten.

title: Berlin city tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Walking from the Reichstag to Alexanderplatz, this audio tour visits an astounding amount of sites where pivotal 20th-century events took place. Rick’s engaging and informative commentary is excellent, despite a few corny moments. Allow at least 3 hours.

title: The “poison cabinet” for controversial literature
desc: The site of the Kongresshalle was once Magnus Hirschfeld’s Institute for Sexual Science, the first place where Nazis burned subversive books. This episode explains how Germans have dealt with sexual, political, or otherwise verboten literature over time.

title: The city airport with surprising longevity
desc: Brandenburg Airport’s opening was delayed by a decade due to mismanagement and corruption, leaving Berlin’s two smaller airports to shoulder the burden. This report from Monocle lovingly eulogizes Berlin’s small Tegel airport before its closure in 2020.

title: The abandoned spy base overlooking Berlin
desc: Teufelsberg is a decommissioned spy outpost built by the United States to eavesdrop on the Soviet Union during the Cold War. In this report for Monocle, Kimberly Bradley explains the layers of history found underneath the base and wonders about its future.

title: Berlin bodies in motion
desc: KDV Dance Ensemble is a Berlin-based dance group led by talented choreographer Kianí del Valle. If this mesmerizing 2016 practice video published by Nowness is any indication, the group’s premiere at Funkhaus in early 2020 must have been spectacular.

title: Provoking a German nation at Bild
desc: Bild is a feisty and influential tabloid newspaper based in Berlin that has infuriated Germany’s left-wing for decades. This story from The Guardian explores the paper’s history and motivation, providing a contemplative look at modern politics in Germany.

title: Reckoning with a checkered family history
desc: As Kaiser Wilhelm II’s heir, Georg Friedrich claims to be the rightful owner of Cecelienhof Palace, now a museum about World War II’s Potsdam Conference. This episode of Noble Blood explains how his brazen legal claim inadvertently opened pandora’s box.

title: The airport that opened nine years late
desc: Inspired by the disastrous opening of Berlin’s Brandenberg Airport, Jöran Mandik started a podcast series called How to Fuck Up an Airport. In this episode of The Europeans, he gives an overview of the airport’s many woes. (Segment starts around ~15:00)

title: Preserving the paper trail of the secret police
desc: Doug Selvage is a historian at the Stasi Archives in Berlin, which preserves records from the brutal East German intelligence agency. In this episode of Spycast, he reflects on the Stasi’s legacy and explains the archives. Tours can be booked in advance.

title: Suspicion and spying between the Allies in postwar Berlin
desc: Bernd von Kostka is the director of the Allied Museum in Berlin, which documents how the mutual victors of World War II quickly fell into a 45-year Cold War. In this episode of Spycast, he shares stories of espionage in divided and occupied postwar Berlin.

title: A secret tunnel to help neighbors flee East Berlin
desc: Memorials near Bernauer Strasse 97 commemorate a series of dramatic attempts by free West Berliners to liberate East Berliners through a makeshift tunnel in 1964. This riveting episode of 99% Invisible describes the daring escape that freed 57 people.

title: Ich bin von Kopf bis Fuß auf Liebe eingestellt
creator: Marlene Dietrich
desc: Known in English as “Falling in Love Again,” this smoky number made Marlene Dietrich a star in the 1930 film The Blue Angel. Born in Berlin’s Schöneberg district, she became the eternal face of the city’s daring cabaret glamour.

title: Die Moritat von Mackie Messer
creator: Kurt Weill & Bertolt Brecht
desc: Better known as “Mack the Knife,” this jaunty tune about a smooth-talking murderer comes from The Threepenny Opera, Brecht and Weill’s biting 1928 musical. It premiered at the Theater am Schiffbauerdamm — pure satirical, Weimar-era Berlin.

title: Yü-Gung (Fütter mein Ego)
creator: Einstürzende Neubauten
desc: Einstürzende Neubauten — “collapsing new buildings” — made music by banging scrap metal and power tools. This 1985 track’s subtitle means “feed my ego”: raw West Berlin industrial noise from the scene around Kreuzberg’s club SO36.

title: Mein kleiner grüner Kaktus
creator: Comedian Harmonists
desc: The title means “my little green cactus.” The Comedian Harmonists, a dazzling Berlin close-harmony group, made playful hits like this in the early ’30s — until the Nazis banned them for having Jewish members. Pure Weimar charm and wit.

title: Heroes
creator: David Bowie
desc: David Bowie wrote his most beloved anthem in 1977 at Hansa Studios, a stone’s throw from the Berlin Wall. It imagines two lovers kissing in the Wall’s shadow — defiant hope in a divided city. He lived nearby in Schöneberg in his “Berlin years.”

title: Looking for Freedom
creator: David Hasselhoff
desc: On New Year’s Eve 1989, weeks after the Wall fell, American TV star David Hasselhoff sang this cheesy pop anthem atop the Brandenburg Gate to a euphoric crowd. Kitschy as it is, it became an unlikely soundtrack to Berlin’s reunion.

title: 99 Luftballons
creator: Nena
desc: The title means “99 balloons.” In Nena’s 1983 hit, toy balloons drifting over the Wall are mistaken for an enemy attack and trigger a war — a catchy Cold War nightmare from the city where the world’s two armies stared each other down.

title: Du Hast
creator: Rammstein
desc: The title means “you have,” but sounds just like “you hate” — a deliberate pun. Rammstein, formed in Berlin in 1994, pile crushing guitars onto rolling, theatrical German. This 1997 track made them Germany’s biggest metal export.

title: For an Angel
creator: Paul van Dyk
desc: After the Wall fell, Berlin became the world’s techno capital, its giant Love Parade flooding the streets with ravers. Paul van Dyk, an East-German-raised DJ, made this soaring 1998 trance anthem — a defining sound of those euphoric years.

title: Mein Block
creator: Sido
desc: The title means “my block.” Sido grew up in the Märkisches Viertel, a vast concrete housing estate in northern Berlin. This raucous 2004 song turns his tower-block world into a cartoonish anthem — a landmark for Berlin rap.

title: Schwarz zu Blau
creator: Peter Fox
desc: The title means “black to blue,” the sky as night fades to dawn. Peter Fox stumbles home through a gritty, beloved Berlin, past the döner shops and chaos of Kottbusser Tor in Kreuzberg. A brutally honest love letter to the city.

title: Berlin lebt
creator: Capital Bra
desc: The title means “Berlin lives.” Capital Bra — who came as a child from the former Soviet Union — became the most chart-topping rapper in German history. This 2018 hit, in melodic street slang, is a swaggering shout-out to his adopted city.

title: Sky and Sand
creator: Paul Kalkbrenner
desc: Berlin techno producer Paul Kalkbrenner wrote this hypnotic, slow-building track for Berlin Calling, a 2008 film about a DJ coming undone in the city’s all-night clubs. It became an anthem of the scene that revolves around temples like Berghain.

title: Discovering a forgotten section of the Berlin Wall
desc: In 1999, historian Christian Bormann made an unexpected discovery: a long-forgotten stretch of the Berlin Wall. In this video from Vice News, the “German Indiana Jones” explains his detective work and shares his hopes for the city to preserve the wall.

title: Light, air and gardens for ordinary tenants in the 1920s
desc: Six Berlin housing estates built between 1910 and 1933 were listed as World Heritage in 2008. The best known is Bruno Taut’s Horseshoe Estate in Britz, Neukölln, its long curved block wrapped around a pond.

title: American and Soviet tanks face off at a Friedrichstraße crossing
desc: Checkpoint Charlie was the Friedrichstraße crossing for foreigners and Allied personnel from 1961 to 1990, and in October 1961 US and Soviet tanks stood muzzle to muzzle there. A replica guard hut now stands in the street.

title: Bunkers built for the Nazis lie under a busy station
desc: Berlin is honeycombed with wartime air-raid shelters. Volunteers from the Berliner Unterwelten association lead tours into the bunkers beneath Gesundbrunnen station, built in the early 1940s.

title: Cargo planes land every few minutes to feed a blockaded city
desc: When the Soviets cut road and rail links in June 1948, the Western Allies flew in food and coal for almost a year. Tempelhof was the main landing ground; the Airlift Memorial, with three prongs for the three air corridors, stands outside it.

title: Waiting fifty years to be proven right
desc: Peter Higgs worked at this university for decades on a theory of how particles get mass, then waited half a century for proof. When CERN finally confirmed it in 2012, colleagues had to reassure a stunned Higgs that the discovery was real.

title: What an 18th-century economist can still teach us
desc: Smith spent his final years revising The Wealth of Nations in this house, turning it into a meeting place for the finest minds of the Scottish Enlightenment. Freakonomics visits the restored building to ask what he can still teach a modern economy.

title: Reliving referendum night from inside the room
desc: Yes campaigners gathered outside this building as results confirmed Scotland had voted 55% to stay in the UK. Osborne, Chancellor at the time, and former Shadow Chancellor Balls reconstruct referendum night with people who were there.

title: From a modest pageant to a global spectacle
desc: What began in 1950 as a modest military pageant on this esplanade has grown into an annual show drawing bands and dancers from as far as Japan and Trinidad. Performers describe marching and piping in formation against a floodlit castle backdrop.

title: A drained loch becomes a Victorian pleasure ground
desc: Once a semi-rural mill pond, this stretch was drained and tunnelled under by Victorian engineers, who built a vast outdoor leisure ground here complete with a giant serpent-shaped rowing boat, before it settled into the quiet park it is today.

title: A Stuart prince holds court at Holyrood as the Jacobites rise
desc: In September 1745 Charles Edward Stuart took Edinburgh and held court for six weeks at the Palace of Holyroodhouse, the royal palace at the foot of the Royal Mile. The episode follows the Jacobite cause to its defeat at Culloden in 1746.

title: A planned Georgian grid gives the cramped city room to breathe
desc: From the 1760s Edinburgh’s better-off families left the crowded Old Town for James Craig’s New Town of straight streets and squares. Charlotte Square, at its western end, holds the Georgian House, a townhouse kept as it was around 1800.

title: A New Town boy grows up to unify electricity, magnetism and light
desc: James Clerk Maxwell was born in 1831 at 14 India Street, a Georgian townhouse in the New Town, and schooled at the Edinburgh Academy. His equations tied light to electromagnetism and laid groundwork for radio, relativity and much of modern physics.

title: Seventeen tiny coffins turn up hidden in the rocks of Arthur’s Seat
desc: In 1836 boys hunting rabbits found seventeen small carved coffins, each holding a dressed wooden figure, in a rock niche on the hill. Eight survive at the National Museum of Scotland on Chambers Street; nobody knows for certain why they were made.

title: Newsreel cameras catch the festival in its twelfth summer
desc: A British Pathé newsreel from the 1959 Edinburgh International Festival, then only twelve years old. The Usher Hall, the domed concert hall on Lothian Road, has been the festival’s main orchestral venue since the first season in 1947.

title: A Catalan architect’s partner revisits the parliament he never saw finished
desc: Enric Miralles died in 2000, four years before the Scottish Parliament building opened at Holyrood. His partner and co-architect Benedetta Tagliabue walks through an exhibition of the drawings, models and leaf-and-boat motifs behind the design.

title: Masons and conservators keep the castle on the rock standing
desc: Edinburgh Castle sits on a plug of volcanic basalt, and its walls, batteries and chapels need constant care. Historic Environment Scotland, which runs the fortress, shows the stonemasons and conservators who keep the rock-top site sound.

title: Rich and poor share a staircase in the tenements of Auld Reekie
desc: Before the New Town, nearly everyone lived along the Royal Mile, the spine of the Old Town, in tall tenements where lawyers, merchants and labourers occupied different floors of the same building and waste went out of the windows.

title: Scotland’s crown jewels sit in a fortress built on an old volcano
desc: A short walk through Edinburgh Castle on its volcanic rock: the Esplanade, the tiny 12th-century St Margaret’s Chapel, the Crown Room holding the Honours of Scotland, and the gun fired at one o’clock most days since 1861.

title: Scotland’s national gallery walks through its Impressionist rooms
desc: The Scottish National Gallery, the temple-fronted building on the Mound, holds a strong group of French paintings by Monet, Degas, Gauguin, Cézanne and Van Gogh, many of them given by Scottish collectors.

title: Eight uninvited theatre companies start the world’s biggest arts festival
desc: In 1947 eight companies turned up unasked at the first Edinburgh International Festival and staged their own shows. The Fringe’s former chief executive explains its open-access rule: no selection panel, anyone with a venue can perform.

title: Two cities, one medieval and one Georgian, face each other across a valley
desc: This UNESCO/NHK film looks at the World Heritage site as a pair: the Old Town’s tall tenements and closes running down the Royal Mile ridge, and the ordered New Town laid out across the drained Nor’ Loch, now Princes Street Gardens.

title: Writers and drinkers share the same Old and New Town pub tables
desc: Edinburgh was the first UNESCO City of Literature, home to Scott, Stevenson and Burns in his day. The clip visits the Writers’ Museum in Lady Stair’s Close and the traditional pubs on Rose Street, the New Town’s narrow back lane.

title: The Queen’s floating palace retires to a dock in Leith
desc: HMY Britannia carried the royal family on nearly a thousand official voyages from 1954 to 1997. Decommissioned that year, she is now moored at Ocean Terminal in Leith, Edinburgh’s port, and open to visitors.

title: Three bridges from three centuries cross the Firth of Forth side by side
desc: The red cantilever Forth Bridge of 1890, the Forth Road Bridge of 1964 and the Queensferry Crossing of 2017 stand together at South Queensferry, on Edinburgh’s western edge. The film compares how each generation of engineers spanned the firth.

title: A queen’s secretary is murdered in her supper room at Holyrood
desc: The Palace of Holyroodhouse, at the foot of the Royal Mile, grew beside a 12th-century abbey. In 1566 David Rizzio, Mary, Queen of Scots’ secretary, was stabbed in her rooms in the palace’s northwest tower, which visitors can still enter.

title: A cobbled spine runs downhill from the castle to the palace
desc: The Royal Mile is the chain of streets that links Edinburgh Castle to the Palace of Holyroodhouse, lined with tall tenements, narrow closes and St Giles’ Cathedral. It is the backbone of the medieval Old Town.

title: A forgotten warren of rooms lies sealed inside an 18th-century bridge
desc: South Bridge, finished in 1788, carries a street over the Cowgate valley on nineteen arches. The chambers inside its arches housed cobblers, taverns and later the very poor before being filled in; some were rediscovered in the 1980s off Niddry Street.

title: The world’s first cloned mammal ends up in a museum gallery
desc: Dolly was cloned from an adult cell at the Roslin Institute, just south of the city, and born in 1996. After her death in 2003 she was preserved and put on display at the National Museum of Scotland on Chambers Street, where she still stands.

title: A gallery in an old fruit market breaks into the warehouse next door
desc: The Fruitmarket, a free contemporary art gallery founded in 1974 in a former fruit and vegetable market, expanded into the neighbouring warehouse in 2021. It sits on Market Street, right beside Waverley Station.

title: An American choir fills a crowned Scottish kirk with song
desc: St Giles’ is Edinburgh’s High Kirk, known for its open stone crown spire and as the pulpit of the reformer John Knox. It stands halfway along the Royal Mile in the Old Town.

title: Cavalry charges a crowd demanding the vote
desc: On this site in 1819, cavalry charged 60,000 peaceful demonstrators calling for parliamentary reform, killing at least 15 people. Outrage over the massacre helped found The Manchester Guardian and fed directly into the Great Reform Act of 1832.

title: A human alarm clock wakes 1860s Manchester
desc: Before alarm clocks were affordable, cotton mill workers in this industrial suburb hired knocker-uppers, who tapped bedroom windows with long poles to rouse them for 2am shifts, a profession that survived in parts of Britain into the 1970s.

title: A Nobel Prize starts with pencil lead and sticky tape
desc: Andre Geim and Kostya Novoselov peeled layers off ordinary graphite with tape until they isolated graphene, a material one atom thick, at the University of Manchester in 2004. This museum holds the actual tape dispenser used in the experiment.

title: The largest bomb on British soil since WWII, still unsolved
desc: An IRA truck bomb devastated this building and nearby streets in June 1996, injuring over 200 people though killing none. Decades later, journalists investigate why no one was ever charged, tracing leads across the Irish border.

title: Survivors find hope after a concert bombing
desc: Four years after a bomb killed 22 people leaving a concert here in 2017, survivors and bereaved families return to the arena to read letters to their past selves and describe how they have slowly rebuilt their lives.

title: A room-sized machine runs the world’s first stored program
place: Coupland Street (site of the Manchester Baby computer)
desc: In June 1948 a machine filling a room in the University of Manchester’s engineering building on Coupland Street ran a program held in its own memory. Built by Freddie Williams, Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill, the ‘Baby’ is the ancestor of modern computers.

title: A New Zealand physicist finds the nucleus and splits the atom
desc: Ernest Rutherford ran the physics laboratory at the University of Manchester from 1907 to 1919. In the Coupland Street building now named after him, his team found the atomic nucleus in 1911, and in 1917 he split the atom.

title: A mother and her daughters launch the suffragettes from their parlour
desc: The Women’s Social and Political Union first met in October 1903 in the Pankhurst family house at 62 Nelson Street, now the Pankhurst Centre museum. The episode follows Emmeline and her daughters Christabel, Sylvia and Adela, and the rifts that split them.

title: A French maverick turns up his collar and ends a 26-year wait
desc: Manchester United paid Leeds about £1.2 million for Eric Cantona in November 1992. Gary Lineker, Alan Shearer and Micah Richards recall how he changed the mood at Old Trafford, the club’s stadium, and the ban after his kung-fu kick at Crystal Palace.

title: A stoppage-time goal snatches the league title from the neighbours
desc: On the last day of the 2011–12 season Sergio Agüero scored against QPR at 93:20, giving Manchester City their first top-flight title in 44 years, on goal difference over United. The hosts revisit his decade at the Etihad Stadium, City’s home ground.

title: A sceptical surgeon watches a mesmerist and coins ‘hypnotism’
desc: In November 1841 the Swiss mesmerist Charles Lafontaine performed at the Manchester Athenaeum, a club on Princess Street. James Braid, a surgeon practising in the city, went to debunk him, began his own experiments and gave the practice a new name.

title: A bridge swings aside so ocean ships can sail inland
desc: The Manchester Ship Canal opened in 1894 to make the city a seaport. At Barton a road bridge and the Bridgewater Canal’s aqueduct both pivot on islands in the water, the aqueduct still full of water as it turns. This 1930s archive film shows it at work.

title: A cotton manager bankrolls a revolution from his office
desc: Engels spent some twenty years running his family’s Manchester cotton business, sending money to Marx in London. In 1845 the two read side by side in an alcove of the reading room at Chetham’s Library, where the desk is still in place.

title: A folk fan shouts “Judas” as Dylan plugs in
desc: On 17 May 1966 Bob Dylan played the Free Trade Hall on Peter Street, acoustic first, then loud with the band. After the heckle he called the shouter a liar and launched into “Like a Rolling Stone”. The bootleg was long mislabelled as the Albert Hall.

title: Walking the brick mills that earned the name Cottonopolis
desc: Ancoats was the world’s first industrial suburb, its canal-side spinning mills built from the 1790s and worked by thousands. Local explorer Martin Zero goes inside the surviving buildings, many derelict for decades before becoming flats.

title: A Gothic town hall built to show off a cotton fortune
desc: Alfred Waterhouse’s town hall on Albert Square opened in 1877, a Gothic Revival statement from a city grown rich on cotton. The film reads its clock tower, vaulted corridors and the Great Hall, lined with Ford Madox Brown’s murals of local history.

title: Slum clearance moves a city into homes nobody asked for
desc: Don Haworth’s 1974 BBC film follows Manchester Corporation’s huge rehousing drive, run from the Town Hall, through a council tenant and a council official. It shows terraced streets cleared and residents moved to flats they never chose.

title: A trapdoor in a canal bed drains into a buried river
place: Rochdale Canal lock 89, Whitworth Street West
desc: Near lock 89 on the Rochdale Canal, close to Whitworth Street West, an arrow carved in the quayside marks a hatch in the canal bed. It drains into the River Tib, culverted almost 20 feet below the streets. Martin Zero goes looking for where it leads.

title: A young German mill heir writes up the slums he walks past
place: Site of Little Ireland, River Medlock
desc: Friedrich Engels came to Manchester in 1842 to work in his family’s cotton firm and spent his spare hours in districts like Little Ireland, a flood-prone pocket by the River Medlock near today’s Oxford Road station. His 1845 book described what he saw.

title: London’s 130-year-old coffee shop
place: Algerian Coffee Stores, Old Compton Street
desc: Marisa Crocetta is a third-generation owner of Algerian Coffee Stores, founded in 1887. In this video from Culture Trip, she thoughtfully reflects on how her family’s shop has been a mainstay in the changing Soho neighborhood since its founding in 1887.

title: A boys’ club doorway becomes an indie-music pilgrimage site
desc: Salford Lads Club opened in 1904 to keep working-class boys off the streets. The Smiths posed outside its red-brick entrance in 1986, and fans still come. Historic England goes inside to the gym, the billiard room and the club’s long social history.

title: Prisoners take the roof and hold a jail for 25 days
desc: In April 1990 inmates at Strangeways, the Victorian prison north of the city centre, rioted over overcrowding and squalid conditions. ITN’s news footage shows the rooftop protest that became the longest prison riot in British history.

title: A round library modelled on the Pantheon opens to the public
desc: Manchester Central Library, the domed rotunda on St Peter’s Square, opened in 1934 as one of the largest public lending libraries in Britain. This tour goes through the restored reading room and the archives added in its 2014 refurbishment.

title: Perfume alchemy at Floris London
desc: Since 1730, Floris has been crafting aromatic concoctions for high-brow Londoners wishing to add a bit of fragrance to their lives. In this quick video from The Economist, the 9th-generation owner Edward Bodenham gives us a look around the historic shop.

title: Kew Gardens and the Great Pagoda
desc: This joyful and earnest video from Half Asleep Chris offers a fun whirlwind tour of London’s Kew Gardens. Chris starts at the Great Pagoda, a 250-year-old structure embossed on the UK’s rarest coin.

title: Searching for the home of Sherlock Holmes
desc: In this video, vlogger and coin collector Half-Asleep Chris takes us on an entertaining and delightfully nerdy search for 221b Baker Street, the fictional home of the fictional detective Sherlock Holmes.

title: Number 10 Downing Street’s nearby lookalike
desc: The famous door to the Prime Minister’s residence at 10 Downing Street is barely visible to onlookers due to a massive iron fence and heavy security. This video from Half-Asleep Chris takes a fun look at the door’s nearby doppelganger at 10 Adam Street.

title: Sunday roast at London’s only Michelin-Star pub
desc: Even if you don’t plan to eat a meal at the Harwood Arms, this video from Culture Trip offers a mouth-watering look at how the traditional Sunday Roast fits into the broader culture and cuisine of London.

title: Venturing into a Victorian-era underwater ballroom
desc: Beneath a lake in Surrey is a submerged ballroom built by a devious business tycoon. The room is the last remnant of an estate that mostly burned down. Atlas Obscura co-founder Dylan Thuras tells its story—and warns not to visit—in this video.

title: Creating a restaurant without waste
desc: In 2011, Chef Douglas McMaster set out to create a zero-waste restaurant. This cinematic short film from The Atlantic documents the failures and frustrations of transforming an environmentally sustainable restaurant into an economically viable one.

title: Painting one of the world’s most massive murals
desc: In the rapidly-changing Hackney Wick neighborhood, street artist Ben Eine undertook a project to slather an enormous parking lot with a typographic mural. This video from Canvas documents the logistical complexity of covering such a vast canvas.

title: Using modern technology to understand ancient cultures
desc: This beautifully filmed video from Google Arts & Culture sheds light on how the search giant has partnered with the British Museum to preserve and digitize Ancient Mayan artifacts and make them accessible to more people around the world.

title: Transforming painting studios into public galleries
desc: In 2016, the Newport Street Gallery was named Building of the Year by the Royal Institute of British Architects. This video from Architects’ Journal highlights the subtle ways in which the architect blended historic buildings with new ones.

title: Trading at the Royal Exchange in 16th century London
desc: Founded in 1566, the Royal Exchange was once a gathering point for wealthy merchants and nascent corporations. In this video, tour guide Julian McDonnell shares a bit of history about trading guilds and the streets where they worked.

title: Inside the London headquarters of Bloomberg
desc: In 2018, the London headquarters of Bloomberg was awarded Building of the Year by the Royal Institute of British Architects. In this video from Architects’ Journal, the architects describe the compelling design and engineering behind the building.

title: Expanding and reimagining the Tate Modern
desc: Opened in 2016, the expansion of the Tate Modern was designed by Swiss architects Herzog & De Meuron. In this video from Architects’ Journal, the designers describe their goal to create a street-like space stretching vertically through the building.

title: One final drink for convicted criminals
desc: In the 1600s, condemned criminals were marched along Oxford Street to be hanged at Tyburn Gallows. In this video, tour guide Julian McDonnell tells the story of how a nearby church offered the prisoners a liquid respite from their horrible fate.

title: The City of London: a city within a city
desc: Deep inside the city of London, a statue of a dragon proudly guards the entrance to... the City of London. Confused? This delightful animated video from CGP Grey will help you sort it all out, providing a fast-paced history lesson along the way.

title: Cleopatra’s Needle: A bit of ancient Egypt in London
desc: On the bank of the Thames in central London is an Egyptian obelisk dating from 1475 BC. In this video from Joolz Guides, tour guide Julian McDonnell shares the story of how it got to London and spotlights some easily overlooked details nearby.

title: Frangosyriani
creator: Markos Vamvakaris
desc: The title means ‘the Catholic girl from Syros.’ The patriarch of rebetiko wrote this tender love song after fleeing his island for Piraeus as a boy, building the port’s hashish-den sound around Karaiskaki Square.

title: Ta Paidia tou Peiraia
creator: Melina Mercouri
desc: The title means ‘The Children of Piraeus’; abroad it’s ‘Never on Sunday.’ Mercouri’s Oscar-winning ode to dockside joy still echoes over Mikrolimano, the little fishing harbor of yachts and tavernas below Piraeus.

title: Synnefiasmeni Kyriaki
creator: Vassilis Tsitsanis
desc: The title means ‘Cloudy Sunday.’ Tsitsanis wrote this grief-soaked anthem in occupied Greece and it became the nation’s unofficial hymn. Kolonos held ‘Bizelia,’ the poor-quarter tavern that was his first Athens stage.

title: Dimitroula Mou
creator: Haris Alexiou
desc: The title means ‘My little Dimitra,’ a flirty rebetiko standard. Alexiou revived it as a newcomer working the Plaka tavernas below the Acropolis, where the 1970s rebetiko revival filled the old town’s cellars.

title: Pote tha Kanei Xasteria
creator: Nikos Xylouris
desc: The title means ‘When will the skies clear again?’ — a centuries-old Cretan freedom song. Xylouris sang it inside the Polytechnic during the 1973 student revolt against the junta; it’s forever tied to that gate.

title: As Kratisoun oi Horoi
creator: Dionysis Savvopoulos
desc: The title means ‘Let the dances last’ — half-blessing, half-farewell to youth. Savvopoulos forged his live legend at Kyttaro, the boîte where his theatrical rock nights became an Athenian ritual.

title: Ena to Chelidoni
creator: Grigoris Bithikotsis
desc: The title means ‘One swallow alone.’ Theodorakis set Elytis’s poem and Bithikotsis sang it into a freedom hymn. Fitting for the Pnyx, the hill where ancient Athenians invented the public assembly.

title: O Mpampis o Flou
creator: Pavlos Sidiropoulos
desc: The title means ‘Blurry Babis,’ a drifting, druggy outsider. Sidiropoulos was the doomed voice of Greek rock, and of Exarcheia — the square and its bars where the country’s counterculture drank, argued, and played.

title: Afti Ti Zoi (feat. Guru)
creator: Goin’ Through
desc: The title means ‘This life.’ Athens hip-hop pioneers Goin’ Through landed a crossover hit with Gang Starr’s Guru rapping over it. Their circuit ran through the central city around Syntagma and its clubs.

title: Monaxia Mou Ola
creator: Pyx Lax
desc: The title runs roughly ‘my loneliness, my everything.’ Pyx Lax turned working-class heartache into stadium singalongs; their roots lie past the Iera Odos, the ancient road running west toward the blue-collar suburbs.

title: I Zoi Mas Einai Ligi
creator: Imam Baildi
desc: The title means ‘Our life is short.’ The Falireas brothers splice their father’s 1950s rebetiko 78s onto hip-hop and brass — pure Metaxourgeio, the frayed central district where old Athens leaks into the new.

title: Mavri Ellada
creator: Negros tou Moria
desc: The title means ‘Black Greece.’ Born in Ambelokipi to Ghanaian parents and raised in Kypseli, the rapper maps an Athens of migrants and margins the postcards skip — claiming Greekness on his own terms.

title: Running Out of You
creator: Keep Shelly in Athens
desc: This dream-pop duo’s name puns on Kypseli, the dense central neighborhood of 1930s apartment blocks. Their hazy, homesick sound is the most literally Athenian thing here — the city is folded into the band’s very name.

title: Mantissa
creator: Marina Satti
desc: The title means ‘Fortune-teller.’ Satti’s flash-mob video dances down Odos Athinas, the gritty market street linking Omonoia to the Acropolis; the song became an anthem of hope for a crisis-worn generation.

title: An alliance that grew into an empire
desc: What began as a Greek defense pact against Persia had its treasury moved here in 454 BC and became something closer to an Athenian empire, funded by allies who had little say in how their tribute was spent.

title: Fishing a 2,000-year-old computer from the sea
desc: Sponge divers hauled a corroded bronze lump from a shipwreck in 1901; this museum has held it ever since. It turned out to be a 2,000-year-old mechanical computer that tracked planets, eclipses, and the Olympic calendar with startling precision.

title: Colonels seize Greece in a bloodless coup
desc: On April 21, 1967, army colonels seized power in Greece in a bloodless coup centered here. Resistance fighter Gerasimos Nortaras tells Witness History what followed: capture and brutal torture for refusing to name fellow fighters.

title: Refugees turn exile into rebetiko
desc: Refugees arriving from Smyrna and Constantinople in the 1920s brought café music styles into neighborhoods like this one, where they fused into rebetiko, the bouzouki-driven Greek blues still played live in Athens basements today.

title: Stephen Fry picks his three favorite Athens myths
desc: Recorded from lockdown in the UK, the writer and self-declared Hellenophile shares the myths that mean the most to him, and explains why this quiet, green neighborhood beneath the Acropolis will always hold a piece of his heart.

title: A flâneur retraces his childhood, block by block
desc: The journalist and author of Walking in Athens has made it his mission to walk every neighborhood of the city at least once. Here he retraces the streets of his own childhood in Kypseli, once fashionable and now rapidly changing again.

title: A fashion designer stages her biggest show at sunset
desc: Athens-born designer Mary Katrantzou built her career on the London and Paris runways before staging a show at home, choosing this clifftop temple for what she calls the biggest challenge of her career, drawing on the many faces of her home city.

title: A city appoints someone to protect it from its own summers
desc: In 2021 Athens named Eleni Myrivili Europe’s first chief heat officer, working from City Hall on Kotzia Square. She explains how a dense, concrete city with little shade is trying to plant, cool and warn its way through longer heatwaves.

title: A neighbourhood of bookshops, squats and graffiti goes its own way
desc: Exarchia, the district around Exarchia Square near the Polytechnic, has been home to students, publishers, anarchists and squats since the 1970s. DW reporters look at how it lives with its reputation, tourism and a growing police presence.

title: Island builders tuck a whitewashed village under the Acropolis
desc: Anafiotika is a cluster of whitewashed houses and stepped lanes on the Acropolis’s north slope, built in the 1800s by workers from the island of Anafi. It sits just above Plaka, Athens’ oldest neighbourhood.

title: Gold masks, bronze gods and grave markers fill one great museum
desc: Greece’s largest archaeological collection runs from Mycenaean gold to Roman marble. It fills a neoclassical building on Patission Street, a short walk north of Omonia Square in central Athens.

title: A 1961 newsreel camera takes in a fast-growing capital
desc: British Pathé’s 1961 colour film shows Athens as visitors saw it then, ancient monuments alongside the street life of a fast-growing capital. Syntagma Square, in front of the parliament building, was its busy centre.

title: A Venetian shell hits Ottoman gunpowder stored in the Parthenon
desc: In 1687, during a Venetian siege, the Ottoman garrison kept gunpowder inside the Parthenon, and one mortar round blew out its middle. The broken temple still stands on the Acropolis, the rock above central Athens.

title: A crown jewel nearly slips from Spanish hands
desc: By 1505, Spanish viceroys ruled from this castle over a kingdom so valuable it rivaled Venice and Paris in size. French forces nearly seized the city in a 1528 siege, one crisis in a decades-long tug-of-war for control of southern Italy.

title: Seeing the history of humanity at the Gulbenkian Museum
desc: Travel writer Rick Steves asserts that Lisbon’s Gulbenkian Museum is “one of the most enjoyable museum experiences in all of Europe.” In this video, he gives a fast-paced tour of the museum’s collection, which spans five millennia of human creativity.

title: Lisbon tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Starting at the grandiose Praça do Commércio and ending at cozy Camões Square, this fun and informative walking tour meanders through Lisbon’s Baixa, Bairro Alto, and Chiado neighborhoods. Allow at least 3 hours and bring some cash for a funicular ticket.

title: Fado music: The presence of absence
desc: Fado is a soulful and sorrowful Portuguese music genre. This engaging discussion from the BBC deftly jumps from one facet of fado to another, unfolding a nuanced view of its history, performers, and broader context. For more, visit Lisbon’s Fado Museum.

title: The many voices of Fernando Pessoa
desc: Housed in the building where he lived, Casa Fernando Pessoa is a small museum dedicated to the 20th-century Portuguese poet. In this episode of The Forum, scholars analyze Pessoa’s frequent use of pseudonyms, then reflect on his life, death, and influence.

title: What fueled Calouste Gulbenkian
desc: Lisbon’s fantastic Gulbenkian Museum houses the private art and antiquity collection of a single man — oil tycoon Calouste Gulbenkian. This slightly dry episode of The Forum explains his business acumen and how his philanthropic legacy landed in Portugal.

title: Lisbon in four voices
desc: This episode of the Sunday Times Travel Podcast shares the voices of four Lisbon locals. After stories about magical nightlife, historic trams, and soulful music, the episode ends in Largo do Carmo to hear about the Carnation Revolution in 1974.

title: Rice fields and endless beaches in Comporta
desc: An hour south of Lisbon, Comporta is a town that mixes rustic rural charm with little moments of high-end luxury frippery. This story from Condé Nast name-drops an overwhelming amount of people and places, yet still paints a lucid picture of the area.

title: Rival powers during the Age of Discoveries
desc: Ferdinand Magellan was Portuguese but circumnavigated the globe on behalf of Spain. This inquisitive discussion uses Magellan’s fateful voyage to explain Spain and Portugal’s rivalry during the Age of Discovery. For more, visit Lisbon’s Maritime Museum.

title: Retribution and revenge after a failed assassination
place: Beco do Chão Salgado column, Belém
desc: A strange column in Lisbon’s Belem area is affixed with a plaque that forever forbids the land’s use. This riveting episode of Noble Blood vividly explains how the landowners made a grave mistake in 1758 — they tried to assassinate Portugal’s King José I.

title: A peek into Afro-Portuguese culture in Lisbon
place: Site of the Casa dos Escravos, near Praça do Comércio
desc: In 1486, Portugal formalized its slave trade in a quasi-government entity called the House of Slaves, located near today’s Praça do Comércio. This quick video from Travel Coterie showcases a tour guide focused on Lisbon’s complex African cultural heritage.

title: A building that engages the public
desc: This wordless video from Dezeen showcases the swoopy white curves of the Maat Museum, an architectural marvel that enlivens and enriches the riverside promenade. If you want to see it in person, it’s a lovely stroll along the river from Lisbon’s center.

title: Unique finds at Mercado de Ribeira
desc: Adjacent to the modern and upscale Time Out Market is lively Mercado de Ribeira, filled with produce and fish stalls. In this quick video, the owner of Pastéis de Belém stops by the century-old market to try hearty acorn bread from the Alentejo region.

title: The forgotten Portuguese soldiers of World War I
place: Monument to the Dead of the Great War, Avenida da Liberdade
desc: Along Avenida de Liberdade is a dramatic monument to the Portuguese heroes of World War I. This clear and engaging video from The Great War explains Portugal’s role in fighting Germany and how political turmoil at home overshadowed the troops’ sacrifices.

title: Saudade, saudade
creator: MARO
