desc: “Saudade” is the untranslatable Portuguese ache of longing for what’s gone — the feeling fado is built on. Lisbon-born Maro wrote this hushed, half-English ballad for her late grandfather and carried it to Eurovision 2022, a whisper amid the spectacle.

title: Canção Verdes Anos
creator: Carlos Paredes
desc: The title means “green years,” meaning youth. Carlos Paredes was the master of the Portuguese guitar — the teardrop-shaped, 12-string instrument at the heart of fado. He wrote this gorgeous, wistful piece for a 1963 film set in Lisbon.

title: Mundu Nôbu
creator: Dino d’Santiago
desc: The title means “new world” in Cape Verdean Creole. Dino d’Santiago fuses his island heritage — morna, kizomba — with electronic beats and Portuguese song. He’s the sound of a younger, multicultural Lisbon shaped by its African roots.

title: Amar Pelos Dois
creator: Salvador Sobral
desc: The title means “to love for both of us.” Salvador Sobral’s tender, old-fashioned ballad, written by his sister, won the 2017 Eurovision — Portugal’s first win ever. The prize brought the 2018 contest to Lisbon’s Altice Arena.

title: Sobre(tudo)
creator: Sam the Kid
desc: The title puns on “above all” and “everything.” Sam the Kid — a revered rapper-producer from the Chelas estates of eastern Lisbon — made this 2002 landmark of Portuguese hip-hop: sharp, street-level storytelling about city life.

title: Canção de Engate
creator: António Variações
desc: The title roughly means “pick-up song.” António Variações — a Lisbon barber turned wildly original pop star and gay icon — fused fado with new wave before his early death in 1984. Picture the downtown bars where he held court at night.

title: Desfado
creator: Ana Moura
desc: The invented title plays on “fado,” hinting at undoing one’s fate. Ana Moura loosens fado toward pop and rock — she’s sung with Prince and the Rolling Stones. This 2012 record became one of the best-selling Portuguese albums ever.

title: Sound of Kuduro
creator: Buraka Som Sistema
desc: Buraka Som Sistema took kuduro — the frantic dance music of Angola — and blew it up for the world’s clubs. This 2008 banger is pure Lisbon energy, born in suburbs like Buraca, home to the city’s Angolan and Cape Verdean communities.

title: Ó Gente da Minha Terra
creator: Mariza
desc: The title means “oh, people of my land.” Mariza grew up in Mouraria, the very neighbourhood where fado was born, and became the face of its revival. Her signature song is a trembling tribute to her people and their shared sorrow.

title: Ainda
creator: Madredeus
desc: The title means “still” or “yet.” Madredeus wrap fado’s sadness in something dreamier, almost hymn-like. Their music is the soul of Wim Wenders’ 1994 film Lisbon Story, drifting through the lanes of Alfama, where the band appears on screen.

title: Canção do Mar
creator: Dulce Pontes
desc: The title means “song of the sea.” Dulce Pontes’ soaring 1993 version made this melody famous worldwide, even reaching Hollywood films. It holds Lisbon’s longing for the ocean — best felt watching the Tagus widen toward the Atlantic.

title: A Casa da Mariquinhas
creator: Alfredo Marceneiro
desc: Marceneiro’s most famous fado — a wry, knowing portrait of a notorious house and the lives passing through it — and the purest example of his weathered, old-tavern voice. Hear classic fado explained at the Museu do Fado in Alfama.

title: Sweet treats at a 200-year-old pastry shop
desc: Confeitaria Nacional has been in the same family for five generations. This video from Portugal Daily View showcases their famous king’s cake (bolo rei), and dessert-like breads made from cornmeal (broas castelares) and sweet potato (broas de especie).

title: Lisboa Menina e Moça
creator: Carlos do Carmo
desc: The title pictures Lisbon as both young girl and grown woman. Carlos do Carmo, fado’s great male voice, made this tender love letter to the city, naming old quarters like Alfama. Hear it from an Alfama viewpoint over the tiled rooftops.

title: Grândola, Vila Morena
creator: José Afonso
desc: Named for a town in southern Portugal, this banned folk song was the secret radio signal that launched the 1974 revolution toppling Portugal’s dictatorship. The near-bloodless coup ended at Largo do Carmo, rifles filled with red carnations.

title: Uma Casa Portuguesa
creator: Amália Rodrigues
desc: The title means “a Portuguese house.” Amália Rodrigues, the Queen of Fado who carried the music worldwide, sings of a humble home rich in love, bread, and wine. Portugal honoured her with a tomb in the National Pantheon.

title: A city shaped by an earthquake and the Marquês de Pombal
desc: In the center of Praça do Comércio stands a statue of the Marquês de Pombal, the heavy-handed leader who rebuilt Lisbon after the devastating 1755 earthquake. In this video, travel guide Rick Steves describes how he shaped the city’s urban planning.

title: New life for a street in the Cais do Sodre neighborhood
desc: Rua Nova do Carvalho—known as “Pink Street”—is the nightlife hub in what was once a seedy neighborhood frequented by sailors and prostitutes. This video from Portugal Daily View visits its unique bars: Sol e Pesca, Pensão Amor, O Povo, and Velha Senhora.

title: Street fashion in the heart of Lisbon
desc: This video from The New York Times visits Praça de Camões in Lisbon’s center to interview several casually cool fashionistas about their sartorial choices for the day. It’s fun to hear the voices of people you might otherwise quietly pass on the street.

title: Inside the oldest tile factory in Portugal
desc: Since 1741, Fábrica Sant’Anna has been contributing to the astounding array of tiles that adorn buildings around Lisbon. In this video from Great Big Story, proud tilemaker Francisco Tomás explains the factory’s process and a broader historical context.

title: The Portuguese dish that inspired Japanese tempura
desc: Tempura is typical in Japanese cuisine, but the technique arrived in Japan via stranded Portuguese sailors. In this video from Great Big Story, the chef of Pap’Açorda tells the story of peixinhos da horta, the battered green bean dish that inspired Japan.

title: How to spend 36 Hours in Lisbon
desc: This big-picture overview of Lisbon from the New York Times visits some expected hotspots like Pastéis de Belém and Sintra’s Pena Palace. It also highlights more offbeat places to eat and drink like theatrical Pensão Amor and tricky-to-find Park Bar.

title: An exotic rhinoceros ends up in the city’s pavements
desc: A rhinoceros sent from India arrived in Lisbon in 1515 and caused a sensation. Portugal’s black-and-white stone pavements, calçada portuguesa, are laid by hand; the wave pattern of Rossio square is the city’s best-known example.

title: Crusaders bound for the Holy Land stop to take a Moorish city
place: São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge)
desc: In 1147 English, Flemish and German crusaders sailing east joined Portugal’s first king, Afonso Henriques, in a four-month siege of Muslim-held Lisbon. The hilltop Castelo de São Jorge stands on the citadel they captured.

title: Twelve-string guitars and songs of longing from the old quarters
desc: Fado grew up in Lisbon’s poorer waterfront districts in the 19th century and was added to UNESCO’s intangible heritage list in 2011. The Museu do Fado sits at the foot of Alfama, beside the Chafariz de Dentro square.

title: Soldiers with carnations in their rifles end a dictatorship in a day
desc: On 25 April 1974 young army officers toppled Europe’s longest-running authoritarian regime almost without bloodshed. Crowds filled Largo do Carmo, the square where the prime minister surrendered at the barracks. Reporter Adelino Gomes recalls what he saw.

title: An economics professor runs Portugal for four decades
desc: Tom Holland and Dominic Sandbrook end their series on Portugal with the 20th century: two world wars, the Fátima visions and António Salazar, who ruled from São Bento, the palace that houses parliament and the prime minister’s residence.

title: A playboy double agent gambles under Ian Fleming’s gaze
desc: Serbian double agent Dusko Popov passed through neutral Lisbon while feeding the Germans British-approved lies. He knew Ian Fleming, and a night at the Casino Estoril, the seaside gambling hall west of the city, is often cited as a seed of Casino Royale.

title: Five ships sail from a river to circle the globe
place: Guadalquivir riverfront, Paseo de las Delicias (area)
desc: In August 1519, five ships and over 200 men set out from this river to find a western route to the Spice Islands. Magellan, a Portuguese captain sailing for a Spanish crown that had rejected his offer, would not survive to complete the voyage himself.

title: Monks translate a forbidden Bible, then pay with their lives
desc: A handful of monks near Seville secretly embraced Lutheran ideas and began translating scripture into Spanish. The Inquisition burned nineteen people at the stake here in 1559, then seventeen more in 1567, for the crime of Protestant belief.

title: A Christian king rebuilds his palace in Islamic style
desc: Pedro I so admired Moorish design that he borrowed builders from the Emir of Granada to rebuild this palace after the Reconquista, even while murdering rivals within its walls. Later, Ferdinand and Isabella ran their New World empire from these rooms.

title: A fictional seducer gets a statue of his own
place: Don Juan Tenorio statue, Plaza de los Refinadores
desc: Tirso de Molina invented Don Juan in a 1630 Seville-set play, and the womanizer proved so durable that this square erected a statue calling him the pride of his myth. Cervantes, who set other tales here, reportedly wrote famous work during a jail stint.

title: A wine that sailed around the world gets its English name
desc: English merchants mangled the Moorish name for this town, Sherish, into sherry, now used worldwide for its fortified wine. In the 1500s, sherry became the first wine to complete a voyage around the globe, carried aboard Spanish exploration fleets.

title: Fallen bitter oranges are turned into power for a water plant
place: Patio de los Naranjos, Seville Cathedral
desc: Seville’s streets are lined with tens of thousands of bitter orange trees, and each winter tonnes of fruit hit the pavement. The city water company now ferments the juice into biogas.

title: Six giant timber mushrooms shade a medieval market square
place: Las Setas (Metropol Parasol), Plaza de la Encarnación
desc: The engineers behind Las Setas explain how J. Mayer H.’s lattice of glued timber panels was made to stand over Plaza de la Encarnación, a square where digging for the project had uncovered Roman houses now shown in a museum beneath it.

title: One city block holds a cathedral, a palace and an empire’s paperwork
place: General Archive of the Indies (Archivo de Indias)
desc: An NHK film for UNESCO on the three neighbouring buildings listed together in 1987: cathedral, Alcázar and the Archivo de Indias, the former merchants’ exchange that now stores the records of Spain’s rule over the Americas.

title: Four kings carry an explorer’s coffin inside a vast cathedral
desc: Built on the site of the Almohad great mosque, Seville’s cathedral is among the largest Gothic churches anywhere. Inside, the tomb of Christopher Columbus is held aloft by statues of the kings of Castile, León, Aragón and Navarre.

title: Whitewashed lanes wind through the old Jewish quarter
desc: Santa Cruz was Seville’s judería until the pogrom of 1391 and the expulsion that followed. A short walk through its tight streets and small plazas, built narrow to keep out the sun.

title: A tax collector in a city jail dreams up Don Quixote
place: Site of the Royal Prison, Calle Sierpes
desc: Cervantes was locked up in Seville’s Royal Prison in 1597 over shortfalls in the taxes he collected, and later wrote that his knight was “engendered in a prison.” A plaque on Calle Sierpes, the shopping street, marks where the jail stood.

title: Europe’s frying pan rethinks how people work and live in summer
desc: A Focus on Europe report on how Seville protects outdoor workers and older residents as summers pass 40°C, and why planners say the city’s streets must change. Calle Tetuán is one of the shopping streets roofed with canvas awnings in July.

title: Moorish courtyards survive inside a Christian king’s palace
desc: The Real Alcázar was rebuilt in the 1300s by Pedro I with Mudéjar craftsmen, so its tiled halls and pools look Moorish. It is still a royal residence, next to the cathedral in the old centre of Seville.

title: Hand claps, guitar and stamping heels in flamenco’s home city
desc: Flamenco grew out of Andalusia’s Roma, Moorish and Spanish traditions, and Seville is one of its centres. The city has a flamenco dance museum in the Santa Cruz quarter and small tablaos across the old town.

title: A week of horses, dresses and sherry in a tented city
place: Feria de Abril fairground, Los Remedios
desc: The Feria de Abril began as a livestock fair in 1847 and now fills a grid of over 1,000 striped casetas for a week after Easter. It is held on the fairground in the Los Remedios district, across the river.

title: La raja de tu falda
creator: Estopa
desc: The title cheekily eyes “the slit of your skirt.” Estopa are two brothers from working-class Cornellà, on Barcelona’s edge, who turned rumba catalana into raw guitar-rock. This 1999 debut single sold by the truckload — streetwise and instantly huge.

title: Hooded brotherhoods carry floats through the streets at Easter
desc: During Holy Week about 60 brotherhoods carry heavy floats of Christ and the Virgin from their parish churches to the cathedral and back, accompanied by robed penitents and brass bands. The processions fill the old centre.

title: Seville’s two football rivals settle scores in rowing boats
place: Guadalquivir River by the Torre del Oro (area)
desc: Since 1960 Sevilla FC and Real Betis have raced eights on the Guadalquivir, a river regatta that draws crowds to the banks. The course runs through the city on the river below the Torre del Oro and the Triana quarter.

title: La Santa Espina
place: Barcelona Cathedral square (Pla de la Seu)
creator: Enric Morera
desc: The title means “the holy thorn.” Enric Morera’s 1907 sardana — the circle dance that is Catalonia’s own — became so potent a symbol of Catalan identity that dictators banned it. Sardanas are still danced on weekends outside the Cathedral.

title: Gitana Hechicera
creator: Peret
desc: The title means “sorceress gypsy.” Peret, the king of rumba catalana, forged the genre in the Roma community around Gràcia’s Plaça del Raspall. This 1967 hit, dedicated to Barcelona, later closed the 1992 Olympics — the city dancing to its own beat.

title: L’Estaca
creator: Lluís Llach
desc: The title means “the stake.” Lluís Llach’s 1968 song — if we all pull together, the stake we’re tied to will fall — became the anthem of resistance to Franco, sung in Catalan when the language was suppressed. It later spread worldwide as a freedom hymn.

title: Mediterráneo
creator: Joan Manuel Serrat
desc: Joan Manuel Serrat, born in Barcelona’s Poble-sec, is Catalonia’s most beloved singer-songwriter. This 1971 hymn to the sea he grew up beside is often voted the greatest Spanish song ever — the Mediterranean itself, in a voice from the barri.

title: El ventilador
creator: Gato Pérez
desc: The title names the “fan” — the whirling guitar-strum that drives rumba catalana. Gato Pérez, an Argentine who fell for the genre in Barcelona’s Gràcia and Raval, revived it in the late 1970s with sharp, streetwise lyrics about the city itself.

title: Barcelona
creator: Montserrat Caballé & Freddie Mercury
desc: The city’s own anthem, sung by two operatic voices: the Barcelona-born soprano Montserrat Caballé and Freddie Mercury. Written for the 1992 Olympics that transformed the city, it soars over Montjuïc, where the Games were held.

title: Clandestino
creator: Manu Chao
desc: The title means “stowaway,” or undocumented. Manu Chao, the French-Spanish troubadour who made Barcelona his home, distilled the city’s restless, multicultural spirit into this 1998 song — the anthem of migrants and drifters, in a stew of languages.

title: Al mar!
creator: Manel
desc: The title means “to the sea!” Manel, four friends from Barcelona, led a revival of witty, literate indie-pop sung in Catalan. This 2008 singalong, all handclaps and wordplay, became a rallying cry for a young, proudly Catalan-speaking generation.

title: El Cant dels Ocells
place: Palau de la Música Catalana concert hall
creator: Pau Casals
desc: The title means “the song of the birds” — a centuries-old Catalan carol. The cellist Pau Casals made it his signature and a symbol of Catalan peace, playing it in exile and at the UN. Its home is a hall like the Palau de la Música.

title: Malamente
creator: Rosalía
desc: The title means “badly.” Rosalía, who trained in flamenco at Barcelona’s conservatory before conquering the world, broke through with this 2018 track — flamenco palmas and hand-claps welded to trap and avant-pop. A new sound, born in the city.

title: Fiebre
creator: Bad Gyal
desc: The title means “fever.” Bad Gyal, from the coastal town of Vilassar de Mar just north of Barcelona, pioneered a Catalan take on dancehall and reggaeton. This slinky 2018 hit is Auto-Tuned, sun-soaked, and defiantly of the Mediterranean coast.

title: Ay mamá
creator: Rigoberta Bandini
desc: Roughly “oh, mama.” Rigoberta Bandini, a Barcelona pop auteur, turned this 2022 song — an ode to mothers and to breasts, tender and cheeky at once — into a feminist singalong that nearly went to Eurovision and became an instant Catalan pop classic.

title: Boig per tu
creator: Sau
desc: The title means “mad about you.” Sau’s 1990 ballad is one of the best-loved songs in Catalan — so cherished that Shakira later recorded it for her Catalan partner. A tender staple of rock català, sung back word for word across the city.

title: Allied liberators find a starving city running on the black market
desc: Keith Lowe, author of “Naples 1944”, on the city the Allies entered in October 1943: wrecked by German demolitions, then hit by typhus and inflation. The glass-roofed Galleria Umberto I arcade filled with soldiers and black-market traders.

title: A prince-composer catches his wife with her lover and kills them both
place: Palazzo Sansevero, Piazza San Domenico Maggiore
desc: In October 1590 Carlo Gesualdo, Prince of Venosa, had Maria d’Avalos and the Duke of Andria killed in her rooms off Piazza San Domenico Maggiore. He went unpunished and went on to write some of the strangest madrigals of the age.

title: A wartime eruption buries a village under Vesuvius lava
desc: In March 1944, with Allied troops already in Naples, Vesuvius erupted for eleven days. Lava swallowed much of San Sebastiano al Vesuvio, the town on the volcano’s slope. Angelina Formisano, then nine, remembers the evacuation.

title: A city founded by a siren never stops singing
place: Teatro di San Carlo opera house
desc: Joanna Robertson traces Neapolitan song from sixteenth-century protest villanelle to the San Carlo opera house, where impresario Domenico Barbaja drew Rossini and Donizetti, and on to “Funiculì, Funiculà”, written to sell a funicular.

title: Nelson arrives a hero and stays to settle a bloody score
desc: In 1798 Nelson lands in Naples after the Nile and falls in with Sir William and Emma Hamilton at Palazzo Sessa, their palace above the bay. Within a year the court has fled, a republic has fallen and Admiral Caracciolo has been hanged.

title: Pompeii’s mosaics and Roman marbles fill a former university
desc: Naples’ National Archaeological Museum holds the best finds from Pompeii and Herculaneum and the Farnese collection of ancient sculpture. It occupies a 16th-century building at the top of Via Toledo, in the old centre.

title: Residents of the Gomorrah towers watch them come down
desc: The Vele, giant sail-shaped housing blocks in the northern suburb of Scampia, became a byword for drug dealing and the Camorra. France 24 visits as one block is demolished and residents try to remake the estate’s reputation.

title: Neapolitans adopt the skulls of the forgotten dead
desc: The Fontanelle Cemetery is a tufa quarry cave in the Sanità district filled with the bones of plague and cholera victims. For generations, locals tended individual skulls, praying for these anonymous souls in purgatory and asking favours in return.

title: Street fighters drive the Germans out before the Allies arrive
desc: Over four days in late September 1943, Neapolitans, many of them teenagers, rose against the German occupiers as Allied troops closed in. Some of the first clashes broke out on the Vomero, the residential hill above the old city.

title: A street priest takes on the cult of teenage gangsters
desc: Murals and shrines across Naples honour young Camorra members who died violently. Father Luigi Merola, once parish priest at San Giorgio Maggiore church in the Forcella district, now runs a youth centre and argues against making them heroes.

title: Before the Margherita, pizza was cheap street food for the poor
desc: Max Miller recreates pizza as 19th-century Neapolitans ate it, folded and sold on the street by vendors to working people. Antica Pizzeria Port’Alba, beside the old city gate near Piazza Dante, claims roots in this era of pizza as everyday food.

title: Daily life spills out along the street that splits the old city
desc: Spaccanapoli is the long, narrow street that runs straight through the historic centre, following the line of the ancient Greek city. Rick Steves walks it among shrines, laundry, scooters and shopkeepers, with Vesuvius looming over the bay.

title: Ancient erotic art is locked away from respectable eyes
desc: Frescoes, statues and charms dug up at Pompeii were judged too explicit for public view and shut in a ‘Secret Cabinet’ for over a century. The collection is now open in Naples’ National Archaeological Museum.

title: In vacanza da una vita
creator: Irene Grandi
desc: The title means “on holiday from a lifetime.” Irene Grandi, born and raised in Florence, became one of Italy’s favourite pop-rock voices. This bright, restless 1994 song was her breakthrough — a young woman itching to break free and live.

title: A loaf baked the day Vesuvius erupted, still in eight slices
desc: Carbonised round loaves scored into wedges were found in bakery ovens buried in AD 79. Examples are kept at the National Archaeological Museum of Naples, the city’s great museum of finds from Pompeii and Herculaneum.

title: Euridice
creator: Jacopo Peri
desc: Opera was invented in Florence, and this is the earliest one to survive. Jacopo Peri staged it at Palazzo Pitti in 1600 for a Medici royal wedding, singing Orpheus himself — the fruit of a circle of thinkers trying to revive ancient Greek drama.

title: Ecco la primavera
creator: Francesco Landini
desc: The title means “here comes the spring.” Francesco Landini, the blind organist who was medieval Florence’s greatest composer, wrote this joyful ballata. He played the organ at San Lorenzo, the Medici church where he was buried.

title: O Fiorentina
creator: Narciso Parigi
desc: The title means “oh, Fiorentina.” Narciso Parigi’s 1959 song became a double anthem — for the city and for its football club — and it still roars from the terraces of the Stadio Artemio Franchi on match days, a whole stand in purple.

title: Requiem in C minor
creator: Luigi Cherubini
desc: Luigi Cherubini, born in Florence in 1760, became one of Europe’s most admired composers; Beethoven thought him the greatest of the age. His career unfolded in Paris, but his home city named its conservatory — still training musicians today — after him.

title: Amarilli, mia bella
creator: Giulio Caccini
desc: The title means “Amaryllis, my lovely one.” Giulio Caccini, a singer at the Medici court at Palazzo Pitti, belonged to the circle that invented opera. This tender 1602 song launched a radical new style — a single, plainly expressive voice.

title: Disperato
creator: Marco Masini
desc: The title means “desperate.” Marco Masini, a Florentine cantautore with a knack for raw, bruising ballads, broke through with this 1990 song of heartbreak and despair. He went on to win Sanremo and to court controversy with his blunt lyrics.

title: Siberia
creator: Diaframma
desc: Diaframma led Florence’s dark, arty post-punk wave in the early 1980s — a cult band who kept turning down Sanremo and the majors to stay free. This icy, intense 1984 track is their landmark, and the sound of a very different, underground Florence.

title: Luglio
creator: Riccardo Del Turco
desc: The title means “July.” Riccardo Del Turco, from Fiesole in the hills above Florence, had Italy’s biggest hit of summer 1968 with this sunny love song — so catchy it was covered across Europe. He later ran a bar back home in the city.

title: El Diablo
creator: Litfiba
desc: Litfiba took their name from the telex code of Via de’ Bardi, the street where they rehearsed; a mural to them stands there now. This snarling 1990 hit made the Florentine band one of Italy’s biggest rock acts, gritty and Mediterranean at once.

title: Se mi rilasso collasso
creator: La Bandabardò
desc: The title means “if I relax, I collapse.” La Bandabardò — named in homage to Brigitte Bardot — brought rowdy, acoustic folk-rock and a busker’s spirit to the Florence scene from the 1990s on. This 2004 song is one of their sing-along staples.

title: Governo Punk
creator: bnkr44
desc: The title means “punk government.” bnkr44 are a young self-made collective from Villanova, near Empoli in Florence’s province, who blend pop, rap, and rock. They took this scrappy anthem to Sanremo in 2024 — the sound of Tuscany’s newest generation.

title: La Porti un Bacione a Firenze
creator: Odoardo Spadaro
desc: The title means “take a big kiss to Florence.” Odoardo Spadaro’s 1937 song is the city’s tender anthem, sung from the point of view of an emigrant longing for home. Picture it from Piazzale Michelangelo, the terrace with all Florence laid out below.

title: A poet dreams of a homecoming that never came
desc: Dante was baptized in this octagonal building and spent his exile dreaming of returning to be crowned with a laurel wreath here. Florence never let him back, and still refuses to return his remains, buried instead in Ravenna since 1321.

title: A goddess born from sea foam and Medici money
desc: Commissioned by a Medici cousin, this painting of Venus arriving on a scallop shell hangs a short walk from where it was made. Botticelli himself is buried nearby at Ognissanti, alongside the Vespucci family who likely modeled for him.

title: A condemned astronomer keeps working from house arrest
desc: Convicted of vehement suspicion of heresy for insisting the earth moves, Galileo spent his final nine years confined to this hillside villa — well treated, still working, producing what he thought his best science here while going blind.

title: An 11-year-old apprentice becomes king of the booksellers
desc: Vespasiano da Bisticci began work on this street, then called Via dei Librai, as an 11-year-old in 1433 and spent the next 50 years dominating the manuscript trade. He refused to stock printed books, insisting they would shame his handwritten volumes.

title: An English mercenary gets a painted horse in the cathedral
desc: Florence hired soldiers rather than fielding its own army, and two of its captains are honoured on the north wall of the cathedral. Uccello painted the Englishman John Hawkwood in 1436 and Andrea del Castagno added Niccolò da Tolentino twenty years later.

title: A banking family’s chapel sets the rules for Renaissance building
desc: The Pazzi Chapel sits in the first cloister of Santa Croce basilica and is attributed to Filippo Brunelleschi. Grey pietra serena stone on white plaster marks out its proportions. The film is by the Opera di Santa Croce, which runs the complex.

title: Charcoal drawings turn up in a sealed room below the Medici tombs
desc: Rediscovered in 1975 beneath the New Sacristy, this small storeroom is covered in wall drawings attributed to Michelangelo, who is thought to have hidden here in 1530. It opened to small groups of visitors in 2023.

title: A mafia car bomb tears into the Uffizi in the night
place: Via dei Georgofili, behind the Uffizi
desc: In May 1993 a car bomb planted by the Sicilian Mafia exploded in Via dei Georgofili, the narrow street behind the Uffizi gallery, killing five people. The episode follows one damaged painting by Bartolomeo Manfredi through its long restoration.

title: Leonardo and Michelangelo are hired to paint rival battles
place: Hall of the Five Hundred, Palazzo Vecchio
desc: In 1504 the republic hired Leonardo and Michelangelo to paint two huge battle scenes facing each other in the council hall of the Palazzo Vecchio. Neither was finished, and historians still argue over what lies under Vasari’s later frescoes.

title: Builders argue for years over how many doors a church needs
desc: Brunelleschi designed Santo Spirito, the Augustinian church in the Oltrarno, but died soon after work began. His successors fought over the facade, especially whether it should have four doors, as he wanted, or three. The bare front was never clad.

title: The Arno bursts its banks and buries the city in mud
desc: On 4 November 1966 the Arno flooded Florence, burying churches, archives and workshops in mud and fuel oil. Volunteers from around the world, the “mud angels”, dug out books here at the National Central Library and art in the churches nearby.

title: Twenty-seven men a side fight over a ball in a sand-covered square
desc: Every June the four historic quarters of Florence play calcio storico, a Renaissance ball game with punching, wrestling and almost no rules. Piazza Santa Croce is covered in sand and ringed with stands, and the matches draw fighters from boxing and MMA.

title: Violin makers and framers keep working south of the river
desc: The Oltrarno, the district on the far bank of the Arno around Santo Spirito, is where many of Florence’s workshops still are. The film visits a picture framer and a violin maker, then sits down to a bistecca of Chianina beef.

title: Monks still chant in a marble church above the city
desc: San Miniato al Monte, a Romanesque church in green and white marble begun in 1013, stands on the hill south of the Arno. Olivetan monks still sing vespers there, a short walk uphill from the Piazzale Michelangelo terrace.

title: A fortress town hall becomes a Medici palace
desc: The Palazzo Vecchio, with its tall crenellated tower, was built around 1300 to house the republic’s government. When the Medici became dukes they moved in and filled it with grand halls, including the Hall of the Five Hundred.

title: Florentines line up for a sandwich of cow’s fourth stomach
desc: Lampredotto is the abomasum, a cow’s fourth stomach, simmered in broth with tomato and herbs, then sliced into a bread roll with green sauce. It has been sold from carts and market counters, like those around the San Lorenzo central market, for centuries.

title: A whole Renaissance city still packed inside its old walls
desc: Florence’s centre was listed as World Heritage in 1982 for the cathedral and Brunelleschi’s dome, the Palazzo Vecchio, the Uffizi and the bridges over the Arno. Most of it can be crossed on foot in half an hour.

title: Goldsmiths keep shop on the one bridge the Germans spared
desc: The Ponte Vecchio has carried shops since the Middle Ages; butchers were moved out for goldsmiths in 1593. A private Medici corridor runs along its roof, and it was the only Florence bridge left standing by retreating German troops in 1944.

title: The Medici offices become the world’s first great picture gallery
desc: Vasari designed the Uffizi in the 1560s as offices for the Medici; it now holds Botticelli, Leonardo and Titian. The long U-shaped building runs from Piazza della Signoria down to the Arno.

title: An arcade for abandoned babies sets the Renaissance in motion
desc: Brunelleschi designed this foundling hospital in 1419, its loggia hung with Andrea della Robbia’s blue-and-white roundels of swaddled babies. It faces Piazza della Santissima Annunziata, north of the Duomo.

title: Galileo’s finger points skyward from a glass reliquary
desc: Admirers removed three fingers and a tooth when Galileo’s body was moved to a new tomb in 1737. The middle finger is displayed in an egg-shaped case at the Museo Galileo, the science museum behind the Uffizi on the Arno.

title: A blind traveler meets Rome’s she-wolf
desc: This fun and empathy-building Atlas Obscura episode relays the childhood experience of Matthew Shifrin, a blind kid from the US who visited the Capitoline Museum and was allowed to touch the iconic bronze she-wolf sculpture nursing Romulus and Remus.

title: Testaccio: A foodie neighborhood in a foodie city
desc: Once home to the city’s slaughterhouse, Testaccio is now a food haven. This tour of neighborhood’s culinary hits begins at the delightful Mercato di Testaccio. Other stops: pizza at Trapizzino, wine at Palombi, pasta at Felice, and mains at Piatto Romano.

title: A private corridor lets the Medici cross the river unseen
desc: Giorgio Vasari built the kilometre-long passage in 1565 so Cosimo I could walk from the Palazzo Vecchio to the Pitti Palace. It runs through the Uffizi and along the top of the Ponte Vecchio, the city’s old bridge of goldsmiths.

title: Cats and the ghost of Julius Caesar
desc: On busy Largo di Torre Argentina is the spot where Julius Caesar was betrayed and stabbed. This episode of This Is Love tells the story of former opera singer Silvia Viviani, who created a sanctuary for Rome’s stray cats amidst the ruins over 30 years ago.

title: A safe haven from Nazis in the Vatican
desc: During WWII, Vatican City sat at the heart of German-occupied Rome, offering a base for secret rescue operations. This BBC Witness History episode reveals how Monsignor O’Flaherty orchestrated a daring escape network hidden inside Rome’s walls.

title: Miserere
creator: Gregorio Allegri
desc: A setting of Psalm 51, “have mercy on me.” For nearly two centuries the Vatican forbade copying it, so Allegri’s ethereal Miserere could be heard only here in the Sistine Chapel — until the teenage Mozart famously wrote it down from memory.

title: Behind the Trevi Fountain, Rome’s baroque masterpiece
desc: Rome’s Trevi Fountain isn’t just a postcard icon — it’s fed by an ancient aqueduct and was completed in 1762 with dramatic marble sculptures. This episode of Rebuilding the Renaissance explores the history and artistry behind Rome’s most beloved fountain.

title: The controversial beheading of the Roman Virgin
desc: In 1599, Beatrice Cenci was publicly beheaded on Rome’s Ponte Sant’Angelo for the murder of her abusive father. This chilling episode of Noble Blood recounts her crime, punishment, and the legend of her ghost that still haunts the bridge.

title: Una storia importante
creator: Eros Ramazzotti
desc: The title means “an important story.” This 1985 song launched Eros Ramazzotti, who grew up in the Cinecittà district named after Rome’s legendary film studios — the “Hollywood on the Tiber” where Fellini and the great epics were shot.

title: Zitti e Buoni
creator: Måneskin
desc: The title means “quiet and good” — a sarcastic “shut up and behave.” Måneskin, four teenagers who busked on the Via del Corso, won Eurovision 2021 with this glam-rock blast and made Rome the unlikely capital of a rock revival.

title: Sicut cervus
creator: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
desc: The Latin title means “as the deer longs for water.” Palestrina, the towering master of Renaissance church music, served as choirmaster at Santa Maria Maggiore; his serene, interweaving voices are the sound of Counter-Reformation Rome itself.

title: Arrivederci, Roma
creator: Renato Rascel
desc: The title means “goodbye, Rome.” Renato Rascel’s 1955 song is the city’s great farewell — every visitor’s bittersweet promise to return, traditionally sealed by tossing a coin over your shoulder into the Trevi Fountain.

title: La Dolce Vita (tema)
creator: Nino Rota
desc: The title means “the sweet life.” Nino Rota scored Fellini’s 1960 film about glamour and emptiness among Rome’s celebrities and paparazzi — a world centered on the cafés and hotels of the Via Veneto, then the most glamorous street on earth.

title: E lucevan le stelle
creator: Giacomo Puccini
desc: The title means “and the stars were shining.” In Puccini’s opera Tosca, a condemned man sings this heartbreaking dawn farewell atop Castel Sant’Angelo — the riverside fortress where, moments later, Tosca herself leaps from the ramparts.

title: Pini di Roma
creator: Ottorino Respighi
desc: The title means “Pines of Rome.” Respighi’s blazing 1924 orchestral showpiece paints the city’s umbrella pines from dawn to dusk; its thunderous finale imagines Roman legions marching home along the ancient Appian Way.

title: Roma nun fa’ la stupida stasera
creator: Armando Trovajoli
desc: In Roman dialect, “Rome, don’t play dumb tonight.” From the 1962 musical Rugantino, it’s a tender plea to the city to nudge two lovers together — best imagined under the Baroque fountains of Piazza Navona on a warm Roman night.

title: La società dei magnaccioni
creator: Gabriella Ferri
desc: A rowdy old Roman tavern singalong — roughly “the society of big eaters,” whose refrain shrugs “we like to eat and drink, and we don’t like to work.” It was made famous by Gabriella Ferri, “la Testaccina,” the great voice of working-class Testaccio.

title: Roma Capoccia
creator: Antonello Venditti
desc: Roman dialect for “Rome, boss of the world.” Venditti wrote this aching love letter to his city at fourteen, naming the Colosseum and St. Peter’s dome. The “fontanone” he sings of is the Acqua Paola, crowning the Janiculum with all Rome below.

title: I migliori anni della nostra vita
creator: Renato Zero
desc: The title means “the best years of our lives.” Renato Zero, Rome’s flamboyant and fiercely beloved showman, turned this 1995 song into a generational singalong. He first found his audience back in the 1960s at the city’s legendary Piper Club.

title: Solo guai
creator: Carl Brave x Franco126
desc: The title means “nothing but trouble.” Carl Brave and Franco126, from the 126 crew around Piazza San Cosimato in Trastevere, make dreamy, slang-soaked rap that maps everyday Roman life — Peronis, scooters, and the cobblestones underfoot.

title: I tuoi particolari
creator: Ultimo
desc: The title means “your little details.” Ultimo, who grew up in the gritty San Basilio estates on Rome’s northeastern edge, took this 2019 ballad to second place at Sanremo. Months later he filled the Stadio Olimpico — the local boy’s homecoming.

title: Architectural thinking behind London Bridge Station
desc: In 2019, the new London Bridge Station was shortlisted for Building of the Year by the Royal Institute of British Architects. In this video from Architects’ Journal, the architect describes the humanist approach to designing the complex station.

title: The London airport without air traffic controllers on-site
desc: As you fly into London City Airport, air traffic controllers are keeping a close eye on the plane — from 80 miles away. In this video, Tom Scott gets a tour of the remarkable control center that blends smart technology with a big dose of risk aversion.

title: Riding a historic Routemaster double-decker bus
desc: Most iconic double-decker buses that ply London’s streets are a 2012-era design. This video from Half-Asleep Chris shows how you can still climb aboard the historic Routemaster buses on route 15 each weekend. His enthusiasm for these buses is contagious.

title: Studying “The Knowledge” to drive a black cab in London
desc: A traffic circle below Trafalgar Square marks the center of a six-mile radius of 25,000 roads that have to be memorized by drivers of London’s black cabs. In this video from Quartz, cabbie Kevin Tuite offers insight into the “hardest test in the world.”

title: Serving the community’s needs at the Library of Things
place: Library of Things, Upper Norwood Library Hub
desc: This video from Time Out heads down to South London, where three young women started a library where people in the community can borrow physical objects like power tools, camping gear, or kitchen equipment. What a smart and inspiring idea.

title: Five decades of getting the Tube where it’s going
desc: Frank Kelly is a delightful and jovial signal box operator who has worked at the Edgeware Road tube stop since 1963. Thankfully, the worryingly archaic 1920s equipment he used during his career is retiring along with Frank. BBC London tells his story.

title: The Dagenham Idol: A carving as old as the Pyramids of Giza
desc: Carved from wood in around 2250 BC, the Dagenham Idol is one of the oldest known depictions of a human form in Europe. In this video from Londonist, historian Robert Kingham stops by Valence House Museum to explain the neolithic woodcarving.

title: Taking a leap of faith to start The Nunhead Gardener
desc: This video from Monocle Films tells the story of a couple who quit their ho-hum corporate jobs to start a garden center. They converted unloved indoor and outdoor spaces alongside a train station to create a green oasis that has become a community hub.

title: Introducing Shakespeare to a new generation
desc: More than 20,000 state school students attended a shortened performance of Romeo and Juliet at the Globe Theatre in 2019. The young audience in this video from BBC London was wonderfully electric. It’s fun to see new generations experience Shakespeare.

title: How a tube station sheltered people and art in World War II
desc: Despite being a hub on the London Underground, significant portions of Piccadilly Circus tube station have been collecting dust since the 1920s. This video from BBC London explains how abandoned parts of the station got a second life during the Blitz.

title: The worldly collections of Sir John Soane
desc: Sir John Soane was a prolific architect and avid traveler who collected art and antiquities, leaving behind a house full of treasures upon his death in 1837. This video from ArtFundUK goes inside the underrated museum to hear from curators and visitors.

title: The rise and fall of the Crystal Palace
place: Site of the Crystal Palace, Crystal Palace Park
desc: Opened in 1851 for the Great Exhibition, the Crystal Palace was an architectural marvel that sadly burned down in 1936. This thought-provoking video from Amor Sciendi shows how the building became an important symbol of human imagination and ingenuity.

title: The only commercial vineyard in London
desc: Forty Hall Vineyard in Enfield is staffed by volunteers seeking the therapeutic effects of a community at work together in the sunshine. This video from BBC London takes a peek inside the relatively young vineyard to hear from the owner and volunteers.

title: Symbolism and surprise in The Ambassadors by Hans Holbein
desc: On view at the National Gallery is a portrait of two French Ambassadors painted in 1533 by German Hans Holbein. This video from Amor Sciendi explains some easy-to-miss meaning and symbolism, then reveals a surprise in the painting at around 1:40.

title: Outside and inside at The Barbican
desc: The Barbican is a bold yet controversial complex of housing and civic spaces completed in 1979. This thoughtful video from the Architecture Foundation shows how The Barbican is “a fortress within the city” that reveals surprising beauty once inside.

title: Preserving the history of aviation and motorsports
desc: Brooklands Museum is on a mission to celebrate the history of innovation in aviation and motorsports. This video from ArtFundUK shows the museum’s unique work, like teaching hands-on courses to preserve historical aircraft or renovating a racing circuit.

title: A city with six airports
desc: Heathrow, Gatwick, Luton, Stansted, Southend, and City — why does London have so many airports? In this hilariously zany video, Jay Foreman explains how airports emerged all over London, primarily built on former airstrips used by the Royal Air Force.

title: In praise of the London Olympics Aquatics Centre
desc: Zaha Hadid was an acclaimed British architect who designed the Aquatics Centre for the London Olympics in 2012. In this quick video from Dezeen, famed architect Richard Rogers celebrates Hadid’s design and how it continues to resonate with people.

title: Meet the master distiller behind Beefeater Gin
desc: Beefeater is one of the world’s most popular gin brands, led by their friendly and down-to-earth master distiller Desmond Payne. In this beautifully-filmed video from Gin Foundry, he shares his love of gin and how he approaches creating new products.

title: Concocting homemade gin at Sacred Spirits
desc: Somewhere in Highgate is a unique gin distillery started by Ian Hart and Hilary Whitney in their house. Ian is like a mad scientist with a gentle demeanor, using a highly unorthodox vacuum distilling process that he explains in this video by Gin Foundry.

title: The curious single station stub on the Tube map
desc: Near the top of the London Underground map, one station inexplicably juts out of the Northern Line: Mill Hill East. This fun video from Jay Foreman explains the on-the-ground realities that led to this lonely anomaly of a Tube stop.

title: Teaching kids to dance for a half-century
desc: In 1962, Irene hayes founded Superarts, a dance studio dedicated to offering inexpensive classes for kids in Southwark. At age 87, Irene continues hands-on instruction that has led her students to star in major musicals. BBC London tells her story.

title: Stories from a neighborhood in flux
desc: Documentary filmmaker Zed Nelson spent four years creating a film about the gentrifying Hackney neighborhood. In this thought-provoking episode of Monocle On Culture, he shares how making the film revealed more nuance and complexity than he anticipated.

title: Inventing a new way to shop at Selfridges
desc: In 1908, Harry Gordon Selfridge opened a novel shopping concept: the department store. In this podcast episode, Tim Harford describes the radical innovations at Selfridges, like bringing merchandise out into the open or providing restrooms for women.

title: Breadmakers on the rise
desc: Gail’s Artisan Bakery is a rapidly-growing chain that started on Hampstead High Street in 2005. This episode of The Entrepreneurs hears from the bakery’s co-founder about how Gail’s has reduced food waste by repurposing ingredients and giving to charity.

title: The seedy streets of Hockley in the Hole
desc: Now a typical pub on a modest street, The Coach was once a popular hub in an unruly neighborhood called Hockley in the Hole. In this episode of London History podcast, tour guide Hazel Baker shares stories of amateur boxing, cockfighting, and bear bating.

title: Finding remnants of Newgate Prison inside a pub
desc: For nearly 500 years, Newgate Prison served as the main prison in London. In this quick video, tour guide Julian McDonnell ventures beneath The Viaduct Tavern, a pub where a few historic prison cells remain in the basement.

title: Rethinking British cuisine with Elizabeth David
desc: In Chelsea, a blue plaque adorns the longtime home of Elizabeth David, who revolutionized British cuisine via her cookbooks and columns in Harpers Bazaar. This episode of Encyclopedia Womannica podcast describes how her extensive travel inspired her work.

title: How a smelly river pushed parliament to address The Great Stink
place: River Thames by the Palace of Westminster
desc: In the sweltering summer of 1858, London’s open sewers had filled the city’s air with an inescapable stench of human excrement. In this podcast episode, host Tim Harford explains how the event accelerated the adoption of new toilet and sewer technology.

title: A little square that brims with history
desc: Down a tiny lane called Pickering Place is one of London’s smallest public spaces. In this video, tour guide Julian McDonnell shares stories about the area. Most interestingly, it was home to the embassy of Texas before joining the United States in 1845.

title: Raising the drawbridge at Tower Bridge
desc: Seeing Tower Bridge fold open for a boat to go underneath is a fascinating experience. In this video from Londonist, Will Noble does something much more fun: summit the control tower and raise the drawbridge for a huge cruise ship coming up the Thames.

title: How long is a foot? How long is a yard?
desc: Throughout the British Empire, people used the imperial system to measure distances. In this video, tour guide Matt Gedge points out public plaques that established the correct length of feet and yards — plus defunct units like pole, links, and chain.

title: The phantom gates of Londinium
desc: Roman Londinium was a walled city with gates controlling how and where people entered and exited. This video from Londonist visits the sites where each of the gates stood, and it’s surprisingly compelling despite all of the gates being destroyed long ago.

title: The keeper of musical instruments
desc: In this episode of the National Trust podcast, joyful and curious curator James Grasby visits Fenton House in North London to discover a treasure trove of musical instruments dating as far as 1540. Historical harpsichords are surprisingly fascinating.

title: The oldest remaining church in London
desc: St. Bartholomew the Great is a gorgeous 900-year-old medieval church. In this video, tour guide Julian McDonnell takes us inside for a quick look around. To quote Yoda from Return of the Jedi: “When 900 years old you reach... look as good you will not.”

title: Fighting home-grown fascism at the Battle of Cable Street
desc: On October 4, 1936, a gang of British fascists poured into the east end of London to provoke the area’s Jewish community. This episode of Witness History describes how anti-fascists prevailed that day, later memorialized by a bold mural on Cable Street.

title: The Notting Hill race riots of 1958
desc: As a community of immigrants from the West Indies grew in postwar Notting Hill, so did racial tensions. This episode of Witness History describes how white gangs wielding firebombs eventually gave way to an annual carnival celebrating Caribbean culture.

title: A siege at the Iranian Embassy
desc: In May 1980, an insurgent group held 19 hostages at the Iranian Embassy in London for six days. This episode of BBC Witness History shares firsthand accounts of how the standoff ended: with a dramatic capture of the embassy by British special forces.

title: The Bethnal Green tube station disaster
desc: In March 1943, 173 people were crushed to death as they sought refuge in an air-raid shelter at Bethnal Green tube station. This episode of BBC’s Witness History podcast relays a harrowing firsthand account of a woman who survived the tragedy as a child.

title: Inside the archives of the Museum of London
place: Mortimer Wheeler House (Museum of London stores)
desc: Like most museums, the Museum of London only displays a portion of its collection at any given time. This video from Londonist visits Mortimer Wheeler House, its unexpectedly museum-like storage warehouse. The archivist saying “ornate urinal” was a treat.

title: The first black woman to become a member of parliament
desc: In June 1987, Dianne Abbott gave a speech at Hackney Town Hall after her unexpected electoral victory to become a member of parliament. In this episode of BBC Witness History podcast, the daughter of working-class Jamaican immigrants shares her story.

title: A harrowing history of the Tyburn Tree
desc: Near the Marble Arch tube station is an easily-overlooked memorial to the Tyburn Tree, where executioners hung London’s condemned for half a millennia. Tour guide Matt Gedge offers a thoughtful history of the grim gallows in this video from Londonist.

title: What happens when you lose something on the Tube?
desc: Transport for London’s Lost Property Office is the hub for 300,000 items lost by Londoners in transit each year. In this video from Londonist, manager Paul Cowan gives a tour of the office and explains the logistical complexity dealt with by his team.

title: Protesting the Miss World beauty pageant
desc: In 1970, Sally Alexander joined dozens of feminist women as they stormed Royal Albert Hall’s stage to protest the Miss World competition. In this BBC Witness History episode, she reflects on her arrest that night and the protest’s long-term impact.

title: The poisoning of a former KGB agent
desc: Alexander Litvinenko fled to London after exposing corruption within the Russian government. After a casual lunch at Itsu in central London, he fell gravely ill, suspecting Russian agents poisoned him. This episode of BBC Witness History tells his story.

title: Harry Houdini at the Hippodrome
desc: In 1904, the up-and-coming escape artist Harry Houdini performed to an eager crowd of 4000 people at the Hippodrome in London. This episode of BBC’s Witness History podcast tells the story of the handcuff escape challenge that propelled him into stardom.

title: A journey through British postal history
desc: Opened in 2017, the Postal Museum houses unexpected and engaging exhibits, including a ride on the Mail Rail, a historic underground train used for sorting and delivery. This video from ArtFundUK describes why they named it Museum of the Year in 2018.

title: A supermarket made from steel
desc: The giant metallic mass of the Camden branch of Sainsbury’s supermarket looks otherworldly, especially for something as mundane as a supermarket. This episode of Monocle On Design describes why the 1988 building became listed for historic preservation.

title: Glimpses of the past at an abandoned tube station
desc: In 1994, Aldwych Tube Station closed due to low ridership and high maintenance costs. In this video, Time Out tours the neglected station, which still contains a 70s-era subway train, original posters on the walls, and props from its use as a movie set.

title: Behind the screens at Piccadilly Circus
desc: In this video, Londonist goes on a tour of the giant digital advertisements overlooking Piccadilly Circus. Historical photos in the video show the area changing over time. If the comments on YouTube are any indication, the new screen is... controversial.

title: A 90-year tradition of handmade ballet shoes
place: Freed of London shop, St Martin’s Lane
desc: Freed of London has been producing handmade ballet shoes for over 90 years. This video from National Geographic profiles the hardscrabble yet optimistic craftspeople who have been making the shoes for decades, including a sweet couple who met on the job.

title: A male tree in need of a female mate
desc: David Cooke supervises the lovely Victorian-era Palm House, an iconic building inside Kew Gardens. In this video from Great Big Story, he tells the story of a lonely tree brought to London from South Africa more than 115 years ago.

title: Exploring the ins-and-outs of Southwark Cathedral
desc: In this video from Londonist, charming and engaging tour guide Vicki Pipe points out some easily-overlooked details in Southwark Cathedral. She then climbs to the roof past a gang of practicing bellringers for a spectacular vista over London.

title: Inside London’s 900-year-old secret garden
desc: Constructed in the 12th century, St. Dunstan-in-the-East is a church that was mostly destroyed during World War II, leaving only its ruined husk behind. It is now a peaceful and tucked-away garden, nicely highlighted in this video from Great Big Story.

title: Falling back in love with print periodicals
desc: In 2007, Tyler Brûlé founded Monocle, a slightly highfalutin design and culture magazine. In this video, he introduces his new shop Kioskafé, which aims to be “an optimistic rebuttal to the mistaken narrative that people aren’t buying print products.”

title: How Phonica Records became a Soho institution
desc: This video from Culture Trip offers a peek inside Phonica Records, a vinyl-oriented record store that specializes in dance music. The shop serves as a community hub for a local music scene and occasionally transforms into a tiny dance club at night.

title: How the equestrian statue ended up at Trafalgar Square
desc: Statues of King Charles I are rare because they were melted down after his beheading in 1649. In this video, guide Julian McDonnell explains how a scheming man saved and hid an equestrian statue of Charles before its eventual arrival at Trafalgar Square.

title: How the historic City of London chooses a mayor
desc: Overlooking the Bank tube stop stands the Mansion House, an ornate building that serves as the home of the Lord Mayor of the City of London. This fun and fast-paced video from CGP Gray describes the hilariously complicated process of becoming the mayor.

title: Making Freddie Mercury’s commemorative plaque
place: Freddie Mercury’s family home, 22 Gladstone Avenue, Feltham
desc: The blue commemorative plaques affixed to many buildings across London are so ubiquitous that they blend into the backdrop of the city. This surprisingly inspiring video shows how each plaque is lovingly hand-made by artisans Frank and Sue Ashworth.

title: Making hat history for 350 years at Lock & Co
place: Lock & Co hatters, St James’s Street
desc: This video from Londonist visits Lock & Co, the world’s oldest hat shop. Roger Stephenson describes how his family’s business has connections to Lord Nelson, Winston Churchill, Queen Elizabeth, Charlie Chaplin, and even the fictional Mad Hatter.

title: Marie Stopes: Bringing birth control to London
place: Site of Marie Stopes’s first clinic, 61 Marlborough Road
desc: In 1921, London’s first clinic where women could access birth control opened at 61 Marlborough Road. This episode of Witness History tells the story of Marie Stopes, a family planning pioneer (and unfortunate eugenics advocate) who opened the clinic.

title: Questioning the legacy of Jack the Ripper
place: Jack the Ripper Museum, Cable Street
desc: Jack the Ripper was an infamous serial killer who murdered as many as 11 impoverished women in the east end of London in the 1880s. This video from CBC shows the debate surrounding his legacy, now propagated by gimmicky museums and campy walking tours.

title: Queen Elizabeth’s life told through banknotes and coins
desc: Starting in 1934, the image of Queen Elizabeth II has appeared on paper currency throughout the British Commonwealth. This video from Half-Asleep Chris admiringly tells her unlikely life story through the clever use of stop-motion animation.

title: The bombing of the Houses of Parliament
desc: In May 1941, at the end of the weeks-long bombing campaign known as the Blitz, the Houses of Parliament were nearly destroyed. This video from Half-Asleep Chris describes how 51 countries contributed to the postwar reconstruction of the House of Commons.

title: Modern furniture with mid-century influences
desc: Pinch is a furniture company with a retail shop in the Pimlico neighborhood. In this episode of Monocle On Design, the calm and reflective co-founders describe their embrace of raw wood textures and aim to make “gentle” furniture that ages gracefully.

title: The bookshop that the LGBTQ community calls home
desc: Gay’s The Word has served as a bookshop and hub for the LGBTQ community in London since 1979. This excellent video from BBC London allows the sweet and thoughtful staff to tell the story of the “rare and precious” shop in their own words.

title: The golden post box of Westminster
place: Gold post box near Westminster Abbey
desc: The Royal Mail commemorated the 2012 Olympics by slathering a post box in gold paint, starting with one near Westminster Abbey. This video from Half-Asleep Chris shows how the golden boxes popped up across the UK to honor gold medal winners.

title: The strike that dealt a blow to Fleet Street
desc: In its heyday as the newspaper industry’s spine, Fleet Street bustled with gifted journalists and hardscrabble pressmen. This episode of BBC Witness History recounts a union strike against Rupert Murdoch in 1986 that hastened the street’s fall from grace.

title: The last remnants of London’s extensive tram network
desc: One of the only remaining signs of London’s once-massive network of trams is an unused tunnel underneath King’s Way in Holborn. In this hysterical video, Jay Foreman tells a history of electric trams in the city before double-decker buses became common.

title: The meaning of man versus centaur on the Elgin Marbles
desc: Housed at the British Museum since 1816, the marbles taken from the Parthenon are highly controversial — Athens wants them back. This podcast episode from the BBC explains how Athenians may have read the sculptures when the Parthenon opened in 432 BCE.

title: The mice of Philpot Lane
desc: Clinging to the facade of a historic office building in the City of London is a tiny sculpture of mice fighting over a piece of cheese. This 60-second video from Londonist tells the story of how it got there.

title: The monument to the Great Fire of London
place: Monument to the Great Fire of London
desc: Just north of London Bridge stands a dramatic column that memorializes the Great Fire of London in 1666. In this 60-second video from Londonist, author Mark Mason offers a few interesting tidbits of trivia about the monument itself.

title: The vampire craze at Highgate Cemetery
desc: London has seven spooky and overgrown Victorian-era cemeteries. Highgate became the epicenter of a bizarre 1970s vampire-hunting trend that rapidly escalated out of control. Atlas Obscura co-founder Dylan Thuras excitedly tells the story in this video.

title: The trailblazing female founders of the Royal Academy of Arts
desc: Working in an environment that was openly hostile to women, painters Angelica Kauffman and Mary Moser helped found the Royal Academy of Arts. This delightful episode of Bow Down describes how they navigated the absurd gender discrimination of the era.

title: Visiting a wacky homemade arcade
desc: Tim Hunkin is a cartoonist and engineer who created Novelty Automation, an arcade filled with jokey satirical games like Pet Or Meat, Instant Eclipse, or Auto-Frisk. This video from Great Big Story will make you intrigued enough to visit.

title: Meet an up-and-coming director in Theatreland
desc: This video from BBC London stops by Donmar Warehouse in London’s West End theatre district to interview Ola Ince, a young woman of color who started directing plays before she turned 30. Her fearlessness and aspiration are commendable.

title: Past and present on display at Tate Britain
desc: Tate Britain was wholly overhauled and remodeled in 2013. In this video from ArtFundUK, the museum’s director Penelope Curtis describes how interior spaces were altered to create a museum experience that blends historical and contemporary British art.

title: The past, present, and future of Battersea Power Station
desc: The four chimneys of London’s iconic power plant have loomed over the south bank of the Thames since 1955. In this episode, the host of Londonist Out Loud goes on-site for an insightful chat about the station with author Peter Watts. Gets going at ~2:45.

title: Seeing the world through the eyes of William Morris
desc: William Morris was an influential designer who championed craftsmanship in an age of mass-production and industrialization. This podcast episode from the National Trust visits the lovely Red House, where he lived at the peak of his career in the 1860s.

title: Swimming in the ponds of Hampstead Heath
desc: In this slightly overdramatic video from The Economist, a cabbie shares his favorite overlooked place in London: the bathing ponds in the sprawling open space of Hampstead Heath. A dip in these ponds looks like a delightful adventure.

title: A cultural stew inside BBC Broadcasting House
desc: Producing content in 35 languages, the BBC World Service is “a kind of United Nations based in London.” This episode of The Food Programme describes a diverse global cookbook compiled by staff from dozens of countries working in BBC’s Broadcasting House.

title: Exploring the church built by The Knights Templar
desc: Temple Church was built as the headquarters of The Knights Templar, a fighting force aligned with the Catholic Church. In this video, tour guide Julian McDonnell pokes around the church that sparked recent interest due to The Da Vinci Code book and movie.

title: From the Douro to the Thames
place: Bar Douro restaurant, Flat Iron Square
desc: Max Graham’s father founded Churchill’s Port, one of the top makers of the boozy and complex Portuguese wine. In this episode of The Menu, Max describes his own business venture, Bar Douro, which aims to bring tasty Portuguese culinary classics to London.

title: A train station for the recently deceased
desc: At 121 Westminster Bridge Road are the remnants of a London Necropolis Railway station. The grim service shuttled the dead—and their living relatives—to Brookwood Cemetery for 90 years. The first part of this episode of Ridiculous History tells the story.

title: How London ended up with 32 boroughs
desc: Why is there a Finsbury Town Hall, but not a corresponding borough named Finsbury? In this hilarious Monty Pythonesque video from Jay Foreman, we go on a delightful tour of the problems and wacky compromises that led to the city’s 32 current boroughs.

title: Sibling stars in the London restaurant scene
desc: Karam, Sunaina, and Jyotin Sethi have built an empire of 15 diverse restaurant brands in London. In this episode of The Menu, the sibling trio explains their culinary journey, starting with Trishna, a Michelin-star Indian restaurant they opened in 2008.

title: Bringing tastes of the Philippines to London
desc: Chef Budgie Montoya aims to introduce and normalize Filipino cuisine with western eaters. The first part of this episode of The Menu describes his restaurant Sarap, which serves modern twists on Filipino flavors like lechón, kinilaw, or calamansi limes.

title: The nonchalant fashion of Beau Brummell
desc: Gazing into Picadilly Arcade is a statue of the dapper 19th-century socialite Beau Brummell. This fun episode of Articles of Interest explains how his minimalist and military-inspired attire influenced the uniformity of the ho-hum men’s suits worn today.

title: Air-raid shelters hiding in plain sight
desc: Scattered along the Northern Line are ten deep-level shelters built to protect people from World War II bombing. Starting at Clapham South, air-raid shelter enthusiast Geoff Marshall gives an above-ground tour of ones still visible from the street.

title: The Berners Street Hoax
desc: In 1809, the woman living at 54 Berners Street had undoubtedly the weirdest day of her life. This episode of the Futility Closet podcast tells the story of an elaborate practical joke that caused mayhem as hundreds of people suddenly arrived at her door.

title: How London is losing its appetite for jellied eels
desc: Jellied eels were once a popular dish in the east end of London, but have fallen out of favor as tastes change. This video from Great Big Story visits suppliers of live eels and a restaurant in Greenwich that proudly serves up a wiggly bowl of the fish.

title: British Library tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: The treasures room at the British Library is among the most underrated small museums in Europe. This excellent tour offers context for what’s on display: Gutenberg bibles, early printings of Shakespeare, an original copy of the Magna Carta, and much more.

title: Pulling on the thread of colonialism
desc: Like many western museums, the British Museum’s epic collection has a dark side: many pieces were stolen during wars or unscrupulous colonial exploits. This video from Vox explains the long-simmering debate about whether or not to return stolen artifacts.

title: Westminster tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Starting on Westminster Bridge in front of Big Ben and ending in Trafalgar Square, this engaging tour focuses on the government, history, war, and politics — all without being too academic or overbearing. Double the suggested 1 hour for a more casual pace.

title: British Museum tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: This useful introductory tour of the British Museum veers around the galleries to seek out its most notable Egyptian, Assyrian, and Greek artifacts. Double his suggested 90 minutes for a more relaxed pace, or finish the tour before exploring on your own.

title: Historic London tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Starting at the Church of St Clement Danes and ending at London Bridge, this tour spans the oldest parts of London. The vivid commentary and variety from stop-to-stop make it a delightful stroll. Best on a weekday around lunchtime. Allow at least 4 hours.

title: St. Paul’s Cathedral tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: St. Paul’s Cathedral has been an icon of London since it rose from the ashes of the Great Fire of London in 1666. This engaging tour explains the church itself and the many people buried there. Allow at least an hour, or two if you plan to climb the dome.

title: The spectacle of the suffragettes
desc: In 1910, dozens of women were physically and sexually assaulted by police in Parliament Square as they protested their lack of voting rights. This video from Vox vividly describes how the event triggered a more radical and militant era for suffragettes.

title: Reclaiming public space with congestion charges
desc: A busy road once stretched in front of The National Gallery before its pedestrianization in 2002. This report from Vox describes how London has taken significant measures to reduce the negative impacts of cars and how New York can learn from its example.

title: Dressing the judiciary with wigs and robes
desc: Founded in 1689, Ede & Ravenscroft is a London tailor with an unusual focus: making traditional wigs for the judiciary system. This video from Great Big Story shows how they stitch the horsehair wigs by hand and explains why modern judges still wear them.

title: John Snow and the Broad Street Pump
desc: In 1854, Physician John Snow discovered that Cholera is a water-borne disease, leading to the end of an epidemic that killed 616 people. This slick and engaging video from Vox tells the story of the Broad Street Pump, now marked by a public memorial.

title: Grime: The raw sounds of East London
desc: Grime is a music genre that emerged from an underground music community in the Bow E3 area of East London. This 2017 report from Vox explains the “raw form of energy” and quick tempo of the genre first popularized by Dizzee Rascal in the early 2000s.

title: Wealth far beyond Buckingham Palace
desc: Nestled among buildings near Waterloo Bridge is Savoy Chapel, part of a vast array of real-estate holdings tied to the royal family. This Vox report explains how the inconspicuous chapel invites a larger question: How does the royal family make money?

title: Brick Lane walking tour with author Tarquin Hall
desc: Starting at the venerable bagel shop Beigel Bake and ending at the contemporary Whitechapel Gallery, this fabulous walking tour meanders down colorful Brick Lane — a street shaped by Huguenots, Jews, Bangladeshis, artists, and more. Allow at least an hour.

title: The tastemaker of the contemporary art world
desc: Saatchi Gallery is a fabulous (and free) contemporary art gallery in the posh Chelsea neighborhood. This 2016 report from Vox recounts how the influence of the gallery’s founder Charles Saatchi has led to dizzyingly pricey bids at high-end art auctions.

title: Having a pint with Charles Dickens
place: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese pub, Fleet Street
desc: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese is a 350-year-old pub frequented by Charles Dickens. Starting there, this report from Monocle stops by more pubs mentioned in Dickens novels: George and Vulture, The Spaniards Inn, The One Tun, the George Inn, and The Grapes.

title: Fifty years of humane public housing at Dawson’s Heights
place: Dawson’s Heights housing estate, East Dulwich
desc: Completed in 1972, Dawson’s Heights is a public housing building in South London that feels both geometric and organic, as if made haphazardly from toy blocks. This story from Monocle explains how the 50-year-old design has engendered a sense of community.

title: Regret and revival at the Millennium Dome
desc: The Millennium Dome is a tent-like venue that barely opened in time for the New Year in 2000. This piece from The Guardian recounts the disjointed design process, rushed construction, public skepticism, infighting, and mixed-emotions the project roused.

title: The simple joys of Gasholder Park
desc: Near King’s Cross Station is a small circular park built inside the structure of the mammoth cast-iron frame of a 170-year-old gas tank. This report from Monocle admires the creativity, ingenuity, and simplicity of the project, completed in 2017.

title: A modern look at ancient Stonehenge
desc: Two hours from London stands Stonehenge, the neolithic site that has captivated imaginations for thousands of years. This casual and cheerful episode of You’re Dead to Me pairs a historian with a comedian to explain the massive and mysterious stone circle.

title: Thirty years at The River Café
desc: Opened in 1987, The River Café is a high-end Italian restaurant known for its inventive yet simple food. In this chatty and engaging episode of Bon Appétit Foodcast, owner Ruth Rogers candidly shares stories about running such a long-lasting restaurant.

title: Spending time with pastry chef Claire Ptak
desc: Violet is a bakery in East London specializing in high-end cupcakes, brownies, pies, cookies, and other sweet treats. This cheerful episode of Bon Appétit’s Foodcast chats with American owner and acclaimed pastry chef Claire Ptak about her work and life.

title: The origins of punk style
desc: Punk music may have originated in America, but the iconic style came from London. This fun episode of Articles of Interest takes a thought-provoking look at how the safety-pin aesthetic emerged from designer Vivienne Westwood’s shop at 430 Kings Road.

title: The Union of Women Matchmakers goes on strike
desc: In July 1888, female workers at the Bryant & May Factory in East London walked out, demanding safer working conditions. This episode of This Day in History Class explains how the “match girls” inspired others to speak out against blatant workplace dangers.

title: Regent’s Canal nature walk with conservationist Kabir Kaul
desc: Starting at Islington tunnel, this short walk along Regent’s Canal contains many quick interviews with conservationists and designers involved in keeping London green and wild. The walk to Kingsland Basin only takes 30 minutes, so amble while you listen.

title: Fond memories of Eel Pie Island
desc: Given its small size, London’s Eel Pie Island has a big history. This episode of The Kitchen Sisters shares stories about the island’s fishy name and how it became a destination for rock icons like David Bowie, Mick Jagger, Pink Floyd, and Black Sabbath.

title: Roman ruins hiding in a modern city
place: London Mithraeum (Temple of Mithras), Bloomberg building
desc: In this London History episode, tour guide Ian McDiarmid explains Londinium, founded by the Romans in 47 AD. Archaeologists recently restored some of the city’s best-preserved Roman ruins: The Temple of Mithras inside the modern Bloomberg headquarters.

title: Back to Black
creator: Amy Winehouse
desc: Amy Winehouse’s haunting 2006 title track turned heartbreak into modern soul. The late singer was the heart of Camden’s music scene; a bronze statue of her now stands in Camden’s Stables Market, near the pubs and stages she made her own.

title: A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square
creator: Vera Lynn
desc: This dreamy 1939 song imagines a nightingale singing on a magical night in Berkeley Square, an elegant garden square in Mayfair. A favourite of the war years, recorded by Vera Lynn and many others, it became a symbol of a romantic London.

title: Waterloo Sunset
creator: The Kinks
desc: The Kinks’ gentle 1967 classic watches lovers meet by Waterloo Station as the sun sets over the Thames. Ray Davies turns an ordinary evening on Waterloo Bridge into something quietly beautiful — for many, the greatest song ever written about London.

title: West End Girls
creator: Pet Shop Boys
desc: The Pet Shop Boys’ cool, half-spoken 1984 synth-pop hit moves between London’s glamorous West End — the theatre-and-shopping heart of town near Soho — and the grittier East End, sketching the city’s divides over an icy beat.

title: Zadok the Priest
creator: George Frideric Handel
desc: Handel wrote this thunderous choral anthem for a coronation in 1727, and it’s been sung at every British coronation since. The German-born composer made London his home and is buried in Westminster Abbey, where monarchs are still crowned.

title: Land of Hope and Glory
creator: Edward Elgar
desc: Elgar’s grand, swelling melody — officially “Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1” — is a patriotic singalong known to every Briton. Its home is the Last Night of the Proms, the flag-waving finale of the summer concerts at the Royal Albert Hall.

title: Life on Mars?
creator: David Bowie
desc: David Bowie’s surreal 1971 ballad is one of his most loved songs. Bowie was born in Brixton, South London; since his death in 2016, the colourful Bowie mural near Brixton station has become a shrine where fans still leave flowers.

title: London Calling
creator: The Clash
desc: The Clash’s urgent 1979 anthem sounds an alarm over a London of unrest and a rising Thames. The punk band came up around Ladbroke Grove in west London, near where the Notting Hill Carnival riots of 1976 first fired their music.

title: Our House
creator: Madness
desc: Madness — the cheeky “Nutty Boys” of Camden Town — built bouncy ska-pop out of everyday London life. This warm 1982 hit remembers the happy chaos of a crowded family home, the sound of working-class North London in the early ’80s.

title: Parklife
creator: Blur
desc: Blur’s 1994 Britpop romp, narrated in a broad cockney accent by actor Phil Daniels, celebrates the small rhythms of London life — joggers, pigeons, and the daily grind in the park. It became an anthem of ’90s “Cool Britannia.”

title: Hometown Glory
creator: Adele
desc: Adele wrote her first single at sixteen — a piano ballad in praise of the place that raised her. “Hometown Glory” is a love letter to her corner of South London around West Norwood, the streets she didn’t want to leave behind.

title: Fix Up, Look Sharp
creator: Dizzee Rascal
desc: Dizzee Rascal helped invent grime — London’s raw, electronic answer to hip-hop — as a teenager on the estates of Bow, East London. This hard-hitting 2003 track, from his prize-winning debut, announced a sound the whole city would claim.

title: Back to Life
place: Site of the Africa Centre, King Street
creator: Soul II Soul
desc: Soul II Soul’s smooth, bass-heavy 1989 number one defined a new Black British sound. The collective, led by Jazzie B, built its name at legendary Sunday club nights at the Africa Centre in Covent Garden before conquering charts worldwide.

title: Vossi Bop
creator: Stormzy
desc: Stormzy, from Croydon in South London, is Britain’s biggest rapper and the first Black British solo act to headline Glastonbury. This swaggering 2019 number one mixes street slang with sly digs at the government — modern London at full volume.
