title: Introvert
creator: Little Simz
desc: Little Simz, from Islington in North London, is one of Britain’s most acclaimed rappers. This cinematic 2021 track, with blaring horns and sharp self-reflection, opens her award-winning album and shows how far London rap has travelled.

title: Four centuries of history at Fortnum & Mason
desc: Opened in 1707, the venerable London department store Fortnum & Mason has so much history that they have an on-staff archivist. This video from Londonist goes on a whirlwind tour of the store’s history and most well-known offerings.

title: The fake houses of Leinster Gardens
desc: The neoclassical buildings at 23 and 24 Leinster Gardens aren’t buildings at all — they’re just facades. This video from Half-Asleep Chris describes the odd compromise that resulted from a tube line needing to cut through an affluent London street.

title: The first public drinking fountain in London
place: First public drinking fountain, St Sepulchre’s Church
desc: On the corner outside St. Sepulchre’s Church sits London’s first public drinking fountain, which opened to fanfare in 1859. This episode of 99% Invisible explains the fascinating societal contexts surrounding the dawning age of public drinking fountains.

title: Exploring off-limits areas in St. Paul’s Cathedral
desc: Many nooks and crannies within St. Paul’s Cathedral are not accessible by visitors. This video from Londonist takes us on a surprisingly adventurous tour through cramped spaces, rooftop traverses, and harrowing viewpoints usually closed to the public.

title: The much-loved corpse of Jeremy Bentham
place: Jeremy Bentham auto-icon, University College London
desc: In a chair at the end of a hallway in London’s University College sits the corpse of eccentric philosopher Jeremy Bentham. This video from Atlas Obscura tells the hilariously odd story of how he became an auto-icon — a statue made from a dead body.

title: The German ambassador’s canine companion
desc: In this video, tour guide Julian McDonnell tells the story of a German ambassador whose dog has been buried in London since 1934. The footage of the reluctant-Nazi ambassador’s coffin parading through the streets of London is genuinely shocking.

title: Royal accouterments at Hampton Court Palace
desc: In this video from CBS Sunday Morning, host Jane Pauley takes a trip just outside London to Hampton Court Palace, home of King Henry VIII. An enthusiastic curator provides a look at some regal clothing and decorative frippery in the palace’s archives.

title: Preparations for the death of a monarch
desc: Since her coronation, Queen Elizabeth’s handlers have been quietly preparing the procedures and logistics in the event of her death. In this episode of The Omnibus, Ken Jennings and John Roderick banter as they relay details about the unusual occurrence.

title: Re-discovering the lost art of globemaking
desc: This video from Great Big Story goes behind the scenes at one of the world’s only remaining workshops making handmade globes. The process is incredibly labor-intensive, requiring three woodworkers, three globemakers, three painters, and one cartographer.

title: King’s Cross: Redeveloping a neighborhood at a human scale
desc: This video from Monocle Films illuminates the thinking behind the new buildings and public spaces in the King’s Cross neighborhood. The architects and planners describe their efforts to make the redeveloped area vibrant, engaging, and inviting for all.

title: Introducing the Victoria & Albert Museum
desc: This official video published by the Victoria & Albert Museum highlights the history and mission of a longstanding institution that offers one of the world’s most exciting and rewarding museum experiences.

title: Designing a stadium that adapts to different needs
desc: Hosting the Olympics has often led to long-term financial woes and underused infrastructure in a city. This video from Architects’ Journal shows the great lengths the architects took to design London’s Olympic Stadium with its future in mind.

title: British monarchs from 1066 to the present day
desc: British history has so many famous royals that it is hard to keep all of the Richards and Elizabeths and Henrys and Marys and Williams straight. This funny and frenetic video from CGP Gray will make you feel better because, well... it’s very complicated.

title: A modern home for the Design Museum
desc: In this video, two journalists from the Financial Times tour the Design Museum’s new building in Kensington as it opened in 2016. They share thoughts about the building’s form and show how the collection goes beyond merely presenting designed objects.

title: A close look at three pieces in the National Portrait Gallery
desc: The fabulous National Portrait Gallery can be overshadowed by the National Gallery, its neighbor in Trafalgar Square. In this video from the auction house Christie’s, the museum’s director shares stories about three portraits in their collection.

title: Among the world’s most expensive places to build
desc: The unusual shape of the Leadenhall Building—more popularly known as the Cheese Grater—is influenced by one of London’s many rules and regulations governing construction. This video from The Economist explains why new buildings are so costly.

title: Crossing the Thames by ferry in the 18th century
desc: With only one bridge spanning the Thames until 1750, many Londoners crossed the river by ferry. In this video from Londonist, tour guide Vicky Pipe recounts how ferrymen waited for passengers exiting Bankside’s plentiful theatres, brothels, and pubs.

title: The dinosaurs of Crystal Palace Park
place: Crystal Palace dinosaurs, Crystal Palace Park
desc: In 1854, the world’s first sculptures of dinosaurs dazzled the public at the Great Exhibition. In this video, Tom Scott describes why the beloved (yet scientifically inaccurate) dinosaurs are legally required to remain preserved in their current state.

title: Central Saint Martins: a hub for students of art and design
desc: Adapting a historic grain warehouse, Stanton Williams Architects designed a new home for London’s University of the Arts. This video from Monocle showcases the clever space-planning and beautiful raw textures that surround the students as they learn.

title: Rothko: The simple expression of complex thought
desc: The Rothko Room at the Tate Modern can be a profoundly moving art experience. This fast-paced video from The Art Assignment offers a thoughtful primer to Rothko’s massive minimalist paintings. Pro tip: visit while listening to the album ( ) by Sigur Rós.

title: Building a new line on the London Underground
desc: This video from Bloomberg begins with some dull complaints about the city’s traffic. Still, it quickly gets interesting by offering a beneath-the-surface look at the new Crossrail tube line under construction. The tunnel boring machines are incredible.

title: Patterns in the pavement to help people get around
desc: Just south of St. Pancras station is the advocacy organization Royal National Institute of Blind People. In this video, Tom Scott decodes the meaning of the tactile shapes and patterns in London’s sidewalks that help partially-signed people navigate.

title: Studying tiny bees in a big museum
desc: Unbeknownst to most visitors, London’s Natural History Museum employs 300 scientists who study the natural world. In this video from Google Arts & Culture, we go behind the scenes to meet a team researching how honey bees carry air pollutants.

title: Helping kids see themselves in the stories they read
desc: Only one percent of nearly 10,000 children’s books published in the UK in 2017 featured non-white main characters. This video from BBC London showcases Round Table Books in Brixton, which promotes books that reflect the wide diversity of London’s kids.

title: Building a residential skyscraper on reclaimed land
place: One Park Drive tower, Canary Wharf
desc: This video from B1M takes a look at the creation of One Park Drive, a cylindrical tower built on reclaimed land in London’s trendy Canary Wharf neighborhood. The video is so pro-development that it feels like an advertisement, but it’s interesting anyway.

title: Inside the awe-inspiring Cast Courts at the V&A Museum
place: Cast Courts, Victoria and Albert Museum
desc: The Victoria & Albert Museum houses two rooms packed with full-size copies of famous art, including the massive Trajan’s Column from Rome and Michelangelo’s David from Florence. This stunning drone footage nicely captures the experience of visiting.

title: The heyday of London’s early punk music scene
place: Site of the Roxy club, Neal Street
desc: In the late 1970s, the Roxy rapidly became the heart of London’s burgeoning punk scene. This episode of The History Listen vividly recounts how punks were influenced and intertwined with the reggae community. The club at 41 Neal Street no longer exists.

title: Building human towers ten people high
desc: Teams build human towers up to ten people high in squares like this one, a tradition older than 200 years where the lightest climber, usually a child, tops the structure. The Catalan phrase for teamwork, fer pinya, comes straight from it.

title: The bell tolls for Whitechapel Bell Foundry
desc: Before closing in 2017, Whitechapel Bell Foundry had been in business since 1570. Some of the factory’s bells are genuinely famous — Big Ben and the Liberty Bell among them. This slightly cheesy video from CBS Sunday Morning tells the shop’s story.

title: From Londinium to the present day
desc: London’s storied history began as the Roman settlement Londinium, some remnants of which can still be seen near Tower Bridge today. In this video from CBS Sunday Morning, Jane Pauley provides a quick primer on significant events that shaped the city.

title: The pioneering women of British Modernism
desc: Tate Britain showcases British art from the 16th century to the present day. In this video from the auction house Christie’s, art historian Katy Hessel provides a passionate and energetic primer on women who shaped modern art in Britain.

title: A building adorned with brick and wicker
place: Barrett’s Grove apartment building, Stoke Newington
desc: In 2017, the apartment building Barrett’s Grove was shortlisted for Building of the Year by the Royal Institute of British Architects. In this video by Architects’ Journal, the architect describes their goal to make durable and high-quality housing.

title: Allies turn on each other mid-war
desc: In May 1937, street fighting erupted here and across Barcelona as anarchists and Communists turned on each other mid-war over the telephone exchange — the May Days that Orwell, fighting nearby, wrote into Homage to Catalonia.

title: A museum shows only the art someone tried to ban
place: Museum of Forbidden Art (Museu de l’Art Prohibit)
desc: The Museu de l’Art Prohibit, in a modernista mansion on Carrer de la Diputació, collects works that were censored, banned or attacked for political, religious or social reasons. Its founders talk about the collection and about censorship under Franco.

title: A coppersmith’s son from Reus becomes Barcelona’s strangest architect
desc: Casa Vicens, a tiled summer house in Gràcia finished in 1885, was Antoni Gaudí’s first major commission. This episode follows his childhood illnesses, his schooling and the early jobs that led him here, decades before the Sagrada Família.

title: A protest against a colonial war ends with churches on fire
desc: In July 1909 reservists shipped from Barcelona’s port to fight in Morocco, and the protests that followed turned into a week of riots and burned convents. Historians explain why some call it a revolution and how the city earned the name “Rose of Fire.”

title: A bus driver hijacks his own bus to reach a forgotten hillside
desc: Torre Baró, a neighbourhood on the Collserola hills, was built by migrants from the 1950s with no water, power or buses. The story of driver Manolo Vital, told in the film El 47, comes with its director, its actors and residents who live there now.

title: Car workers occupy their factory and face Franco’s police
desc: On 18 October 1971 workers at SEAT’s Zona Franca car plant struck over sacked colleagues. A 12-hour standoff with police left worker Antonio Ruiz Villalba dead. Two men who were there recall one of late Francoism’s defining labour fights.

title: A showpiece prison spends a century filling with political inmates
desc: La Model, a star-shaped prison in the Eixample, opened in 1904 as an example of modern reform. Under Franco it held thousands of political prisoners. It closed in 2017 and is now a memorial site; a guide and the Puig Antich sisters tell its story.

title: Commuters still ride tunnels dug a hundred years ago
desc: Barcelona’s first metro line opened on 30 December 1924 between Plaça de Catalunya and Lesseps, a stretch now on line 3. The episode covers station-name stories, the buskers who play underground and the ghost stations opened for the centenary.

title: Gaudí’s teacher builds a concert hall out of glass and tile
place: Palau de la Música Catalana concert hall
desc: The Palau de la Música Catalana, a concert hall finished in 1908, and the Sant Pau hospital are the best-known works of Lluís Domènech i Montaner. Marking a century since his death, the episode covers his buildings, his teaching and his politics.

title: Three chefs from elBulli open the world’s best restaurant
desc: Disfrutar, a restaurant on Carrer de Villarroel in the Eixample, was named the world’s best in 2024. Chef Eduard Xatruch shows the kitchen and explains how he and his two partners design dishes around memory and emotion as much as taste.

title: A supercomputer hums inside a deconsecrated chapel
desc: MareNostrum, the Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s machine, sits inside Torre Girona, a former chapel on the university campus. Researchers explain what 314 petaflops means, what it is used for, and the quantum computer being built next door.

title: A region votes to leave Spain and the state says no
desc: Vox explains the history behind Catalonia’s push for independence and the disputed 2017 referendum. The Parliament of Catalonia sits in the old arsenal in Ciutadella Park, where the declaration was voted and then suspended.

title: Residents push back against the visitors filling their streets
desc: Residents of Barcelona say rising rents and crowds of visitors are pushing them out. DW reports on the protests and the city’s curbs on tourist flats. Barceloneta, the old fishermen’s quarter by the beach, has long been a flashpoint.

title: A teenage Picasso learns to paint in a medieval street
desc: Picasso spent his formative years in Barcelona, and the museum in five Gothic palaces on Carrer Montcada holds the student work that shows how fast he mastered academic painting, plus his late variations on Velázquez’s Las Meninas.

title: A temporary pavilion is torn down, then rebuilt as a legend
desc: Mies van der Rohe designed Germany’s pavilion for the 1929 International Exposition on Montjuïc: marble, onyx and glass walls under a floating roof. It was dismantled in 1930 and rebuilt on the same site in 1986. This film explains its open plan.

title: Medieval lanes give way to beaches built for the 1992 Games
desc: A short walk through the Barri Gòtic, the old Roman and medieval core around the cathedral, then down to the sand at Barceloneta, the former fishermen’s district whose beaches were remade when the city hosted the Olympics.

title: A sweep of Gaudí’s houses, from dragon roofs to a hidden crypt
desc: Design historian Paul Greenhalgh starts at Palau Güell, the dark, lavish townhouse Gaudí built off the Rambla for his patron, then works through Casa Batlló, La Pedrera and the Colònia Güell crypt, placing them within Art Nouveau.

title: Rival architects line up their showpieces on one boulevard
desc: Around 1900 Barcelona’s new rich commissioned Modernista houses along Passeig de Gràcia, the grand avenue of the Eixample. On one block Gaudí’s Casa Batlló, with its bone-like balconies, stands beside buildings by Puig i Cadafalch and Domènech i Montaner.

title: A tree-lined boulevard runs from the old city down to the port
desc: Rick Steves walks La Rambla, the promenade that follows a filled-in riverbed from Plaça de Catalunya to the Columbus monument, past flower stalls, the Boqueria market and the Liceu opera house.

title: Grids of streets are handed back from cars to neighbours
desc: Barcelona’s ‘superilles’ group nine blocks of Cerdà’s grid together and push through-traffic to the edges, leaving the inner streets for play, trees and benches. The first big one was tried out in Poblenou, the old industrial district.

title: A 1934 cruise ship drops anchor and passengers go ashore
desc: Unissued newsreel footage of Barcelona two years before the Spanish Civil War, shot on a Mediterranean cruise stop. Ships then tied up at the old port, at the foot of the Rambla and the Columbus column.

title: A Japanese sculptor spends his life carving for Gaudí’s basilica
desc: Etsuro Sotoo came to Barcelona in 1978 to cut stone and stayed for decades, carving musician angels and fruit for the Sagrada Família. His work is on the Nativity façade of the basilica in the Eixample district.

title: A concert hall and a hospital dressed in glass, tile and mosaic
place: Palau de la Música Catalana concert hall
desc: Both are by Lluís Domènech i Montaner, Gaudí’s contemporary: the Palau de la Música, a concert hall under a stained-glass skylight in La Ribera, and Sant Pau, a hospital laid out as a garden of pavilions near the Sagrada Família.

title: Nearly 100,000 seats for one football club in Les Corts
desc: Camp Nou opened in 1957 as FC Barcelona’s home ground and grew into the largest football stadium in Europe. It stands in the Les Corts district on the city’s west side, where a major rebuild began in 2023.

title: The woman who fights bulls
desc: This video from BBC Reel tells the story of a rejoneador—a bullfighter on horseback—who practices their brutal craft in bullrings throughout Spain, including Las Ventas in Madrid. Unexpectedly, the bullfighter Lea Vicens is a young woman born in France.

title: Jamón Jamón: Getting to know Spanish ham
desc: In this video from Devour Tours, Lauren Aloise visits Mercado Jamón Ibérico to explain the ins-and-outs of eating ham in Spain. Arguably the best in the world—jamón ibérico de bellota—is from black-hooved, acorn-fed pigs native to the Iberian peninsula.

title: Theater during the Spanish Golden Age
place: Corral de Comedias theatre, Alcalá de Henares
desc: Built in 1601 on the outskirts of Madrid, Corral de Comedias de Alcalá de Henares is among the oldest preserved theaters in Europe. This detailed video from Crash Course provides a thorough and engaging introduction to Renaissance-era theater in Spain.

title: The hidden restaurant near Plaza de España
place: Cafetería Yulong Zhou, Plaza de España underpass
desc: In an underground walkway in a parking garage near Plaza de España is tricky-to-find Cafetería Yulong Zhou. In this fun video from Great Big Story, we meet the charming owners of a restaurant specializing in authentic dishes from Qingtian in China.

title: The disappearing barquilleros
desc: This video from Culture Trip visits Plaza Mayor to see Julian Cañas, a hawker of homemade waffles rolled into cylinders. The traditional treat is now mass-produced, so there are few people like him left in Madrid. His pride and dedication are palpable.

title: Five classic tapas to try in Madrid
place: La Casa del Abuelo tapas bar
desc: In this video from Devour Tours, James Blick visits La Casa del Abuelo to explain five traditional tapas. He tries lightly fried prawns in oil, breaded calamari, langoustine croquettes, green peppers from Galicia, and the tasty pork dish Secreto Ibérico.

title: Breathing new life into Franco-era military apartments
desc: On the surface, Edificio Princesa may seem like an imposing 1970s concrete apartment building. This video from Monocle explains how the building has a more compelling story that mirrors changes in Spain as it transitioned from dictatorship to democracy.

title: The oldest restaurant in the world
desc: Opened in 1725, Sobrino de Botín has been going strong for 295 years. In this video from Great Big Story, a longtime staff member shares the restaurant’s classic, unembellished approach to food. The top dish: suckling pig with potatoes and jamón ibérico.

title: Archiving the world’s art and cultural treasures
desc: Factum Arte uses high-res scanning and 3D printing to accurately replicate works of art, from Veronese paintings to Egyptian tombs. In this video from Great Big Story, director Adam Lowe explains their noble mission to record our cultural heritage.

title: Suiting up matadors at Fermín Tailor Shop
place: Fermín bullfighters’ tailor shop (not open to visitors)
desc: Antonio López Fuentes runs an unusual tailoring business — all of his clients are bullfighters. In this video from Great Big Story, he describes his passion for outfitting matadors and shows the labor and time involved in making an outfit. (Not visitable)

title: Street racing with daredevil bike messengers
desc: This video from Nowness offers a cinematic peek into Madrid’s bike messenger subculture, notable for its illegal and dangerous races across the city. At the end of the video, they ride underneath the historic Segovia Viaduct in the La Latina neighborhood.

title: Colegio Estudio: A school infused with idealism
desc: Founded by three women in the 1940s under the dark cloud of fascism in Spain, Colegio Estudio is a cheery school dedicated to progressive democratic values. This video from Monocle Films looks at how their 1966 campus reinforces the school’s lofty ideals.

title: Touching art at the Prado
desc: In 2015, the Prado Museum held an exhibit featuring tactile recreations of famous masterpieces to give visually-impaired people a hands-on experience with art. In this video from PBS NewsHour, Alison Stewart describes the 3D printing process called Didú.

title: Memories of bullfighting on Plaza Mayor
desc: In this video, Rick Steves stops by lovely Plaza Mayor—once a bullfighting ring—to share some historical moments the square has witnessed. Just off of the plaza, he visits La Torre del Oro, a tiny bar slathered wall-to-wall with bullfighting memorabilia.

title: Looking closely at Las Meninas by Velasquez
desc: Las Meninas by Diego Velasquez is not only a highlight of the Prado Museum but a standout in art history more broadly. In this video from Nerdwriter, Evan Puschak takes a detailed and rewarding look at its complex visual composition and deeper symbolism.

title: The high-speed train to Barcelona
desc: Since 2006, passengers have been able to leave Madrid’s Atocha Station and zip toward Barcelona in a high-speed train traveling 350km per hour. In this video from Smithsonian Channel, Teddy Wilson explains the technology underpinning the speedy train.

title: What it’s like to be held hostage during a failed coup
desc: In 1981, 350 politicians in newly-democratic Spain met at Madrid’s Congress of Deputies to elect a new prime minister. This episode of Witness History describes what happened next: an armed far-right military leader held them hostage and attempted a coup.

title: A day trip to monumental El Escorial
desc: An hour outside Madrid is El Escorial, a complex built during the 16th-century reformation. In this video, Rick Steves explains its many functions — a regal palace, mausoleum for generations of Spanish royalty, a religious school, library, and monastery.

title: A more sustainable world one garden at a time
place: Desert City botanical garden, San Sebastián de los Reyes
desc: Describing itself as an “experimental botanical gardens,” Desert City aims to increase the adoption of eco-friendly plants like cactuses and succulents. This video from Dezeen doesn’t tell much of a story but has beautiful footage of this unique project.

title: An assemblage of flavors at Mercado San Miguel
desc: Madrid has many terrific food markets, including posh Mercado San Miguel, which keeps its fanciness in check by still having plenty of adventurous food. In this video, a food tour guide from Devour Tours shares some of her favorite restaurants and bites.

title: The pact to forget a fascist past
desc: In 1977, Spain passed “the pact of forgetting,” a law providing amnesty to people on all sides of the Spanish Civil War and Franco’s regime. This 99% Invisible episode explains how the Valley of the Fallen near Madrid makes avoiding the issue difficult.

title: The culture of eating tapas in Madrid
desc: In this video from Monocle, food writer Helena Vaello explains the culture and norms around tapas in Madrid and some key terminology: tapas, pintxos, and raciones. The video shows many tapas bars, including highly-rated La Colmada and Casa Macareno.

title: Confronting Spain’s past via Franco’s resting place
desc: In late 2019, the remains of fascist dictator Francisco Franco were exhumed from his grandiose tomb in the Valley of the Fallen northwest of Madrid. This video by PBS NewsHour explains the controversy of moving Franco’s coffin to a less lauded location.

title: Surviving the bombing of Guernica
desc: Picasso’s famous painting Guernica—on display at the Reina Sofia Museum in Madrid—drew global attention to the brutal bombing of the Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. This episode of Witness History relays horrific firsthand accounts of survivors.

title: The assassination of Spain’s new prime minister
place: Claudio Coello 104 (site of 1973 Carrero Blanco bombing)
desc: In December 1973, a Basque separatist group assassinated Luis Carrero Blanco, Spain’s prime minister of only six months. This episode of Witness History recounts the grisly bomb attack outside San Francisco de Borja church and its political aftershocks.

title: The bladesmith of Toledo
desc: Fabrica Zamorano is a third-generation swordmaking shop in Toledo, a short train ride from Madrid. Despite pronouncing “Toledo” like it’s in Ohio instead of Spain, this video is an excellent introduction to the town’s millennia-old blade-making tradition.

title: Procuring the perfect paella
desc: AlliOli is one of the few places to get authentic Valencian-style paella in central Madrid. This fun video from Great Big Story explains Wikipaella, a website that officially blesses restaurants outside Valencia for their traditional paella prowess.

title: Terror on the transit system
desc: On 11 March 2004, a series of bombs exploded on commuter trains bound for Atocha Station, killing 191 people. In this graphic episode of Witness History, a paramedic describes the fear, worry, and shock as his team responded to the synchronized attacks.

title: Christmas traditions in Madrid
desc: Every year, Plaza Mayor transforms into a lively Christmas market. In this episode of Notes from Spain, Madrid native Marina Diez and her British husband visit the plaza to share insights and stories about the city’s many holiday traditions.

title: Seeing flamenco outside of Andalusia
desc: This episode of Notes from Spain briefly explains Madrid’s flamenco scene, then plays audio from a performance. Both places mentioned have since closed, but it’s worth seeing a show at a well-regarded venue like Las Carboneras. Live flamenco is terrific.

title: Madrid tour with travel writer Rick Steves
desc: Round trip from Puerta del Sol, this walk provides a lively introduction to Madrid’s history, culture, traditions, and food. There are many snack stops in the first half, so consider starting hungry and eating anywhere mentioned. Allow at least 3 hours.

title: Attending a bullfight at Las Ventas bullring
desc: This lengthy episode of When In Spain opens with a brief history of bullfighting, the famously controversial tradition in Spain. Next, the British host attends a fight at Las Ventas with his aficionado friend, who contextualizes what he sees and hears.

title: The sorrowful demise of Federico García Lorca
place: Lorca statue, Plaza de Santa Ana
desc: At the center of Plaza de Santa Ana is a statue honoring poet and playwright Federico García Lorca. This episode of Witness History describes how a fascist death squad killed the likable and imaginative writer as Franco’s right-wing rose to power in 1936.

title: Imagining a cathedral and making it a reality
place: Justo Gallego’s cathedral, Mejorada del Campo
desc: Justo Gallego became deeply devout when he saw priests shot by Franco’s troops during the Spanish Civil War. In this video from Great Big Story, he shares how his faith drove him to slowly build an incredible homemade cathedral for the last 50 years.

title: Relaxing in the gardens of El Escorial
place: Friars’ Garden, Royal Monastery of El Escorial
desc: In this chatty episode of Notes From Spain, hosts Marina Diez and Ben Curtis venture north of Madrid to visit El Escorial, a charming town known for its massive palace and monastery. They advise visiting the mausoleum and easy-to-miss gardens in the back.

title: The scandal that sullied the People’s Party
desc: In 2007 at the hotel Gran Meliá Fénix, a whistleblower covertly recorded politician Francisco Correa Sanchez implicating himself in fraud. The recordings set off the Gürtel Case, a €120 million corruption scandal chronicled in this story from The Guardian.

title: The peculiar world of The Garden of Earthly Delights
desc: One of the Prado’s highlights is The Garden of Earthly Delights, a wonderfully strange painting by Hieronymus Bosch. In this jokey and diversion-filled episode of The Omnibus, the quick-witted hosts banter about the bizarre triptych. (Gets going at ~9:30)

title: Exploring the historic barrio of La Latina
place: Mercado de la Cebada market, La Latina
desc: Mercado de la Cebada is a charmingly scrappy market in the heart of the La Latina neighborhood. In this episode of When In Spain, host Paul Burge tours La Latina on foot as he explains its traditional-yet-gentrifying character and notable places to stop.

title: Getting to know Madrid’s Romani people
desc: In Puerta del Sol, it’s easy to spot Madrid’s Romani community, often pejoratively called gypsies. In this fascinating interview from When In Spain, an American photographer explains how he slowly befriended members of the oft-maligned ethnic group.

title: Stellar streets and squares in Madrid
desc: In this episode of When In Spain, a Brit and American living in Madrid share tips about their favorite little parts of town, starting with Plaza de Olavide. Their affection for Madrid is contagious. See the podcast’s show notes for each place they visit.

title: Dark legacies of the idealistic International Brigade
desc: In November 1936, thousands of foreign fighters from dozens of countries marched along Gran Via to join Spanish Republicans resisting Franco’s fascism. This report from The Guardian explains the thorny legacy of International Brigade troops decades later.

title: Reporting on the transition to democracy
desc: After Franco died in 1975, Spain entered a tumultuous few years as the dictatorship was dismantled. In this episode of When In Spain, a British reporter recounts how King Juan Carlos I encouraged reform and a democratic parliament in the fragile nation.

title: Day-tripping to royal Aranjuez
desc: This episode of When In Spain ventures a half-hour from Madrid to Aranjuez, a charming town with a massive 16th-century palace. The host extends his visit to the royal abode by seeing San Antonio Plaza, Calle de Principe, Casa Pablo, and Prince’s Garden.

title: The barrels and bodegas of the Sherry Triangle
desc: The venerable bar La Venencia is among the best places to enjoy sherry in Madrid. In this episode, sherry fanatic Annie Manson explains the long traditions and complex tastes of sherry-making. Don’t miss the handy sherry guide in the podcast’s show notes.

title: Sights and sounds of El Rastro market
desc: El Rastro is an enormous Sunday flea market going strong since 1740. Recorded at the market, this episode of “When In Spain” gives a short history of the market, offers tips for a visit, and vividly describes the endless antiques and bric-a-brac for sale.

title: Lady Madrid
creator: Pereza
desc: Pereza, a scruffy Madrid rock duo, made this swaggering anthem that treats the city itself like a lover — restless, nocturnal, impossible to quit. A staple of 2000s Spanish radio and a guitar-driven valentine to the capital.

title: Concierto de Aranjuez (Adagio)
creator: Joaquín Rodrigo
desc: Spain’s most beloved piece of classical music, written in 1939 for guitar and orchestra. Its aching slow movement evokes the gardens of the royal palace at Aranjuez, a lavish retreat just south of Madrid — fountains, birdsong, and faded grandeur.

title: La Verbena de la Paloma
creator: Tomás Bretón
desc: Zarzuela is Spain’s own comic light opera, and this 1894 favourite unfolds during the Verbena de la Paloma — a rowdy summer street party still held each August in the old La Latina quarter. The sound of traditional Madrid at play.

title: Madrid
creator: Agustín Lara
desc: Mexican composer Agustín Lara wrote Madrid’s most affectionate anthem without ever living there — a chotis, the city’s own old-fashioned dance. It name-checks the Gran Vía, calle de Alcalá, and the famous Chicote bar, toasting the old capital.

title: Madrid
creator: Burning
desc: Burning, a beloved Madrid rock-and-roll band, cut this gritty 1978 ode to their city, casting it as a tattooed, hard-drinking femme fatale you can’t help loving. The raw sound of Madrid’s rock scene just before La Movida exploded.

title: Pongamos que hablo de Madrid
creator: Joaquín Sabina
desc: The title means “let’s say I’m talking about Madrid.” Joaquín Sabina, the city’s great rogue songwriter, paints a grimy, tender 1980 portrait of a Madrid where even the birds, he sings, see a psychiatrist. A true anthem of the city.

title: La chica de ayer
creator: Nacha Pop
desc: The title means “yesterday’s girl.” Antonio Vega’s wistful 1980 song is the unofficial hymn of La Movida — the wild creative explosion of post-Franco Madrid. It nods to El Penta, the Malasaña bar that still plays it at closing time.

title: Quiero ser libre
creator: Los Chichos
desc: The title means “I want to be free.” Los Chichos, a Roma group formed in Madrid in 1973, made rumba the streetwise sound of the city’s rough edges — the music of the “quinqui” crime films and cassette decks of ’70s working-class Madrid.

title: Corazón Partío
creator: Alejandro Sanz
desc: The title means “broken heart,” in clipped Madrid slang. Madrid-born Alejandro Sanz fused pop with flamenco soul on this 1997 megahit — inescapable across Spain for years, and the song that made him a Latin superstar.

title: Hoy no me puedo levantar
creator: Mecano
desc: The title means “today I can’t get up” — too wrecked from a night out. Mecano, who became Spain’s biggest pop band, bottled La Movida’s all-night hedonism in this 1981 synth-pop romp from the bars of Malasaña. It later named a hit musical.

title: Cayetano
creator: Carolina Durante
desc: A “cayetano” is slang for a posh, preppy rich kid — the type linked to Madrid’s upscale Barrio de Salamanca. Carolina Durante’s snotty 2018 punk-pop hit skewers him gleefully, an instant anthem for the city’s indie youth.

title: A quién le importa
creator: Alaska y Dinarama
desc: The title means “who cares.” Alaska, the queen of La Movida, turned this 1986 synth-pop song into a defiant anthem of being yourself no matter what people say — long embraced in Chueca, Madrid’s vibrant LGBT neighbourhood.

title: Tú Me Dejaste de Querer
creator: C. Tangana
desc: The title means “you stopped loving me.” Madrid’s C. Tangana left trap behind to reinvent Spain’s roots music on his 2021 album El Madrileño (“the man from Madrid”). This rumba-flamenco heartbreaker smashed national streaming records overnight.

title: Rumba
creator: Natos y Waor
desc: Natos y Waor are the raw, hard-living face of Madrid hip-hop, rapping the city’s nights, friendships, and excess. This 2022 track captures the sound of young Madrid today: streetwise Spanish rap with a melodic, melancholy edge.

title: Copenhague
creator: Vetusta Morla
desc: Vetusta Morla were Madrid’s best-kept secret for years before their acclaimed 2008 debut made them indie heroes. From the northern suburb of Tres Cantos, they make thoughtful, layered rock — this one a tender song named after a faraway city.

title: The ghost station of the Madrid metro
desc: Between the Iglesia and Bilbao stops on Metro Line 1, you’ll see historic Chamberí station whizz by out the window. This slightly clunky video from Tim Traveller tours the forgotten station, now a museum, and explains why Madrid abandoned it in 1966.

title: A football temple gets a steel skin and a roof that closes
desc: Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabéu, opened in 1947 on the Paseo de la Castellana, has been wrapped in a steel facade and given a retractable roof and a pitch that slides away into storage beneath the stands.

title: Fifty thousand Romans gather for spectacle and blood
desc: Vespasian began this amphitheater using treasure from a conquered province, finishing it under his son Titus in 80 AD with a hundred days of inaugural games. It could hold roughly 50,000 spectators and flood for staged naval battles.

title: A dome with a hole in it survives two thousand years
desc: Hadrian rebuilt this temple around 126 AD with the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever constructed, still standing without a single crack. Its open oculus lets in rain, sun, and the occasional bird, exactly as intended for nearly two thousand years.

title: A reluctant sculptor becomes a painter under protest
desc: Pope Julius II forced this commission on Michelangelo, who considered himself a sculptor and resented painting at all. Contrary to popular myth, he stood on scaffolding rather than lying on his back, craning his neck in constant pain for four years.

title: Three thousand fans watch gladiators practice for free
desc: Slaves lived, trained, and slept at this barracks just steps from the Colosseum, connected to the arena by underground tunnels. Public training sessions drew crowds of up to 3,000, and the site itself stayed hidden until a chance discovery in 1937.

title: A funeral gone wrong burns down the Senate
desc: This marketplace-turned-political-heart of Rome hosted triumphal processions, riots, assassinations, and speeches that changed history. One funeral cremation got so out of hand it accidentally set fire to the Senate building itself.

title: Rome on Film: A Self-Guided Tour of La Dolce Vita Locations
creator: GeoBeat Audio Tour
desc: A film-locations walk through the Rome of La Dolce Vita and Roman Holiday. From a Triton fountain in a busy square, it follows movie backdrops past the coin-tossing fountain and the famous stairway, ending on a panoramic garden terrace.

title: A church sits on a church that sits on a pagan temple
desc: The basilica of San Clemente near the Colosseum is a stack of eras: a twelfth-century church with gold apse mosaics, a fourth-century church below it, and at the bottom Roman houses and a temple to Mithras, with water still running past.

title: Unpaid imperial troops loot Rome while the pope hides in a fortress
desc: In May 1527 mutinous troops of Emperor Charles V stormed Rome and plundered it for months. Pope Clement VII fled along a raised passage from the Vatican to Castel Sant’Angelo, the papal fortress on the Tiber, and was besieged there.

title: SS planners sketch a raid to carry off the pope
desc: In 1943, after Italy changed sides, Hitler is said to have floated a plan to occupy the Vatican and seize Pope Pius XII. The tiny state behind St Peter’s Square was never entered, and how far the plan went is still argued over.

title: Romans dump millions of oil jars into a hill of their own
desc: Monte Testaccio is a hill about 35 metres high made almost entirely of broken amphorae that once carried olive oil to ancient Rome. Classicist Garrett Ryan explains how it was stacked, what the stamps on the shards reveal, and why it was never cleared.

title: Artichokes are flattened and fried twice in the old Ghetto
place: Jewish Ghetto, Via del Portico d’Ottavia
desc: Carciofi alla giudia, whole artichokes fried until they open like crisp bronze flowers, are the signature dish of Rome’s Jewish community. Food writer Elizabeth Minchilli watches them made on Via del Portico d’Ottavia, the main street of the old Ghetto.

title: A new metro line digs straight through two thousand years
desc: Building Metro C under the historic centre meant excavating as it went. Archaeologist Darius Arya tours the Colosseo and Porta Metronia stations, opened in 2025, where finds from the dig are displayed along the way down to the platforms.

title: Crowds fill St Peter’s Square as a long papacy ends
desc: John Paul II died on 2 April 2005 after nearly 27 years as pope. Pilgrims had kept vigil below his window in St Peter’s Square, and millions came to Rome for the funeral held there six days later.

title: Young Swiss men sign up to guard the pope for a few years
desc: The Pontifical Swiss Guard has protected popes since 1506. Recruits must be Catholic Swiss men, sworn in each 6 May, the date 147 guards died in the 1527 Sack of Rome. Their barracks are inside Vatican City by the Porta Sant’Anna.

title: Nearly three thousand years of building inside the old city walls
desc: Listed in 1980 and enlarged in 1990, the site covers Rome inside the Aurelian Walls, from the Forum and Colosseum to Renaissance palaces, plus Vatican-owned churches such as St Paul Outside the Walls. The Roman Forum lies at its heart.

title: Romans bathe 1,600 at a time in a vast imperial spa
desc: Emperor Caracalla opened these baths in 216, with hot, warm and cold halls, a pool and libraries. Their brick walls still stand some 30 metres high south of the Circus Maximus, and host summer opera.

title: Early Christians bury their dead under an old Roman road
place: Catacombs of San Callisto, Appian Way
desc: The Appian Way left Rome for the south in 312 BC, lined with tombs. Below the fields beside it, early Christians dug kilometres of burial tunnels such as the Catacombs of San Callisto, a few kilometres outside the walls.

title: The world’s smallest country holds one of its largest art collections
desc: Vatican City covers under half a square kilometre, yet takes in St Peter’s Basilica, the Sistine Chapel and the Vatican Museums. It lies across the Tiber from the centre of Rome, ringed by its own walls.

title: Europe’s oldest Jewish community lives beside a Roman theatre
place: Jewish Ghetto, Via del Portico d’Ottavia
desc: Jews have lived in Rome for over 2,000 years; in 1555 a papal bull walled them into a ghetto by the Tiber. The quarter, with its domed Great Synagogue, lies beside the Portico of Octavia and Theatre of Marcellus.

title: Ivy-covered lanes across the river keep a village feel
desc: Trastevere, ‘across the Tiber’, is a working-class district of cobbled lanes, trattorias and the mosaic-filled church of Santa Maria in Trastevere. It sits on the west bank of the river, south of the Vatican.

title: Stray cats rule the ruins where Caesar was stabbed
desc: Largo di Torre Argentina is a sunken square of four Republican temples and part of Pompey’s theatre, where Julius Caesar was killed. Volunteers run a cat shelter in one corner, a short walk from the Pantheon.

title: Fifty thousand Romans file in for a day of blood and bread
desc: The Flavian Amphitheatre opened in AD 80 and held around 50,000 spectators, who came for beast hunts, executions and gladiator fights. It stands at the east end of the Roman Forum, Rome’s ancient civic centre.

title: Butter, cheese and a restaurant’s claim to a famous pasta
desc: Alfredo di Lelio served his fettuccine with butter and Parmesan in Rome in the early 1900s, and Hollywood visitors made it famous abroad. Alfredo alla Scrofa still serves it on Via della Scrofa, near Piazza Navona.

title: Cardinals locked in to choose a pope still have to eat
desc: Since 1878 papal elections have been held in the Sistine Chapel, with the cardinals shut away until a new pope is chosen and smoke signals the result. The chapel is part of the Vatican’s Apostolic Palace, beside St Peter’s Basilica.

title: Priests in goatskins run through the city each February
place: Site of the Lupercal cave, Palatine Hill
desc: The Lupercalia began at the Lupercal, the cave where the she-wolf was said to have nursed Romulus and Remus, and lasted into Christian times. Its site lies at the foot of the Palatine Hill, above the Circus Maximus.

title: Building the Crossrail Place Roof Garden
place: Crossrail Place Roof Garden, Canary Wharf
desc: This mesmerizing timelapse video from Architect’s Journal doesn’t have any sound, but it’s still an interesting look at the elaborate process required to build the publicly accessible Crossrail Place Roof Garden at Canary Wharf.

title: Looking closely at The Gare St. Lazare by Claude Monet
desc: It can be deeply satisfying to gaze at a single painting for an extended period. In this video from Google Arts & Culture, the frontman of the band Pulp narrates a slow and meditative look at a single Monet painting found in London’s National Gallery.

title: Becoming an auctioneer at Christie’s
desc: Founded in 1766, the London-based auction house Christie’s has sold billions of dollars worth of one-of-a-kind objects to its affluent clientele. In this video, their head auctioneer Hugh Edmeades offers a glimpse into the weird world of auctioneering.

title: A private pub just for Beefeaters
place: Yeoman Warders’ Club, Tower of London
desc: The Yeoman Warders—more commonly known as Beefeaters—are ceremonial guardians of the Tower of London. In this video from CBS Sunday Morning, host Jane Pauley goes behind the scenes to visit the Yeoman Warder’s private hangout.

title: The Globe Theatre in the Shakespeare era
desc: In this video from HarvardX, professor Stephen Greenblatt vividly describes the neighborhood surrounding the Globe Theatre during Shakespeare’s lifetime. His story about closures during the bubonic plague brought to mind the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

title: The ever-changing structure of the Serpentine Pavilion
desc: Every summer, a new architect is asked to build a temporary pavilion outside the Serpentine Gallery in Hyde Park. Although this video from Google Arts & Culture is a tad pretentious, it’s an excellent look at a yearly transformation of a public space.

title: Burlington Arcade’s behavior police
desc: At the historic Burlington Arcade shopping center in London’s Mayfair neighborhood, a private police force donning frock coats and top-hats has kept the local riff-raff in check for more than 200 years.

title: The time-ball at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich
desc: There’s something seriously endearing about videos by Half-Asleep Chris, and this one about the time-telling ball perched atop the Royal Observatory in Greenwich is no exception. Chris takes a fun look at Greenwich’s critical role in global timekeeping.

title: London’s only disability-friendly drag show
desc: Wayne Allingham is a disabled drag queen who founded “Disabled, Queer, and Here” nights at the Royal Vauxhall Tavern. This video from Culture Trip reveals the warmth, fun, and inclusivity of London’s community of people who are both LGBTQ and disabled.

title: A king pays Rubens to paint his father into heaven
desc: Charles I commissioned Rubens’s ceiling for the Banqueting House on Whitehall to glorify James I. In 1649 Charles walked beneath it to his execution on a scaffold outside. It is the only Rubens ceiling still in its original place.

title: A widow sculpts her husband for a square off Pall Mall
desc: The bronze of Captain Robert Falcon Scott in Waterloo Place was made by his widow, the sculptor Kathleen Scott, after his death returning from the South Pole in 1912. It shows him in polar gear and was unveiled in 1915.

title: A Victorian railway subway survives the palace it served
desc: Under Crystal Palace Parade lies a vaulted subway of red and cream brick that once led first-class passengers from their train into the Crystal Palace. The palace burned in 1936; the subway is opened up on certain days.

title: Steel gates rise from the river to keep the sea out
desc: The Thames Barrier at Woolwich has ten steel gates that lie on the riverbed and swing up when a surge tide threatens. Finished in 1982 after the deadly 1953 North Sea flood, it is closed more often each decade.

title: Green huts where cabbies still stop for a fry-up
desc: From 1875 a charity put up green wooden shelters so cab drivers could get a hot meal without leaving their horses. Thirteen survive and still serve food, including the one on the west side of Russell Square.

title: Ornate cast iron hides inside a sewage pumping station
desc: Crossness, on the marshes by the Thames at Abbey Wood, was built in 1865 as part of Joseph Bazalgette’s sewer network. Its giant beam engines sit within a painted cast-iron interior, now restored by volunteers.

title: A flat-pack iron church still stands in a Kilburn street
place: St Gabriel’s Tin Church, Cambridge Avenue
desc: Victorian congregations could order a prefabricated church of corrugated iron. Kilburn’s was put up on Cambridge Avenue in 1863, later fitted out inside as a mock ship by sea cadets, and is now a community space.

title: Parliament’s crumbling palace waits for a huge repair
desc: The Palace of Westminster, rebuilt by Barry and Pugin after the 1834 fire, has leaking roofs, asbestos and decades of patched-up wiring. MPs have argued for years over whether to move out so it can be fixed.

title: Spies move into a riverside ziggurat at Vauxhall
desc: Terry Farrell’s stepped building at Vauxhall Cross opened in 1994 as the headquarters of the Secret Intelligence Service. It was hit by an RPG in 2000 and has appeared in several James Bond films.

title: Soldiers and a home secretary besiege an East End house
place: Sidney Street, Stepney (Siege of Sidney Street site)
desc: In January 1911 police and Scots Guards surrounded two Latvian anarchists in a house on Sidney Street, Stepney. Home Secretary Winston Churchill came to watch; the house caught fire and both men died.

title: Richard Rogers turns an insurance market inside out
desc: The Lloyd’s building, finished in 1986, puts its lifts, stairs and pipes on the outside so the trading floor stays open beneath a tall glass atrium. It stands on Lime Street in the City of London and was listed Grade I in 2011.

title: One Beefeater’s whole job is keeping the ravens at the Tower
desc: Legend says the kingdom will fall if the ravens leave the Tower of London, so at least six are kept there, looked after by a Yeoman Warder called the Ravenmaster. The Tower stands on the north bank of the Thames beside Tower Bridge.

title: Two battleship guns guard a war museum in a former asylum
desc: The Imperial War Museum’s London branch moved in 1936 into the old Bethlem Royal Hospital in Lambeth, the asylum known as Bedlam. Two 15-inch naval guns stand in front of its domed entrance in Geraldine Mary Harmsworth Park.

title: A Soviet tank parks on a Bermondsey corner and never leaves
desc: The T-34 on Mandela Way was put there in 1995 by a local developer after he was refused permission to build on the plot, and artists have repainted it many times since. It sits on a scrap of land off the Old Kent Road in Southwark.

title: Salt beef and bagels around the clock on Brick Lane
desc: Beigel Bake has baked bagels at 159 Brick Lane since 1974, a holdover from the East End’s Jewish community, and it never closes. The queue for salt beef beigels is often longest late at night.

title: Norse ships pull down the wooden bridge across the Thames
desc: In 1014, according to later Norse sagas, Olaf Haraldsson helped King Æthelred retake London by tying ropes to the bridge and rowing until it fell. Today’s London Bridge crosses at nearly the same spot between the City and Southwark.

title: Steel gates rise from the riverbed to hold back the North Sea
desc: Opened in 1984, the Thames Barrier’s rotating gates lie flat on the river bed and swing up to stop storm surges reaching central London. It spans the river at Woolwich Reach, with a visitor centre on the south bank.

title: A brewery vat bursts and a wave of beer floods the slums
place: Site of the Meux Brewery, Tottenham Court Road
desc: In October 1814 a vat at the Meux Horse Shoe Brewery burst, sending over a million litres of porter into the St Giles rookery and killing eight people. The brewery stood where the Dominion Theatre is now, at Tottenham Court Road.

title: A rich city quietly stockpiles water for the worst day
desc: Swiss law has long required a fallout-shelter place for every resident, and Zurich’s water supply is planned with the same caution. Tom Scott looks at how the city prepares to keep people sheltered and drinking water flowing in a crisis.

title: The capital bans dogs for sixty years and cats take over
desc: In 1924 Reykjavík banned dogs over tapeworm fears and a housing shortage. By the 1980s thousands were kept illegally, and a finance minister refused to pay fines for his dog Lucy. The ban was lifted in 1984; cats, never restricted, still roam the streets.

title: Inspired and innovative architecture from Bjarke Ingels
desc: Led by its young and visionary founder, Copenhagen-based Bjarke Ingels Group has become one of the world’s most respected architecture firms. This quick video from B1M showcases five ambitious projects in the US, UK, Taiwan, and the United Arab Emirates.

title: The puzzle a Budapest professor accidentally invented
desc: In this episode of Stuff You Should Know, Josh and Chuck untangle the Rubik’s Cube and the Hungarian professor behind it — the inventor who said the puzzle’s twisting core came to him as he watched the Danube swirl around the pebbles.

title: Chico Fininho
creator: Rui Veloso
desc: Chico Fininho is a drifting, drug-loving character — and the title of Portugal’s breakthrough rock song, sung in Portuguese rather than English. Its 1980 release lit the fuse on a rock boom from Lisbon’s Rock Rendez Vous club.

title: A 67-es út
creator: Republic
desc: The title means “Route 67.” Republic’s 1994 song follows a lonely drive out of the city and became a Hungarian standard. The band was from Budapest — and grooves cut into the real Route 67 now “sing” the tune as cars drive over it.

title: Don Quijote
creator: Neoton Família
desc: Named for the deluded fictional knight, this 1980 disco track by Neoton Família was a smash far beyond Hungary — even a hit in Japan. It’s proof that, even behind the Iron Curtain, Budapest had its own glittering pop machine.

title: Ha én rózsa volnék
creator: Zsuzsa Koncz
desc: The title means “if I were a rose.” Sung by Zsuzsa Koncz in 1973, this gentle song slipped quiet criticism past the communist censors and became a soft protest anthem — from a Budapest where dissent had to hide in metaphor.

title: Add már, uram, az esőt!
creator: Kati Kovács
desc: The title means “Lord, send the rain already!” Kati Kovács belts this 1972 song with one of the great Hungarian voices. Decades later, Christina Aguilera sampled it for her hit “WooHoo.” Kovács was a Budapest stage and screen star.

title: Gyöngyhajú lány
creator: Omega
desc: The title means “the girl with pearl hair.” Omega’s dreamy 1969 track is the most beloved Hungarian rock song ever — so good that Kanye West sampled it and the Scorpions covered it. The band formed here in Budapest in the early 1960s.

title: African Reggae
creator: Nina Hagen
desc: Nina Hagen, the wild “godmother of punk,” fled communist East Germany for West Berlin, where she unleashed her operatic shriek and outrageous style. This 1979 track is the sound of the city’s fearless, anything-goes underground.

title: Andaluza (Danza Española No. 5)
creator: Enric Granados
desc: Enric Granados, the great Catalan pianist-composer, ran his music academy in Barcelona until he drowned at sea in 1916. This lilting “Spanish Dance No. 5” is his most beloved miniature — Andalusian in colour, but pure Barcelona salon craft.

title: Riverside
creator: Agnes Obel
desc: Agnes Obel, born in Copenhagen, makes hushed, haunting piano music. This 2010 song, the standout from her debut, drifts along just as its title suggests — fragile and cinematic. It made her one of Denmark’s most quietly admired exports.

title: Take Me into Your Skin
creator: Trentemøller
desc: Anders Trentemøller, Copenhagen’s master of moody electronica, opened his acclaimed 2006 debut with this slow-building, cinematic instrumental. He’s a fixture of the city’s club scene and ended a world tour with two shows in Christiania.

title: Move Your Feet
creator: Junior Senior
desc: Junior Senior, a Danish duo signed to Copenhagen’s beloved indie label Crunchy Frog, made this irresistible 2002 disco-punk romp. Its low-res pixel-art video became as famous as the song — pure, sunny early-2000s fun, recorded in the city.

title: Ma il cielo è sempre più blu
creator: Rino Gaetano
desc: The title means “but the sky is always bluer.” Rino Gaetano’s breathless 1975 epic rattles off every kind of Italian in one long list, saints and scoundrels alike. The cult cantautore grew up in Rome and came up through its scrappy folk clubs.

title: Stratosfear
creator: Tangerine Dream
desc: Long before techno, Tangerine Dream were inventing electronic music in 1970s West Berlin — vast, hypnotic synthesizer landscapes. This 1976 piece shows the pioneering sound that would echo through every Berlin nightclub for decades to come.

title: The poet who parachuted back into occupied Hungary
desc: In this episode of Stuff You Missed in History Class, the hosts honor Hannah Szenes — the Budapest-born poet who parachuted behind enemy lines to save Hungarian Jews and was executed, at 23, in the military prison on Magrit Boulevard (now demolished).

title: Eating with five senses at Restaurant Alchemist
desc: This quick video from VisitCopenhagen offers a peek inside Restaurant Alchemist, which provides an immersive experience for diners in what they call “holistic cuisine.” The 3-5 hour dinner includes 50 tastes, and the price is, um, you don’t want to know.

title: Fighting against Danish food waste
desc: In 2008, reactions to her online rant about food waste motivated Selina Juul to create Stop Wasting Food, one of the top organizations fighting waste in Denmark. This video from BBC News shares how she has influenced new policies at stores like REMA 1000.

title: Saving shops with history
desc: This short documentary highlights Lojas Com História, an advocacy group trying to protect hundreds of unique historical shops in Lisbon like pharmacy Drogaria Oriental. The thought-provoking video shows how rampant tourism erodes local charm and history.

title: The study of Danish happiness
desc: Meik Wiking is the CEO of the Happiness Research Institute in Copenhagen. In the first two-thirds of this episode, he shares thoughts on “hygge” culture and why Denmark consistently ranks at the top of the United Nations’ yearly World Happiness Report.

title: A young star in the fashion world
desc: Olivier Rousteing is the young Creative Director at Balmain, one of the major fashion houses in Paris. This video from the New York Times visits his office, where he discusses his approach to fashion, his A-List pop star pals, and his unlikely life story.

title: An Amsterdam spa with a Parisian past
desc: In this video, Gessell and Jessica from Amsterdam Calling visit Spa Deco, a luxury spa with an unusual story. Much its lovely Art Deco interior was rescued from the wrecking ball when the Parisian department store Au Bon Marché was slated for demolition.

title: Building for people with architect Francis Kéré
desc: Francis Kéré is an acclaimed architect based in Berlin. In the first part of this episode of Monocle On Design, he shares the thought-provoking rationale for the unusual (and award-winning) clay brick school he designed for his home town in Burkina Faso.

title: The right to wind in your hair
desc: Cycling Without Age provides volunteer “pilots” to help older people get around by bike, creating heartwarming multigenerational bonds along the way. This clip from Great Big Story describes how the Copenhagen-based service has expanded into 41 countries.

title: The open and accepting mentality of fashion of Berlin
desc: This video from The New York Times features Berliners describing their sartorial choices. Their style will inevitably become dated, but the spirit won’t: “I like Berlin because you can wear whatever you want without getting strange looks from people.”

title: The Green Vic: Aiming to be the world’s most ethical pub
desc: Randy Rampersad is trying to ensure his pub behaves ethically by sweating every little detail — who the pub hires, how it recycles or uses carbon, where its products come from, and more. He outlines his aspirations in this video from BBC London.

title: A new life in London after surviving the Holocaust
desc: Ruth Posner was just sixteen when she came to London as a refugee after surviving a Nazi concentration camp. This video from BBC London shows how Ruth and other holocaust survivors in the city share details about their horrific ordeal with new generations.

title: Founders on a mission to fight food waste
desc: Germany wastes 18 million tons of food per year. This video from Shopify spotlights the co-founders of Sirplus, an inspirational supermarket that sells food that wholesalers, markets, or bakeries would have discarded. They have five locations in Berlin.

title: Making art on found paper
desc: Tina Berning is a skilled artist and illustrator who embraces the unplanned accidents that occur when painting and drawing on recycled surfaces. This video from Shopify goes inside her studio in Mitte to see her beautiful and delicate work.

title: Making paper with hands, heart, and mind
desc: This alluring video from National Geographic profiles Gangolf Ulbricht, an expert papermaker in Berlin. The process is messy and industrial, yet seems to be therapeutic and perhaps even spiritual for him. This video will give you a new respect for paper.

title: Tapas crawl through Legazpi and Delicias neighborhoods
desc: In this video from Spain Revealed, tour guide James Blick goes on a non-touristy tapas crawl through six scrappy neighborhood bars starting at Taberna Martín. He expertly explains each dish he eats, including huevos rotos, torreznos, and brocheta iberica.

title: Searching for stories on the banks of the Thames
desc: Nicola White is a mudlarker, a person who walks along the banks of a river scavenging for tiny treasures in the mud. She calls the Thames “a giant liquid storybook,” which seems right given everything she has found. Her story about the grenade was great.

title: Outdoor spaces in Lisbon that are loved by locals
desc: This video from Booking.com follows a few Lisboetas to their favorite places, including two unique outdoor hangouts. First, we visit Mirador da Senhora do Monte perched above the city. Then, we hop a few metro stops east to modern Parque das Nações.

title: Starting a new life in London after fleeing Poland
desc: Bozena Merrick left Poland in 1985 to seek political asylum in England. This video from 1000 Londoners shows how she transformed her own life, then started a psychotherapy practice by embarking on a dramatic renovation of a quirky historic building.

title: Wahaca and the art of cooking sustainably
desc: Thomasina Miers co-founded Wahaca, a trendy chain of Mexican street food restaurants found throughout London. In this video from Culture Trip, the chef shares her thoughts on contributing to a more sustainable food system.
